card.headline: Alert, bright-eyed and chewing the cud
card.look: A healthy cow holds her head and ears up, has clear bright eyes and a smooth coat, and spends much of her resting time calmly chewing the cud. She comes to feed and water eagerly, walks evenly, and passes soft, well-formed dung.
card.action: Spend five minutes every morning and evening watching each animal, and write down anything different so you notice problems early.

detail.summary: Before you can spot a sick cow, you need to know what a healthy one looks, sounds and behaves like. This page sets out the normal signs, normal temperature, heart and breathing rates, cud chewing and dung, and gives a simple daily health-check routine. Farmers who know their animals' normal behaviour catch illness earlier. Early action is usually cheaper and gives the animal a better chance of recovery.
detail.cause: Good health in cattle rests on a few basics working together. The first is good feed and clean water. Cattle are ruminants, which means they have a four-part stomach. The biggest part, the rumen, is a large fermentation tank full of helpful microbes that break down grass, napier and hay. The cow keeps the rumen healthy by chewing the cud. She brings food back up, chews it again and mixes it with saliva, which neutralises acid. A steady supply of fibre, enough energy and protein, minerals such as calcium, phosphorus, salt and trace elements, and plenty of clean water keep the rumen and the whole body working. The second basic is protection from disease: vaccination, tick and worm control, clean housing and careful buying of new stock. The third is low stress. That means shade, dry and comfortable resting space, gentle handling, enough room at the feeder and no sudden changes in diet. When any of these slips, the cow's defences weaken. The first sign is often a small change in behaviour, appetite, cud chewing, milk yield or dung, long before she looks obviously sick.
spread: Sudden changes in feed, such as a switch from dry hay to lush wet-season grass or a big increase in dairy meal, upset the rumen microbes and can lead to bloat, acidosis (too much acid in the rumen) or diarrhoea.

Ticks, biting flies and tsetse carry serious diseases such as East Coast Fever, anaplasmosis (gall sickness), babesiosis (redwater) and trypanosomiasis. Poor tick control is one of the most common ways a healthy herd becomes sick in East Africa.

New animals bought from markets or neighbours can bring in diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, brucellosis and ticks. This is why new stock should be kept apart for a few weeks first.
Dirty or shared water points, communal dips and grazing areas allow worms, germs and ticks to pass between herds, especially in pastoral and communal grazing systems.

Mouldy feed, such as damp maize, poorly stored dairy meal or spoiled silage, can contain mycotoxins. These are poisons made by moulds that lower appetite, immunity and milk yield, and some can pass into milk.
Heat stress during the hottest months, especially for exotic breeds like Friesians with no shade, reduces feeding and milk and weakens the body's defences.
Wet, muddy or dirty zero-grazing units raise the risk of mastitis (udder infection), foot rot and calf diarrhoea.
Mineral shortages, especially of phosphorus and salt, are common on many Kenyan soils. They show up as poor growth, chewing bones or soil, weak fertility and lower milk.
detail.atRisk: Every animal benefits from a daily check, but some need closer watching. Newborn calves in their first weeks are the most fragile. They can go downhill within hours from diarrhoea, pneumonia or failing to get enough colostrum, the first milk. Cows in the three weeks before and after calving, called the transition period, are at higher risk of milk fever, retained afterbirth, mastitis and ketosis. High-yielding exotic and crossbred dairy cows such as Friesian, Ayrshire and Jersey in zero-grazing units need more attention during hot weather and when feed changes. Animals just brought from a market need extra care, as do those recovering from transport or a long dry season. The start of the long and short rains brings more ticks, flies, worms and lush grass that can cause bloat. Free-range and pastoral herds that share grazing, water and dips face more tick-borne and infectious disease. Zero-grazed animals depend entirely on what the farmer gives them, so mineral and water shortages are more common in those herds.

early: Alert and aware: head up, ears moving towards sounds, eyes following you as you approach, and a calm reaction to people she knows.
Bright, clear eyes with no tears, crust or cloudiness. The white of the eye shows thin pink blood vessels, and the eyes are not sunken.
A clean, moist nose with at most a little clear moisture. Cows lick their noses often, which is normal.
A smooth, glossy coat that lies flat, with skin that is soft and moves freely over the ribs. A pinch of skin on the neck should spring back in about two seconds or less.
A normal rectal temperature of about 38.0–39.5 °C in adults. Calves can sit slightly higher. Readings rise a little in the afternoon and in hot weather.

A resting heart rate of roughly 48–84 beats per minute in adult cattle, and faster in calves. The breathing rate at rest is roughly 20–40 breaths per minute, counted by watching the flank rise and fall. It is higher in heat and after walking.

Cud chewing: a healthy cow spends many hours a day ruminating, usually when lying down and relaxed. She gives roughly 40–70 steady chews per mouthful before swallowing. When you watch a group at rest, most should be chewing.
Good appetite and drinking: she comes to the feeder when fresh feed arrives and drinks freely and often. A milking cow needs a great deal of water, especially in hot weather.

Dung that is soft but formed. In dairy cows it should make a pile like thick porridge with rings and a small dip in the middle. It should not be watery, hard balls, or contain blood, mucus or a lot of undigested grain. Urine is clear to pale yellow.

The left side of the belly, the rumen area, is slightly filled but not tight or bulging, and steady rumen movements can be felt, about one to three a minute. She walks evenly on all four feet, lies down and gets up easily, and has a soft, even udder and normal-looking milk.
advanced: Standing alone, away from the herd, with head low, ears drooping, or a dull, uninterested look.
Off feed or eating much less, refusing dairy meal, or not coming to the feeder when others do.
Few or no animals chewing cud at rest, or a single cow that has stopped ruminating.
A temperature above about 39.5 °C in an adult, especially above 40 °C, or a temperature below about 38 °C. A low reading can be just as serious, for example in milk fever or shock.
Fast, heavy or noisy breathing at rest, breathing with an open mouth, coughing, or a thick yellow or green nose discharge.
A sudden drop in milk yield, or clots, watery milk, blood in the milk, or a hot, hard or painful quarter of the udder.
A swollen left flank (possible bloat), a tucked-up belly, kicking at the belly, or grinding the teeth, which is often a sign of pain.
Watery, bloody, very smelly or very hard dung, or no dung at all. Red or dark brown urine is another warning sign.

Lameness, swollen joints or feet, swollen lymph nodes (the glands under the ear, in front of the shoulder or above the udder), skin lumps, ticks clustered in the ears, tail or udder, sunken eyes, or a skin pinch that stays up.

lookalikes.name: Normal panting in hot weather
lookalikes.howToTell: On hot afternoons cattle, especially Friesians, breathe faster and may seek shade or stand near water. This is a normal cooling response. If the cow eats, chews cud and her rectal temperature returns to normal once she is cool in the evening, it is heat load, not illness. A cow that pants in the cool morning, refuses feed, or has a high temperature in the shade needs a vet.

lookalikes.name: Being on heat (oestrus)
lookalikes.howToTell: A cow on heat may be restless, bellow, mount others or stand to be mounted. She may eat less, drop a little milk for a day and have clear, stretchy mucus from the vulva. This lasts about a day and her temperature stays normal. Note the date for breeding. Cloudy, yellow or smelly discharge, fever or illness lasting longer than a day is not heat.

lookalikes.name: Normal discharge after calving
lookalikes.howToTell: For the first two to three weeks after calving, a cow normally passes reddish-brown, odourless discharge as the womb cleans itself. If the discharge smells bad, is grey or pus-like, continues beyond about three weeks, or she has a fever and is off feed, call the vet. That points to a womb infection.

lookalikes.name: Looser dung on fresh, lush grass
lookalikes.howToTell: When the rains come and animals move onto young green grass, dung often becomes softer for a few days while the rumen adjusts. The cow stays bright, eats well and has a normal temperature. Watery dung with blood or mucus, a dull animal, fever, or diarrhoea spreading through calves is not normal and needs a vet.

detail.diagnosis: This is a home health check you can do yourself, and it tells you when to call the vet. Do it calmly and at the same time each day, for example at morning and evening milking or feeding. First, watch from a distance for two or three minutes before touching anything. Who is standing alone? Who is not eating or chewing the cud? Count the breaths by watching the right flank rise and fall for 30 seconds, then double the number. Look at the eyes, nose, coat, dung and urine, and how each animal walks. Next, take the temperature with a digital thermometer from an agrovet. Restrain the cow safely in a crush or by tying her head. Stand to the side of her back leg, never directly behind. Lift the tail, apply a little petroleum jelly or soapy water to the tip, and gently insert it into the rectum. Tilt it so the tip touches the rectal wall, not a ball of dung. Hold it until it beeps, then read and record the result. Clean and disinfect the thermometer after every animal so you do not spread disease. To check heart rate, you can feel the pulse under the base of the tail, in the middle groove, or listen with a stethoscope on the left chest just behind the elbow. Count for 15 seconds and multiply by four. To check the rumen, press a closed fist firmly into the hollow of the left flank and wait. You should feel a slow roll or push one to three times a minute. Pinch the skin on the neck to check for dehydration; it should flatten quickly. Check the udder and milk at milking, and strip the first squirts onto a dark cup to look for clots. Score body condition on the common 1–5 scale by feeling the ribs, spine and pin bones. Very thin or very fat both signal a problem. Keep a simple notebook or phone record for each animal, including temperature, milk yield, appetite, dung, heat dates, treatments and vaccinations. When you call the vet, these records, plus a note of when you first noticed the change, help the vet work out the problem quickly.
firstSteps: Learn each animal's normal behaviour. Do a short check every morning and evening, and do the first check before feeding so you can see who comes eagerly to the feeder.
Buy and keep a digital thermometer, petroleum jelly, a torch, gloves, disinfectant, a notebook and the phone numbers of your vet and County Veterinary Officer in one clean box.
Take and record the temperature of any animal that seems different, and take a few readings from healthy animals too, so you know your herd's normal range.
If an animal looks unwell, separate her into a clean, shaded, dry pen. Give her clean water and good roughage, and keep her calm.

Do not give antibiotics, dewormers or other drugs on guesswork. Wrong or incomplete treatment wastes money, can hide the real problem, and adds to antimicrobial resistance, which is when germs stop responding to drugs.
Call your vet early and describe what you see: temperature, appetite, cud chewing, dung, milk and how long it has been going on. Do not move sick animals to market or to other farms.
Wear gloves and wash your hands with soap after handling sick animals, discharges, afterbirths or aborted calves, and keep milk from a sick cow separate until the vet advises.
detail.vetTreatment: Healthy herds still need a vet, but for prevention rather than emergencies. A good plan, made with your vet or County Veterinary Officer, usually includes several parts. The first is vaccination against the main diseases in your area. In Kenya this commonly covers foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, anthrax and blackquarter, and brucellosis for young heifers where recommended. In some areas the plan also includes East Coast Fever immunisation by the infection-and-treatment method, which only trained, authorised people can do, and rabies, plus CBPP or other campaigns in pastoral zones. Schedules vary by county and risk, so follow local advice. Other parts of the plan are a tick-control programme, using the right acaricide (tick-killing chemical) at the right interval and strength, and a deworming plan based on age, season and, ideally, dung tests rather than routine guessing. Calves and in-calf cows need the most attention. The vet also handles pregnancy checks, breeding and artificial insemination advice, and hoof trimming and foot care. Mastitis screening, for example with the California Mastitis Test, is another part, along with castration, dehorning and disbudding done properly with pain control, and advice on feeding, minerals and body condition. Any medicine the vet uses has a withdrawal period. This is the time after treatment when milk or meat must not be sold or eaten because drug residues may remain. Always ask the vet for the withdrawal period and keep to it. Use antibiotics only when a vet has diagnosed a bacterial infection, and always finish the course as prescribed.
prevention: Feed a balanced diet with plenty of long fibre such as napier, hay, maize stover or Rhodes grass, plus energy and protein suited to the animal's stage and milk yield. Make any change in feed slowly over one to two weeks.
Provide unlimited clean, fresh water close to the feeding area, and clean troughs regularly. Milking cows drink far more than many farmers expect, especially in the dry season and in heat.
Give a good mineral supplement and salt all year. Many Kenyan soils are short of phosphorus, and shortages harm fertility, growth and milk yield.
Store feed dry, off the floor and away from leaking roofs. Do not feed mouldy maize, hay, dairy meal or silage, because mould poisons reduce appetite, immunity and milk.
Follow a vaccination calendar agreed with your vet, keep records, and make sure every calf gets enough colostrum within the first few hours of life.
Control ticks and worms on a planned schedule, check ears, tail, udder and between the legs for ticks, and ask the vet about acaricide resistance if ticks keep surviving.
Keep housing dry, clean and well ventilated. Scrape dung daily, provide soft bedding, give enough feeder space and shade, and clean teats and hands before milking.
Quarantine new or returning animals for about three to four weeks, buy from known sources with health records, and limit visitors, shared equipment and contact with other herds where you can.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan smallholding, one cow is often a large part of the family's income. Missing the early signs of illness can quickly turn into lost milk, a dead calf, an expensive vet bill or a forced sale at a low price. Many costly problems start quietly: a slight fever, less cud chewing, a small drop in milk, or a cow that hangs back at the feeder. Mastitis, tick-borne diseases, milk fever, calf diarrhoea and poor fertility are much cheaper to deal with early. A daily health check costs nothing but a few minutes. It helps a farmer act early and spot repeated problems such as poor minerals or bad hygiene. It also gives the vet useful information, keeps calving intervals shorter and protects the herd's value when selling. Good records also help farmers get better prices and access to dairy cooperatives and buyers, who increasingly want proof of vaccination and drug-residue-free milk.
detail.humanHealth: A healthy-looking cow can still carry infections that affect people, such as brucellosis and bovine tuberculosis. Always boil or pasteurise milk before drinking it. Wash your hands with soap after handling animals, dung, afterbirths or aborted calves, and wear gloves when assisting calving. Respect withdrawal periods after any treatment so that drug residues do not reach your family or customers through milk and meat.
detail.outlook: Cattle that are well fed, given clean water, vaccinated, protected from ticks and worms, and kept in clean, low-stress conditions usually stay productive for many lactations. When problems do arise, the outlook is usually best when the farmer notices the first small change, takes the temperature, isolates the animal and calls the vet promptly. Delays, guesswork treatment, poor nutrition and dirty housing all make recovery less likely and more costly. Learning what normal looks like in your own herd is one of the most valuable skills a farmer can build.

faqs.q: How often should I take my cow's temperature?
faqs.a: You do not need to take every cow's temperature every day. Take it whenever an animal looks or behaves differently: eating less, not chewing cud, dropping milk, standing alone, or breathing fast. It is also worth checking daily in the days after calving, after buying a new animal, and during a disease outbreak nearby. Taking a few readings from healthy animals helps you learn what is normal on your farm. Readings are often slightly higher in the hot afternoon, so compare readings taken at similar times.

faqs.q: Is a dry nose a sign that my cow is sick?
faqs.a: Not on its own. A healthy cow's nose is usually moist because she licks it often, but it can look dry for a while when she has been lying in the sun or sleeping. A dry nose matters only when it comes with other signs, such as fever, poor appetite, no cud chewing, a crusty or cracked nose, or discharge. Always look at the whole animal and take the temperature rather than judging by the nose alone.

faqs.q: My cow lies down a lot. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Healthy dairy cows spend many hours a day lying down, often around half the day. Lying comfortably and chewing cud is a very good sign, and it also helps milk production. Be worried if she cannot get up, struggles to rise, lies stretched flat on her side, lies with her head tucked into her flank, or refuses to rise when others get up to feed. Lying down shortly after calving with cold ears and a wobbly walk can mean milk fever, which is an emergency.

faqs.q: How do I know my cattle are drinking enough water?
faqs.a: Watch the trough. Healthy cattle drink several times a day, especially after milking and feeding. Dung should be soft and formed, urine pale, the eyes not sunken, and a skin pinch on the neck should flatten quickly. Hard, dry dung, dark urine, sunken eyes and falling milk can point to too little water. If water must be carried, give enough for the whole herd and refill often, especially in the dry season. Even a short shortage lowers milk yield.

faqs.q: When should I call the vet instead of waiting?
faqs.a: Call quickly if a cow has a temperature above about 40 °C or below about 38 °C. Also call if she has stopped eating and chewing cud, has a swollen left side, is breathing hard at rest, or is straining to calve for a long time without progress. Other reasons to call are red urine, bloody diarrhoea, sudden lameness in several animals, or blisters in the mouth or on the feet. Sudden deaths, or several animals getting sick at once, also need a vet straight away. With any sudden death, do not open the carcass; call the vet, because some diseases, like anthrax, are dangerous to people. When in doubt, a phone call to your vet costs little and can save the animal.

faqs.q: What should I keep at home to check my cattle's health?
faqs.a: A digital thermometer and petroleum jelly are the most useful tools. Add a torch for checking eyes and the mouth, disposable gloves, soap, disinfectant and clean cloths, and a dark strip cup or plate for checking milk. A notebook or phone app for records completes the kit, along with your vet's and County Veterinary Officer's contacts. A weigh band from an agrovet helps you track growth and condition. Keep medicines only as advised by your vet, store them properly, and record every treatment with its withdrawal period.

products.role: A source of calcium and phosphorus that, when mixed into the ration as advised, helps prevent the mineral shortages common on many Kenyan soils. This supports strong bones, growth, fertility and milk production as part of a balanced diet.

A mycotoxin binder that can be added to dairy meal or home-mixed concentrates to help reduce the effect of aflatoxin and ochratoxin from imperfectly stored feed. It works alongside, never instead of, keeping feed dry and throwing away visibly mouldy feed.

healthy.imagePrompt: A healthy black-and-white Friesian dairy cow standing in a clean, well-bedded Kenyan zero-grazing shed, head and ears up, bright clear eyes, glossy coat, calmly chewing cud beside a full water trough.
healthy.seoDescription: Know what a healthy cow looks like: normal temperature 38–39.5 °C, heart and breathing rates, cud chewing, dung and a simple daily health check for farmers.

card.headline: Swollen glands below the ear
card.look: The animal has a hard, swollen lump below the ear and another in front of the shoulder. It has a high fever, stops eating and looks dull, and brown ticks are often found on the ears.
card.action: Call your vet or animal health officer today, because treatment works best in the first few days of fever.

aka: Corridor disease (the form caught from buffalo)
detail.summary: East Coast Fever (ECF) is a tick-borne disease of cattle caused by a tiny blood parasite called Theileria parva. The brown ear tick passes it on. It is one of the biggest killers of cattle in Kenya and East Africa, especially dairy cows of exotic breeds and young calves. Without early treatment many sick animals die within a few weeks of the first signs.
detail.cause: ECF is caused by Theileria parva, a single-celled parasite (a protozoan, a microscopic organism that is not a bacterium or a virus). An infected brown ear tick bites the cow and injects the parasite with its saliva while it feeds. The parasite enters the animal's white blood cells, called lymphocytes, which normally fight infection. Inside these cells it makes them multiply out of control, a little like a cancer. This is why the lymph nodes swell so much. Lymph nodes are the glands that filter infection, such as the ones below the ear and in front of the shoulder. The infected cells spread through the body and the immune system breaks down. In the late stage, fluid leaks into the lungs. This is called pulmonary oedema, and it causes the laboured breathing and the froth at the nose. Most animals that die of ECF die because they cannot breathe. The disease usually appears about one to three weeks after an infected tick bite, often around 8 to 12 days. Animals that recover often stay carriers. A carrier has the parasite in its blood without looking sick, and ticks can pick it up from it.
spread: The main carrier is the brown ear tick (Rhipicephalus appendiculatus). It is a small, reddish-brown tick that likes to attach inside and around the ears, and also on the eyelids, tail and udder.

A young tick (larva or nymph) picks up the parasite by feeding on an infected or carrier animal. It passes the infection on at its next life stage, as a nymph or an adult, when it feeds on a new animal.
The parasite is not passed from the female tick into her eggs. Infection keeps going on a farm because ticks keep feeding on carrier cattle.
ECF does not spread directly from cow to cow by contact, milk, coughing or sharing water. It needs the tick.

Ticks are carried onto farms on new animals bought from markets. They also come on cut-and-carry grass and fodder in zero-grazing units, and on animals grazing roadsides, communal land or bushy pasture.
Tick numbers, and so ECF cases, often rise during and after the long and short rains, when grass is green and ticks are active.
African buffalo can carry a form of Theileria parva. Where cattle share grazing with buffalo, near parks and conservancies, ticks can pass a severe form called Corridor disease to cattle.
When dipping or spraying is skipped, done badly, or done with an acaricide (tick-killing chemical) that ticks have become resistant to, ticks build up quickly and outbreaks follow.
detail.atRisk: Exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle such as Friesian, Ayrshire, Jersey and Guernsey are most at risk. In them the disease is often severe and many die if not treated. Calves of all breeds are very vulnerable, especially those born to unvaccinated mothers in tick areas. Indigenous zebu cattle raised in areas where ECF is common often survive mild infection as calves and gain some natural resistance, but they can still get sick and die. This is especially true when they are moved to a new area or are stressed. Cattle brought from tick-free or low-ECF areas into high-risk areas are in great danger. High-risk areas include much of central, western, Rift Valley and coastal Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin. Farms with poor or irregular tick control are at risk, and so are zero-grazing units that cut fodder from roadsides or bushy areas. Cattle on communal grazing, or grazing near wildlife, are also at risk. Risk rises in the rainy seasons and the weeks after them.

early: A swollen, firm lymph node just below the ear, at the base of the jaw. It is often on the same side where ticks were feeding. It can be felt and often seen.
A swollen lymph node in front of the shoulder, felt as a sausage-shaped lump under the skin.
High fever. The animal feels hot, and a thermometer in the rectum often reads 40°C or more. The fever keeps going for days.
Dullness, standing apart from the herd, and a drop in appetite and chewing the cud.
A sudden, sharp fall in milk yield in dairy cows.
Watery eyes and a clear runny nose.
Brown ear ticks found in or around the ears, or recent signs of heavy tick burden.
advanced: Fast, laboured breathing with the neck stretched out. There may be a cough and loud breathing sounds.
Frothy, foamy discharge from the nose. This comes from fluid in the lungs and is a serious warning sign.
Many lymph nodes in the body become swollen, not just the ones near the ear and shoulder.
Rapid weight loss, weakness and wobbly walking. Many animals end up lying down and unable to rise.
Cloudy or bluish-white eyes, and pale gums and inner eyelids.
Diarrhoea, sometimes with blood or mucus, in the late stage.
Occasionally, nervous signs such as circling, head-pressing or staggering. This is sometimes called 'turning sickness'.
Death, often within about one to three weeks of the first fever if no treatment is given.

lookalikes.name: Anaplasmosis (gall sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gall sickness causes pale, then yellow, gums and eyes (jaundice). Dung is often hard, dry and constipated. There is usually fever, but lymph nodes are not greatly swollen, and froth at the nose is not typical. It is mostly seen in adult cattle. The two diseases can happen together, so a vet test is the only way to be sure.

lookalikes.name: Babesiosis (redwater)
lookalikes.howToTell: Redwater usually causes red or coffee-coloured urine, with pale or yellow gums from loss of blood cells. Fever is high. Lymph nodes are not usually the big feature. It is spread by blue ticks rather than brown ear ticks.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater
lookalikes.howToTell: Heartwater often shows nervous signs such as high-stepping, chewing movements, twitching eyelids, circling and paddling of the legs. Sudden death is common. It is linked to the colourful bont ticks (Amblyomma) rather than brown ear ticks, and does not cause large lymph node swellings.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: Nagana is spread by tsetse flies in bush areas. It usually develops slowly over weeks or months, with wasting, pale gums and a staring coat. Lymph nodes may be mildly enlarged, but the fast, severe illness with froth at the nose seen in ECF is less usual. A blood test tells them apart.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer first examines the animal. They feel the lymph nodes, take the temperature, listen to the chest and check for ticks. In ECF areas, swollen nodes with a high fever and ticks on the ears strongly suggest the disease. To confirm it, the vet may take a small sample from a swollen lymph node using a fine needle. This is called a lymph node biopsy or smear. They also take a blood smear. These are stained and looked at under a microscope for the parasite inside white blood cells. These parasite clusters are called schizonts or 'Koch's blue bodies'. Laboratories such as county veterinary labs and the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete can do further tests like PCR, which detects the parasite's genetic material, or blood tests for antibodies. If an animal dies, a post-mortem examination often shows lungs full of froth and fluid, greatly enlarged lymph nodes, small white spots in the kidneys, and ulcers in the stomach. Before the vet arrives, write down when the animal first looked sick and its temperature readings. Note when it was last dipped or sprayed, which acaricide you used, and any recent purchases or movement of animals. Note also whether you cut fodder from outside the farm. Tell the vet whether the animal was vaccinated against ECF, and any drugs already given.
firstSteps: Call your vet or animal health officer as soon as you notice swollen glands and fever. Early treatment greatly improves the chance of survival, and waiting even a few days can be fatal.
Take the animal's temperature with a rectal thermometer if you have one, and write it down with the time. Keep recording it so the vet can see how the illness is progressing.
Keep the sick animal in a shaded, well-ventilated and quiet place, away from the rest of the herd. Avoid making it walk long distances, because exertion worsens breathing problems.
Provide plenty of clean, fresh drinking water within easy reach. Offer soft, palatable feed such as fresh green grass or good hay, even if it eats only a little.

Check the sick animal and the rest of the herd carefully for ticks, especially in the ears, around the eyes, tail and udder. Ask your vet about spraying or dipping the herd with an effective acaricide to stop further spread.
Do not give any drugs, injections or herbal mixtures before the vet sees the animal unless the vet tells you to. Wrong or late treatment can hide signs, waste money and reduce the chance of recovery.
Check the other cattle daily for swollen glands, dullness or a drop in milk. Catching the next case early saves lives.
Stop buying new animals or moving cattle off the farm until the outbreak is under control. Do not cut fodder from tick-infested roadsides or bush during this time.
detail.vetTreatment: The main specific treatment for ECF is an anti-theilerial drug. Buparvaquone is the most widely used. Parvaquone and halofuginone have also been used. These drugs act directly against the Theileria parasite. They work best when given early, while the animal is still eating and before breathing problems set in. Once froth at the nose and severe breathing distress appear, many animals die even with treatment. Alongside this, the vet may give supportive treatment. This can include anti-inflammatory drugs to bring down fever and inflammation, drugs to help clear fluid from the lungs, and vitamins. Antibiotics such as oxytetracycline may be given to control secondary bacterial infections like pneumonia. Antibiotics do not reliably cure ECF itself, and they should only be used when prescribed. Unneeded antibiotics add cost and help bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), so future treatments stop working. All treatment must be prescribed and given by a qualified vet or animal health officer. Doses depend on the drug, the animal's weight and its condition. Many of these drugs have long withdrawal periods, the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be sold or eaten. Buparvaquone in particular has a long meat withdrawal period. Always ask your vet and read the label for the exact milk and meat withdrawal times. Expect the animal to need close nursing for one to several weeks. Recovery can be slow, and milk yield may take a long time to return.
prevention: Keep up regular, effective tick control by dipping, spraying or using pour-on acaricides. Ask your vet or agrovet to advise how often, because this depends on the season and how many ticks are in your area. Treat more often during and after the rains, when ticks are most active.

Pay close attention to the ears, which are the favourite site of the brown ear tick. When hand-spraying, make sure the inside and back of the ears, the eyelids, tail brush and udder are well soaked. Some farmers also use tick grease in the ears.

Mix and use acaricides exactly as the label says. Watch for signs that ticks are surviving treatment, because ticks can become resistant. Ask your vet about switching to a different class of acaricide if control fails.

Talk to your vet about ECF vaccination by the Infection and Treatment Method (ITM). ITM uses a live vaccine, such as the Muguga cocktail, given together with a long-acting antibiotic. It must be given by trained, authorised vaccinators, and the vaccine has to be kept in liquid nitrogen. It can give strong, long-lasting protection, especially for calves and exotic dairy cattle. Vaccinated animals may become carriers, so follow local guidance. Vaccination does not replace tick control.

In zero-grazing units, avoid cutting fodder from roadsides, bushy areas or places where other cattle graze. Inspect fodder and the animals often for ticks, and keep the area around the unit slashed and clean.
Quarantine newly bought cattle for a few weeks. Treat them for ticks before they join the herd, and check them for swollen glands and fever. Buy from known, healthy herds where possible.
Keep grass short around sheds, fences and kraals, and reduce bush where ticks hide. Where possible, keep cattle from grazing where buffalo or other wildlife pass.

Give good nutrition, clean water and shade, and reduce stress. A well-fed animal copes better with infection. Check animals daily, feeling the glands below the ear and in front of the shoulder so you notice early swelling.
detail.impact: ECF is one of the most costly cattle diseases for Kenyan farmers. On a smallholder dairy farm, losing a single exotic cow can wipe out a family's main source of daily income, as well as the money and years spent raising her. Even when animals survive, milk yield often falls sharply and may not fully recover in that lactation. Pregnant cows may abort, recovered animals can lose a lot of body condition, and fertility can suffer. Calf deaths reduce replacement stock and slow herd growth. Farmers also carry the costs of treatment, vet visits, acaricides and lost milk sales during withdrawal periods. For many families, fear of ECF is one reason they keep fewer improved dairy breeds. At community level, frequent ECF outbreaks limit dairy development and food security.
detail.humanHealth: East Coast Fever does not infect people. The Theileria parasite only affects cattle and buffalo. However, the drugs used to treat it, especially buparvaquone and antibiotics, can leave residues in milk and meat. Do not sell or consume milk or meat from treated animals until the withdrawal period stated by your vet and on the label has passed. Acaricides used for tick control are also poisonous to people. Wear gloves, long sleeves and boots when mixing and spraying. Do not eat, drink or smoke while working with them. Wash well afterwards, and store chemicals away from children, food and water sources.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mostly on how early treatment starts and on the type of animal. Cattle treated with an anti-theilerial drug in the early stage, when they have swollen glands and fever but are still eating and breathing normally, often recover. Once the animal is breathing with difficulty, has froth at the nose or is lying down, the chance of survival drops sharply, even with treatment. Exotic breeds and young calves generally do worse than local zebu cattle from ECF areas. Animals that recover may take weeks to regain condition and milk yield. Many stay carriers for a long time, so continued tick control on the farm remains important.

faqs.q: Can I treat East Coast Fever myself with drugs from the agrovet?
faqs.a: ECF treatment should be prescribed and given by a vet or animal health officer. The right drug, dose and supportive care depend on the animal's weight and stage of disease. Many farmers lose animals because they first try cheap antibiotics alone, or give the wrong dose, and waste precious days. Antibiotics on their own do not reliably cure ECF. Call the vet early. The first few days of fever are when treatment works best.

faqs.q: My cow recovered from ECF. Is she safe now?
faqs.a: A recovered cow usually has strong protection against the same type of parasite, but she may stay a carrier. A carrier carries the parasite in her blood without looking sick, and ticks can pick it up from her and pass it to other cattle. Keep up good tick control on the whole herd. Also watch her condition and milk yield, as full recovery can take time.

faqs.q: Does the ECF vaccine mean I can stop dipping or spraying?
faqs.a: No. The ITM vaccine protects against East Coast Fever, but it does not protect against other tick-borne diseases like gall sickness, redwater and heartwater. It also may not cover every local strain of the parasite. Ticks also cause damage, stress and skin wounds on their own. Continue regular tick control, though your vet may advise you on a suitable routine for vaccinated animals.

faqs.q: I practise zero-grazing. How can my cows get ECF if they never go out?
faqs.a: Ticks can be carried in with cut fodder, especially grass cut from roadsides, swampy edges or bushy places where other cattle graze. They can also come in on new animals, or on people's clothes and equipment. Cut fodder from clean, well-managed plots where possible. Check your cows' ears and bodies for ticks regularly, and keep up tick control even in zero-grazing units.

faqs.q: How do I know if the swelling below the ear is ECF and not something else?
faqs.a: In ECF the lymph node below the ear, and the one in front of the shoulder, become firm and enlarged. This usually comes with a high fever, dullness and a drop in milk. Other problems such as abscesses or lumpy jaw can cause swellings too. Only a vet examination and a lymph node or blood smear can confirm ECF. If you see swollen glands with fever, treat it as an emergency and call the vet.

faqs.q: When can I sell milk again after my cow is treated?
faqs.a: This depends on the drugs used. Anti-theilerial drugs and antibiotics each have their own milk and meat withdrawal periods, and some are long. Ask your vet to tell you clearly, and check the product labels. During this time, discard the milk safely rather than selling it or feeding it to people. Some buyers and milk cooperatives test for residues, and sending milk with residues can lead to rejection or penalties.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help a feverish, weak animal stay hydrated and keep drinking during illness and recovery. Use it as supportive care alongside the vet's prescribed anti-theilerial treatment and good nursing. It does not treat the Theileria parasite.

east-coast-fever.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a dull Friesian dairy cow in a simple Kenyan smallholder shed, with a clearly visible firm swelling just below the ear at the base of the jaw and a few small brown ticks on the ear, soft natural daylight, no people, no text.
east-coast-fever.seoDescription: East Coast Fever in cattle: spot swollen glands, high fever and froth at the nose early, act fast, and prevent it with tick control and ITM vaccination.

card.headline: Pale, then yellow, eyes and gums
card.look: The cow becomes weak and dull, with very pale pink or white gums and eyelids that later turn yellow. She often breathes fast, stops eating and passes small, hard, dry dung.
card.action: Keep the animal calm and still in shade with water, avoid chasing or moving her, and call your vet immediately.

aka: Ndigana baridi (Swahili, used especially in Tanzania)
detail.summary: Anaplasmosis, widely called gall sickness, is a tick-borne blood disease of cattle caused by a tiny bacterium called Anaplasma marginale. It destroys red blood cells, so the animal becomes severely anaemic (short of blood), weak and later yellow (jaundiced). It matters because it can kill valuable adult dairy and beef cattle, cuts milk sharply, causes abortion and leaves recovered animals as lifelong carriers that can infect others. It is common across Kenya and East Africa wherever ticks and biting flies are found.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Anaplasma marginale, a very small bacterium of the rickettsia group that lives inside red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. After an animal is infected, the bacteria multiply quietly inside red cells for several weeks before signs appear. The animal's own immune system then recognises the infected red cells and removes them, mainly in the spleen. When large numbers of red cells are destroyed, the blood becomes thin and watery and cannot carry enough oxygen, so the animal tires quickly, breathes fast and its heart races. The broken-down red cells release a yellow pigment called bilirubin, which the liver cannot clear fast enough, so the gums, eyes and skin turn yellow. Because the red cells are destroyed inside the body rather than burst in the bloodstream, the urine usually does not turn red, which helps tell it apart from redwater. Lack of oxygen also slows the rumen and gut, causing constipation, and in severe cases affects the brain, making some animals excitable or aggressive just before collapse.
spread: Ticks are the main natural spreaders: in East Africa the blue tick (Rhipicephalus decoloratus) and related one-host ticks pick up the bacteria from infected cattle and pass it to others when they feed.

Biting flies such as horse flies (tabanids) and stable flies can carry infected blood on their mouthparts from one animal to the next, especially when they are disturbed while feeding during the rains.
Reusing the same needle or syringe on several animals during vaccination, deworming or treatment can transfer infected blood and is a very common cause of outbreaks on farms.
Instruments used for dehorning, castration, ear tagging, tattooing or hoof trimming can spread the disease if they are not cleaned and disinfected between animals.
Recovered animals remain carriers for life, carrying low levels of bacteria in their blood without showing signs, so they act as a hidden source of infection for ticks and flies.
Infected cows can occasionally pass the infection to their calves before birth.
Stress such as transport, hard work, calving, poor feeding, heat or other diseases can turn a quiet carrier infection into clinical disease.
detail.atRisk: Adult cattle suffer most: calves under about six months are naturally quite resistant and usually get only mild disease, animals of one to two years can become seriously ill, and cattle over two years often get severe disease that can be fatal. Exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle such as Friesians, Ayrshires and Jerseys, especially those raised in zero-grazing units with strict tick control and then exposed later in life, are at higher risk than indigenous Zebu, Boran or Sahiwal cattle that grew up in tick-infested areas and gained immunity young. Cattle moved from low-tick highland areas to warmer, tick-heavy areas, or newly bought animals mixed with local herds, are at particular risk. Cases often rise during and after the long and short rains when ticks and biting flies increase. Herds where dipping or spraying is irregular, where one needle is used for the whole herd, or where acaricide (tick chemical) has stopped working well are also more exposed. Pregnant and high-yielding cows can be hit hard.

early: A sudden drop in milk yield, often the first thing a dairy farmer notices.
Fever, with the animal feeling hot to the touch, although this can be short and easily missed.
Dullness, standing apart from the herd, reduced appetite and less chewing of the cud.
Gums, inner eyelids and the inside of the vulva look paler pink than normal, and later almost white.
Tiring quickly when walking and lagging behind the herd.
Faster breathing and a faster heartbeat, especially after any movement.
advanced: Yellow colour (jaundice) of the eyes, gums, vulva and thin areas of skin, often appearing several days into the illness.
Constipation with small, hard, dry dung that may be coated in mucus, and a quiet rumen.
Marked weakness, staggering, lying down and difficulty getting up.
Rapid weight loss and a dull, rough coat.
Some animals become excitable or aggressive and may charge, because the brain is short of oxygen.
Abortion in pregnant cows, and temporary loss of fertility in bulls.
Sudden collapse and death, sometimes triggered by handling, chasing or transport.

lookalikes.name: Babesiosis (redwater)
lookalikes.howToTell: Redwater, also tick-borne, usually causes a high fever and red, brown or 'coca-cola' coloured urine because red cells burst in the bloodstream. In gall sickness the urine is usually normal or dark yellow, constipation is more typical, and the illness is often slower. Both can occur together, so a blood test is the best way to know.

lookalikes.name: East Coast Fever (ndigana)
lookalikes.howToTell: East Coast Fever causes clearly swollen lymph glands, especially in front of the shoulder and below the ear, high fever, breathing difficulty, coughing and froth from the nose. Severe paleness and jaundice with constipation, without big swollen glands, points more to gall sickness.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater
lookalikes.howToTell: Heartwater, spread by the bont tick, mainly shows nervous signs such as high-stepping walk, circling, chewing movements, twitching and paddling of the legs. Gall sickness mainly shows paleness, yellowing and weakness, although very anaemic animals can also become agitated.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana) or chronic liver fluke
lookalikes.howToTell: Both cause slow, long-lasting anaemia and wasting over weeks to months. Nagana occurs in tsetse fly areas and often causes watery eyes and swollen lymph glands; liver fluke is linked to wet, swampy grazing and often causes swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw). Gall sickness usually comes on faster and more severely in adult cattle.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the gums, eyes and vulva for paleness and yellowing, take the temperature, listen to the heart and rumen, check for swollen lymph glands and look at the urine colour to rule out redwater. The quickest test is a thin blood smear stained and viewed under a microscope, where the bacteria appear as tiny dark dots at the edge of the red cells. The vet may also measure the packed cell volume (PCV), a simple test of how much blood the animal has left, which shows how severe the anaemia is and guides treatment. In carriers or animals already treated, the smear may look clear, so blood tests for antibodies (serology such as ELISA) or DNA tests (PCR) at a county or national veterinary laboratory may be used. At post-mortem, typical findings are a pale or yellow carcass, thin watery blood, a greatly enlarged spleen, an enlarged orange-yellow liver and a swollen gall bladder full of thick dark bile, which gave the disease the name gall sickness. Before the vet arrives, note when signs started, any change in milk yield, urine colour, dung consistency, your dipping or spraying dates and the acaricide used, any recent injections, dehorning or castration, and whether new animals have joined the herd.
firstSteps: Keep the sick animal calm and still, ideally where she already is or a short, slow walk to a shaded pen; do not chase, rope-wrestle, truck or force her to walk, because severely anaemic cattle can collapse and die from stress.
Provide clean fresh water and good fresh fodder within easy reach, and shade from the sun, so she does not need to move far.
Call your vet or the nearest animal health service provider as soon as you notice paleness, yellowing or a sudden milk drop, because early treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.
Separate the animal from the herd if this can be done gently, and check the rest of the herd for ticks, paleness, dull behaviour and milk drops.
Do not give any injections or drugs yourself from the agrovet before the vet has examined the animal, as wrong drugs or doses can be dangerous and can hide the true diagnosis.
Record the animal's signs, temperature if you have a thermometer, urine colour, dung, and your recent tick control and injection history to share with the vet.

Remove visible ticks carefully by hand while wearing gloves, and make sure your herd's tick control is up to date, but avoid stressful dipping or crush handling of the sick animal until the vet advises.
If milking, keep the cow comfortable and milk her gently; if she has been treated, follow the vet's advice on withholding milk.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and given or supervised by a vet. The main drugs used are tetracycline antibiotics such as oxytetracycline, often a long-acting form, which stop the bacteria multiplying and work best when given early in the disease. Imidocarb dipropionate is another option used by vets, which also acts against babesia (redwater), useful when both infections are suspected. In very severe cases with dangerously low blood levels, a vet may give a blood transfusion from a healthy donor cow, along with supportive care such as fluids and gentle feeding. Treatment kills enough bacteria for the animal to recover, but it usually does not fully clear the infection, so most recovered animals stay carriers. Recovery of blood levels is slow and can take several weeks, and the animal should be handled as little as possible during this time. Both oxytetracycline and imidocarb leave residues, and withdrawal periods for milk and meat must be followed strictly; imidocarb in particular has a very long meat withdrawal period, so always check the product label and your vet's instructions before selling milk or animals for slaughter. Because these are antibiotics or antimicrobials, use them only when a vet confirms they are needed, complete the course as directed, and never use them as routine prevention without veterinary advice, to slow the development of drug resistance.
prevention: Keep regular tick control by dipping, spraying or pour-on at the interval your vet or extension officer recommends for your area, mixing acaricide at the correct strength and wetting the whole body, including ears, tail brush, udder and between the legs.
If ticks seem to survive dipping, ask your vet about acaricide resistance and rotate between different chemical groups as advised instead of simply making the mixture stronger.
Use a new or sterilised needle for every animal during vaccination, deworming and treatment, and never use one needle for the whole herd.
Clean and disinfect dehorning, castration, tagging and hoof-trimming tools between animals.
Reduce biting flies by clearing dung and stagnant water around the boma or zero-grazing unit and using fly control approved for cattle.
Quarantine newly bought cattle for a few weeks, treat them for ticks, watch for paleness or weakness, and ask your vet about blood testing animals from unknown sources.
Take extra care when moving cattle from low-tick to high-tick areas, and discuss a protection plan with your vet before moving valuable exotic animals.

In areas where the disease is common, talk to your vet about 'endemic stability', where young calves meet the infection while naturally resistant and build immunity; live vaccines are used in some countries, but availability in Kenya is limited, so ask your County Veterinary Officer about current options.
Feed cattle well with enough energy, protein, minerals and clean water, and reduce stress around calving and transport, so carrier animals are less likely to break down with disease.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan dairy farm, gall sickness can mean a sudden collapse in milk yield from your best cow, followed by weeks or months before she returns to good production, if she survives. Deaths of adult exotic or cross-bred cows are a major financial loss, as these animals are expensive to replace. Pregnant cows may abort, losing both the calf and a lactation, and affected bulls may be temporarily infertile, delaying breeding. Treated animals lose weight, and milk must be thrown away during the withdrawal period. Vet fees, drugs, possible blood transfusions and extra labour add to costs. On pastoral and beef farms, weight loss reduces sale value and deaths can be high in herds with poor immunity. Outbreaks caused by shared needles can affect several animals at once.
detail.humanHealth: Anaplasma marginale, the cause of gall sickness in cattle, is not known to infect people, so caring for sick cattle does not give you this disease. The main human risk comes from drug residues: milk and meat from cattle treated with oxytetracycline or imidocarb must not be consumed or sold until the full withdrawal period on the label or set by your vet has passed. Wear gloves when removing ticks, as ticks can carry other infections that affect people, and wash your hands afterwards.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mainly on how early treatment starts and how old the animal is. Animals treated in the early stage, before severe anaemia and jaundice, usually have a reasonable chance of recovery. Once the animal is very pale or yellow, down, or showing aggression, the outlook becomes guarded to poor, and some die even with treatment, especially if stressed by handling. Calves and young stock usually recover well, while cattle over two years and high-producing exotic cows have a higher risk of death. Recovery is slow, with weight and milk taking weeks to months to come back. Survivors become carriers that are usually protected against severe disease again but can infect other cattle through ticks, flies and needles.

faqs.q: Why is it called gall sickness?
faqs.a: When cattle that died of this disease are opened, the gall bladder, which stores bile from the liver, is often very swollen and full of thick, dark bile, and the carcass looks yellow. Farmers noticed this and named it gall sickness. The swollen gall bladder is a result of the disease, not the cause; the real problem is the destruction of red blood cells.

faqs.q: Can I buy oxytetracycline at the agrovet and treat the cow myself?
faqs.a: It is much safer to call a vet. Gall sickness can look like redwater, East Coast Fever or heartwater, and each needs a different approach. A vet can confirm the diagnosis, choose the right drug, handle a weak animal without killing her from stress, and advise on milk and meat withdrawal. Wrong doses or wrong drugs waste money, can harm the animal and add to antibiotic resistance.

faqs.q: My cow died soon after we drove her into the crush. Why?
faqs.a: Cattle with gall sickness have very little blood left to carry oxygen. Chasing, struggling in a crush, walking long distances or loading onto a lorry suddenly increases the body's oxygen demand, and the heart cannot keep up. This is why sick animals should be kept calm, moved slowly or not at all, and treated where they stand if possible.

faqs.q: If my cow recovers, can she still infect the rest of the herd?
faqs.a: Yes. Most recovered cattle remain carriers for life, with a low level of bacteria in their blood. Ticks, biting flies and shared needles can carry this blood to other animals. Good tick control, fly control and using one needle per animal keep the risk low. The carrier cow herself is usually protected from severe illness afterwards.

faqs.q: How is gall sickness different from redwater?
faqs.a: Both are tick-borne blood diseases that cause paleness and weakness. In redwater the red cells burst in the blood vessels, so the urine often turns red or brown and fever is usually high. In gall sickness the red cells are removed inside the body, so urine is usually not red, yellowing and constipation are more typical, and adult cattle are most at risk. They can occur together, so a vet's blood test is the best way to know.

faqs.q: Can milk from a sick cow be used?
faqs.a: Milk from a sick cow is not a source of gall sickness for people, but a sick cow's milk is often poor in quality and the cow needs rest. Once she is treated, the drugs pass into the milk, so you must discard milk for the full withdrawal period given on the drug label or by your vet. Do not give this milk to calves without asking your vet, and never sell it.

products.role: During recovery, after the vet has started treatment, K-DIGEST can be used as a supportive aid for liver function and digestive stress, helping a cow whose liver is working hard to clear bile pigments and whose rumen has slowed, as she returns to eating; it does not treat the infection and should be used alongside the vet's treatment plan.

RE-COVER oral rehydration solution can help support fluid intake in a weak, recovering cow that is drinking poorly, offered in her water or given only as your vet advises; avoid forceful drenching of a very weak or anaemic animal, as stress and choking are risks, and remember it does not replace veterinary treatment.

anaplasmosis.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of the lower eyelid gently folded down on a Friesian dairy cow in a Kenyan zero-grazing shed, showing pale whitish-yellow tinged membranes and a yellowish tint to the white of the eye, natural daylight, no people's faces, no text.
anaplasmosis.seoDescription: Anaplasmosis (gall sickness) in cattle: spot pale then yellow gums, weakness and constipation, act fast, and prevent it with tick control and clean needles.

card.headline: Dark red-brown 'coffee' coloured urine
card.look: A feverish, dull cow stops eating, passes urine the colour of strong tea, coffee or port wine, and her gums and eye whites turn pale, then yellow. Blue ticks are often found on the animal or in the herd.
card.action: Call your vet at once and move the cow quietly into shade with water. Never chase or stress her, because a badly anaemic cow can collapse and die.

detail.summary: Babesiosis, commonly called redwater, is a tick-borne blood disease of cattle. It is caused by tiny parasites that live inside red blood cells and burst them. This causes high fever, severe anaemia (shortage of blood), jaundice and the typical red-brown urine. It is an emergency: exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle can die within days without treatment. Early treatment by a vet usually saves the animal.
detail.cause: Redwater is caused by Babesia, a single-celled parasite called a protozoan. It is not a bacterium and not a virus. In East Africa the main species is Babesia bigemina. Babesia bovis is more dangerous and occurs where the Asian blue tick (Rhipicephalus microplus) has become established. When an infected tick feeds, it injects the parasites into the cow's blood. They enter the red blood cells and multiply, and each cell bursts as new parasites are released to invade more cells. As millions of red cells are destroyed, the cow runs a high fever and becomes anaemic. Her blood cannot carry enough oxygen, so she weakens, breathes fast and her heart pounds. The red pigment from burst cells (haemoglobin) spills into the blood and passes out in the urine, turning it red-brown. The liver is overwhelmed breaking down this pigment, so the gums, eyes and skin turn yellow (jaundice). With Babesia bovis, infected red cells also stick inside the small blood vessels of the brain. This causes the 'cerebral' form, with nervous signs, which is very often fatal. Kidney damage, shock and lack of oxygen are what usually kill the animal.
spread: The main carrier is the blue tick (Rhipicephalus decoloratus). It is a one-host tick, which means it spends its whole life on one animal before dropping off to lay eggs.
An infected female tick passes the parasite into her eggs. The next generation of ticks then infects new cattle, so pasture can stay dangerous even after the original sick animals are gone.

The Asian blue tick (Rhipicephalus microplus) carries both Babesia bigemina and the more deadly Babesia bovis. It has spread into parts of East Africa and is often harder to control with some acaricides (tick-killing chemicals).
Recovered cattle and many local zebu cattle carry low levels of the parasite in their blood without looking sick. Ticks feeding on them can pick it up and pass it on.
It can also spread through blood on shared needles, dehorning or castration tools, and through blood transfusions. Use a clean needle for each animal.
Outbreaks are often triggered when dipping or spraying is stopped or done badly, when the rains bring a surge of ticks, or when cattle from tick-free areas are moved onto tick-infested land.
Redwater does not pass directly from cow to cow by contact, breath or milk. Ticks or blood are needed.
detail.atRisk: Adult cattle that have never met the parasite are most at risk, especially exotic dairy breeds such as Friesian, Ayrshire, Jersey and Guernsey, and their high-grade crosses. Animals moved from tick-free highland farms or bought from zero-grazing units and then put out to graze in tick areas are classic victims. Calves under about nine months have natural protection: they usually get only mild disease and then become immune. That is why herds where calves meet ticks early are often stable, while herds where tick control suddenly fails get serious outbreaks in adults. Indigenous zebu (such as Boran and East African Shorthorn Zebu) are more resistant to both ticks and disease, though they can still fall sick. Risk rises during and after the long and short rains when tick numbers rise. Free-range, communal grazing and pastoral systems carry more tick exposure, but zero-grazed cows can also be infected through ticks brought in on fodder or visiting animals. Pregnant cows, newly calved high-yielders and stressed or poorly fed animals tend to suffer worse disease.

early: High fever, often above 40°C (normal is about 38.5°C). Check with a rectal thermometer, as the cow may feel hot and look dull before anything else shows.
Dullness and standing apart from the herd, with drooping ears and head held low.
Reduced appetite and stopping chewing the cud.
A sudden, sharp drop in milk yield in dairy cows.
Faster breathing and a fast, pounding heartbeat you can feel or see on the left side of the chest.
Gums, the inside of the eyelids and the vulva start to look paler pink than normal.
Blue ticks are found on the ears, neck, dewlap, belly, udder, between the legs or under the tail.
advanced: Red-brown, coffee- or port-wine-coloured urine that stays coloured when left in a container. True blood would settle as a red layer at the bottom.
Very pale, almost white gums and eyes, later turning yellow (jaundice).
Severe weakness, staggering and lying down and unable to rise.
Constipation with hard, dry dung, or sometimes diarrhoea.
Abortion in pregnant cows because of the high fever. Bulls may become temporarily infertile.
Nervous signs in the cerebral form: incoordination, grinding teeth, pressing the head against walls, aggression or 'madness', paddling, fits and coma.
Rapid loss of condition. Death can follow within a few days, sometimes within 24 hours of signs appearing in the cerebral form.

lookalikes.name: Anaplasmosis (gall sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gall sickness also causes fever, pale gums and strong jaundice, and is also tick-borne. However, the urine usually stays normal in colour or is only dark yellow, not red-brown. It tends to develop more slowly, and constipation is very common. The two diseases often occur together, so a blood smear is needed to be sure.

lookalikes.name: East Coast Fever (ECF, ndigana)
lookalikes.howToTell: ECF is spread by the brown ear tick. It causes clearly swollen lymph nodes (glands) below the ear and in front of the shoulder, watery eyes, coughing, laboured breathing and froth from the nose near death. It does not cause red urine or marked jaundice.

lookalikes.name: Leptospirosis
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial disease can cause red urine and jaundice, mainly in calves, along with abortion storms and 'milk drop' with thick, clotted milk in cows. Ticks are not involved. It is diagnosed with blood and urine tests, and it can infect people.

lookalikes.name: Post-calving haemoglobinuria and kale or rape poisoning
lookalikes.howToTell: Red urine without high fever in a high-yielding cow a few weeks after calving points to low phosphorus. Red urine in cattle fed large amounts of kale, rape or other brassicas points to plant poisoning. A normal temperature and no ticks make redwater less likely, but your vet should still check.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects redwater from fever, red-brown urine, pale or yellow gums and the presence of blue ticks. To confirm it, the vet takes a drop of blood, ideally from a small prick on the ear tip or tail. Babesia bovis gathers in these small vessels. The vet makes a thin smear on a glass slide, stains it and looks under a microscope for the pear-shaped parasites inside red cells. A packed cell volume test (PCV, which measures how much blood the cow has left) shows how severe the anaemia is. In animals that have already been treated or are carriers, parasites may be hard to find. In that case laboratory tests such as PCR (which detects the parasite's genetic material) or serology (blood tests for antibodies) can help. These are also useful for checking a herd's immunity. If an animal dies, a post-mortem by the vet or a Veterinary Investigation Laboratory typically shows yellow tissues, a large dark spleen, an enlarged liver, a swollen gall bladder with thick bile and dark urine in the bladder. With Babesia bovis, the brain often looks cherry-pink, and a brain smear confirms it. Important: if an animal dies suddenly with dark blood oozing from the nose, mouth or anus, do not open the carcass, because it could be anthrax. Call the vet. To help your vet, write down when you first noticed signs, the temperature readings, what the urine looks like (keep a sample in a clean, closed container), when the herd was last dipped or sprayed and with what product, any recent purchases or animal movements, and how many animals are affected.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer immediately. Redwater can kill within days, and early treatment makes the biggest difference.
Move the sick animal slowly and calmly into a shaded, quiet pen close by. Do not chase, drive long distances or wrestle her, as a severely anaemic cow can collapse and die from stress.
Provide clean, fresh drinking water within easy reach, plus soft, palatable fodder. Do not force-drench a weak or nervous animal, because liquid can go into the lungs.
Take and record her rectal temperature, and note the colour of her urine and gums. Keep a urine sample in a clean, closed bottle for the vet.
Check her and the rest of the herd for ticks. Hand-pick or carefully remove ticks from the sick animal without crushing them on your skin.
Check every other animal's temperature twice a day for the next week, especially exotic and recently bought cattle. Report any fever early.
Keep animals with nervous signs in a safe pen away from people and walls, as they may charge or fall. Do not try to restrain a fitting animal alone.
Do not buy and inject drugs from the agrovet yourself. The wrong drug or dose can kill an anaemic cow or leave dangerous residues. Wait for the vet's diagnosis and prescription.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and given by a vet. Redwater is treated with specific anti-protozoal drugs that kill Babesia. The commonly used active ingredients are diminazene aceturate and imidocarb dipropionate. Imidocarb can also give the animal some protection against reinfection for a period of weeks, and vets sometimes use it under supervision to protect newly introduced animals. These drugs work best early, before the anaemia becomes severe. Many animals start to improve within a day or two: the fever falls and the urine colour clears. Severely anaemic animals may also need a blood transfusion from a healthy donor cow, fluids, anti-inflammatory drugs to bring the fever down, and vitamin and iron support to rebuild blood. Cerebral cases need intensive care and often do not survive. Antibiotics alone do not cure redwater, because Babesia is not a bacterium. However, a vet may prescribe an antibiotic such as oxytetracycline if gall sickness (anaplasmosis) is also present, which is common. Use antibiotics only when prescribed and finish the course as directed. Misuse breeds antimicrobial resistance, meaning medicines stop working for animals and people. All these drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods: the time you must wait before milk can be sold or drunk, or the animal slaughtered. For imidocarb the meat withdrawal period is very long, often several months. Follow the exact period on the label and the vet's advice. Recovery of full strength and milk yield can take several weeks, and the cow needs good feed, rest and tick protection meanwhile.
prevention: Keep tick control regular and effective. Dip or spray at the interval your vet or extension officer recommends for your area, usually more often during the rains. Always mix the acaricide at the correct strength on the label.

Spray thoroughly. Wet the whole body, including the ears, under the tail, the udder or scrotum, between the legs and the belly, where blue ticks hide. Hand-dress these spots with a tick grease if needed.
Slow down acaricide resistance. Ask your vet or agrovet about rotating between different chemical groups rather than using the same product for years. Report it if ticks survive dipping.

Do not stop or suddenly reduce tick control in a herd that has been heavily dipped for years. Adults in such herds often have no immunity and can suffer a severe outbreak. Discuss any change in your tick programme with a vet first.

Take special care with new animals, especially exotic cattle from tick-free areas. Treat them for ticks on arrival, keep them apart and watch their temperature for several weeks. Ask your vet whether protective treatment is advisable.

Let young calves meet low numbers of ticks under close observation where your vet advises it. Calves under nine months usually get only mild disease and become immune. This is part of building 'endemic stability', a herd that is naturally protected.
Ask your vet about vaccination. Live redwater vaccines are used in some countries, but their availability in Kenya is limited and they must be handled and given by a vet.
Use a clean needle for every animal, and disinfect dehorning, castration and ear-tagging tools between animals to avoid spreading infected blood.
Manage pasture and fodder. Slash long grass and bush around homesteads and night bomas. Avoid bringing tick-infested cut fodder into zero-grazing units, and keep stray or neighbours' animals away.
Feed animals well, with balanced energy, protein and minerals, so they cope better if infected.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, redwater can be very costly. A single dead in-calf Friesian or high-grade cross can wipe out many months of milk income and years of breeding investment. Animals that survive often lose much of their milk for weeks, lose body condition and may abort their calves. Bulls can be temporarily infertile after the fever, delaying calving across the herd. Vet call-outs, anti-protozoal drugs, blood transfusions and the long withdrawal periods for some drugs add further losses, as milk and meat cannot be sold during that time. Ongoing dipping or spraying is a regular expense, and resistant ticks force farmers onto pricier acaricides. The fear of redwater, together with ECF and gall sickness, also holds back farmers from keeping more productive exotic breeds in tick areas, limiting farm income and growth.
detail.humanHealth: The Babesia species that cause redwater in Kenyan cattle are not known to infect people. There is no risk from touching a sick cow or drinking properly boiled milk from her. The main human risk is drug and chemical residues. Anti-protozoal drugs, antibiotics and acaricides can pass into milk and meat. Do not drink or sell milk, or slaughter a treated animal, until the full withdrawal period on the label and your vet's advice has passed. Imidocarb in particular has a very long meat withdrawal period. When mixing and applying acaricides, wear gloves, long sleeves and boots, avoid splashing your skin and eyes, and wash afterwards. Ticks can carry other diseases that affect people, so remove them with gloves or tweezers rather than crushing them with bare fingers. If an animal dies suddenly with dark blood from its openings, do not open the carcass, as this could be anthrax, which is dangerous to people. Call the vet.
detail.outlook: With early diagnosis and prompt treatment by a vet, most cows with redwater caused by Babesia bigemina recover. Improvement is often seen within one to two days. The outlook gets much worse once the animal is severely anaemic, lying down or showing jaundice for several days, and the cerebral form caused by Babesia bovis is often fatal even with treatment. Exotic breeds, heavily pregnant or freshly calved cows, and animals with mixed infections such as gall sickness or ECF also do worse. Survivors usually remain carriers with long-lasting immunity to that Babesia species, which protects them as long as they keep meeting ticks. Full return to milk and body condition may take several weeks of good feeding and rest.

faqs.q: My cow is passing red urine. Can she get better on her own?
faqs.a: Some calves and resistant local zebu recover from mild infections without treatment. However, an adult exotic or cross-bred cow with red urine and fever is in serious danger and can die within days. Do not wait to see. Call the vet immediately, because the treatment works best early, before she loses too much blood.

faqs.q: Why do my local zebu cattle stay healthy while my Friesian gets redwater?
faqs.a: Indigenous zebu have natural resistance to ticks and to Babesia, and many were exposed as calves, so they are immune carriers. Friesians and other exotic breeds are more sensitive, carry more ticks, and are often bought from tick-free areas with no immunity. Mixing them with carrier zebu on tick-infested grazing puts the Friesian at high risk unless tick control is excellent.

faqs.q: Is redwater the same as gall sickness?
faqs.a: No, although they look similar and often occur together. Both are tick-borne and cause fever, anaemia and jaundice. Redwater is caused by Babesia and gives red-brown urine. Gall sickness (anaplasmosis) is caused by a different germ, Anaplasma, and the urine usually stays normal coloured. They need different medicines, which is why the vet's blood smear matters.

faqs.q: Can I drink or sell milk from a cow being treated for redwater?
faqs.a: The disease itself does not pass to people through milk. However, the drugs used to treat it do get into milk and meat. You must throw away milk and avoid slaughtering the animal for the full withdrawal period stated on the drug label and by your vet. For some drugs, such as imidocarb, the meat withdrawal period lasts several months.

faqs.q: I dip every week but still get redwater. What is going wrong?
faqs.a: Common reasons are acaricide mixed too weak, poor coverage of the ears, tail and udder, and ticks that have become resistant to the chemical you use. New animals or neighbours' cattle can also bring ticks in. Ask your vet or extension officer to check your mixing and spraying method. Consider testing for resistance and rotating to a different chemical group. Also remember that a herd kept almost tick-free for years has little natural immunity, so even a few infected ticks can cause disease.

faqs.q: Can I buy the redwater injection from the agrovet and give it myself?
faqs.a: It is not safe to do this without a vet. Wrong diagnosis is common, because gall sickness, ECF and others look similar. A wrong drug or dose can kill a weak, anaemic cow. Some drugs also need careful handling and have long withdrawal periods. Call a vet to confirm the disease and prescribe the right treatment. While you wait, keep the cow calm, shaded and watered.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help keep a feverish, dehydrated cow drinking and support her fluid and electrolyte balance during recovery, given alongside the vet's anti-protozoal treatment. Offer it only in drinking water to animals that can swallow normally, and never drench a weak, lying-down or nervous animal.

Supports liver function and digestion during recovery, after jaundice has put the liver under strain and appetite has dropped. It is an aid to help the cow get back on feed alongside the vet's treatment and good nutrition. It does not kill Babesia.

babesiosis.imagePrompt: A dull, weak dairy cow standing with head lowered in a farm yard, pale gums visible, a puddle of dark red-brown coffee-coloured urine on the ground behind her, a few ticks on the legs.
babesiosis.seoDescription: Redwater (babesiosis) in cattle: spot coffee-coloured urine, fever and pale gums early, what to do before the vet comes, and tick control to prevent it.

card.headline: High-stepping walk and constant chewing movements
card.look: A cow with a high fever stops eating, then walks with exaggerated high steps, chews or twitches her lips and eyelids, circles or presses her head against walls. Late cases go down, paddle their legs and may die suddenly.
card.action: Call your vet at once, because heartwater can usually only be treated successfully if treatment starts early, while the animal has fever but before severe nervous signs.

detail.summary: Heartwater is a serious tick-borne disease of cattle, goats, sheep and wild ruminants, caused by a tiny bacterium carried by bont ticks. It causes high fever followed by nervous signs such as a high-stepping walk, chewing movements, circling and convulsions, and can kill within days. Exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle brought into tick areas are hit hardest. Fast vet treatment in the fever stage can save many animals, but once convulsions start most die.
detail.cause: Heartwater is caused by Ehrlichia ruminantium, a very small bacterium of the rickettsia group (germs that can only live inside the cells of an animal). It was formerly called Cowdria ruminantium, which is why the disease is also called cowdriosis. It is carried by bont ticks (Amblyomma species; in East Africa mainly Amblyomma variegatum). When an infected tick feeds, the germ enters the blood and grows inside the cells lining the small blood vessels, especially in the brain, lungs and heart.
