These damaged vessels become leaky, so fluid seeps out into the tissues and body spaces. Fluid builds up around the heart (this gave the disease its name), in the chest and lungs, and in the brain. Swelling and damage in the brain cause the typical nervous signs, and fluid in the lungs causes difficult breathing. Signs usually appear about two to four weeks after an infected tick has fed, although this varies.
spread: Heartwater spreads through the bite of infected bont ticks. These are large, colourful ticks with shiny brown and orange or whitish patterned backs, banded legs and long mouthparts.
Bont ticks pick up the germ when they feed as larvae or nymphs on an infected animal, keep it as they moult, and pass it on when they feed as nymphs or adults on the next animal.
Recovered cattle, goats, sheep and many wild ruminants such as buffalo and antelope can carry the germ without looking sick, so they keep ticks infected on shared grazing.
Bont ticks are most active during and after the long and short rains, when grass is long and bushy areas are wet, so cases often rise in these seasons.
Moving susceptible cattle, especially exotic dairy breeds, from tick-free highland areas into lowland or coastal tick areas is a classic trigger for outbreaks.
Suddenly stopping or weakening tick control, such as missed dipping, cheap or wrongly diluted acaricide, or ticks that resist the acaricide, can lead to heavy tick loads and new cases.
Heartwater does not spread directly from cow to cow by contact, coughing or milk. It needs the tick, although infected blood on shared needles could in theory pass it on.
detail.atRisk: Exotic breeds such as Friesian, Ayrshire, Guernsey and Jersey, and their crosses, are far more likely to get severe disease than indigenous zebu and Boran cattle, which often show only mild fever or none at all. Young calves, roughly in their first few weeks of life, have a natural resistance and usually survive infection, and in tick areas this early exposure helps them build immunity. Animals at greatest risk are older calves, heifers and cows that have never met the germ before, for example dairy stock bought from tick-free highland farms and taken to the coast, the Lake Victoria basin, the Rift Valley lowlands or semi-arid ranching areas. Risk is higher during and after the rains, on farms bordering bush or wildlife areas, in free-range and pastoral herds sharing grazing with goats, sheep and wildlife, and on farms where dipping or spraying has become irregular. Zero-grazed cattle are not completely safe, because ticks can come in on cut fodder, visiting animals or nearby grazing.

early: High fever, often above 40°C (normal for cattle is about 38 to 39.5°C), checked with a rectal thermometer, usually the first sign.
Dullness, standing apart from the herd, and reduced or no appetite and cud chewing.
A sudden drop in milk yield in dairy cows.
Faster breathing, and sometimes mild diarrhoea.
Bont ticks attached under the tail, around the udder, groin, scrotum, brisket or between the toes, sometimes with painful swellings where they feed.
Mild nervous signs starting: twitching of the eyelids or lips, frequent licking or chewing movements, or an unsteady walk.
advanced: A high-stepping, stiff or wobbly walk, as if the animal is stepping over invisible objects.
Constant chewing movements, tongue pushing out, and grinding of teeth.
Walking in circles, pressing the head against walls or fences, or blindly bumping into things.
Aggression or excitement, sudden bellowing, or charging at people.
Going down and lying on the side with the legs paddling or running in the air, the head and neck bent backwards, and rolling or flickering eyes.
Laboured breathing and sometimes froth at the nose from fluid in the lungs.
Sudden death, sometimes with no warning signs, especially in very susceptible animals.

lookalikes.name: Rabies
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabies also causes strange behaviour, aggression and going down, but it usually has no high fever, and you often see drooling saliva, hoarse bellowing, straining and paralysis of the throat. It follows a dog or wild animal bite and always kills. Because rabies can kill people, treat any nervous cow as a possible rabies case: do not put your hand in its mouth and call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Redwater (cerebral babesiosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Redwater, spread by blue ticks, also causes high fever and sometimes nervous signs, but the animal usually passes red or dark brown urine, and the gums and eyes look pale or yellow from anaemia and jaundice. A vet can tell them apart with a blood smear.

lookalikes.name: East Coast fever (including turning sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: East Coast fever, spread by the brown ear tick, causes fever with clearly swollen lymph nodes, especially below the ear and in front of the shoulder, plus coughing, difficult breathing and froth from the nose. A rare brain form called turning sickness causes circling, but the swollen glands usually point to East Coast fever. A vet confirms with a lymph node or blood smear.

lookalikes.name: Anthrax
lookalikes.howToTell: Anthrax also causes sudden death, but dead animals often have dark, tarry blood that does not clot oozing from the nose, mouth or anus, and the carcass swells quickly. Never open or skin an animal that died suddenly; call the vet first, as anthrax is dangerous to people.

detail.diagnosis: A vet suspects heartwater from the high fever, nervous signs, bont ticks on the animal or herd, the season and the animal's history, such as recent arrival from a tick-free area. In a live animal, blood can be sent for PCR, a laboratory test that detects the germ's genetic material, though results take time, so treatment usually starts before they return. The most common confirmation is after death: the vet takes a small piece of brain and makes a crushed smear, which is stained and examined under a microscope for clusters of the germ inside small blood vessels. At post-mortem the vet may also find clear or straw-coloured fluid around the heart and in the chest, fluid-filled lungs with froth in the airways, an enlarged spleen and a swollen, congested brain. You can help by recording the temperature and when signs started, noting recent movements, purchases and dipping dates, collecting a few ticks in a closed container, and keeping any dead animal whole and covered, away from dogs, until the vet sees it. Do not open a carcass yourself, because anthrax can look similar.
firstSteps: Call your vet or the County Veterinary Officer immediately, and describe the fever, nervous signs and ticks, because early treatment is the main chance of survival.
Take the rectal temperature of the sick animal and of the rest of the herd, especially exotic and newly bought cattle, and tell the vet which ones have fever.
Move the sick animal gently to a quiet, shaded, well-bedded place away from walls, ditches and water troughs where it could fall, get stuck or drown during fits.
Keep people, especially children, away from a nervous or aggressive animal, and never put your hand into its mouth, because rabies cannot be ruled out without a vet.
Offer clean, fresh water and soft feed within reach, but never force-drench a cow that is down, fitting or struggling to swallow, as liquid can go into the lungs.
Check all cattle, goats and sheep for bont ticks under the tail, around the udder, groin, scrotum and between the toes, and arrange tick control for the whole herd with your vet or agrovet.
Write down the dates of first signs, recent purchases or movements, your last dipping or spraying, and the acaricide used.
Do not give any drug, including antibiotics, painkillers or fever remedies, without your vet's advice, and do not open any animal that dies before the vet examines it.
detail.vetTreatment: The vet will usually treat with an antibiotic from the tetracycline group, such as oxytetracycline or doxycycline, which is the standard treatment for heartwater. Unlike many diseases, heartwater is caused by a bacterium, so antibiotics do work, but only if given early. Animals treated during the fever stage, before strong nervous signs, often recover; once an animal is down and convulsing, treatment frequently fails. The vet may add supportive care, such as an anti-inflammatory drug to reduce swelling and fever, careful fluid therapy, and sometimes a sedative to control fits. The vet may also treat other exposed animals with fever, and advise on a programme for in-contact stock. Doses, routes and repeats must be decided by the vet. Tetracyclines leave residues in milk and meat, so you must follow the withdrawal period the vet gives you before selling or drinking milk or slaughtering the animal. Use antibiotics only as prescribed and complete the course, because careless use of agrovet antibiotics drives antimicrobial resistance (germs that no longer respond to medicines) and leaves residues in food. Recovered animals can be weak for one to two weeks and need rest, shade, water and good feed.
prevention: Control bont ticks with regular dipping, spraying or pour-on acaricides as advised by your vet or extension officer, paying special attention to the hidden places they attach: under the tail, udder, groin, scrotum, brisket and feet.
Use the correct acaricide dilution, wet the whole animal including the hidden areas, keep to the recommended interval, and rotate acaricide groups on advice if ticks seem to survive treatment.
Treat goats and sheep for ticks too, as they share heartwater and bont ticks with cattle.

Before moving exotic or cross-bred cattle from a tick-free area to a heartwater area, talk to your vet about protecting them, which may include strict tick control and preventive treatment under vet supervision during the first weeks.
Quarantine and inspect new animals for ticks before mixing them with the herd, and buy from sellers who can tell you about their tick control.

In tick areas, discuss with your vet whether to keep a stable tick-control plan that allows young calves some natural exposure while they are resistant, rather than switching between intensive and no tick control, which can leave adult animals with no immunity.
Keep grass short and clear bush around homesteads and night bomas, and check cut fodder brought to zero-grazing units for ticks.

Vaccines exist in some countries, such as a live blood vaccine in South Africa, but there is no widely available heartwater vaccine in Kenya, so tick control and early vet treatment remain the main tools.
detail.impact: Heartwater can kill valuable dairy cows and in-calf heifers within days, wiping out years of investment for a smallholder. Even animals that survive lose milk for weeks, may abort, and need costly vet treatment. Fear of heartwater and other tick-borne diseases limits the spread of high-yielding exotic dairy breeds into lowland, coastal and semi-arid parts of Kenya. Farmers also carry the ongoing cost of acaricides, labour for dipping or spraying, and lost milk during drug withdrawal periods. Bont ticks also damage teats and udders, leading to abscesses and mastitis, and reduce the value of hides.
detail.humanHealth: Heartwater is not considered a meaningful risk to people; only a very small number of possible human infections have ever been reported, and this remains uncertain. The real human health concerns are different. First, a cow with nervous signs could have rabies, which is deadly to people, so wear gloves, avoid saliva and never put your hand in the mouth until a vet has ruled rabies out. Second, tetracycline antibiotics leave residues in milk and meat, so do not drink or sell milk or slaughter treated animals until the vet's withdrawal period is over. Third, never open or eat an animal that died suddenly without a vet's check, because anthrax can look similar.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mainly on how early treatment starts and how susceptible the animal is. Cattle treated by a vet in the fever stage, before strong nervous signs, often recover. Once an animal is down, paddling or convulsing, most die even with treatment. Indigenous zebu and animals that have had heartwater before often survive with mild illness, while newly introduced exotic dairy cattle can die quickly. Recovered animals usually have good immunity for some time, but they may carry the germ and keep infecting ticks, so tick control must continue.

faqs.q: Can I buy oxytetracycline at the agrovet and treat heartwater myself?
faqs.a: Tetracyclines are the drugs used for heartwater, but they must be prescribed by a vet who confirms the diagnosis and sets the right drug, dose and course. Many diseases look similar, such as redwater, East Coast fever and rabies, and they need different treatment. Wrong or partial doses waste money, fail the animal and build antibiotic resistance. If you see a cow with fever and ticks, call the vet quickly; speed matters more than anything else.

faqs.q: My cow is already lying down and paddling. Is there any hope?
faqs.a: Once heartwater reaches the convulsing stage, most animals die even with treatment, because the brain and lungs are badly damaged. A vet can still try treatment and supportive care, and some animals do pull through. Keep her quiet, shaded and safe from injury. Check the rest of the herd for fever, because catching the next case early gives a much better chance.

faqs.q: Why did my Friesian die while my neighbour's zebu cattle are fine?
faqs.a: Indigenous zebu and Boran cattle have lived with bont ticks and heartwater for generations and are naturally more resistant. Many were also infected as young calves, when they are naturally protected, so they built immunity early. A Friesian brought from a tick-free farm has no such protection, so the same tick bite can make it very ill.

faqs.q: Should I stop dipping so my animals build up immunity?
faqs.a: No, do not stop tick control on your own. Bont ticks also carry other diseases and damage teats and udders, and stopping suddenly can expose your whole herd to heavy infection. In some tick areas vets advise a steady, balanced tick-control plan that lets young calves get some natural exposure. This is a decision to make with your vet or extension officer for your farm and breeds.

faqs.q: Is there a heartwater vaccine in Kenya?
faqs.a: A live blood-based vaccine is used in South Africa, but it needs careful handling and follow-up treatment, and there is currently no widely available heartwater vaccine for Kenyan farmers. Researchers are working on better vaccines. For now, the best protection is good tick control, careful management of new animals and fast vet treatment.

faqs.q: Can heartwater spread from a sick cow to my other cows?
faqs.a: Not by contact, breath or milk. It spreads only through bont ticks that have fed on an infected animal. But if one animal has heartwater, infected ticks are on your grazing, so others may be infected too. Check the whole herd for fever and ticks, and tighten tick control for cattle, goats and sheep.

products.role: During recovery, once the vet has started treatment and the animal is standing and drinking normally, RE-COVER can be added to drinking water to help replace fluids and salts lost through fever and poor intake and to ease heat stress. It does not treat heartwater. Never drench it into an animal that is down, fitting or struggling to swallow.

heartwater.imagePrompt: A black-and-white Friesian dairy cow in a dry Kenyan paddock walking with an exaggerated high-stepping front leg, head held low and jaw mid-chew, with a few large colourful bont ticks visible on the udder and under the tail, natural daylight, realistic farm photo.
heartwater.seoDescription: Heartwater in cattle: spot the fever, high-stepping walk and chewing signs, act fast before the vet arrives, and control bont ticks to prevent it in Kenya.

card.headline: Heavy drooling with blisters in mouth
card.look: Cattle drool long strings of saliva, smack their lips and stop eating. Blisters or raw red patches show on the tongue, gums, teats and between the claws, and animals limp or refuse to stand.
card.action: Stop all animal movement on and off your farm immediately and report to your County Veterinary Officer today.

detail.summary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a very contagious viral disease of cattle and all other cloven-hoofed animals, including goats, sheep, pigs, camels and wild animals such as buffalo. It causes fever, painful blisters in the mouth, on the feet and on the teats, and a sudden, sharp drop in milk. Most adult cattle survive, but young calves can die suddenly, and the loss of milk, weight and draught power can hurt a farm for months. FMD is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer.
detail.cause: FMD is caused by a virus from the picornavirus family (genus Aphthovirus). There are seven main types, called serotypes: O, A, C, SAT1, SAT2, SAT3 and Asia1. Several of these, including O, A, SAT1 and SAT2, have been reported in East Africa. Immunity to one type does not protect against another, which is why an animal can catch FMD more than once and why the vaccine must match the types circulating in your area. The virus usually enters through the nose and throat, multiplies there, and then spreads through the blood. It settles in the skin of the mouth, feet and teats, where it forms fluid-filled blisters (vesicles). These blisters burst within a day or so, leaving raw, very painful sores. The pain is what stops the animal eating and walking. In young calves the virus can attack the heart muscle, causing sudden death even before blisters appear. Some recovered cattle and many African buffalo can carry the virus in their throat for months without looking sick.
spread: Direct contact between animals is the main route: an infected cow passes virus to others through saliva, breath, milk, dung and the fluid from burst blisters, often before it looks sick.
Breathing in virus in the air spreads it within and between nearby herds, especially in crowded bomas, zero-grazing units and markets.

People carry it on boots, clothes, hands and even in their nose and throat for a short time after handling sick animals, so visitors, milk collectors, AI technicians and traders can move it from farm to farm.
Vehicles, milk cans, feed sacks, ropes, tools and hay or cut grass from infected farms can carry the virus.
Buying, borrowing or bringing back animals from markets, shows or other farms is one of the most common ways FMD arrives on a new farm.
Sharing grazing, water points and dips, especially in the dry season when herds gather, spreads it quickly in pastoral areas.
Contact with African buffalo and other wildlife near parks and conservancies can bring SAT-type viruses into cattle.
Raw milk, milk by-products and meat from infected animals can carry the virus, and feeding kitchen waste containing meat to pigs can start outbreaks.
detail.atRisk: All cattle of every age and breed can get FMD, and goats, sheep, pigs and camels on the same farm can catch it too. High-yielding exotic dairy breeds such as Friesian and Ayrshire usually show more severe disease and bigger milk losses than local zebu cattle, which often show milder signs but still spread the virus. Young calves are at the greatest risk of death. Unvaccinated herds, or herds whose vaccination has lapsed or used a vaccine that does not match the local virus type, are most at risk. Outbreaks in Kenya often rise when animals are moved a lot, for example during dry seasons when pastoralists move herds in search of grass and water, and around market and festive periods. Farms near livestock markets, stock routes, national parks with buffalo, or busy roads, and farms that buy in animals often, face the highest risk.

early: Sudden high fever, dullness and loss of appetite, often in several animals within a few days.
A sharp, sudden drop in milk yield in dairy cows, sometimes before any blisters are seen.
Lots of saliva hanging in strings from the mouth, with frothing and a smacking or sucking sound of the lips.
Small blisters or pale, raised patches on the tongue, gums, dental pad (the hard pad in the upper front of the mouth) and inside the lips.
Shifting weight from foot to foot, kicking or shaking the feet, and reluctance to walk as blisters form between the claws and along the top of the hoof.
Blisters on the teats, making cows restless and resistant at milking.
advanced: Burst blisters leaving raw, red, bleeding-looking sores in the mouth; skin on the tongue may peel off in sheets.
Severe lameness, with animals lying down for long periods and refusing to get up.
Rapid loss of body condition because the animal cannot eat or walk to feed and water.
Teat sores leading to mastitis (infection of the udder) with swollen quarters and clotted or watery milk.
Secondary infection of foot sores, with swelling, bad smell and, in some cases, the hoof horn coming loose or sloughing off months later.
Young calves dying suddenly with little warning, sometimes with breathing difficulty, because the virus has damaged the heart.
Abortion in some pregnant cows, and in recovered animals long-term problems such as poor fertility, chronic lameness, heat intolerance with heavy panting, and a rough, hairy coat.

lookalikes.name: Foot rot
lookalikes.howToTell: Foot rot is a bacterial infection that usually affects one foot of one or a few animals, with swelling above the hoof and a foul smell between the claws. There is no drooling and no mouth blisters, and it does not race through the whole herd in a few days like FMD.

lookalikes.name: Malignant catarrhal fever (MCF)
lookalikes.howToTell: MCF, linked to wildebeest calving in Maasai areas, causes high fever, mouth sores and drooling, but also cloudy eyes, thick discharge from the nose and swollen lymph glands. It usually affects individual animals rather than spreading rapidly from cow to cow, and most affected animals die.

lookalikes.name: Bovine viral diarrhoea / mucosal disease (BVD)
lookalikes.howToTell: BVD can cause mouth erosions and some lameness, but the sores are shallow erosions rather than fluid-filled blisters, and severe diarrhoea is a main sign. It does not usually cause the sudden, herd-wide drooling and lameness of FMD.

lookalikes.name: Mouth injury or chemical burns
lookalikes.howToTell: Sharp thorns, rough feed, or swallowing caustic chemicals or dip wash can cause drooling and mouth sores, but usually in one animal, without fever spreading through the herd and without blisters on the feet and teats.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will suspect FMD from the pattern: fever, drooling, mouth and foot blisters, lameness and milk drop spreading quickly through the herd. Because it is notifiable and other diseases can look similar, the diagnosis must be confirmed in the laboratory. The vet will take samples such as fluid or skin from fresh blisters, saliva, throat fluid, or blood, under strict biosecurity, and send them to the national veterinary laboratory. Tests find the virus and identify its serotype, which is vital for choosing the right vaccine for the area. Blood tests can also show if animals have been infected in the past. If a calf dies, a post-mortem may show a streaky, pale heart muscle ('tiger heart'). Before the vet arrives, keep all animals on the farm, note when signs started and how many animals of each species are sick, record any recent purchases, visitors, market trips or shared grazing, and keep your vaccination records ready. Do not move or sell any animal or carcass.
firstSteps: Report the suspected case right away to your County Veterinary Officer, the area veterinary or livestock officer, or the nearest government veterinary office, because the law requires it.
Stop all movement of animals, milk, manure, feed and equipment on and off the farm, and do not take animals to market, shows or shared grazing until the vet advises.
Separate sick animals from healthy ones as much as your housing allows, and keep goats, sheep and pigs away from affected cattle.
Give sick animals clean, fresh water within easy reach and soft, palatable feed such as fresh green grass, soft hay or mashes, because a sore mouth makes hard feed painful.
Provide shade, dry, soft bedding such as dry grass or sawdust, and a clean, mud-free floor to protect painful feet and reduce secondary infection.
Milk affected cows gently and keep their milk separate; do not sell it or take it to the collection centre, and follow your vet's advice on disposal or boiling.

Keep visitors out, set up a footbath or washing point with water and soap or a disinfectant your vet recommends at the gate, and change clothes and boots after handling sick animals before visiting other farms or markets.
Write down daily which animals are sick, how they are eating and walking, and any deaths, and do not give any drugs unless a vet has prescribed them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no drug that kills the FMD virus, and antibiotics do not cure it. Treatment is supportive, aimed at reducing pain, keeping the animal eating and drinking, and preventing secondary bacterial infection while the animal's own immune system clears the virus, which usually takes one to two weeks for the sores to heal. A vet may prescribe anti-inflammatory pain relief from the NSAID group (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as meloxicam or flunixin), gentle antiseptic mouth washes, and antiseptic or astringent dressings for feet and teats. Antibiotics are only used when there is a real secondary infection such as infected foot sores, mastitis or pneumonia, and only on a vet's prescription; using them without need wastes money and adds to antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working. Any drug given carries a milk and meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait before milk or meat can be used, and you must follow it exactly. Your vet and the County Veterinary Office will also lead the outbreak response, which can include quarantine of the farm or area, closure of markets, controls on milk and animal movement, and ring vaccination of nearby healthy herds. Expect recovery to be slow in high-yielding cows, with milk yield sometimes not returning fully in that lactation.
prevention: Vaccinate all cattle regularly with an FMD vaccine that matches the serotypes in your area, such as the multivalent vaccines made in Kenya by KEVEVAPI, and follow the booster schedule your vet or County Veterinary Office gives, because protection from FMD vaccines is short-lived compared with many other vaccines.
Keep written vaccination records for every animal, and join county or community vaccination campaigns, since vaccination works best when most herds in an area are covered.
Buy animals only from known, healthy sources with a movement permit, and keep new animals separate for at least two to three weeks before mixing them with your herd.
Limit visitors, traders and service providers in your cattle area, provide a footbath or washing point, and ask anyone who has been at a market or another farm to change or clean boots and clothes.
Clean and disinfect milk cans, vehicles, ropes and tools that move between farms, and avoid sharing equipment with neighbours during outbreaks.
Avoid shared grazing, watering points and markets when FMD is reported nearby, and follow any quarantine or movement ban announced by the authorities.
Reduce contact between cattle and buffalo or other wildlife where possible, especially near parks and conservancies.
Do not feed kitchen waste containing meat or raw milk scraps to pigs or other livestock, and keep good general nutrition and housing so animals cope better if infection does occur.
detail.impact: FMD is one of the most costly livestock diseases in Kenya. Dairy farmers lose milk suddenly, often for weeks, and high-yielding cows may not return to full production that lactation; mastitis from teat sores can permanently damage quarters. Beef and draught animals lose weight and cannot work, which can delay ploughing in the planting season. Calf deaths, abortions, poor fertility and long-term lameness reduce the future value of the herd. On top of farm losses, quarantines close livestock markets and restrict movement and milk sales across whole areas, cutting income for farmers, traders and milk collectors, and FMD blocks access to export markets for meat and live animals. Treatment, extra labour for nursing, and lost sales together can be a heavy blow for a smallholder family.
detail.humanHealth: FMD is not considered a significant risk to human health; human infection is extremely rare and mild. It is a different disease from 'hand, foot and mouth disease' that affects children, which is caused by a different virus and does not come from cattle. The bigger human concern is that people can carry the FMD virus on their hands, clothes, boots and briefly in their nose and throat, and spread it to other farms. Wash hands and change clothes after handling sick animals, avoid visiting other livestock for a few days, and do not sell or move milk or meat from affected farms against vet advice. If your vet treats animals, respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods so drug residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: Most adult cattle recover within about two weeks if they are nursed well, given water and soft feed, and protected from secondary infection, and deaths in adults are usually low. Young calves are at much higher risk of sudden death from heart damage. Recovery is slower and losses greater in high-yielding exotic dairy cows, animals in poor condition, and those that develop infected feet or mastitis. Some recovered animals stay chronic poor doers with reduced milk, poor fertility, lameness or heat intolerance, and some may carry the virus for a time. Immunity after infection protects mainly against the same serotype, so animals can get FMD again from a different type.

faqs.q: My cattle were vaccinated. Why did they still get FMD?
faqs.a: There are several possible reasons. The vaccine may not have matched the serotype causing the outbreak, because protection against one type does not cover another. FMD vaccine protection also fades after some months, so if boosters were late, immunity may have dropped. Poor storage, such as vaccine not kept cold, can also make it weak. Vaccinated animals that do get infected often have milder disease. Talk to your County Veterinary Office about which vaccine and schedule suit your area.

faqs.q: Can I sell or drink milk from cows with FMD?
faqs.a: Do not sell milk or take it to the collection centre from an infected farm unless the veterinary authorities allow it, because milk carries the virus and spreads it to other farms. Follow your vet's instructions on disposal or boiling. FMD itself is not a real danger to people, but if the cow is on any medicine you must also respect the withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics cure FMD?
faqs.a: No. FMD is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may prescribe antibiotics only if there is a secondary bacterial infection, such as badly infected feet or mastitis. Using antibiotics without need wastes money, leaves residues in milk and meat, and helps create drug resistance.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report FMD? Will my animals be killed?
faqs.a: FMD is notifiable under Kenyan law because it spreads so fast and affects whole regions and trade. Reporting allows the County Veterinary Officer to confirm the disease, find the virus type, vaccinate surrounding herds and set up quarantine so neighbours are protected. In Kenya the usual response is quarantine, movement control and vaccination rather than mass culling. Quarantine means no animals, milk or animal products may leave or enter the affected farm or area without permission until the vets lift it.

faqs.q: How long does the quarantine last and when can I sell animals again?
faqs.a: It depends on the outbreak and the decision of the veterinary authorities. Quarantine usually stays in place until no new cases have been seen for a set period and the vets are satisfied the outbreak is over. Keep your animals at home, follow the County Veterinary Office instructions, and ask them directly when movement permits will resume.

faqs.q: Can my goats and sheep spread FMD to my cattle?
faqs.a: Yes. Goats, sheep, pigs and camels can all catch FMD and spread it, even when goats and sheep show only mild signs. During an outbreak keep all cloven-hoofed animals on the farm, separate species where you can, and include them in vaccination if your vet advises.

foot-and-mouth-disease.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a Friesian dairy cow's head in a Kenyan zero-grazing shed, with long strings of clear saliva hanging from its mouth and small pale blisters visible on the gums and tongue tip, natural daylight.
foot-and-mouth-disease.seoDescription: Foot-and-mouth disease in cattle: spot drooling, mouth and foot blisters, lameness and milk drop, report to your vet, nurse sick cows and prevent outbreaks in Kenya.

card.headline: Firm round lumps all over skin
card.look: Many firm, raised, round lumps from coin-size up to about 5 cm appear over the neck, back, legs, udder and head, often with fever, watery eyes and a sudden drop in milk. Swollen glands in front of the shoulder and swollen legs are common.
card.action: Isolate the sick animal, stop all cattle movement on and off the farm, and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, because lumpy skin disease is a notifiable disease in Kenya.

aka: Knopvelsiekte (Afrikaans name used in southern Africa)
detail.summary: Lumpy skin disease (LSD) is a viral disease of cattle that causes fever and firm lumps (nodules) in the skin and sometimes in the mouth, throat and lungs. It is common in Kenya and East Africa, especially during the rains when biting flies are plentiful. Few animals die, but sick cows lose a lot of milk and weight, may abort or become infertile, and their hides are damaged, so the money lost can be large. It is a notifiable disease, which means the law requires you to report it to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: LSD is caused by the lumpy skin disease virus, a member of the capripox group of viruses (the same family as sheep pox and goat pox). Once a biting insect or tick carries the virus into a cow, it multiplies and travels through the blood. This stage brings fever and makes the lymph nodes (glands that filter infection, such as the large one in front of the shoulder) swell. The virus then settles in the skin and the tissues under it, where it damages small blood vessels and causes swelling and dead tissue. This is what forms the firm nodules. The same damage can happen in the lining of the mouth, nose, windpipe, lungs, gut, udder and reproductive organs, and in the legs, where fluid builds up and causes swelling and lameness. Over time the centre of a nodule can die and form a hard plug of dead skin called a 'sitfast', which may fall out and leave a hole that heals slowly and can become infected by bacteria or invaded by fly maggots. Pneumonia and mastitis from bacteria are common complications in weakened animals.
spread: Biting flies are the main way LSD spreads: stable flies, mosquitoes and horse flies feed on a sick cow and carry the virus on their mouthparts to the next animal.
Certain ticks, including some common in Kenya such as blue ticks and bont ticks, can also carry and pass on the virus.
Spread is fastest during and just after the long and short rains, when insect numbers rise, and in low-lying, warm or wet areas.
Moving infected or newly bought cattle into a herd, or bringing cattle together at markets, dips, watering points and communal grazing, brings the virus to new farms.
Reusing the same needle on several animals during treatment or vaccination can carry the virus from one cow to another.
Infected bulls can shed the virus in semen, so natural mating and semen from unscreened bulls can carry the disease.
An infected pregnant cow can pass the virus to her unborn calf, and calves may be born with skin lesions.
The virus survives well in dry scabs, hides and dirty surroundings for a long time, and saliva, nasal discharge and milk from sick cows can contaminate shared feed and water.
detail.atRisk: All ages and breeds of cattle can get LSD, but exotic dairy breeds such as Friesian (Holstein), Ayrshire, Jersey and Guernsey, and their crosses, usually suffer much more severely than local Zebu and Boran cattle. High-yielding cows in milk, pregnant cows, young calves and animals that are thin or stressed tend to become very sick. Unvaccinated herds are at greatest risk, as are herds where the yearly vaccination has been missed. Risk is highest during and after the long and short rains when flies and mosquitoes multiply. Zero-grazing units can still be affected because flies move freely between farms, while free-range and pastoral herds face extra risk from shared grazing, watering points, dips, markets and long-distance movement. Herds near livestock markets, stock routes or wildlife areas, and farms that often buy in new animals, are especially exposed. Buffalo and some other wild animals may be involved in the disease cycle, although their exact role is not fully understood.

early: Fever, often high, with the cow looking dull, standing apart and eating less.
A sudden and sharp drop in milk yield in milking cows, often noticed before the lumps appear.
Watery eyes, clear nasal discharge and extra drooling of saliva.
Swollen lymph nodes that you can feel as firm, enlarged lumps in front of the shoulder and in the flank just in front of the back leg.
Small, firm, round raised lumps appearing in the skin, often first on the neck, head, back, udder, perineum (area under the tail) or legs; the hair over them stands up.
Lumps that feel hard and deep in the skin, not just on the surface, and may be painful when touched.
advanced: Many nodules, from a few to hundreds, covering much of the body, sometimes joining together into larger swollen patches.
Nodules whose centres die and form hard, dark plugs (sitfasts) that later drop out, leaving deep open sores that may attract flies and maggots.
Swelling of the legs, brisket (lower chest) and dewlap with fluid, causing stiffness, reluctance to walk and lameness.
Sores in the mouth, nose and throat causing thick discharge, bad breath, difficulty eating and heavy drooling.
Noisy or laboured breathing and coughing from lesions in the windpipe and lungs, or from pneumonia.
Marked weight loss, weakness, mastitis with swollen painful quarters, and in pregnant cows, abortion.
In bulls, swollen and painful testicles that may lead to temporary or permanent infertility; in cows, missed heats and failure to conceive for months.

lookalikes.name: Pseudo-lumpy skin disease (bovine herpes mammillitis virus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by a different virus and usually milder. The lumps are shallow, on the surface only, often with a flat or sunken centre, and they heal within a few weeks without deep sitfasts. Fever is mild and the lymph nodes are not greatly swollen. A vet often needs lab tests to tell the two apart.

lookalikes.name: Insect bites or allergic hives (urticaria)
lookalikes.howToTell: Soft, puffy swellings that appear suddenly, often after a change of feed, a spray or heavy insect attack, and disappear within hours to a few days. There is usually no fever, no milk drop, no swollen glands and no hard nodules that later scab or slough.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis, 'rain scald')
lookalikes.howToTell: A bacterial skin infection seen in wet weather, especially along the back. It forms crusty scabs with tufts of matted hair that look like a paintbrush and peel off to show raw, moist skin underneath. The lesions are on the surface, not deep firm nodules, and the cow is usually not feverish.

lookalikes.name: Warts (papillomatosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Grey, rough, cauliflower-like growths mostly on the head, neck and shoulders of young cattle. They grow slowly over weeks, the animal stays bright and eats well, and there is no fever, milk drop or leg swelling.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will often strongly suspect LSD from the typical deep skin nodules, fever, swollen glands and the season, especially if neighbouring farms are affected. Because it is notifiable, confirmation is usually done through the government veterinary laboratories. The vet may take small skin biopsies (samples) from fresh nodules, scabs, swabs from the nose or mouth, and blood in special tubes. These are tested by PCR, a laboratory test that detects the virus's genetic material and gives a reliable answer. Blood tests for antibodies can show past infection, and tissue examination under the microscope can support the diagnosis. If an animal dies, a post-mortem examination may show nodules in the mouth, windpipe, lungs and gut. To help the vet, keep the sick animal confined and calm in a crush or safe pen, write down when signs started, how many animals are affected, temperatures if you have a thermometer, milk records, vaccination dates and the vaccine used, and any recent purchases, market visits or movements. Do not move animals or sell hides while waiting for results.
firstSteps: Report your suspicion at once to your County Veterinary Officer, the nearest government veterinary office or your local vet; LSD is notifiable in Kenya and early reporting helps protect your neighbours' herds as well as yours.
Stop all movement of cattle on and off your farm: do not sell, buy, lend, take animals to market, or send them to shared grazing or communal dips until the vet advises you.
Separate sick animals from healthy ones in a shaded, well-ventilated pen, ideally screened from flies, and use separate buckets, feed troughs and equipment for them.
Give sick cattle unlimited clean, fresh water and soft, palatable feed such as fresh green grass, good hay and moistened concentrate, because mouth sores and fever make eating hard.

Reduce flies and ticks around the farm by clearing manure and stagnant water, keeping your normal tick and fly control routine with registered products as advised by your vet, and keeping sick animals indoors in shade during peak fly times.
Do not treat with antibiotics, injections or home remedies on your own; wait for the vet, and never reuse one needle between animals.
Protect your herd through hygiene: wash hands, boots and clothes after handling sick cattle, and handle healthy animals first and sick animals last.
Keep records of every sick animal, its temperature if you can measure it, milk yield and changes from day to day, and keep milk from sick cows separate until the vet tells you what to do with it.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the LSD virus, so treatment focuses on supporting the animal while its own immune system fights the infection, and on preventing complications. Your vet may give anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving drugs (NSAIDs such as meloxicam or flunixin) to bring down fever, reduce leg swelling and help the cow eat and move. Antibiotics do not cure the virus, but the vet may prescribe them, for example oxytetracycline or penicillin-streptomycin, when there are signs of bacterial complications such as infected sores, pneumonia or mastitis. Use antibiotics only as prescribed and complete the course exactly, because misuse breeds bacteria that no longer respond to treatment (antimicrobial resistance). Open sores and sitfasts are cleaned and dressed, and fly repellent wound sprays are used to prevent maggots. Vitamin injections, fluids and good nursing may also be advised for weak animals. All drugs used have milk and meat withdrawal periods, which is the time you must wait after the last dose before milk can be sold or drunk or the animal slaughtered; your vet will tell you these, and you must follow them. Alongside treatment, the veterinary services will usually organise vaccination of healthy cattle on your farm and in the surrounding area (ring vaccination) and enforce movement restrictions. Recovery is slow: fever may settle in days, but nodules and sores can take weeks to months to heal, and milk yield and fertility may take a long time to return.
prevention: Vaccinate all cattle every year with a registered LSD vaccine; live vaccines made in Kenya (for example by KEVEVAPI) are widely available through agrovets and veterinary offices, and your vet will advise on the right product and timing.

Vaccinate before the long and short rains, when flies increase, rather than waiting for an outbreak, and include calves from the age your vet recommends, usually after the protection from their mother's colostrum wears off.
Make sure vaccines are kept cold from purchase to use, are given by a trained person, and that a new needle is used for each animal.

Control biting flies and ticks with a regular spraying or dipping programme using registered acaricides and insecticides, and reduce fly breeding by removing manure, wet bedding, rotting feed and stagnant water.
Quarantine newly bought cattle for at least a few weeks, buy only from herds with a known vaccination history, and ask for movement permits; avoid buying animals from areas with current outbreaks.
Limit contact with other herds at markets, communal grazing, dips and watering points during outbreaks, and keep visitors, traders and their vehicles away from your animals.
Use semen from reputable AI providers whose bulls are tested and vaccinated, and avoid hiring bulls of unknown health status.
Keep cattle well fed with good forage, minerals and clean water so that they are in strong condition, because thin and stressed animals suffer worse disease.
detail.impact: LSD rarely kills large numbers of cattle, but it is very costly on a Kenyan farm. Dairy cows can lose most of their milk for weeks, and some never return to their full yield in that lactation, which hurts farmers who depend on daily milk income from cooperatives or local sales. Sick animals lose weight and condition quickly, and beef and draught animals may be unable to work or walk to grazing. Abortions, missed heats and infertile bulls delay calving and reduce the number of calves born, with effects that last into the next year. Hides are scarred and lose value. Mastitis and pneumonia add vet and drug costs, and milk must be discarded during drug withdrawal periods. Quarantines and movement restrictions can stop sales, close markets and disrupt AI services, and when an exotic dairy cow is badly affected, the farmer may lose a valuable animal through death or forced culling. Annual vaccination costs far less than one serious outbreak.
detail.humanHealth: Lumpy skin disease is not known to infect people, so it is not a zoonosis. The main human-health concern is drug residues: if sick cows are treated with antibiotics or other medicines, their milk and meat must not be sold or eaten until the withdrawal period set by your vet has passed. Milk from any sick or feverish cow should be kept separate, and milk you do use should always be boiled. Wash your hands after handling sick animals and their sores to avoid carrying the virus on your skin and clothes to healthy cattle.
detail.outlook: Most cattle with LSD survive, and deaths are usually low, but recovery is slow and can take several weeks to a few months. Animals with only a few nodules and mild fever often recover fully. The outlook is worse for exotic breeds, high-yielding cows, young calves and pregnant cows, and for animals with many nodules, mouth and throat lesions, severe leg swelling, pneumonia or infected sores with maggots. Some animals stay thin, have long-term scarring, lose part of the udder, or remain infertile, and some farmers decide to cull them. Cattle that recover usually have strong, long-lasting immunity to LSD. Early reporting, good nursing, fly control and prompt vet care for complications all improve the chances of a good recovery.

faqs.q: Can I drink or sell milk from a cow with lumpy skin disease?
faqs.a: LSD is not known to infect people, but milk from a sick, feverish cow is often poor quality and may come from an udder with mastitis. If the cow is being treated with antibiotics or other drugs, the milk must be discarded until the withdrawal period your vet gives you is over. Keep milk from sick cows separate, ask your vet before using it, and always boil milk before drinking. During an official quarantine, follow any instructions from the veterinary office on milk sales.

faqs.q: My cows were vaccinated but one still got lumpy skin disease. Why?
faqs.a: No vaccine gives 100% protection. A cow may get sick if the vaccine was not kept cold and lost its strength, if it was given too late and the cow was already infected, if the yearly booster was missed, or if the cow was weak or sick when vaccinated. Some vaccinated animals also show a mild local swelling or a few small lumps after vaccination, which a vet can help you tell apart from true disease. Vaccinated herds generally have far fewer and milder cases, so keep vaccinating every year and report any sick animal.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate my healthy cattle when there is an outbreak nearby?
faqs.a: Yes, vaccination of healthy cattle is a key part of controlling an outbreak, and the veterinary services often organise ring vaccination around affected farms. Vaccinating an animal that is already showing signs will not cure it. Let the vet or trained vaccinator decide which animals to vaccinate, and insist on a new needle for every animal so that the virus is not spread from cow to cow.

faqs.q: How long will the lumps take to go away?
faqs.a: The fever often settles within one to two weeks, but the nodules take much longer. Small nodules may shrink slowly over a few weeks, while larger ones can form hard plugs that fall out and leave sores that take a month or more to heal. Some lumps and scars can remain for many months. Keep sores clean, protect them from flies and maggots, and call your vet if a sore smells bad, swells or produces pus.

faqs.q: Can I sell my animals or take them to market during an outbreak?
faqs.a: No, not while your farm or area is under restriction. Because LSD is notifiable, the County Veterinary Officer can impose movement restrictions, which means cattle cannot be moved, sold, taken to markets or slaughterhouses, or brought in, without permission. Markets in affected areas may be closed. These rules stop the virus being carried to new herds. Breaking them can spread the disease and may be an offence, so wait until the veterinary office lifts the restrictions.

faqs.q: Will my bull or cows be able to breed again after lumpy skin disease?
faqs.a: Many recover their fertility, but it can take months. Bulls with swollen, painful testicles may become temporarily infertile, and some become permanently infertile. Cows may miss heats or fail to conceive for a while, and pregnant cows may abort. Ask your vet to examine breeding animals after recovery, and keep breeding records so you can make good decisions about which animals to keep.

lumpy-skin-disease.imagePrompt: A Friesian dairy cow standing in a Kenyan farmyard with many firm, round, raised skin nodules clearly visible across its neck, shoulder and flank, the hair standing up over each lump, photographed in natural daylight.
lumpy-skin-disease.seoDescription: Lumpy skin disease in cattle: spot firm skin nodules, fever and milk drop early, report to your vet, and protect your herd with vaccination and fly control.

card.headline: Laboured breathing with neck stretched out
card.look: A feverish cow or bull stands apart with its head and neck stretched forward, elbows turned out and mouth open, breathing hard and coughing, especially after walking. It may grunt and flinch when you press gently on the side of its chest.
card.action: Keep the whole herd at home, separate any coughing animal and report to your County Veterinary Officer straight away, because CBPP is a notifiable disease.

detail.summary: Contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP) is a serious, highly contagious lung disease of cattle caused by a bacterium-like germ called a mycoplasma. It causes fever, coughing, painful and difficult breathing, and can kill animals or leave them thin and weak for months. Many animals that seem to recover keep the germ hidden in their lungs and can infect other cattle later. Because it spreads quickly through herds, markets and grazing areas and damages livestock trade, CBPP is a notifiable disease in Kenya and must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: CBPP is caused by Mycoplasma mycoides subspecies mycoides. A mycoplasma is a very small germ, similar to a bacterium but with no cell wall, which is why some common antibiotics such as penicillin do not work against it. When a healthy animal breathes in droplets coughed out by a sick animal, the germ settles in the lungs. It causes strong inflammation (swelling and heat) of the lung tissue and of the pleura, the thin lining that covers the lungs and the inside of the chest wall. The lung becomes heavy, solid and full of fluid, and yellow fibrin (a sticky, clotting material) and straw-coloured fluid build up in the chest. This makes each breath painful and reduces the space for air, so the animal struggles to breathe. Often only one lung is badly affected. In animals that survive, the body may wall off dead pieces of lung inside a tough capsule called a sequestrum. The live germ can hide inside this capsule for a long time, and these 'carrier' animals can start shedding the germ again, especially when stressed. In young calves the germ can also settle in the joints and cause painful, swollen joints. The time from infection to showing signs (the incubation period) varies widely, commonly several weeks and sometimes several months, so infected animals can be moved and sold before anyone notices a problem.
spread: The main route is breathing in droplets coughed out by an infected animal, so close, repeated contact between cattle is what spreads the disease most.
Spread is fastest where cattle are packed together: night bomas and kraals, crowded water points, dips, livestock markets, holding grounds, trucks and trekking routes.

Bringing in new cattle from markets, dowry exchanges, restocking or cross-border trade is a common way the disease enters a clean herd, because animals can look healthy during the long incubation period.
Chronic carrier animals that recovered from earlier illness can keep the germ walled off in their lungs and later shed it again, quietly re-infecting the herd.
Drought and seasonal migration, when many herds share scarce grazing and water, greatly increase contact between herds and the chance of spread.
Stress from long walks, poor feeding, transport and other diseases can make carriers shed more and make exposed animals sicker.

The germ does not survive long outside the animal in sunlight and dry conditions, so spread through equipment, pasture or water is much less important than direct animal-to-animal contact, though very close contact with fresh discharges, urine or infected afterbirth may play a small part.
detail.atRisk: All cattle can catch CBPP, of any breed, sex or age, including local Zebu, Boran and dairy breeds. Water buffalo can also be infected; goats and sheep are not affected by this germ. Herds that have never been exposed or vaccinated tend to suffer the most severe illness and deaths, while herds in long-affected areas may show milder or slower-spreading disease with many carriers. Young calves are more likely to show swollen, painful joints rather than only lung signs. In Kenya the disease has mostly affected pastoral and agro-pastoral systems, especially in northern, north-eastern and border counties where cattle are moved long distances, mix at markets and water points, and cross borders with neighbouring countries. Risk rises during droughts and dry seasons when herds concentrate around water and grazing, and when cattle are trekked to markets. Zero-grazing and smallholder dairy farms are at lower risk but can be infected by buying animals from markets or affected areas without checking and quarantining them.

early: Fever: the animal feels hot, its ears and muzzle may be warm and dry, and a thermometer in the rectum shows a temperature clearly above normal.
Dullness and reduced appetite; the animal lags behind the herd, chews the cud less and may stand alone in shade.
A dry, short cough, most noticeable in the morning, after walking or when the animal is driven quickly.
Faster breathing than other cattle at rest, with the flanks moving more than normal.
A drop in milk yield in lactating cows.
In some animals, especially in partly protected herds, the early signs are mild and easy to miss, so a slow trickle of coughing animals over weeks should raise suspicion.
advanced: Hard, laboured breathing with the head and neck stretched forward, mouth open and sometimes the tongue out.
Standing with the elbows turned outwards and the back arched, refusing to lie down or lying only on the chest, to ease chest pain.
Grunting or groaning with each breath, and a soft, painful, wet cough.
Clear pain when you press firmly between the ribs or tap on the chest: the animal flinches, groans or moves away.
Frothy saliva at the mouth and nasal discharge, sometimes with swelling under the chest or throat.
Rapid weight loss, weakness and reluctance to walk; some animals collapse and die within days to a few weeks.
In calves, hot, swollen and painful knees, hocks or other joints, with lameness.
Animals that survive the acute stage may stay thin, with a lingering cough and poor body condition for months.

lookalikes.name: Pasteurellosis / shipping fever pneumonia (Mannheimia and Pasteurella bacteria)
lookalikes.howToTell: This pneumonia often follows stress such as transport, weaning or bad weather and tends to appear in a group soon after the stress event, often with a lot of nasal discharge. It usually responds quickly to vet-prescribed antibiotics. CBPP spreads more slowly through a herd over weeks to months, causes marked chest pain and the typical outstretched neck, and needs lab or post-mortem confirmation by a vet to tell the two apart.

lookalikes.name: East Coast fever (theileriosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: East Coast fever is tick-borne and causes clearly swollen lymph nodes (glands), especially below the ear and in front of the shoulder, along with fever, watery eyes and, at the end, frothy discharge from the nose as the lungs fill with fluid. CBPP does not cause the large swollen glands, and it spreads by contact rather than ticks. A vet can confirm East Coast fever with a blood or gland smear.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm (verminous bronchitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Lungworm mainly affects young cattle grazing wet pasture, especially during and after the rains, and causes coughing and fast breathing but usually little fever or chest pain. Signs improve after vet-advised deworming. CBPP affects adults and young stock, causes high fever and painful breathing, and is linked to contact with other herds rather than pasture.

lookalikes.name: Bovine tuberculosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Tuberculosis is a slow, long-lasting disease with gradual weight loss and a soft cough in a few animals, developing over months to years, and usually without sudden high fever. CBPP can cause acute illness with fever and painful breathing in several animals over weeks. Both need vet testing, and tuberculosis can infect people, so a vet should investigate any herd with chronic coughing.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will suspect CBPP from the history (new animals, market contact, a spreading cough in the herd) and from examining sick animals: taking their temperature, watching their breathing, listening to the chest with a stethoscope and pressing or tapping the chest to check for pain and areas that sound dull. Confirmation needs laboratory tests, so the vet or veterinary officer will usually take blood samples from several animals in the herd for antibody tests such as the complement fixation test (CFT) or competitive ELISA (c-ELISA). These tests work best for checking the herd as a whole rather than proving whether one single animal is or is not infected. Samples of nasal swabs, chest fluid or lung tissue can be sent for culture or PCR (a test that detects the germ's genetic material). A post-mortem (opening a dead or culled animal) is very useful: the vet looks for a heavy, solid lung with a 'marbled' pattern, yellow fibrin, straw-coloured fluid in the chest, the lung stuck to the chest wall, and sometimes walled-off sequestra. Do not open dead animals yourself; leave this to the vet. To help, prepare a clear history: when the first animal got sick, how many are coughing, any deaths, recent purchases, market visits, shared water or grazing, vaccination dates and where your cattle have moved. Keep sick animals restrained in a crush or yard so the vet can examine them safely.
firstSteps: Report your suspicion immediately to the County Veterinary Officer, the nearest government vet or animal health office, or through your local chief or extension officer; this is a legal requirement for CBPP.
Stop all movement of cattle onto or off your farm or boma, and do not sell, give away, exchange or take any animals to market until a vet tells you it is safe.
Separate coughing or feverish animals from the rest of the herd, ideally in a pen or area several metres away and downwind, and keep them away from neighbours' cattle and shared water points.

Give sick animals shade, shelter from wind and rain, clean fresh water close by and soft, good-quality feed so they do not have to walk far; avoid driving or chasing them, as exercise makes breathing harder.
Do not give any antibiotics or other drugs on your own; incomplete or wrong treatment can hide the disease, create carriers and make diagnosis harder, so wait for the vet's instructions.
Write down which animals are sick, their ear tags or descriptions, their temperatures if you have a thermometer, dates signs started and any deaths, so the vet can trace the outbreak.
If an animal dies, cover the carcass, keep dogs and people away, do not eat or sell the meat, and wait for the vet, who may want to do a post-mortem.
Tell neighbours who share grazing or water with you so they can watch their herds and keep them apart from yours.
detail.vetTreatment: Because CBPP is notifiable, decisions about treatment are made with the government veterinary services, and what is allowed can depend on the local situation and current national policy. Control in Kenya relies mainly on reporting, movement control, vaccination and, in some situations, removing infected animals, rather than on treating individual animals. Where treatment is permitted, a vet may prescribe antibiotics that act against mycoplasma, such as tetracyclines (for example oxytetracycline), macrolides (for example tylosin) or fluoroquinolones (for example danofloxacin). Penicillin-type antibiotics do not work because the germ has no cell wall. Antibiotics can reduce fever, ease breathing and cut deaths, but they do not reliably clear the germ from the lungs, and treated animals can still become chronic carriers that spread disease later. For this reason, using antibiotics without vet control is risky for your herd and your neighbours. Vets may also give anti-inflammatory drugs to ease pain and fever. Treatment must only be given as prescribed by a vet, with the full course completed. Misuse and under-dosing of antibiotics also drives antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people. All these drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods: you must not sell or drink milk, or slaughter animals for meat, until the withdrawal time stated by the vet and on the product label has passed. Expect the vet to examine and sample the whole herd, advise on vaccination of healthy animals, and explain quarantine rules and whether any animals should be culled.
prevention: Vaccinate: in areas where CBPP occurs, the government-approved live vaccine (commonly the T1/44 strain, produced in Kenya) is the main tool, usually given in campaigns or by vets; protection does not last for life, so cattle need repeat vaccination as advised, and some animals develop swelling at the injection site, which the vet can advise on.
Join and support county vaccination campaigns, and keep records of which animals were vaccinated and when.
Buy cattle only from known, healthy herds, ask about their vaccination and disease history, and avoid buying from areas under quarantine.
Quarantine every new animal for several weeks away from your herd and watch it for cough, fever or breathing problems before mixing; ask a vet to check or test it if possible.
Limit contact with other herds at water points, dips, grazing areas and markets where you can, especially during droughts and migration.
Respect movement permits and quarantine orders; illegal movement of cattle is one of the main ways CBPP spreads between counties and across borders.

Keep cattle in good body condition with adequate feed, water and mineral supplementation, and reduce stress during transport and trekking, because healthy, well-fed animals cope better with all diseases.
Report any cough spreading through the herd early, so outbreaks are stopped while they are small.
detail.impact: CBPP is one of the most costly cattle diseases in pastoral parts of East Africa. Direct losses include deaths, which can be high in herds never exposed before, and severe weight loss in animals that survive. Lactating cows lose milk, which hits household nutrition and income, and sick bulls and oxen cannot work. Recovered animals often stay in poor condition and may carry the germ, lowering their value. Calves with joint infections may never thrive. Indirect losses are often larger: quarantines and movement bans stop farmers from selling animals when they need cash, markets may close, and traders pay lower prices for cattle from affected areas. Costs of vet visits, testing, vaccination and any treatment add up. For the wider economy, CBPP limits export of live cattle and beef, and outbreaks in one area threaten neighbouring counties and countries.
detail.humanHealth: CBPP does not infect people, and there is no known risk of catching it from handling sick cattle. However, if cattle are treated with antibiotics, their milk and meat can contain drug residues that are harmful to people and add to antimicrobial resistance; always keep to the withdrawal period given by the vet before using or selling milk or meat. Do not eat or sell meat from animals that died of illness, as other dangerous diseases can look similar, and wash your hands after handling sick animals.
detail.outlook: The outlook varies. In herds never exposed before, acute CBPP can kill many animals within weeks, and severely affected animals with very laboured breathing often die even with care. Some animals recover, especially with early vet involvement, rest, good feeding and shade, but many stay thin for a long time and may remain chronic carriers with walled-off lung lesions that can spread the disease again. For this reason the herd, not just the individual animal, is the focus: quick reporting, movement control and vaccination give the best chance of stopping losses. Herds and areas that keep up regular vaccination and controlled movement have far fewer and smaller outbreaks.

faqs.q: My cow is coughing. Does that mean it has CBPP?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many things cause coughing in cattle, including lungworm, dust, other pneumonias and East Coast fever. CBPP is more likely if the animal has fever, painful and laboured breathing with the neck stretched out, and especially if several animals start coughing over a few weeks after contact with other herds or new purchases. Only a vet with lab tests can confirm it, so if you see these signs, report early rather than wait.

faqs.q: Can I just buy antibiotics from the agrovet and treat it myself?
faqs.a: Please do not. CBPP is a notifiable disease, so you must report it, and treatment decisions are made with the veterinary services. Antibiotics may make the animal look better, but they often do not clear the germ, so the animal can become a hidden carrier that infects your herd and your neighbours later. Wrong or incomplete use also leads to drug resistance and leaves residues in milk and meat. Let the vet decide what, if anything, should be given.

faqs.q: What happens after I report CBPP? Will my cattle be taken away?
faqs.a: Veterinary officers will visit, examine and sample your animals and may place your farm or area under quarantine. This means cattle cannot be moved, sold or taken to markets until the restriction is lifted. They will usually vaccinate healthy animals in the area. In some cases, they may advise that infected animals be removed to protect other herds; ask the officer to explain the rules and any support available. Reporting early usually means a smaller, shorter problem for you and your community.

faqs.q: Is CBPP the same disease as the lung disease in goats?
faqs.a: No. The serious lung disease of goats, contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP), is caused by a different mycoplasma and affects goats, not cattle. CBPP affects cattle and buffalo, not goats or sheep. Both are contagious and should be reported, but vaccines for one do not protect against the other.

faqs.q: How often should my cattle be vaccinated against CBPP?
faqs.a: In areas where the disease occurs, vaccination is usually repeated regularly, often yearly, because protection from the vaccine does not last for life. The exact timing depends on local risk and county campaigns, so follow your County Veterinary Officer's advice and keep a record of vaccination dates for each animal. Vaccinate before the dry season movements and before taking animals to markets where possible.

faqs.q: An animal recovered from CBPP. Is it safe to keep or sell it?
faqs.a: Recovered animals can carry the germ hidden in their lungs for a long time and may spread it again, especially when stressed by transport or hunger. Do not sell or move them without vet approval, and never sell them to an unknown buyer to 'get rid of the problem', as this spreads the disease to other farms. Your vet will advise whether to keep, monitor or remove recovered animals.

cbpp.imagePrompt: A thin Zebu cow standing alone in a dry pastoral boma with its head and neck stretched forward, mouth slightly open, elbows turned outwards and flanks heaving as it struggles to breathe, in natural daylight.
cbpp.seoDescription: CBPP in cattle: spot the cough, laboured breathing and outstretched neck, report to your County Vet fast, and protect your herd with vaccination.

card.headline: Sudden death, dark blood from openings
card.look: A cow that seemed healthy is found dead, often bloated, with dark, tar-like blood that does not clot oozing from the nose, mouth or anus. The body stays limp instead of going stiff.
card.action: Do not open, skin, move or eat the carcass: keep people and animals away and call the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.summary: Anthrax is a severe and often fatal bacterial disease of cattle and other grazing animals. It usually kills so fast that the first sign is a dead animal. It is dangerous to people who touch, skin or eat infected carcasses. In Kenya it is a notifiable disease: you must report it, and the right response is to call the vet, lock down the carcass and vaccinate the rest of the herd.
detail.cause: Anthrax is caused by a bacterium called Bacillus anthracis. Outside the body it forms spores. A spore is a tough, sleeping form of the germ that can survive in soil for decades and resists heat, drying and many disinfectants. Cattle swallow spores while grazing on contaminated ground, drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated feed. Inside the animal the spores wake up and multiply very fast in the blood. The bacteria produce powerful poisons (toxins) that damage blood vessels, stop the blood from clotting, cause fluid to leak into tissues and lead to shock and death, often within hours. When the animal dies, its blood is full of bacteria. If the carcass is opened or the blood spills onto the ground, the bacteria meet air and turn back into spores, which contaminate that spot for many years. If the carcass is left closed, the bacteria inside are largely destroyed by decay within a few days. This is why opening a suspected anthrax carcass is the worst thing a farmer can do.
spread: Grazing on pasture where spores are present in the soil, especially at old anthrax sites, old burial spots or places where carcasses were opened in the past.

Weather changes that bring spores to the surface: heavy rains or flooding after a long drought, or the start of the long and short rains, wash and concentrate spores in low-lying areas and around water points.
Very short dry-season grazing, which makes cattle pull up roots and swallow soil along with the grass.
Disturbing soil through ploughing, digging, road building or digging up old burial sites.
Opening, skinning or butchering a carcass, which spills blood full of bacteria and creates new spore-contaminated ground.
Scavengers such as dogs, hyenas and vultures, and flies, which can spread infected blood and tissue from carcasses to new places.
Contaminated feed or materials, such as poorly processed bone meal, meat meal, hides or hair from infected animals.
Moving infected animals or carcass products to markets and other farms, which can carry the disease into new areas.
detail.atRisk: All cattle can get anthrax, whatever their age, breed or sex, and it also affects sheep, goats, camels, pigs and wildlife. Unvaccinated herds are at greatest risk. Free-range and pastoral herds grazing communal land, riverbanks, swamps and low-lying areas are especially exposed, but zero-grazed cattle can also be infected through cut fodder or feed from contaminated land. Outbreaks in Kenya often follow dry spells broken by heavy rain, or happen in the dry season when grazing is short. Areas with a history of anthrax, and farms near where carcasses were opened or buried shallowly, remain risky for many years. Herds in counties where cattle are often moved, traded or slaughtered at home without inspection face higher risk of the disease spreading.

early: Sudden death of an animal that looked healthy the evening before is the most common first sign; many cattle die without any illness being seen.
High fever: the animal feels very hot to the touch, especially the ears and the base of the horns.
Dullness, standing apart from the herd and refusing to eat or chew the cud.
Fast, laboured breathing and a fast heartbeat.
Trembling, staggering or excitement followed by weakness.
A sudden fall in milk yield; milk may be yellowish or tinged with blood.
Pregnant cows may abort.
advanced: Collapse, struggling (paddling the legs) and death, often within a few hours of the first signs.
Dark, thick, tar-like blood that does not clot coming from the nose, mouth, anus or vulva, sometimes also in the urine or dung.
Soft swellings under the skin of the throat, neck, brisket, belly or flanks in some animals that live a little longer.
After death the carcass bloats very quickly and decomposes fast.
The carcass does not go stiff (no rigor mortis), so the legs stay floppy hours after death.
Bloody diarrhoea in some cases before death.

lookalikes.name: Blackquarter (blackleg)
lookalikes.howToTell: Blackquarter mostly kills well-fed young cattle between about 6 months and 2 years. It causes a hot, then cold, swollen leg or shoulder muscle that crackles like paper when pressed because of gas under the skin, and the animal is usually lame first. Anthrax affects any age, has no crackling muscle swelling and causes dark unclotted blood from body openings. Only a vet test can confirm which one it is, so treat every sudden death as possible anthrax until a vet rules it out.

lookalikes.name: Lightning strike
lookalikes.howToTell: Death from lightning usually happens during or just after a storm, often under a tree or near a wire fence, sometimes with several animals together. There may be singe or burn marks on the skin and burnt grass nearby. The carcass stiffens normally and blood clots. Anthrax deaths are not linked to storms and show unclotted blood and no stiffening.

lookalikes.name: Acute poisoning (plants, nitrate, cyanide or pesticides)
lookalikes.howToTell: Poisoning often follows a change of feed, access to wilted sorghum, young sudan grass, certain toxic plants, fertiliser or a recently sprayed area, and several animals may be affected at once. Signs like drooling, frothing, muscle twitching or bright red or chocolate-brown blood point towards poisoning. Blood still clots and the carcass stiffens normally. A vet blood smear is needed to exclude anthrax.

lookalikes.name: Haemorrhagic septicaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial disease, more common in buffalo and cattle in wet seasons, causes high fever, a large hot swelling of the throat and lower neck and noisy, difficult breathing, usually over hours to a day or two. It does not normally cause dark unclotted blood from all body openings with failure of the carcass to stiffen. Laboratory tests by the vet separate the two.

detail.diagnosis: A vet suspects anthrax from the history of sudden death, the dark unclotted blood, rapid bloating and lack of stiffening. The carcass must NOT be opened for a post-mortem. Instead, the vet or animal health officer, wearing gloves and protective clothing, takes a small blood sample from a vein in the ear or tail, or cuts off the tip of the ear, and seals the wound and sample safely. A thin blood smear is stained (commonly with polychrome methylene blue) and looked at under a microscope for the typical square-ended rods with a pink capsule. Samples may also be sent to a regional veterinary laboratory for culture or PCR, a test that detects the germ's genetic material. The farmer can help by keeping the carcass untouched and guarded, writing down when the animal was last seen healthy, what signs were seen, how many animals are sick or dead, where the herd has grazed and watered recently, and the vaccination history of the herd.
firstSteps: Do not open, cut, skin, butcher or move the carcass, and do not let anyone take meat, hides or horns from it, even if neighbours ask.
Call the County Veterinary Officer or your nearest government vet immediately; anthrax is notifiable by law and they will guide you and test the carcass.
Keep people, children, dogs and other animals away by fencing off or guarding the carcass, and cover it with branches, iron sheets or a tarpaulin to keep off vultures, dogs and flies.
Move the rest of the herd away from the area where the animal died and stop grazing and watering there until the vet says otherwise.
Stop all movement of animals, milk, meat and hides into or out of the farm until the vet gives advice.
Do not use or sell milk from sick animals or animals that died, and discard it safely as the vet directs.
Check the rest of the herd often for fever, dullness or swellings, keep any sick animal separate with shade and water, and tell the vet straight away rather than giving any drugs yourself.

Anyone who touched the carcass, blood or milk should wash thoroughly with soap and water, avoid touching their face, and watch for skin sores or illness, going to a health facility and saying they had contact with a possible anthrax case.
detail.vetTreatment: Most cattle with anthrax are found dead, so treatment is often not possible.
