If an animal is found early, while it still has fever and before it collapses, a vet may treat it with antibiotics that anthrax bacteria are usually sensitive to, such as penicillin or oxytetracycline. Even with prompt treatment, many animals still die because the toxins have already done damage. The vet will usually vaccinate the healthy animals in the herd and may advise on giving antibiotics to in-contact animals; because the anthrax vaccine contains live spores, antibiotics given around the same time can stop the vaccine from working, so only the vet should plan this. All treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet. Milk and meat from treated animals must not be used until the drug withdrawal period on the label or set by the vet has passed, and milk and meat from sick animals must never enter the food chain. Antibiotics should be used only as directed to avoid antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. The vet will also arrange safe carcass disposal, usually by burning on site or deep burial covered with soil and disinfectant as the authorities direct, and disinfection of the place where the animal died. Expect quarantine of your farm and sometimes the surrounding area, with restrictions on moving animals and selling milk or meat, usually until a set period after the last case and after vaccination.
prevention: Vaccinate cattle against anthrax every year in areas where it has occurred, ideally before the high-risk season; in Kenya a combined blackquarter and anthrax vaccine is available through agrovets and vet offices, and your vet will advise on timing.
Join county or community vaccination campaigns, as vaccinating whole neighbourhoods protects shared grazing and water points better than single farms.
Never open, skin, butcher or eat cattle that die suddenly; report them and let the vet arrange proper disposal by burning or deep burial.
Avoid grazing cattle on known anthrax sites, old burial places and low-lying flood areas, especially after heavy rains that follow drought.
Provide supplementary feed or hay in the dry season so cattle do not graze too close to the soil and swallow spores.
Buy bone meal and animal-based feeds only from reliable suppliers who process them properly, and avoid feeding carcass products to livestock.
Mark and fence off places where anthrax carcasses were disposed of, and do not dig, plough or build on them.
Control dogs and scavengers around the farm, and quarantine and check newly bought animals and confirm their vaccination history before mixing them with your herd.
detail.impact: Anthrax can kill several animals in a herd within days, and each dairy cow or ox lost is a big blow to a smallholder's savings, milk income and ploughing power. Farms with confirmed cases face quarantine, so milk and animal sales stop for a time, which hurts families who depend on daily milk money. Abortions and milk drop in survivors add to the loss. There are also costs for vaccination, disposal and disinfection. When people eat meat from anthrax carcasses, human illness and deaths can follow, bringing medical costs, lost work and great distress to the community. Because spores stay in soil for years, land can remain a risk long after the outbreak, making annual vaccination a lasting expense that is still far cheaper than the losses.
detail.humanHealth: Anthrax is a zoonosis, meaning it spreads from animals to people, and it can be deadly. People usually get it by handling, skinning or butchering infected carcasses, touching hides, hair or blood, or eating meat from animals that died suddenly. The most common form is skin anthrax: a painless itchy bump that becomes a sore with a black centre, often on the hands, arms or face, sometimes with swelling. Eating infected meat can cause gut anthrax with fever, vomiting, belly pain and bloody diarrhoea, which is often fatal. Breathing in spores is rare but very dangerous. Cooking does not make anthrax meat safe, and it must never be eaten, sold or given away. Never handle a suspected carcass with bare hands; if you must go near, wear gloves, boots and covering clothes, then wash well with soap and water. Anyone with contact who develops a sore, fever or stomach illness should go to a health facility quickly and mention contact with a possible anthrax animal, as human anthrax can be treated with antibiotics when caught early.
detail.outlook: The outlook for an individual animal is very poor. Most die before any signs are noticed, and even animals treated early often do not survive. The outlook for the herd is much better if the death is reported quickly, the carcass is not opened, the rest of the herd is moved off contaminated ground and vaccinated, and the vet's quarantine advice is followed. Vaccination usually stops new cases once immunity develops, though a few animals may still die in the days after vaccination while protection builds. Farms that vaccinate every year in risk areas rarely see repeat outbreaks, while farms where carcasses were opened may face cases for many years.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell the meat if I cook it well?
faqs.a: No. Meat from an animal that died suddenly or is suspected of anthrax must never be eaten, sold or given away, however well it is cooked. Handling and cutting the meat can infect your skin, and eating it can cause gut anthrax, which often kills. In Kenya, people have died after sharing meat from cattle that died this way. Report the death and let the vet dispose of the carcass.

faqs.q: Why must the carcass not be opened?
faqs.a: Inside a closed carcass, the anthrax bacteria are mostly killed as the body decays. When the carcass is opened or the blood spills, the bacteria meet air and turn into spores that can live in the soil for decades and infect animals grazing there in future. Opening the carcass also exposes you directly to the germ. Leaving it closed protects your family, your neighbours and your land.

faqs.q: Do I have to report anthrax, and what happens after I report it?
faqs.a: Yes. Anthrax is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so the law requires you to report suspected cases to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. The vet will test the carcass, arrange safe disposal, and usually vaccinate your herd and nearby herds. Your farm may be placed under quarantine, meaning you cannot move animals in or out or sell milk, meat or hides until the vets lift the restriction. Public health officers may also check on people who had contact.

faqs.q: How often should I vaccinate my cattle against anthrax?
faqs.a: In areas where anthrax has occurred, cattle are usually vaccinated once a year, preferably before the risky season such as the onset of the rains. Many farmers use the combined blackquarter and anthrax vaccine. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer about the right timing for your area, and keep a record of every vaccination. Do not give antibiotics around vaccination time unless the vet advises, because they can stop the live vaccine working.

faqs.q: Can a supplement or vitamin help my cattle against anthrax?
faqs.a: No supplement or vitamin can prevent or treat anthrax. Good nutrition keeps animals generally strong, but it does not protect them from this germ. The only reliable protection is yearly vaccination, avoiding contaminated ground and proper carcass disposal. If you suspect anthrax, the answer is to call the vet and lock down the carcass, not to buy remedies.

faqs.q: Is it safe to graze where an animal died of anthrax?
faqs.a: Treat that spot as dangerous for many years. Fence it off or mark it, and do not graze, dig or plough there. Keep vaccinating your herd every year, because spores can be brought to the surface by rain, flooding or digging. Your vet can advise on how long to keep animals off the wider area after an outbreak.

anthrax.imagePrompt: A dull, sick zebu cow standing alone on a dry, short-grassed Kenyan pasture with head lowered, ears drooping and a soft swelling under the lower neck and brisket, the rest of the herd far in the background, a rope barrier in the foreground, no people.
anthrax.seoDescription: Anthrax in cattle: sudden death, dark unclotted blood from nose and anus. Do not open the carcass. Signs, human risk, reporting and vaccination in Kenya.

card.headline: Crackling swollen leg in young cattle
card.look: A well-grown young animal suddenly goes lame, with a hot, painful swelling on the thigh, shoulder or neck that crackles like dry paper when pressed. The swelling soon turns cold and numb, and the animal is often dull, feverish or already dead.
card.action: Call your vet immediately, separate the sick animal, and do not cut open any animal that dies suddenly until anthrax has been ruled out.

detail.summary: Blackleg is a fast, usually fatal bacterial disease of young cattle. Bacteria that sleep quietly in the animal's muscles suddenly wake up, release poisons and destroy a large block of muscle, often killing the animal within one to two days. It tends to strike the best-fed, fastest-growing young stock on the farm. The good news is that it is almost completely preventable with a cheap, widely available vaccine.
detail.cause: Blackleg is caused by Clostridium chauvoei, a bacterium that forms spores. A spore is a tough, resting form of the germ that can survive in soil for many years, even through dry seasons. Cattle swallow spores while grazing or eating contaminated feed. The spores pass from the gut into the bloodstream and settle in the muscles, where they lie dormant (inactive) without causing any harm, sometimes for months. When something reduces the oxygen in a part of the muscle, for example a bruise from rough handling, a fall, fighting, crowding in a truck or crush, or heavy exercise, the spores 'wake up' in that low-oxygen pocket. They multiply quickly and produce powerful toxins (poisons). These toxins kill the muscle tissue, produce gas bubbles inside it, and leak into the blood, causing fever, shock and heart failure. The gas is what makes the swelling crackle under your hand, and the dying muscle turns dark red to black, which gives the disease its name.
spread: Cattle pick up spores by eating grass, soil or feed contaminated with them; the disease is not passed directly from one live animal to another by contact or breathing.
Carcasses of animals that died of blackleg release huge numbers of spores into the soil if they are opened, eaten by dogs or hyenas, or left to rot, contaminating that ground for many years.
Soil disturbance brings buried spores to the surface, so outbreaks often follow ploughing, digging, road works, flooding or erosion during the long and short rains.
Grazing short, overgrazed pasture close to the soil, especially early in the rains when new grass is short, increases the amount of soil and spores swallowed.

Bruising and muscle injury trigger disease in animals already carrying dormant spores; handling in crushes, loading onto lorries, long trekking, fighting and slipping on wet ground are common triggers.
Occasionally infection enters through wounds such as those from castration, dehorning, ear-tagging or injections given with dirty needles, which is more typical in sheep and goats.
detail.atRisk: Young cattle between about 6 months and 2 years old are most at risk, although cases occasionally occur in calves as young as a few months and in older animals. Strangely, it is the healthiest, best-fed and fastest-growing animals, such as well-managed dairy heifers, feedlot steers and good-condition pastoral weaners, that are hit hardest. Animals that have never been vaccinated, or whose booster is overdue, are the main victims. Risk is higher on farms or grazing areas with a history of blackleg, on land where carcasses were previously opened or buried shallowly, and during and after the rains when soil is disturbed. All farming systems are affected: zero-grazing units buying in fodder or soil-contaminated feed, mixed smallholdings and large pastoral herds alike. Sheep and goats can also get blackleg, usually through wounds.

early: Sudden, severe lameness in one leg in an animal that was healthy the day before; it may refuse to walk or stand stiffly.
A swelling over a heavy muscle, usually the hindquarter (thigh or rump), shoulder, neck, chest or loin, though sometimes in the tongue, throat or heart muscle.
At first the swelling is hot and very painful; the animal flinches when it is touched.
Pressing the swelling gives a crackling, crunchy feeling and sound, like pressing on bubble wrap or dry paper, caused by gas under the skin.
High fever, dullness, loss of appetite, stopping chewing the cud, and fast breathing.
The animal separates itself from the herd and may lie down and be reluctant to rise.
advanced: The swelling spreads and becomes cold and painless as the muscle and nerves die, while the rest of the animal gets worse.
The skin over the swelling darkens, becomes dry, tight and may crack, sometimes oozing a dark, frothy fluid.
Body temperature falls to normal or below as the animal goes into shock, which is a very bad sign rather than improvement.
Trembling, weakness, collapse, lying on its side, and paddling of the legs.
Death usually follows within 12 to 48 hours of the first signs, and many animals are simply found dead in the morning with no warning.
A dead animal often lies with the affected leg stuck out stiffly, the carcass swells quickly, and cut muscle (only if a vet has ruled out anthrax) is dark, dry, spongy and smells like rancid butter.

lookalikes.name: Anthrax
lookalikes.howToTell: Anthrax also causes sudden death, but dead animals often have dark, tarry blood that does not clot oozing from the nose, mouth or anus, the carcass may not stiffen normally, and there is usually no crackling swelling in a leg muscle. Anthrax can kill people and is notifiable in Kenya, so never open, skin or eat any animal that died suddenly until a vet has checked it, often with a simple blood smear test.

lookalikes.name: Malignant oedema (gas gangrene)
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by related clostridial bacteria entering through a wound, it can affect cattle of any age and usually starts near a recent wound such as castration, calving injury or a dirty injection site. The swelling is more soft and jelly-like with less crackling gas, while blackleg typically has no visible wound. Both are deadly and both are prevented by multi-clostridial vaccines, so a vet should confirm which it is.

lookalikes.name: Bloat
lookalikes.howToTell: A bloated animal swells on the left side of the belly, not on a leg or shoulder, and is often seen after eating lush legumes or wet grass. There is no crackling lump in the muscle, and the swelling is a drum-tight belly rather than a localised limb swelling.

lookalikes.name: Injury, fracture or foot problem
lookalikes.howToTell: A kicked, slipped or fractured leg or foot rot also causes sudden lameness, but the animal usually stays alert and keeps eating, has little or no fever, and any swelling does not crackle or turn cold and numb. Foot rot swelling is between the claws and smells foul, not high up in the big muscles.

detail.diagnosis: A vet suspects blackleg from the history (a young, well-grown, unvaccinated animal dying suddenly, often in the rains) together with the crackling swelling in a heavy muscle. Because anthrax can look similar and is dangerous to people, the vet will usually first rule it out, often by taking a blood sample from an ear or tail vein for a smear before any carcass is opened. If anthrax is excluded, a post-mortem (examination after death) shows dark red to black, dry, spongy muscle full of gas bubbles, with a sweet, rancid-butter smell. To confirm, the vet can send muscle samples to a veterinary laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional lab, for tests including a fluorescent antibody test, bacterial culture or PCR (a test that detects the germ's genetic material). Samples should be taken soon after death because other clostridia invade carcasses quickly and can confuse results. You can help by noting when the animal was last seen healthy, its age, vaccination history and dates, any recent handling, transport, injuries, soil disturbance or feed changes, and how many other animals are sick or have died.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer straight away; blackleg moves so fast that hours matter, and treatment only has a chance very early.
Move the sick animal gently to a quiet, shaded, separate pen close by, without chasing, beating or forcing it to walk far, because extra muscle stress makes things worse.
Offer clean drinking water and fresh feed within reach, and keep the animal comfortable and calm while you wait for the vet.
Do not cut, slash, open or skin the swelling or any animal that has died suddenly; this can spread spores into your soil for years and, if it turns out to be anthrax, put your family at serious risk.

Check the rest of the herd, especially other young stock in the same age group, by watching them walk and feeling their hindquarters, shoulders and neck for heat, swelling or crackling, and report any suspects to the vet.
If an animal dies, cover the carcass, keep dogs, children and scavengers away, and do not eat, sell or give away the meat or hide; follow the vet's guidance on burning or deep burial with lime.
Wear gloves and wash your hands and boots well after touching sick or dead animals, and disinfect tools and the area where the animal lay.
Write down dates, times, the animal's age, signs seen and vaccination records so the vet can act quickly and plan vaccination of the rest of the herd.
detail.vetTreatment: Blackleg is a true emergency, and even with fast treatment many animals die because the toxins have already done major damage by the time signs appear. If the animal is caught very early, a vet may give high doses of a penicillin-type antibiotic, sometimes injected both into the muscle and directly around the affected area, along with anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving drugs and fluids to fight shock. In some cases the vet may surgically open the affected muscle to let air in, because these bacteria cannot thrive in oxygen; this must only be done by a vet after anthrax is ruled out, with proper disposal of contaminated material. Only a vet can decide whether treatment is worth attempting and which drugs and doses to use. Antibiotics should never be used 'just in case' from the agrovet without a vet's advice, because misuse fuels antimicrobial resistance (germs that no longer respond to medicines) and wastes money on an animal that may not survive. During an outbreak, the vet will usually advise vaccinating all at-risk stock at once and may, in some situations, recommend antibiotic cover for in-contact animals until the vaccine takes effect, which typically needs one to two weeks. Any treated animal will have a milk and meat withdrawal period (the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be sold or eaten); follow the vet's instructions and the drug label strictly. Survivors may stay lame, lose muscle on the affected leg, or develop skin sloughing over the damaged area, and need good nursing for weeks.
prevention: Vaccinate: this is by far the most important step. Multi-clostridial vaccines and combined blackleg-and-anthrax vaccines, including ones produced locally by KEVEVAPI, are sold through agrovets and vets; follow the label for the first doses and boosters.

Start vaccinating calves at the age recommended on the vaccine label (often from around 3 to 6 months), give the booster if required, and then re-vaccinate all young stock every year, ideally a few weeks before the long rains.
Vaccinate any newly bought animals of risky age and keep a written record of every vaccination date, the vaccine name and batch, so you know who is protected.

Store vaccines in a fridge or cool box (not frozen and not in sunlight), use clean, sterile needles, and vaccinate under the skin or as the label says, because poor handling can make vaccines useless and dirty needles can cause wound infections.

Never open or skin carcasses of animals that die suddenly; burn them or bury them deeply (at least about 2 metres) covered with quicklime, away from water sources and grazing, as your vet or County Veterinary Officer advises.
Avoid grazing young stock on land where blackleg carcasses were buried or where soil has recently been disturbed by ploughing, digging or flooding, especially if they are not vaccinated.
Handle young cattle gently: use good crushes, avoid overcrowding in pens and lorries, stop dogs chasing stock and avoid long hard treks, to reduce the bruising that triggers disease.
Keep wounds from castration, dehorning and tagging clean, and use clean equipment, since related clostridial diseases enter through wounds.
detail.impact: Blackleg hits the animals a Kenyan farmer can least afford to lose: well-grown heifers about to become the next milking cows, and steers close to sale weight. One death can wipe out a year or more of feeding, breeding and care, and several deaths in one season can set a smallholder or pastoral family back badly. Because animals often die without warning, there is little chance to sell them, and carcasses must be destroyed rather than eaten or sold, so there is no salvage value. Treatment attempts add vet costs with a low chance of success, and survivors may stay lame and grow poorly. Contaminated grazing stays risky for years, forcing either strict yearly vaccination or the abandonment of certain fields. Compared with these losses, the cost of vaccinating young stock every year is very small.
detail.humanHealth: Blackleg itself is not considered a significant risk to people; human infection with Clostridium chauvoei is extremely rare. The real danger to people comes from confusing it with anthrax, which looks similar in cattle that die suddenly and can cause serious, sometimes fatal illness in people who handle, skin or eat the carcass. For this reason, never open, skin or eat any animal that died suddenly until a vet has ruled out anthrax, keep children and dogs away, wear gloves when handling sick or dead animals and wash well afterwards. Meat from any animal that died of disease should never be eaten or sold. If an animal is treated with antibiotics and survives, observe the milk and meat withdrawal periods set by the vet and the drug label so residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook for an animal showing signs of blackleg is poor; most affected cattle die, often before anyone notices they are sick. A few animals treated very early by a vet, while the swelling is still hot and the animal is still standing and feverish, may survive, but they can be left with lasting lameness, muscle loss or skin damage. Once the swelling has gone cold and the temperature has dropped, recovery is unlikely. For the herd, the outlook is very good if all at-risk animals are vaccinated promptly and every year, carcasses are disposed of properly and young stock are handled gently; well-vaccinated herds rarely see cases.

faqs.q: Can we eat the meat of a cow that died of blackleg?
faqs.a: No. Meat from an animal that died of any disease should never be eaten or sold. The carcass is full of bacteria and toxins, and cutting it spreads spores into your soil, making future outbreaks more likely. Most importantly, sudden death in cattle can also be anthrax, which can kill people, and you cannot tell them apart safely by eye. Call the vet, keep the carcass closed and covered, and burn or deeply bury it with lime as advised.

faqs.q: Why does blackleg kill my best, fattest calves and not the thin ones?
faqs.a: Nobody fully understands why, but it is a well-known pattern. Fast-growing, well-fed young cattle seem to provide the right conditions in their muscles for the dormant spores to wake up and multiply, and their active, heavy muscles bruise more easily. It does not mean good feeding is wrong. It means well-fed young stock must always be vaccinated.

faqs.q: Can blackleg spread from my sick heifer to the rest of the herd or my neighbour's cows?
faqs.a: It does not spread directly from one live animal to another by touching or breathing. However, animals in the same herd graze the same contaminated ground, so if one gets it, others of the same age are at high risk too. Carcasses that are opened or scavenged put large numbers of spores into the soil, which can then affect your animals and your neighbours' animals for years. That is why proper carcass disposal and vaccinating the whole at-risk group matter.

faqs.q: I have had a blackleg death. Is it too late to vaccinate the others?
faqs.a: It is not too late, and you should vaccinate all young stock straight away on your vet's advice. The vaccine needs around one to two weeks to build protection, so a few more cases can still happen during that time, and your vet may recommend extra measures for in-contact animals. After that, keep up yearly boosters, ideally before the long rains, because the spores will stay in your soil.

faqs.q: Does the blackleg vaccine also protect against anthrax and other diseases?
faqs.a: It depends on which vaccine you buy. A blackleg-only vaccine protects against blackleg. Combined blackleg-and-anthrax vaccines protect against both. Multi-clostridial vaccines protect against blackleg plus related diseases such as malignant oedema and enterotoxaemia. Read the label or ask your vet or agrovet which diseases are covered, and choose one suited to the risks in your area.

faqs.q: Can an animal that survives blackleg go back to normal?
faqs.a: Some survivors recover well enough to be useful, but many are left with a damaged, wasted muscle, a lasting limp or skin that peels over the old swelling. They may grow more slowly or be less productive. Good nursing, soft bedding, shade, easy access to water and good feed help, and your vet will advise whether the animal is likely to have a productive future.

blackleg.imagePrompt: A young brown-and-white Kenyan heifer standing in a grassy smallholder paddock, holding one hind leg off the ground, with a clearly visible swollen, tight-skinned bulge over the upper thigh and rump muscle, dull expression, soft daylight, realistic photograph.
blackleg.seoDescription: Blackleg in cattle: spot the crackling swollen leg and sudden lameness in young stock, what to do before the vet arrives, and how vaccination prevents it.

card.headline: Many cows aborting after heavy rains
card.look: After floods or long heavy rains, several pregnant cows in the herd and the neighbourhood abort within days or weeks, and young calves become weak, feverish and die quickly. Adult cattle may have fever, a runny nose, bloody or smelly diarrhoea and a sudden drop in milk.
card.action: Do not touch aborted calves or blood with bare hands, do not slaughter sick animals, and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately, because this is a notifiable disease that also infects people.

detail.summary: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is a viral disease spread mainly by mosquitoes. It strikes cattle, sheep, goats and camels in waves after unusually heavy rains and flooding. It causes storms of abortions in pregnant animals, kills many young calves, and seriously damages the liver. It also infects people, sometimes fatally, so it is a notifiable disease in Kenya and must be reported to the veterinary authorities at once.
detail.cause: RVF is caused by the Rift Valley fever virus, a Phlebovirus. Some floodwater mosquitoes, mainly Aedes species, lay eggs that already carry the virus in the mud of shallow depressions, dams and low-lying grassland. These eggs can stay alive in dry soil for years. When heavy rains or floods fill these hollows, the eggs hatch and the infected mosquitoes bite livestock. Other mosquitoes, such as Culex, then feed on infected animals and spread the virus further, so cases build up very quickly. Inside the animal, the virus multiplies in the blood and attacks the liver, destroying liver cells (this is called hepatitis, meaning liver inflammation). This liver damage causes weakness, jaundice (yellow colour of the gums and eyes) and bleeding problems. The virus also crosses into the unborn calf, which is why pregnant cows abort at any stage of pregnancy. Young calves have weak defences and the virus overwhelms them fast, which is why deaths are highest in calves.
spread: Bites from infected mosquitoes, mainly Aedes and Culex species, are the main way cattle get infected.
Outbreaks follow unusually heavy or prolonged rainfall and flooding, often linked with El Niño years, when large numbers of infected mosquito eggs hatch at once.
Standing water in dams, swamps, irrigation channels, flooded grazing land and around homesteads allows mosquito numbers to explode.
Moving infected animals to markets, new grazing areas or other counties can carry the virus into new areas where mosquitoes then spread it.
Biting flies and contaminated needles may carry the virus mechanically between animals, especially when one needle is used for many animals during an outbreak.
People catch it mainly through contact with blood, body fluids, meat, organs and aborted calves of infected animals, and also from mosquito bites.
detail.atRisk: All cattle can be infected, but the worst losses are in young calves, which become very sick and many die, and in pregnant cows, which abort. Adult non-pregnant cattle often show milder illness, and some show no signs at all, yet they still carry the virus in their blood for a few days and can feed mosquitoes. Exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle may suffer more than local Zebu, though all breeds are susceptible. In Kenya, outbreaks have hit hardest in the North Eastern and Coast regions, the Rift Valley lowlands and around irrigation schemes, including areas such as Garissa, Tana River, Wajir, Isiolo, Baringo and parts of the coast, but any low-lying, flood-prone area can be affected. Risk is highest during and in the weeks after very heavy long or short rains. Pastoral herds that gather around water points, and zero-grazing units near swamps, dams or irrigated fields, are both exposed. Sheep and goats on the same farm are usually affected even more severely than cattle, and a sudden wave of abortions in shoats is often an early warning for cattle.

early: High fever, with the animal feeling hot to the touch, standing dull and isolated from the herd.
Loss of appetite and refusal to feed or chew cud.
A sudden and sharp drop in milk yield in milking cows.
Clear or slightly thick discharge from the nose and drooling of saliva.
Weakness and reluctance to walk, sometimes with a stiff or wobbly gait.
Young calves become weak, stop suckling, have fever and may die within a day or two of first showing signs.
Pregnant cows abort without warning, often several in the herd or village around the same time.
advanced: Foul-smelling diarrhoea that may contain blood.
Yellow colour (jaundice) of the gums, the whites of the eyes and the inside of the vulva, caused by liver damage.
Bloody nasal discharge or small bleeding spots on the gums and inside the eyelids.
Severe weakness and lying down, unable to rise.
Waves of abortions across the herd and neighbouring herds, with aborted calves often looking swollen or partly decomposed.
Sudden death of calves, sometimes with few signs seen beforehand.
Some adult cattle also die, though adult deaths are usually much fewer than calf deaths.

lookalikes.name: Brucellosis (contagious abortion)
lookalikes.howToTell: Brucellosis causes abortions mostly in the last three months of pregnancy and spreads slowly through a herd over months. It does not usually cause fever outbreaks, mass calf deaths or bloody diarrhoea, and it is not tied to floods. RVF comes as a sudden wave after heavy rains, affects shoats and neighbouring herds at the same time, and kills young calves.

lookalikes.name: Leptospirosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Leptospirosis can also cause abortion, fever and jaundice, and red or dark urine, especially after wet weather. It usually affects a few animals rather than causing a sudden storm across many farms, and calf deaths are not as widespread. Only lab tests can separate them reliably, so report and let the vet test.

lookalikes.name: Bovine viral diarrhoea (BVD)
lookalikes.howToTell: BVD causes diarrhoea, mouth ulcers, abortion and weak calves, but it builds up more slowly and is not linked to mosquito seasons. Mouth sores and erosions are more typical of BVD, while jaundice and sudden wide-area abortions after floods point to RVF.

lookalikes.name: East Coast fever and gall sickness (anaplasmosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: These tick-borne diseases cause fever and weakness. East Coast fever shows swollen lymph nodes (glands) below the ear and in front of the shoulder, with breathing difficulty. Gall sickness shows pale or yellow gums and constipation in adult cattle. Neither causes waves of abortions and calf deaths across many farms right after flooding.

detail.diagnosis: Because RVF is notifiable and dangerous to people, diagnosis is done by veterinary authorities, not by the farmer. The vet will look at the pattern first: heavy rains or floods, many abortions, calf deaths and sick sheep or goats in the area, sometimes with people falling ill with fever. They will examine sick animals for fever, jaundice and diarrhoea. To confirm, the vet takes blood samples from sick and in-contact animals and sends them to a government laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional lab. Tests include PCR, which detects the virus itself, and ELISA, which detects antibodies (the animal's defence proteins), including recent infection. Tissue samples, especially liver, from dead calves or aborted foetuses may also be collected under strict safety precautions. Post-mortem examinations should only be done by trained staff wearing protective clothing, because opening carcasses is a major way people get infected. The farmer can help by keeping a written record of which animals aborted or died and when, which animals are sick, any sheep or goats affected, recent rains and flooding, recent animal movements and purchases, and the vaccination history of the herd. Keep dead animals and aborted calves covered and untouched until the vet advises.
firstSteps: Call your County Veterinary Officer or the nearest government vet immediately and report the abortions, calf deaths and sick animals; it is the law, and it helps protect your neighbours and your family.
Do not touch aborted calves, afterbirths, blood or dead animals with bare hands; if you must move them, use thick gloves or plastic bags over your hands, then wash well with soap and water.
Do not slaughter sick or dying animals for meat, and do not sell or eat meat or drink raw milk from sick animals.
Separate sick and aborting animals from the rest of the herd in a shaded pen, and give them clean water and good fodder within easy reach.
Stop all movement of animals in or out of the farm, including to markets, until the vet advises, because moving animals spreads the disease.
Cover aborted foetuses and dead animals and keep dogs, children and other animals away until the vet tells you how they should be disposed of, usually by deep burial or burning.
Reduce mosquito bites for people and animals: sleep under treated mosquito nets, wear long sleeves in the evening, and drain small pools of standing water around the homestead where you can.
Do not inject any medicines yourself, and do not use one needle on many animals, as this can spread the virus; wait for the vet's instructions.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no drug that kills the Rift Valley fever virus in animals. Treatment is supportive, meaning it helps the animal's body cope while its own defences fight the virus. A vet may give fluids or oral rehydration to sick animals, anti-inflammatory and fever-reducing drugs, and good nursing in shade with water and soft feed. Antibiotics do not cure RVF because it is a virus; a vet may sometimes prescribe an antibiotic only if there is a clear secondary bacterial infection, and unnecessary antibiotic use adds to antimicrobial resistance, which makes future infections harder to treat in both animals and people. Any drug used must be prescribed by a vet, and the milk and meat withdrawal periods on the label must be followed strictly, meaning milk and meat cannot be used for food until that time has passed. During an official outbreak, the Directorate of Veterinary Services will usually impose quarantine and movement restrictions, ban slaughter of livestock in affected areas or allow it only under inspection, close livestock markets, and carry out vaccination of healthy animals in surrounding areas and mosquito control. Under quarantine, you may not move, sell or slaughter animals without a permit. These rules can feel hard, but they stop the disease spreading to new herds and protect people. Expect that some calves and pregnant cows will be lost even with good care, and that the vet will advise on safe disposal of carcasses and aborted material.
prevention: Vaccinate cattle, sheep, goats and camels before the rainy season, especially when the Kenya Meteorological Department or veterinary authorities warn of heavy El Niño rains; vaccines are produced locally by KEVEVAPI and are available through vets and agrovets.
Follow your vet's advice on which vaccine to use, because the common live vaccine can cause abortion or birth defects in pregnant animals, so timing and choice of animals matter.

Vaccinate well ahead of an outbreak, since vaccination during an active outbreak can spread the virus by needles and should only be done under official veterinary direction, using a new needle for each animal.
Reduce mosquito breeding by draining or filling small pools around homesteads and animal pens, clearing blocked drains, and covering water containers.
Keep animals away from swamps, flooded areas and dam edges, especially at dusk and night when mosquitoes bite most, and house zero-grazed cattle in pens away from standing water where possible.
Use insect repellents or approved pour-on and spray insecticides on animals during high-risk rains, as advised by your vet or agrovet, and follow label withdrawal periods.
Avoid buying or moving animals from areas with reported RVF, and listen to county announcements on quarantines and market closures.
Watch sheep and goats closely after heavy rains, because sudden abortions in shoats are often the first sign of RVF in an area; report early.
detail.impact: RVF can wipe out a whole year's income on a Kenyan farm. Pregnant cows abort, so there are no calves to raise or sell, and those cows may take months to get back in calf. Young calves die, which destroys the future dairy or beef herd. Milk yield crashes in sick cows, and milk from sick animals cannot be sold. During outbreaks, livestock markets close and movement and slaughter bans are imposed, so farmers cannot sell animals even when they need cash, and prices drop. Pastoral communities, who depend heavily on livestock for food and income, suffer most. Past outbreaks in Kenya, such as in 1997–98, 2006–07 and 2018, caused heavy livestock losses, human deaths and big disruption to the meat and livestock trade, including export bans. There are also costs for veterinary care, vaccination and lost labour when family members fall sick.
detail.humanHealth: Rift Valley fever is a zoonosis, meaning it passes from animals to people. People become infected mainly by handling blood, body fluids, meat and organs of infected animals, especially during slaughter, skinning, butchering, helping with births and abortions, and handling aborted calves. Herders, butchers, farmers, vets and agrovet staff are most at risk. People can also be infected by mosquito bites, and drinking raw milk from infected animals may be a risk. Most infected people get a flu-like illness with fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, which lasts a few days. A smaller number develop serious illness, including eye damage that can cause loss of sight, brain inflammation, or bleeding fever with jaundice, which can be fatal. Protect yourself: never slaughter or eat sick or dead animals; wear gloves and, if possible, eye protection when handling sick animals, births, abortions or carcasses; wash hands with soap after any contact; boil all milk and cook meat thoroughly; and sleep under treated mosquito nets. RVF does not normally spread from person to person. Anyone who develops fever, headache or eye problems after contact with sick animals during an outbreak should go to a health facility promptly and tell the health worker about the animal contact.
detail.outlook: For adult non-pregnant cattle, the outlook is often fair: many recover with good nursing, though they may lose condition and milk for some time. For pregnant cows, abortion is common and cannot be prevented once the cow is infected, but many go on to breed again after recovery. For young calves, the outlook is poor, and many die quickly despite care. Animals that recover usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity. Recovery depends on the animal's age, pregnancy status, general condition, how early it receives supportive care, and whether liver damage is severe. The best protection for the herd is vaccination before the high-risk rains, not treatment after infection.

faqs.q: Can I sell or eat meat from a cow that is sick with Rift Valley fever?
faqs.a: No. Slaughtering and handling sick animals is one of the main ways people catch RVF, and it can kill. During outbreaks the government usually bans slaughter in affected areas. Report sick animals to the vet and follow their advice on safe disposal of any that die.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from my cows during an outbreak?
faqs.a: Never drink or sell milk from sick cows. Milk from healthy-looking cows in an outbreak area should always be boiled thoroughly before drinking. If your cow has been treated by a vet, also respect the milk withdrawal period given for the drug used.

faqs.q: When should I vaccinate my cattle against Rift Valley fever?
faqs.a: The best time is several weeks before an expected period of heavy rains, especially when forecasts warn of El Niño. Talk to your vet or County Veterinary Officer, because the common live vaccine should not be given to pregnant animals and vaccination during an outbreak should only happen under official direction.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics cure Rift Valley fever?
faqs.a: No. RVF is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may use them only if there is a secondary bacterial infection. Using antibiotics without need wastes money and adds to antimicrobial resistance. Supportive care, quarantine and prevention are what matter.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report it, and what happens after I report?
faqs.a: RVF is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so the law requires you to report suspected cases to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. After reporting, vets will visit, take samples, and may put the area under quarantine, close markets, restrict animal movement and slaughter, and organise vaccination and mosquito control. This protects your neighbours, your herd and your family.

faqs.q: My goats are aborting after the rains. Should I worry about my cattle?
faqs.a: Yes. Sheep and goats often show RVF signs first and most severely. A sudden wave of abortions or kid deaths in shoats after heavy rains is a warning that the virus may be in your area. Report it to the vet right away and protect your cattle and family from mosquitoes.

rift-valley-fever.imagePrompt: A weak young Friesian-cross calf lying listlessly on damp grass with a runny nose and dull eyes, beside a flooded pasture with standing water under a grey rainy sky in rural Kenya.
rift-valley-fever.seoDescription: Rift Valley fever in cattle: spot abortion storms and calf deaths after floods, protect your family, report to the vet, and prevent it with vaccination.

card.headline: Cow aborts in late pregnancy
card.look: A cow or heifer loses her calf in the last three or four months of pregnancy, often with an afterbirth that will not come out. Some cattle in the herd may also have swollen knees, and bulls may have a swollen testicle.
card.action: Isolate the cow, do not touch the aborted calf or afterbirth with bare hands, stop drinking her raw milk, and call your vet to test the herd.

aka: Malta fever or undulant fever (when it infects people)
detail.summary: Brucellosis is a long-lasting bacterial infection of cattle that attacks the womb, udder and reproductive organs. Its best-known sign is abortion in late pregnancy, followed by retained afterbirth, weak calves and poor fertility. Many infected cows look completely healthy and keep shedding the germ in their milk and birth fluids for years. It matters twice over. It quietly reduces calves and milk on the farm, and it is one of the most important diseases people catch from cattle, mainly through raw milk and handling births.
detail.cause: Brucellosis in cattle is caused by a bacterium called Brucella abortus. Cattle can occasionally pick up the related Brucella melitensis from infected goats and sheep. Once the germ enters the body, usually through the mouth, it travels to the lymph nodes. These are the small glands that filter infection. From there it spreads through the blood. In a pregnant cow it is strongly drawn to the placenta, the afterbirth that feeds the unborn calf. There it multiplies in huge numbers and inflames the placenta, so the calf is starved of oxygen and food. The calf may die and be aborted, be born dead, or be born weak. The damaged afterbirth often sticks to the womb and is retained, which can lead to womb infection and later infertility. The bacteria also settle in the udder and its glands, so they pass into milk, often for the rest of the cow's life. In bulls, the germ attacks the testicles and the tubes beside them, causing swelling, pain and poor fertility. In both sexes it can infect joints and the fluid sacs over the knees and hocks, causing firm swellings called hygromas. The bacteria hide inside the animal's own cells. This is why the body struggles to clear them and why the infection is usually lifelong.
spread: The biggest source is the aborted calf, the afterbirth and the fluids from an infected cow's womb, which contain enormous numbers of bacteria and contaminate grass, bedding, water and the ground.

Other cattle become infected when they sniff or lick an aborted calf, the afterbirth or a newborn calf, or eat grass and drink water soiled with birth fluids. Cattle are naturally curious about birth material, so this happens easily.
Infected cows can shed the germ in their milk, so calves fed raw milk from infected cows can become infected.
Some heifer calves born to infected mothers carry a hidden infection. They test negative when young and then abort during their own first pregnancy.
Buying in cattle of unknown health status, especially pregnant heifers or cows from markets, is a common way the disease enters a clean herd.
Shared grazing, watering points, dips and communal bulls, which are common in pastoral and mixed farming areas, let the disease pass between herds.

Infected bulls shed the germ in semen. Natural mating plays a smaller role, but semen from an infected bull used for artificial insemination (AI) is a serious risk, so use AI semen only from a trusted, tested source.
The bacteria can survive for weeks to months in cool, damp, shaded places such as wet bedding, manure and muddy ground, but sunlight and drying kill them faster.
detail.atRisk: Sexually mature cattle are most at risk, especially pregnant heifers and cows, and particularly in their first pregnancy after infection. Young calves can carry the germ but rarely show signs. Bulls can be infected and lose fertility. All breeds are susceptible, from zebu and Boran to Friesian and Ayrshire dairy cows. In Kenya and East Africa, the risk is highest in pastoral and agro-pastoral systems, where large herds mix at grazing and water and cattle are kept alongside goats, sheep and camels. Risk is also high in herds that often buy animals from livestock markets, in herds that share bulls, and in dairy units that bring in replacement heifers of unknown origin. Zero-grazing units are not safe either. Calving in crowded, dirty sheds spreads the germ quickly once one infected animal arrives. Spread is often greatest around the calving season, and wet conditions during the long and short rains help the germ survive longer in the environment.

early: Many infected cattle show no signs at all. They look healthy, eat well and milk normally while shedding the germ, so you cannot rule out brucellosis just by looking.
A pregnant cow or heifer aborts, usually from about the fifth month of pregnancy onwards and most often in the last three months, without having seemed sick beforehand.
The aborted calf may look fresh or slightly swollen, and the afterbirth may look thickened, leathery, yellowish or blotchy, sometimes with a brownish discharge.
The afterbirth is retained, meaning it is still hanging from the vulva more than about 12 to 24 hours after calving or abortion.
Some cows give birth at full term to a dead calf, or to a weak calf that cannot stand or suckle well and may die within days.
Several cows or heifers in the herd abort or produce weak calves within a few weeks or months of each other, especially first-calf heifers or newly bought animals.
advanced: After a retained afterbirth, the cow may develop a smelly, discoloured discharge from the vulva, a sign of infection in the womb.
Cows fail to come back on heat normally, need many services to get pregnant, and the calving interval becomes much longer than expected.
Milk yield drops, especially in cows that aborted or had a womb infection after calving.

Firm or soft, often painless swellings appear over the knees (front legs) and sometimes the hocks. These are fluid-filled sacs called hygromas and are commonly seen in African cattle with brucellosis.
Some animals become lame from swollen, stiff joints.
Bulls may develop a hot, painful, swollen testicle, usually on one side, which later shrinks and hardens. They also lose interest in mating or become infertile.
Over time the herd has fewer calves, more empty cows, and more animals culled for infertility, even though few animals ever look really ill.

lookalikes.name: Leptospirosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Leptospirosis can also cause late abortions and weak calves. It often comes with a sudden drop in milk, with thick, yellowish or blood-tinged milk from all quarters and a soft, floppy udder. Young calves may have red urine or yellow gums. Only blood tests or tests on the aborted calf can reliably separate the two, so your vet will usually test for both.

lookalikes.name: Trichomoniasis and vibriosis (venereal diseases)
lookalikes.howToTell: These are spread by bulls during natural mating. They mainly cause early embryo loss, so cows keep returning on heat, abortions happen early in pregnancy and are often missed, and fertility drops across the herd. Swollen knees and late abortion storms are not typical. They are rare in herds that use only AI.

lookalikes.name: Neosporosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Neospora is a parasite spread through dog faeces. It usually causes abortions in mid-pregnancy, around the fourth to sixth month. The same cow may abort again in later pregnancies, and it does not cause swollen knees or testicles. It is linked to dogs eating afterbirths and fouling feed. Laboratory tests on the fetus and blood are needed to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Rift Valley fever
lookalikes.howToTell: Rift Valley fever comes as sudden outbreaks after heavy rains and flooding with many mosquitoes. There are abortions in cattle, sheep, goats and camels at once, many deaths in young calves and lambs, and people falling ill with fever. It is notifiable and an emergency. Brucellosis, in contrast, spreads slowly and is not tied to mosquito seasons.

detail.diagnosis: You cannot confirm brucellosis by looking at a cow, because many abortions have other causes and many infected cows look healthy. Your vet will take blood samples from the aborted cow and usually from other breeding animals in the herd. A quick screening test called the Rose Bengal test is often done first, and positives are checked with more accurate laboratory tests such as ELISA or the complement fixation test. In dairy herds, milk can be screened with a milk ring test or a milk ELISA, sometimes on bulk tank milk to check the whole herd. The strongest proof comes from growing the bacteria in a laboratory from the aborted calf's stomach contents, the afterbirth, vaginal discharge or milk. This is done in specialised laboratories such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or regional veterinary investigation labs, because the germ is dangerous to lab staff. Your vet may also test for other causes of abortion at the same time. To help, do not throw away or bury the aborted calf and afterbirth before speaking to the vet. Wearing gloves, place them in two strong plastic bags, tie them, and keep them cool and shaded, away from dogs. Write down the cow's details, how many months pregnant she was, the dates of any other abortions, recent purchases, the bull or AI semen used, and any vaccinations given. Brucellosis is not on the list of diseases that must be reported in this guidance. However, your vet may still inform the County Veterinary Officer because it is a serious public health disease, and it is wise to cooperate with any herd testing.
firstSteps: Separate the cow that aborted from the rest of the herd straight away, especially from pregnant cows and heifers. Keep her in a pen or paddock you can clean, until your vet has tested her.
Protect yourself before touching anything. Wear rubber gloves, and ideally boots and a face mask. Never handle the aborted calf, afterbirth or discharges with bare hands, and keep cuts covered.

Collect the aborted calf and afterbirth carefully in double plastic bags for the vet. Once the vet no longer needs them, bury them deeply with lime or burn them, so that dogs, other animals and children cannot reach them.
Do not try to pull out a retained afterbirth yourself. This can damage the womb and expose you to large numbers of bacteria. Call the vet to examine and advise.

Stop drinking, selling or feeding raw milk from the affected cow, and boil all milk from the herd thoroughly until testing is done. Throw away her milk safely or boil it well before giving it to calves.
Clean and disinfect the place where the abortion happened. Remove soiled bedding and manure, spread lime or a disinfectant recommended by your agrovet or vet, and let sunlight reach the area.
Keep the cow comfortable with clean water, shade and good feed, and watch her for fever, smelly discharge or loss of appetite, which suggest a womb infection that needs the vet.
Stop buying, selling, lending or sharing animals or bulls until the herd has been tested, so you do not spread the disease or bring in more.

Call your vet or the County Veterinary Officer to arrange testing. If anyone in the household has recurring fevers, sweats or joint pains, tell them to see a doctor and mention contact with cattle and raw milk.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment of brucellosis in cattle is generally not recommended. The bacteria hide inside the animal's cells, so even long courses of antibiotics rarely clear the infection completely. Treated cows can look better but keep shedding the germ in milk and birth fluids, putting your family and the herd at risk. For this reason, mainstream veterinary guidance focuses on testing, removing infected animals and vaccinating, not treating. In practice, your vet will test the herd and identify positive animals. They will usually advise that positive cows and bulls be separated and culled for slaughter under veterinary guidance, or at least kept apart, never bred again, and their milk never consumed raw. The vet may treat problems that follow an abortion, such as a retained afterbirth or womb infection, to keep the cow alive and comfortable. This might include careful examination and antibiotics or womb treatments chosen by the vet. Any such drug must be prescribed by the vet. You must follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods on the label and the vet's advice, so that drug residues do not end up in milk sold to the dairy or in meat. Do not buy antibiotics from the agrovet to treat suspected brucellosis on your own. It will not cure the cow, wastes money, and adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines that people and animals need. The vet will also plan follow-up testing, usually repeated over several months, until the herd tests clean, and will advise on vaccinating young heifers.
prevention: Vaccinate heifer calves, usually between about three and eight months of age, with a brucellosis vaccine such as Strain 19 (S19), which is produced in Kenya, or RB51 where available. Vaccination is done by or under a vet, because these are live vaccines that can cause abortion if given to pregnant animals and can infect people through needle-stick accidents.

Buy replacement animals only from herds known to be tested and free of brucellosis. Ask for recent negative blood test results, and isolate and re-test new animals for about a month before they join your herd.
Use artificial insemination with semen from a reputable, tested source, or ensure any bull you use or share has tested negative for brucellosis.
Set up a clean calving area away from the main herd. Remove and safely dispose of every afterbirth and aborted calf promptly, wearing gloves, and keep dogs away from calving areas.
Treat every abortion as possible brucellosis. Isolate the cow, call the vet to test her, and do not let other cattle sniff or lick the material.
Test the breeding herd regularly, especially in dairy units, and remove positive animals according to your vet's advice, so the infection does not keep circulating.
Feed calves colostrum and milk from cows known to be negative, or boil or pasteurise milk before feeding it to calves.
Limit mixing with other herds at shared grazing, watering points and markets where possible, and keep goats and sheep tested too, since they can carry related Brucella species.
Keep housing clean and dry, remove wet bedding and manure regularly, and let sunlight into sheds, because drying and sunlight help kill the bacteria.
detail.impact: Brucellosis is a quiet thief on a Kenyan farm. Each abortion means a lost calf and often a cow that takes months longer to get back in calf, so the calving interval stretches and you feed a cow that is not producing. Milk drops in cows that abort or develop womb infections, and dairy income falls. Infertile cows and bulls have to be culled early, often at low prices, and replacements are costly and may bring in more disease if bought untested. In pastoral herds, repeated abortions reduce herd growth and the number of animals available to sell or use for bride price and savings. Testing, veterinary visits and culling all cost money. There is also a hidden cost to the household. People infected through raw milk or births can suffer weeks or months of illness, missed work and long courses of medicine. Herds known to carry brucellosis may find it harder to sell breeding stock, and in some areas raw milk may be rejected by buyers.
detail.humanHealth: Brucellosis is a serious zoonosis, meaning a disease that passes from animals to people. In people it is often called Malta fever or undulant fever. People usually catch it by drinking raw or unboiled milk, or by eating sour milk, yoghurt, ghee or cheese made from raw milk from infected cows, goats, sheep or camels. It also spreads by handling aborted calves, afterbirths and birth fluids with bare hands, especially through cuts or splashes into the eyes and mouth. Herders, farmers, milkers, butchers, slaughterhouse workers, vets and lab staff are at higher risk, and children in households that drink raw milk are also exposed. The illness usually starts like malaria or flu, with fever that comes and goes, heavy night sweats, tiredness, headache, back and joint pains, and loss of weight. It can last for months and sometimes affects joints, the heart or the reproductive organs. Because it is often mistaken for malaria or typhoid, tell your doctor or health centre that you keep livestock and drink milk, so they can test for brucellosis. It needs a long course of specific medicines prescribed by a doctor. To protect your family, always boil milk thoroughly or buy pasteurised milk, and make sour milk and other products only from boiled milk. Wear gloves and wash well with soap after helping with births or handling afterbirths, cover cuts, and keep children away from calving and aborted material. Cook meat well. Vets and farmers should also take care with live brucellosis vaccines, as an accidental needle-stick or splash can infect a person, and should see a doctor if this happens.
detail.outlook: A cow with brucellosis usually survives and often recovers her general health after the abortion. However, she nearly always stays infected for life. Many infected cows abort only once and then carry later calves to term, but they continue to shed the germ in milk and birth fluids, so they remain a danger to the herd and to people. Some cows develop lasting infertility after womb infections, and infected bulls often become permanently less fertile. For the herd, the outlook depends on how quickly you act. Herds that test, remove positive animals, keep calving hygienic, buy only tested stock and vaccinate heifers can bring the disease under control and eventually become free of it, although this takes time and repeated testing. Herds that ignore abortions, keep infected animals breeding and keep buying untested cattle tend to have ongoing losses for years.

faqs.q: Can I cure my cow with antibiotics from the agrovet?
faqs.a: No. Brucella bacteria hide inside the cow's cells, and even long courses of antibiotics rarely clear them. A treated cow may look fine but can still shed the germ in her milk and birth fluids. Using antibiotics this way wastes money, can leave drug residues in milk and meat, and adds to antimicrobial resistance. Your vet may treat a womb infection after an abortion, but the usual advice for confirmed brucellosis is to separate and cull infected animals, not to treat them.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from a herd with brucellosis if I boil it?
faqs.a: Thorough boiling or proper pasteurisation kills Brucella, so boiled milk is much safer. Bring the milk to a full rolling boil, not just warm, and make sour milk, yoghurt and ghee only from boiled milk. Never drink raw milk from a cow that has aborted or tested positive. The safest long-term plan is to test the herd and remove infected cows, because people can still be exposed while milking and handling births.

faqs.q: My cow aborted once and then calved normally. Does that mean she is now clean?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many cows with brucellosis abort only once, usually in the first pregnancy after infection, and then carry later calves to term. They usually remain infected and keep shedding bacteria in milk and at every calving. That makes them a hidden source of infection for other cows, calves and people. Only a blood or milk test arranged by your vet can tell you her status.

faqs.q: Can I vaccinate my adult cows against brucellosis?
faqs.a: Brucellosis vaccines are mainly given to young heifer calves, usually between about three and eight months old. Vaccinating older or pregnant animals with some vaccines, such as S19, can cause abortion and can interfere with blood tests later. In some situations a vet may use special plans for adults, but this is a decision for the vet. The vaccine is live and can infect people, so it should only be given by or under the supervision of a vet.

faqs.q: Can my goats, sheep, camels or dogs get brucellosis from my cattle?
faqs.a: Yes, cross-infection happens. Cattle mainly carry Brucella abortus, while goats and sheep mainly carry Brucella melitensis, which is even more dangerous to people. Each species can occasionally pick up the other's type when they graze and give birth together. Camels can also be infected. Dogs that eat afterbirths or aborted calves can become infected and spread the germ around the farm. Keep dogs away from calving areas and ask your vet about testing other livestock too.

faqs.q: Should I sell an infected cow at the market to recover some money?
faqs.a: Selling an infected cow at a market for breeding passes the disease to another farmer's herd and their family, and it keeps the disease circulating in your area. If your vet confirms brucellosis, the responsible step is to send the cow for slaughter at a licensed slaughterhouse under veterinary guidance, where meat inspection is carried out. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer how to do this properly in your county.

brucellosis.imagePrompt: A Friesian dairy cow standing in a rural Kenyan farmyard with a retained afterbirth hanging from her vulva, and visible firm round swellings over both front knees, natural daylight, realistic photograph.
brucellosis.seoDescription: Brucellosis in cattle: spot late abortion, retained afterbirth and swollen knees, protect your family from raw-milk infection, test and vaccinate heifers.

card.headline: Thin, pale cow with weeping eyes
card.look: The animal slowly loses weight over weeks, with a rough coat, pale gums and inner eyelids, tears running down the face and swollen glands in front of the shoulder. She may lag behind the herd and give less milk, even though she is still grazing.
card.action: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer for a blood test before any trypanocide is given, and keep the animal away from tsetse areas in the meantime.

detail.summary: Trypanosomiasis, often called nagana, is a blood disease of cattle caused by tiny parasites called trypanosomes, carried mainly by tsetse flies. It usually causes slow wasting, anaemia (thin, watery blood), on-and-off fever, poor milk and abortions, and untreated animals may die. It is one of the most costly cattle diseases in tsetse areas of Kenya, such as the Coast, the Lake Victoria basin and lowland areas near game parks and thick bush. With early diagnosis, correct vet treatment and fly control, most herds can be kept productive.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by single-celled parasites called trypanosomes that live and multiply in the blood and body fluids. In East African cattle the main species are Trypanosoma congolense, Trypanosoma vivax and Trypanosoma brucei. When an infected tsetse fly bites, the parasites enter the skin, multiply at the bite site (sometimes causing a small swelling called a chancre), then move into the lymph glands and bloodstream. They come and go in waves, which is why the fever rises and falls. The animal's immune system attacks the parasites, but the parasites keep changing their outer coat, so the body never fully clears them. Over time this damages and destroys red blood cells, causing anaemia, and the long-term fight drains the body's energy and protein, causing wasting. The parasites and the inflammation they cause can also harm the heart, the reproductive organs, the eyes and other tissues, leading to abortion, infertility, weakness and eventually heart failure or death.
spread: The main way it spreads is through the bite of tsetse flies (Glossina species), which pick up trypanosomes when they feed on infected cattle or wild animals and pass them on at later meals.

Trypanosoma vivax can also be carried mechanically by other biting flies such as horse flies (tabanids) and stable flies (Stomoxys), so it can spread in herds even outside tsetse belts once an infected animal arrives.
Wild animals such as buffalo, warthog, bushbuck and antelope carry trypanosomes, often without looking sick, and keep the disease going in areas near parks, reserves and thick bush.
Buying or moving in cattle from tsetse areas can bring infected but healthy-looking carriers into a clean herd.
Reusing the same needle on many animals during vaccination or treatment can transfer infected blood from one animal to another.
Grazing or watering animals near riverine bush, forest edges and thickets, where tsetse rest in shade, greatly increases the number of bites.
Stress from poor feeding, drought, heavy work, pregnancy or other diseases can turn a mild, hidden infection into an obvious illness.
detail.atRisk: Any cattle in or near tsetse-infested areas are at risk, including Kwale, Kilifi, Lamu and Tana River at the Coast, Busia, Homa Bay, Migori and Siaya around Lake Victoria, parts of the Rift Valley lowlands and areas bordering the Maasai Mara, Tsavo, Ruma and Meru parks. Exotic and cross-bred dairy cattle (Friesian, Ayrshire, Jersey and their crosses) are usually hit hardest, while local Small East African Zebu and some Boran lines, such as the Orma Boran, tend to cope somewhat better but can still lose condition and milk. Animals brought into a tsetse area for the first time often suffer badly. Pregnant cows, calves after weaning, working oxen and poorly fed animals are especially vulnerable. Free-range and pastoral herds that graze near bush, rivers and wildlife face the most bites, but zero-grazed animals near bush are not fully safe. Fly numbers and cases usually rise during and after the long and short rains, when bush is green and humid.

early: On-and-off fever: the animal feels hot, is dull for a few days, then seems to improve before becoming dull again.
Clear tears running from the eyes and staining the face, sometimes with slightly cloudy or watery-looking eyes.
Swollen lymph glands, most easily felt as a firm lump in front of the shoulder (prescapular) and in front of the thigh (prefemoral).
A gradual drop in milk yield and slower weight gain, even though the animal still grazes.
Slightly pale gums, inner eyelids and vulva instead of a healthy pink colour.
A small, hot, painful swelling on the skin where the tsetse fly bit, which may go unnoticed.
The animal tires easily, breathes faster after walking and lags behind the herd on the way to water.
advanced: Marked wasting: prominent hip bones and ribs, hollow flanks and a dry, rough, staring coat.
Very pale or almost white gums and eyelids from severe anaemia, with a fast, pounding heartbeat.
Swelling (oedema) under the jaw, brisket or belly, caused by fluid leaking from damaged blood vessels.
Abortion, stillbirths, weak calves, repeat breeding and cows failing to come on heat; bulls may become infertile.
Severe weakness, reluctance to move, lying down for long periods and difficulty getting up.
Cloudy eyes, sometimes leading to partial blindness.
With some Trypanosoma vivax strains, a sudden severe illness with high fever, bleeding spots on the gums or eyes and death within days or weeks.
Collapse and death, often from heart failure or the combined effect of anaemia and wasting, especially in untreated exotic cattle.

lookalikes.name: Anaplasmosis (gall sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gall sickness also causes anaemia and fever, but it usually develops faster, the animal often becomes yellow (jaundiced) around the eyes and gums, and it is commonly constipated with hard, dry dung. It is spread by ticks rather than tsetse. A blood smear examined by the vet separates the two.

lookalikes.name: East Coast Fever (ECF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ECF also causes swollen lymph glands and fever, but the glands swell very large and quickly, the fever is high and constant, and the animal develops laboured breathing, coughing and froth at the nose within days. It is tick-borne and more rapid than the slow wasting of trypanosomiasis. Gland smears and blood smears confirm which one it is.

lookalikes.name: Redwater (babesiosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Redwater causes anaemia and fever, but the classic sign is dark red or coffee-coloured urine, and the illness is usually sudden. Trypanosomiasis rarely causes red urine. Ticks, not tsetse, spread redwater.

lookalikes.name: Heavy worm burden (especially wireworm) or malnutrition
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms and poor feeding also cause pale gums, weight loss and bottle jaw, but there is usually no fever, no tears and no gland swelling, and diarrhoea is common with worms. A dung (faecal egg) test and a blood test help the vet decide. Note that an animal can have worms and trypanosomes at the same time.

detail.diagnosis: Because many diseases cause anaemia and wasting, trypanosomiasis should be confirmed with a blood test rather than guessed. The vet will check temperature, gum and eyelid colour, body condition and lymph glands, and ask about grazing near bush, tsetse and recent cattle movements. A blood sample is taken, often from the ear vein or jugular vein. In the lab, the vet or technician looks for moving parasites in fresh blood, or uses stained blood smears and the buffy coat technique (spinning blood in a fine tube and examining the layer between the cells and the plasma), which is more sensitive. The packed cell volume (PCV) test measures how anaemic the animal is. Because parasites come and go in the blood, one negative test does not always rule the disease out, and repeat sampling may be needed. Some laboratories and research centres can do PCR (DNA) tests or antibody tests, which are useful for herd surveys. At post-mortem, the vet may find a thin, wasted carcass, pale and watery blood, enlarged glands and spleen, fluid in body cavities and a pale, flabby heart. To help, the farmer should write down when signs started, which animals are affected, milk records, recent treatments (especially any trypanocide used, when and by whom), where the herd grazes and waters, and whether tsetse flies have been seen.
firstSteps: Call your vet, a qualified animal health officer or the County Veterinary Officer and ask for a blood test; do not buy and inject trypanocides on a guess, because wrong or under-strength treatment drives drug resistance.
Keep the sick animal near the homestead, away from bushy grazing, riverbanks and forest edges, so it is not bitten again and does not act as a source for flies.
Provide shade, clean fresh water at all times and good quality feed such as fresh fodder, hay and a little concentrate to help it keep its strength.
Avoid working, walking long distances or stressing the animal, since anaemic cattle tire quickly and can collapse.
Check the rest of the herd for tears, pale gums, weight loss and swollen glands, and note any animals that look unwell so the vet can test them too.
Record temperature if you have a thermometer, milk yield, body condition and any abortions, so the vet can see how the disease is progressing.
Use a new or properly sterilised needle for every animal during any injection, and never share needles between cattle.
Do not sell or move suspect animals to other farms or markets until they have been tested and treated, to avoid spreading infection.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment uses specific anti-trypanosome drugs called trypanocides, which must be prescribed and given correctly by a vet or trained animal health worker. The most commonly used are diminazene aceturate, which is mainly used to cure an existing infection, and isometamidium chloride, which can both treat and protect for a period against new infections. Homidium compounds are also used in some areas. The vet chooses the drug based on the test result, the local resistance situation and whether the animal needs cure or protection, and calculates the amount from the animal's actual weight; guessing the weight and under-dosing is a major cause of treatment failure and resistance. Where resistance is suspected, vets may use a 'sanative pair', switching between two drugs that do not share resistance. Antibiotics do not kill trypanosomes and should not be used for this disease unless the vet diagnoses a separate bacterial infection. Severely anaemic or wasted animals may need supportive care such as good feeding, rest, deworming if worms are also present and, rarely, other supportive treatments chosen by the vet. Most animals improve in appetite and alertness within days of the right treatment, but regaining weight, blood and milk takes several weeks, and some badly affected animals never fully recover. Trypanocides have milk and meat withdrawal periods, so ask the vet for the exact times and do not sell milk or slaughter animals until they have passed. Animals in high-tsetse areas can be reinfected, so treatment works best combined with fly control.
prevention: There is no vaccine against trypanosomiasis, so prevention depends on reducing tsetse bites, controlling the parasite with vet-guided drugs and keeping cattle strong.

Treat cattle regularly with insecticides, such as pyrethroid pour-ons, sprays or dips as advised by your vet; spraying the legs and belly, where tsetse mostly bite, can reduce cost while still protecting animals.

Support community tsetse control, such as blue-and-black insecticide-treated targets and traps placed near rivers and bush, in partnership with your county veterinary department and the Kenya Tsetse and Trypanosomiasis Eradication Council (KENTTEC).

Where possible, graze and water cattle away from thick riverine bush and forest edges, especially in the hot middle of the day when tsetse are active, and clear bush around homesteads and watering points.
In high-risk areas, ask your vet whether a preventive (prophylactic) trypanocide programme suits your herd, and follow the advised timing rather than treating randomly.
Test and treat newly bought cattle, especially from tsetse areas, before mixing them with your herd, and buy from known, healthy herds where possible.
Keep cattle well fed with enough energy, protein, minerals and clean water, control worms and ticks, and reduce stress, because well-nourished animals handle infection much better.
Consider local or tolerant breeds or crosses for very high tsetse areas, and talk to your extension officer before bringing pure exotic dairy cattle into such places.
Always use clean needles and good injection hygiene during herd treatments and vaccination campaigns.
detail.impact: Trypanosomiasis is a slow, expensive disease that often drains a farm quietly before anyone realises what is wrong. Dairy farmers lose milk, sometimes heavily, and cows that abort or fail to conceive mean lost calves, longer gaps between calvings and fewer replacement heifers. Beef and pastoral herds lose weight and fetch lower prices at market, and working oxen become too weak to plough during the planting season. Repeated drug treatments, insecticides and vet visits add costs, and buying cheap or fake trypanocides from unreliable sources can waste money and worsen resistance. Deaths, especially among high-value exotic or cross-bred cows, can wipe out years of investment. In many tsetse areas the disease also limits which breeds farmers can keep and which good grazing land can be used, holding back dairy development and household income.
detail.humanHealth: The trypanosomes that commonly infect cattle, such as Trypanosoma congolense and Trypanosoma vivax, do not infect people. However, in parts of East Africa, including areas around Lake Victoria and the Kenya–Uganda border, cattle can silently carry Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense, which causes human sleeping sickness (known in Swahili as malale).
