Cases in Kenya are now rare, but anyone living or working in tsetse areas who develops repeated fever, headache, a painful swelling at a fly bite or unusual sleepiness should visit a health facility and mention tsetse exposure. Wear long sleeves and light-coloured clothing near bush, and avoid handling blood from sick animals with bare cuts on your hands. Trypanocide drugs leave residues, so always respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods your vet gives you.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when the disease is caught early, confirmed by a blood test and treated with the correct drug at the correct dose, especially in local breeds that are otherwise well fed. Animals that are already severely anaemic, very thin or pregnant have a poorer chance, and some may die or remain unproductive even after treatment. Exotic dairy cattle generally do worse than local zebu. Drug resistance in some areas can lead to relapses, which is why follow-up checks and vet advice on drug choice matter. Because cattle in tsetse areas can be bitten and infected again, long-term success depends on combining treatment with fly control, good nutrition and careful grazing management.

faqs.q: Can I just buy a trypanocide from the agrovet and inject my cow myself?
faqs.a: Many farmers do this, but it is risky. Several diseases look like trypanosomiasis, and the wrong drug wastes money while the animal gets worse. Guessing the weight often leads to under-dosing, which fails to clear the parasites and helps them become resistant, so the drug stops working in your area. Some trypanocides also cause painful swellings or side effects if injected wrongly. Ask your vet or animal health officer to test the blood and prescribe and give the right drug, and ask about milk and meat withdrawal times.

faqs.q: Why does my cow keep getting sick again after treatment?
faqs.a: There are three common reasons. First, she may be bitten and infected again if she still grazes near tsetse areas. Second, the parasites in your area may be resistant to the drug used, or the dose was too low. Third, the problem may not have been trypanosomiasis at all, or she may have another disease such as worms or gall sickness at the same time. Ask your vet to retest her and review which drug was used, and work on fly control and grazing away from bush.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for nagana?
faqs.a: No. There is currently no vaccine for trypanosomiasis in cattle because the parasite keeps changing its outer coat, which makes it very hard for vaccines to work. Protection comes from controlling tsetse and biting flies, preventive drugs where your vet recommends them, keeping animals well fed and choosing suitable breeds for high-risk areas.

faqs.q: My cow is pale and thin but has no fever today. Can it still be trypanosomiasis?
faqs.a: Yes. The fever comes and goes in waves, so a normal temperature on one day does not rule it out. Long-standing infections often show mainly as wasting, anaemia and poor milk with little fever. The parasites may also be hard to find in the blood on some days, so your vet may need to test more than once.

faqs.q: Can I drink milk or eat meat from a cow with trypanosomiasis?
faqs.a: The common cattle trypanosomes do not infect people, and well-cooked meat and boiled milk from an animal that was otherwise healthy enough for food are not a known source of sleeping sickness. The bigger concern is drug residues. After treatment with a trypanocide, milk and meat must not be used or sold until the withdrawal period given by your vet has passed. Never slaughter a very sick animal for food without a vet or meat inspector's advice.

faqs.q: Are zero-grazed cows safe from tsetse?
faqs.a: Zero-grazing reduces the risk a lot because animals are kept away from bush where tsetse rest, but it does not remove it completely. Tsetse can fly into sheds near bush or rivers, and other biting flies can spread Trypanosoma vivax inside units. Keep bush cleared around sheds, use insecticides or insecticide-treated nets as advised, and test and treat new animals before they join the herd.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can help feverish, weak animals keep drinking and stay hydrated, especially in hot coastal and lakeside areas, while vet-prescribed trypanocide treatment works. It supports comfort and recovery only; it does not kill trypanosomes.

Vitamins A, D3 and E can support general condition, immunity and fertility in cattle recovering from long-standing wasting, alongside correct trypanocide treatment, good feeding and fly control. It is a recovery aid, not a treatment for the infection or its anaemia.

trypanosomiasis.imagePrompt: A thin zebu-cross cow with a rough coat and visible ribs standing in a bushy East African pasture, close view of its face showing clear tears streaking down from the eyes and pale inner eyelids, natural daylight.
trypanosomiasis.seoDescription: Trypanosomiasis (nagana) in cattle: spot tsetse-borne wasting, anaemia and fever early, act before the vet arrives and protect your herd in Kenya.

card.headline: Drooling, bellowing cow that cannot swallow
card.look: The animal drools thick strings of saliva, bellows in a hoarse or strange voice and seems to be choking. It may be very aggressive or dull and wobbly, strain as if to pass dung, and become paralysed in the back legs.
card.action: Keep everyone, especially children, away from the animal's mouth and saliva, isolate it without handling it, and call the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.summary: Rabies is a viral disease of the brain and nerves that is almost always fatal once signs appear, in cattle and in people. Cattle usually catch it from the bite of a rabid dog, and less often from jackals, hyenas, mongooses or other wild carnivores. A rabid cow is a serious danger to the family, because its saliva can carry the virus and many farmers are exposed while trying to 'clear a choke' by putting a hand in the mouth. Rabies is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: Rabies is caused by the rabies virus, a member of the lyssavirus group. The virus lives in the saliva of an infected animal and enters the body through a bite, a scratch or saliva getting into a fresh wound or onto the moist lining of the eyes, nose or mouth. After entry it may stay quietly near the bite for a long time, then it travels slowly along the nerves to the spinal cord and brain. This silent period, called the incubation period, varies a lot: often a few weeks to a few months, but sometimes longer, and it tends to be shorter when the bite is on the head or neck. Once the virus reaches the brain, it disturbs how the brain controls behaviour, swallowing, voice and movement. This is why the animal becomes aggressive or strangely dull, cannot swallow so saliva pours from the mouth, bellows abnormally and gradually becomes paralysed. At this stage the virus also moves into the salivary glands, so the saliva becomes infectious. There is no cure once signs appear, and death usually follows within a few days to about a week or so.
spread: The main source in Kenya is the bite of a rabid dog, especially unvaccinated village or stray dogs that roam between homesteads and grazing areas.
Wild carnivores such as jackals, hyenas, mongooses and wild cats can carry rabies and may bite cattle at night in bomas or on open grazing, particularly near wildlife areas.
Infection can happen when saliva from a rabid animal enters a fresh wound, a scratch or the moist lining of the mouth, eyes or nose, even without a deep bite.
Cattle bitten while grazing are often not noticed at the time, so the farmer may not know an animal was exposed until weeks or months later.
Spread from one cow to another is uncommon, but a rabid cow's saliva is infectious, so licking, shared feed troughs and water points contaminated with fresh saliva should be treated as a risk.

People are infected mainly through bites from rabid dogs, but farmers, herders and family members can be exposed by putting bare hands into the mouth of a sick cow or by getting its saliva into cuts or eyes.
Rabies does not spread through the air, through dung or through normal handling of an animal that is not sick, but any contact with saliva from a suspected case must be taken seriously.
detail.atRisk: Any cow, bull, heifer or calf of any breed can get rabies; there is no breed resistance. The highest risk is in areas with many unvaccinated dogs, such as villages and peri-urban settlements where dogs roam freely, and in pastoral and free-range systems where cattle graze far from home or are kept in open bomas at night near jackals and hyenas. Herds near game parks, conservancies and forest edges face extra risk from wildlife. Zero-grazing cattle in well-fenced units are at lower risk but are not completely safe, because stray dogs can still get into sheds. Curious young stock that approach strange dogs, and cattle that defend calves, are often bitten on the face and nose. Rabies occurs throughout the year in Kenya; there is no strong rainy-season pattern, but cases tend to cluster where a rabid dog has recently been seen in the area.

early: A change in behaviour: a calm cow becomes restless, nervous, aggressive or unusually alert, or a normally lively cow becomes dull and stands apart from the herd.
Drooling of thick, stringy saliva because the animal struggles to swallow, often with the mouth held slightly open as if it has something stuck in the throat.
Repeated, hoarse or unusual bellowing that sounds different from normal calling, sometimes almost non-stop.
Reduced or no eating and drinking, even though the animal may go to the water trough and appear to try to drink.
Sudden drop in milk yield in a milking cow.
Straining as if trying to pass dung or urine (called tenesmus), with little coming out.
Itching, licking or rubbing at one spot, which may be the old bite site, or an unusual sexual excitement such as mounting.
advanced: Attacking or charging people, other animals or objects, sometimes with head-butting; in the dumb form the animal may instead be very quiet and depressed.
Wobbly walking, knuckling of the fetlocks, swaying of the hindquarters and dragging of the back legs as paralysis develops.
Inability to swallow at all, a dropped jaw, and constant drooling with the tongue sometimes hanging out.
The tail may hang limp and the animal may lose control of the anus and bladder.
Lying down and being unable to get up, with paddling of the legs or convulsions near the end.
Death, usually within a few days to about a week or so after the first signs appear.

lookalikes.name: Choke (something stuck in the gullet)
lookalikes.howToTell: A choked cow also drools and stretches its neck, but it usually starts suddenly after eating root crops, maize cobs or fruits, the animal is otherwise alert and normal in behaviour, and there is often bloat. There is no aggression, strange bellowing or paralysis. Because rabies can look exactly like choke, never put a bare hand into the mouth of any drooling cow; let the vet examine it with gloves and a mouth gag.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater and cerebral East Coast Fever (turning sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: These tick-borne diseases also cause nervous signs such as circling, high stepping, head pressing and convulsions. However, the animal usually has a high fever, many ticks, and in ECF swollen lymph nodes below the ear and in front of the shoulder. Rabid cattle often have little or no fever early on and show typical drooling, voice changes and straining.

lookalikes.name: Milk fever and grass tetany
lookalikes.howToTell: These are metabolic problems of low calcium or low magnesium, usually in high-yielding cows around calving or on lush pasture after the rains. The cow may be excitable, tremble, stagger or go down, but she does not usually drool heavily or bellow strangely, and she often improves quickly after the vet gives calcium or magnesium. Rabies does not respond to these treatments.

lookalikes.name: Lead poisoning and listeriosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Lead poisoning, often from licking old batteries or paint, causes blindness, head pressing, frothing and fits, usually in calves or young stock with access to rubbish. Listeriosis, linked to spoiled silage, causes circling and one-sided facial paralysis with a drooping ear and eyelid. Only a vet and laboratory can reliably tell these apart from rabies, so treat any cow with nervous signs as possible rabies until told otherwise.

detail.diagnosis: There is no reliable test for rabies in a live cow. The vet will make a suspected diagnosis from the signs, how quickly they get worse and the history, such as a dog or wild animal bite or a rabid dog reported nearby. Confirmation is done after death, when the vet or veterinary officer safely removes the head or a brain sample and sends it to an approved veterinary laboratory, where it is tested, commonly with a fluorescent antibody test that detects the virus in brain tissue. Do not try to remove the head or open the carcass yourself; this must be done by trained staff with protective equipment. To help the vet, write down when the signs started, how they changed, whether any dog, jackal or other animal was seen biting or fighting the cattle, which other animals and people had contact with the cow, especially its saliva, and whether your dogs and cattle are vaccinated. Keep the carcass covered and guarded from dogs and scavengers until the vet advises on sampling and disposal.
firstSteps: Do not put your hand into the cow's mouth, do not try to drench it or force feed it, and do not try to clear what looks like a choke; treat every drooling cow with strange behaviour as possible rabies.
Keep children, visitors and other animals well away, and if possible confine the animal in a strong pen or crush on its own without getting close, using gates and ropes from a safe distance.
Call the County Veterinary Officer or your nearest veterinary office straight away and report a suspected rabies case, as the law requires; give them your location and a description of the signs.

If anyone has been bitten, or has had saliva from the cow or a suspect dog in a wound, cut, eyes, nose or mouth, wash the area immediately with plenty of soap and running water for about 15 minutes and take the person to the nearest health facility the same day for rabies post-exposure treatment.
Leave water and some feed where the animal can reach them without you entering its space, and give shade, but do not handle it.
Tie up or confine your dogs, check them and other livestock for bite wounds, and tell the vet about any animal that may have been bitten or in contact.
Stop all movement, sale or slaughter of the sick animal and any in-contact animals, and do not use its milk or meat for people or for feeding dogs.

If the animal dies, do not open the carcass or let dogs and scavengers reach it; cover it and wait for the veterinary officer to take samples and supervise safe disposal, usually deep burial or burning.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no treatment that cures rabies once signs appear, in cattle or in people. Antibiotics, painkillers, vitamins and dewormers will not help, because rabies is caused by a virus that has already reached the brain, and giving drugs only puts the person handling the animal at risk of saliva exposure. The vet's job is to confirm the suspicion, protect people and stop further spread. In most cases the vet will advise that a clearly rabid animal be humanely put down under veterinary supervision in a way that keeps the brain intact for laboratory testing, or will keep it strictly isolated until it dies. The vet will also advise on in-contact and bitten animals: depending on official guidance, these may be vaccinated, placed under quarantine and observation for a long period because the incubation period can be months, or in some situations slaughtered under supervision. Do not use or sell milk or meat from suspected cases or recently bitten animals unless the veterinary officer clears it. Where any veterinary product is used on in-contact animals, follow the vet's instructions on milk and meat withholding periods. Expect the veterinary team to trace and vaccinate dogs in the area, follow up on the animal that did the biting, and work with public health officers to make sure exposed people get post-exposure treatment.
prevention: Vaccinate all your dogs and cats against rabies, starting at the age recommended by your vet and repeating as advised; vaccinating dogs is the single most effective way to protect both cattle and people, and dog vaccination is a legal requirement in Kenya.
Take part in county and national mass dog vaccination campaigns, and encourage neighbours to do the same, because rabies control works only when most dogs in an area are vaccinated.

Ask your vet whether rabies vaccination of cattle is recommended in your area; livestock rabies vaccines exist and are often used for valuable animals in high-risk zones such as near wildlife or where cases have occurred.
Keep cattle in well-fenced bomas or sheds at night, especially near game parks, forests and areas with jackals and hyenas, and repair gaps that let stray dogs in.
Control stray and roaming dogs through responsible ownership: feed, house and confine your own dogs, and report aggressive strays to local authorities rather than handling them yourself.
Check cattle regularly for bite wounds, especially on the nose, face and legs, and report any bite from a dog or wild animal to the vet so that the animal can be watched or vaccinated as advised.
Teach everyone on the farm, including herders and children, never to put bare hands into the mouth of a drooling animal and to report any animal behaving strangely.
Report every suspected case and every bite from a suspected rabid animal, so that veterinary and health officers can act quickly and stop the disease spreading in your community.
detail.impact: Rabies kills the animal it infects, so each case is the loss of a whole cow, bull or heifer, often a dairy animal worth a large share of a smallholder family's savings. Milk from the sick cow, and sometimes from in-contact animals under observation, must be discarded, cutting daily income. Movement restrictions and quarantine on in-contact animals can delay sales, breeding and transport to market. The farm may face costs for veterinary visits, dog vaccination and supervised disposal, and people exposed to saliva need a course of post-exposure treatment, which costs time and money even where vaccine is subsidised. Beyond the farm, rabies harms whole communities: it causes human deaths every year in Kenya, mostly from dog bites, and outbreaks create fear and lost working days. These losses are largely preventable through dog vaccination and quick reporting.
detail.humanHealth: Rabies is a zoonosis, meaning it passes from animals to people, and it is almost always fatal in people once symptoms start. The main risk from a rabid cow is saliva entering a cut, scratch, the eyes, nose or mouth, most often when someone puts a hand in the mouth thinking the cow is choking, or when giving medicine by mouth. Bites from cattle are rare but possible. Never handle the mouth of a drooling cow with nervous signs, wear gloves and eye protection if you must be near it, and keep children away. If exposure happens, wash the wound or area immediately with soap and plenty of running water for about 15 minutes, then go to a health facility the same day; post-exposure vaccination, sometimes with immunoglobulin, is very effective if started promptly and completed. Do not drink milk or eat meat from a suspected rabid animal, and do not let dogs eat the carcass. Do not wait for symptoms in yourself before seeking help, because by then it is too late.
detail.outlook: Once a cow shows signs of rabies, the outlook is hopeless: there is no cure and the animal will die, usually within a few days to about a week or so. Nothing a farmer or vet can give will reverse it. The real outlook depends on what happens around the case: how quickly it is reported, whether people exposed get post-exposure treatment in time, whether other bitten animals are found and managed, and whether dogs in the area are vaccinated. Animals that were bitten but have not yet shown signs may still develop rabies weeks or months later, which is why vets may advise long observation or vaccination. With good dog vaccination coverage and fast reporting, further cases in the herd and in people can be prevented.

faqs.q: My cow is drooling and seems to be choking. How do I know it is not rabies?
faqs.a: You cannot be sure by looking, and that is exactly why rabies is so dangerous. Choke usually starts suddenly during or after feeding on things like cassava, potatoes, maize cobs or mangoes, and the cow is otherwise behaving normally. Rabies often comes with strange bellowing, behaviour changes, straining and wobbly back legs, and sometimes a history of a dog or jackal bite. Because the two can look the same, never put your bare hand in the mouth. Call the vet, keep people away and let the vet examine the animal with protective gear.

faqs.q: Can I treat a rabid cow with antibiotics or other injections from the agrovet?
faqs.a: No. Rabies is caused by a virus that has already reached the brain by the time you see signs, and no antibiotic, vitamin injection or herbal remedy can cure it. Trying to treat the animal only exposes you to its saliva. The right steps are to isolate the animal, protect people and report it to the County Veterinary Officer.

faqs.q: Can we drink the milk or eat the meat of a cow with rabies?
faqs.a: No. Do not drink milk or eat meat from a cow suspected of having rabies, and do not feed the carcass to dogs. Although the main risk to people is through saliva, handling, slaughtering and cutting up a rabid animal can expose people to infected tissue, and authorities advise against using any products from suspected cases. The veterinary officer will advise on safe disposal, usually deep burial or burning.

faqs.q: A dog bit one of my cows but she looks fine. What should I do?
faqs.a: Report it to your vet straight away and try to find out what happened to the dog. If the dog was vaccinated and stays healthy, the risk is lower, but if it was a stray, wild or sick animal, treat the bite seriously. The vet may advise vaccination of the cow, a period of observation that can last several months because rabies can take a long time to show, or other measures under official guidance. Keep a note of the date of the bite and watch the cow closely for behaviour changes, drooling or bellowing.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report rabies? What happens after I do?
faqs.a: Rabies is a notifiable disease under Kenyan law, which means anyone who suspects it must report it to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting lets officers confirm the case, trace people and animals that were exposed, make sure exposed people get treatment, and vaccinate dogs in the area to stop more cases. You may be told not to move, sell or slaughter the sick animal or in-contact animals for a period; these movement restrictions exist to stop the disease spreading to other farms and families. Reporting protects your family and your neighbours.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate my cattle against rabies?
faqs.a: Vaccinating your dogs is the most important step, because dogs are the main source of rabies for both cattle and people in Kenya. Rabies vaccines for cattle do exist and are worth discussing with your vet if you live near wildlife areas, have had cases nearby, have many stray dogs around, or keep valuable breeding or dairy animals. Your vet can tell you whether it makes sense for your herd and arrange the vaccination.

rabies.imagePrompt: A Friesian dairy cow standing alone in a rural Kenyan wooden-fenced pen, head stretched forward with mouth slightly open as if bellowing and long strings of clear saliva hanging from its lips, dry grass and a mud-walled shed in the background, natural daylight.
rabies.seoDescription: Rabies in cattle: spot drooling, bellowing, straining and paralysis, protect your family and report fast. Kenya guide to signs and prevention.

card.headline: Hot, hard, swollen udder quarter
card.look: One quarter of the udder is swollen, hard, hot or painful to touch, and the milk from it has clots, flakes, or looks watery or yellowish. In severe cases the cow also has a fever, stops eating and drops her milk sharply.
card.action: Strip a few squirts from every teat into a dark cup to find the affected quarter, keep that milk out of the bulk can, and call your vet before giving any treatment.

detail.summary: Mastitis is inflammation of the udder, almost always caused by bacteria that enter through the teat canal. It can be clinical, with a swollen quarter and abnormal milk, or subclinical, where the cow looks normal but her milk quality and yield are quietly falling. It is the most common and most costly disease of dairy cows in Kenya and around the world. Most cases can be prevented with good milking hygiene and clean, dry housing.
detail.cause: Mastitis is caused mainly by bacteria that get into the udder through the small opening at the tip of the teat, called the teat canal. Some germs are 'contagious': they live in infected udders and pass from cow to cow during milking, mainly Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus agalactiae. Others are 'environmental': they live in dung, mud, wet bedding and dirty water, and include E. coli, Klebsiella and Streptococcus uberis. Less commonly, Mycoplasma, Trueperella pyogenes, yeasts or fungi are involved. Once inside, the bacteria multiply in the milk-producing tissue. The cow's body sends white blood cells to fight them, and this battle causes heat, swelling, pain and clots in the milk. The white blood cells in the milk are counted as the 'somatic cell count' (SCC), and a high count shows infection even when the milk looks normal. Some bacteria, especially E. coli, release poisons (toxins) into the blood, which can make the cow very ill, cause her to go down, and even kill her. Others, especially Staph aureus, hide deep in the udder, form scar tissue and cause long-lasting infections that come and go and are hard to cure. Damaged tissue may stop making milk permanently, leaving a 'blind' or dry quarter.
spread: Contagious bacteria spread at milking time on the milker's hands, shared udder cloths, and milking machine cups that move from an infected cow to a healthy one.
Environmental bacteria enter the teat when cows lie in wet, muddy or dung-covered bedding, which is common in poorly drained zero-grazing units during the long and short rains.
The teat canal stays open for some time after milking, so cows that lie down straight after milking in a dirty shed are at higher risk.
Incomplete milking leaves milk in the udder, which gives bacteria a place to grow; hand milkers who rush or stop early raise the risk.
Poor milking technique, such as pulling or 'stripping' the teat between finger and thumb, or using dirty milking jelly, damages the teat end and lets germs in.
Teat injuries, cracks, warts, tick bites, flies and pox-like sores on the teats give bacteria an easy entry point.
Calves sucking each other after drinking milk, or sucking an infected dam and then another cow, can carry bacteria to heifers and cows.
Stress, poor nutrition (especially low vitamin E and selenium), and the weeks around calving weaken the cow's defences and make infection more likely.
detail.atRisk: Any cow or heifer with a functioning udder can get mastitis, but the highest risk is in the first weeks after calving and in the first weeks of the dry period. High-yielding exotic dairy breeds such as Friesian, Ayrshire and their crosses are more affected than local zebu cattle, partly because of larger udders and longer lactations. Older cows with many calvings, loose teat sphincters or pendulous udders that touch the ground are at greater risk. Zero-grazing units with wet, dirty floors and little bedding, especially during the long and short rains, see many environmental cases. Farms with hand milking by several workers, shared towels, no teat dipping and no testing tend to have more contagious mastitis. Cows that have had mastitis before, or that have teat injuries or warts, are more likely to get it again.

early: Small clots, flakes or strings appear in the first squirts of milk, best seen when stripped into a dark cup or onto a dark cloth.
One quarter feels warmer, firmer or slightly swollen compared with the others.
The cow kicks, steps away or seems uncomfortable when that quarter is touched or milked.
Milk yield from the cow drops a little without any other obvious reason.
The California Mastitis Test (CMT) on the paddle shows a thick, jelly-like reaction in milk from one or more quarters, even though the milk looks normal (subclinical mastitis).
Your milk collection centre or cooperative reports a high somatic cell count or poor-quality milk from your farm.
advanced: The quarter is very hard, hot, red or bluish, and clearly painful; the cow may walk stiffly or stand with her hind leg held away.
Milk becomes watery, yellow, brown, blood-stained or pus-like, or the quarter produces almost nothing.
The cow has a fever, stops eating, stops chewing cud and her milk drops sharply.
In toxic mastitis the cow becomes weak, dull, cold at the ears and legs, has diarrhoea or sunken eyes, and may go down and be unable to rise.
A cold, blue-black quarter that leaks foul, watery fluid suggests gangrenous mastitis, which is an emergency.
Long-term cases leave lumps or scar tissue in the quarter, a shrunken quarter, or a quarter that has stopped producing milk.

lookalikes.name: Udder oedema (fluid swelling)
lookalikes.howToTell: Oedema is common in heifers and cows just before and after calving. The swelling is usually even on both sides, soft, cool, and leaves a finger mark when pressed, and the milk is normal. Mastitis usually affects one quarter, which is hot and painful, and the milk changes.

lookalikes.name: Blood in milk after calving
lookalikes.howToTell: Pink or red milk in the first days after calving often comes from small burst blood vessels and usually clears on its own. The udder is not hot or painful and there are no clots or pus. If the quarter is also hot and hard, think mastitis.

lookalikes.name: Milk fever (low blood calcium)
lookalikes.howToTell: Milk fever usually hits within days of calving: the cow is cold, wobbly, then goes down with her head turned to her side, and the udder is normal. Severe E. coli mastitis can also make a cow go down, so always check the udder and milk of any down cow and tell the vet.

lookalikes.name: Teat sores from pox, warts or lumpy skin disease
lookalikes.howToTell: These cause scabs, nodules or blisters on the teat skin rather than a hot, hard quarter. The milk is usually normal at first, but sore teats make milking painful and incomplete, which often leads to mastitis, so they need attention too.

detail.diagnosis: A vet diagnoses clinical mastitis by examining the udder, checking the milk from each quarter in a strip cup, and taking the cow's temperature, heart rate and general condition to judge how severe it is. The California Mastitis Test (CMT), a simple paddle test with a reagent, shows which quarters have hidden infection. The most useful step is a milk culture and sensitivity test, where a clean milk sample is sent to a laboratory (county veterinary labs, the Central Veterinary Laboratory at Kabete, KALRO or private labs) to find out which bacteria are present and which drugs will work. This is especially important for repeat cases or when many cows are affected. Many dairy cooperatives can also give somatic cell count results for your bulk milk or individual cows. To help the vet, do not start any tube or injection before they arrive, because this spoils the lab sample. Note which quarter is affected, when you first saw the change, the cow's calving date, her yield, and any past mastitis and treatments. If possible, keep a sample of the abnormal milk in a clean, closed container in a cool place.
firstSteps: Strip a few squirts from each teat into a strip cup or dark cup to find exactly which quarters are affected, and do this before every milking until the vet has seen her.

Keep milk from the affected cow completely separate from the bulk milk, and do not sell it, deliver it to the cooler or feed it to calves; dispose of it in a pit away from water sources and other animals.
Milk the affected cow last, after all healthy cows, and wash and dry your hands well afterwards so you do not carry germs to other udders.
Gently and fully strip out the affected quarter several times a day if the vet advises, to remove bacteria and toxins, using clean hands and without pulling or pinching the teat.
Move the cow to a clean, dry, well-bedded and shaded pen, and give her plenty of fresh clean water and good feed to encourage her to keep eating.
Take her temperature with a thermometer if you have one, and watch closely for fever, refusal to eat, weakness, diarrhoea or going down, which mean the vet must come urgently.
Record the cow's name or number, the quarter affected, the date and the signs, so the vet can make a good decision and you can spot repeat cases later.
Call your vet or animal health officer, and do not use leftover tubes, injections or human medicines without their advice.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how sick the cow is and which bacteria are involved, and it must be prescribed by a vet. For mild to moderate cases, the vet usually uses intramammary tubes, which are antibiotics squeezed into the teat after cleaning the teat end with spirit; commonly used drug groups include penicillins such as cloxacillin, cephalosporins and other combinations. For severe or toxic cases, the vet may add antibiotics by injection, anti-inflammatory painkillers such as flunixin or meloxicam to reduce fever, pain and swelling, and fluids by drip or by mouth to fight dehydration and shock. Frequent stripping of the quarter is often part of the plan. Mild E. coli cases sometimes clear on their own with supportive care, and some vets will not give antibiotics in those cases. Long-standing Staph aureus infections often respond poorly to treatment during lactation; the vet may suggest treatment at drying off, drying off that quarter only, or culling the cow. At drying off, the vet may recommend dry cow therapy and internal teat sealants. All these drugs leave residues, so milk must be discarded for the full withdrawal period on the label or as the vet instructs, and meat also has a withdrawal period if the cow is sold for slaughter. Milk with antibiotic residues can be rejected by processors and harms consumers. Use antibiotics responsibly: complete the full course exactly as prescribed, do not use them for every small change in milk, and avoid using one product over and over without a lab test, because misuse creates antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people.
prevention: Follow a clean milking routine: wash and dry your hands, use a separate clean towel or paper for each cow, check the first squirts in a strip cup, and dry the teats fully before milking.
Dip or spray all teats right after milking with a proper teat dip recommended by your vet or agrovet, so the open teat canal is protected.
Milk fully and gently using the full hand (squeezing method) rather than pulling or stripping between finger and thumb, and use only clean milking salve, not used cooking fat.
Keep cows standing for at least half an hour after milking by giving them fresh feed, so the teat canal closes before they lie down.

Keep the shed, cubicles and walkways clean and dry; remove dung at least daily, improve drainage, and use plenty of clean, dry bedding such as wood shavings or dry grass, especially in the rainy seasons.
Milk cows with known or past mastitis last, and cull cows that keep getting mastitis despite proper treatment, as they spread infection to the rest of the herd.
Test all milking cows with the CMT paddle regularly, for example monthly, and ask your cooperative for somatic cell count results so hidden cases are found early.

Work with your vet on dry cow therapy or teat sealants at drying off, feed a balanced ration with adequate vitamins A and E and selenium, control ticks and flies, keep calves from sucking each other, and service milking machines regularly.
detail.impact: Mastitis takes money from Kenyan dairy farms in many ways. The biggest loss is often hidden: subclinical mastitis lowers milk yield in cows that look healthy, and many farmers never notice. Clinical cases mean milk that must be thrown away during illness and for the withdrawal period after treatment, plus the cost of the vet, drugs and labour. Milk collection centres and processors may reject milk with antibiotic residues or high cell counts, and repeated rejection can damage a farmer's relationship with the cooperative. Damaged quarters may produce less milk for the rest of the cow's life, and badly affected cows are culled early, often at a low price. Severe toxic mastitis can kill a valuable cow. For a smallholder with two or three cows, losing one quarter or one cow can mean a large share of the family's daily income.
detail.humanHealth: Mastitis itself is not passed directly from cows to people in normal handling, but milk from infected cows can affect human health. Some mastitis bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus and certain Streptococcus and E. coli strains, can cause food poisoning or illness, and some Staph toxins are not destroyed by boiling, so milk from a cow with mastitis should not be consumed at all. Milk from treated cows contains antibiotic residues during the withdrawal period, which can cause allergic reactions in sensitive people and contribute to antimicrobial resistance; never sell or drink it. Always boil or pasteurise milk for home use, as raw milk can also carry other serious diseases such as brucellosis and tuberculosis. Wash your hands well after handling infected udders and milk, and cover any cuts on your hands.
detail.outlook: Most mild and moderate clinical cases recover well when caught early and treated correctly, and the milk usually returns to normal. The chance of full recovery depends on the type of bacteria, how quickly treatment starts, the cow's age and condition, and how long the infection has been present. Staph aureus and Mycoplasma infections are often long-lasting and may never fully clear, leaving a cow that keeps flaring up. Toxic E. coli mastitis can be fatal within a day or two if the cow is not treated quickly, though cows that survive often recover the quarter. A badly damaged or gangrenous quarter may be permanently lost, but the cow can sometimes continue milking on three quarters. On a herd level, steady hygiene and testing usually bring mastitis down over time.

faqs.q: Can I just buy a mastitis tube from the agrovet and treat the cow myself?
faqs.a: It is better to call a vet first. Different bacteria respond to different drugs, and using the wrong tube wastes money, delays proper treatment and builds antibiotic resistance. Severe cases also need more than a tube, such as painkillers and fluids. If the vet prescribes tubes for you to use, clean the teat end with spirit first, insert only the tip, finish the full course, and observe the milk withdrawal period on the label.

faqs.q: Can I drink or sell milk from the other healthy-looking quarters?
faqs.a: No. Once a cow is being treated, the drug can pass into all four quarters, so milk from the whole cow must be discarded during the withdrawal period. Even before treatment, a cow with mastitis is unwell and her milk quality is poor. Discard it safely and do not feed it to calves, as it can spread infection and antibiotic resistance.

faqs.q: Why does mastitis keep coming back in the same cow?
faqs.a: Repeat cases are usually caused by bacteria such as Staph aureus that hide in scar tissue where drugs cannot reach well, by treatment courses that were stopped early, or by ongoing problems like dirty bedding, teat damage or poor milking routine. Ask your vet to take a milk sample for culture. Some chronic cows are best treated at drying off, have a quarter dried off, or are culled to protect the rest of the herd.

faqs.q: Is mastitis caused by cold weather or by the cow lying on cold ground?
faqs.a: Cold itself does not cause mastitis; bacteria do. However, the rainy seasons bring mud, wet bedding and dung, which are full of environmental bacteria, so cases often rise during the long and short rains. Keeping the shed dry and well-bedded is the key, not keeping the cow warm.

faqs.q: What is the CMT test and do I need it if the milk looks normal?
faqs.a: The California Mastitis Test is a simple paddle with four cups where you mix milk from each quarter with a special liquid. If the mixture turns thick or jelly-like, there is hidden infection. Many cows with subclinical mastitis have normal-looking milk but lose yield and can infect others, so testing your cows regularly, for example monthly, helps you catch problems early. Paddles and reagent are sold at many agrovets.

faqs.q: Do herbal or home remedies like aloe or onion cure mastitis?
faqs.a: There is no reliable evidence that home remedies cure bacterial mastitis, and putting substances into the teat can push in more germs and cause serious damage. Frequent gentle stripping, a clean dry pen and good feeding help the cow, but proper diagnosis and vet-prescribed treatment are needed. Prevention through clean milking is far cheaper than any remedy.

products.role: Vitamins A and E support healthy teat skin and the cow's natural immune defences, and low vitamin E is linked to more udder infections; used as your vet advises, especially around drying off and calving, AD3E can help correct a deficiency as part of a mastitis prevention plan alongside clean milking and proper vet treatment. It does not treat mastitis.

A cow with a fever or toxic mastitis often drinks and eats less and can become dehydrated; RE-COVER oral rehydration solution can help support fluid intake and recovery while she is being treated, but only alongside the vet's treatment and never as a replacement for it.

mastitis.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a Friesian dairy cow's udder in a clean Kenyan zero-grazing shed, with one rear quarter visibly swollen, red and larger than the others, and a dark strip cup below showing small white clots in the milk.
mastitis.seoDescription: Mastitis in cattle: spot a hot, swollen quarter and clotted milk early, use the CMT test, act before the vet arrives and prevent udder infection.

card.headline: Down cow, head turned to flank
card.look: A cow that calved in the last day or two is lying on her chest, cannot get up, and has her head tucked round towards her side. Her ears feel cold, her eyes look dull, and she may have wobbled or trembled before she went down.
card.action: Call your vet immediately, because milk fever can kill within hours, and prop the cow up on her chest while you wait.

aka: Downer cow (when the cow cannot rise)
detail.summary: Milk fever is a sudden drop in blood calcium that happens around calving, usually in older, high-yielding dairy cows. It is not an infection and the cow usually has no fever. In fact her body temperature is often below normal. Without quick treatment by a vet the cow can go down, bloat and die within hours, but most cows treated early recover well. It also opens the door to other problems such as retained afterbirth, mastitis, displaced stomach and ketosis.
detail.cause: Calcium is the mineral the body needs for muscles, including the heart and gut muscles, to contract. When a cow calves and starts making colostrum (the first thick milk), she suddenly pours large amounts of calcium into the udder. Her body has to pull calcium from her bones and absorb more from her gut to keep up. In the last weeks before calving her body may not have 'switched on' these systems yet, especially if her dry-period diet was high in calcium or potassium. This happens often with older cows, whose bones release calcium more slowly. Blood calcium falls faster than the body can replace it. As calcium drops, the muscles become weak and stop working properly. First the cow trembles and wobbles, then she cannot stand, then the gut stops moving so she becomes constipated and bloated, and finally the heart weakens. Low phosphorus and low or high magnesium can make the problem worse or make the cow slower to respond to treatment. Milk fever is a 'metabolic' disease, which means it comes from the body's chemistry and feeding, not from germs, so it does not pass from cow to cow.
spread: It does not spread from animal to animal. It is triggered by the sudden demand for calcium when milk production starts at calving.

Feeding a lot of calcium in the dry period (the last two to three weeks before calving) is a common trigger. Lucerne, other legumes, high-calcium mineral licks and lime all add calcium. This keeps the cow's calcium-releasing systems 'asleep' until it is too late.

Diets high in potassium, such as heavily fertilised young grass, napier grown on manure-rich soil, or a lot of molasses, make the blood more alkaline. This reduces the cow's ability to mobilise calcium.
Low magnesium in the diet interferes with the hormones that control calcium, so cows on lush pasture or poor rations with no magnesium are at higher risk.
Overfat cows at calving, often from being dried off with poor control of feeding, are more likely to get milk fever and related problems.
Stress around calving, such as a difficult birth, long walking, sudden feed changes, going off feed or cold wet weather, can push a borderline cow into milk fever.
Cows that have had milk fever before are much more likely to get it again at the next calving.
detail.atRisk: Milk fever mostly affects dairy cows from their third calving onwards, because older cows produce more milk and release calcium from their bones more slowly. First-calf heifers rarely get it. High-yielding exotic breeds kept in zero-grazing and semi-intensive units in Kenya are most at risk, especially Jerseys and their crosses. Friesians, Ayrshires and Guernseys are also affected. Local zebu and Boran cattle with lower yields are affected far less often, though it can happen. Most cases occur from the day before calving to about three days after, with the peak in the first 24 hours. Cases can occasionally occur late in pregnancy or weeks into lactation. Risk rises when dry cows are fed the same high-calcium ration or mineral mix as milking cows, when they graze lush grass during the long and short rains, when they are overfat, and when there is a cow with a past history. Dairy goats and sheep can get a similar condition, but the pattern differs.

early: Within hours of calving the cow seems nervous, excited or restless, and may stop eating.
She trembles, especially over the shoulders, flanks and hind legs, and may twitch her ears or grind her teeth.
She walks with a wobbly, stiff or shuffling gait, may sway her hindquarters, and keeps shifting her weight between her back feet.
She stops chewing the cud, and dung output drops or stops.
Her ears, legs and skin feel cooler than normal when you touch them, and her muzzle may look dry.
Milk yield and appetite fall suddenly even though she has just calved.
advanced: She goes down and lies on her chest, unable to rise even when encouraged.
She often turns her head round into her flank, or holds her neck in a kink like an 'S' shape.
Her eyes look dull and staring with large pupils, and she seems drowsy or does not notice what is going on around her.
Her ears and legs feel cold, and a thermometer in the rectum often reads below normal temperature.
Her left side swells with gas (bloat) because the stomach and gut have stopped moving, and she may be constipated with the anus relaxed.
Her heartbeat becomes weak and fast, and in the final stage she lies flat on her side, cannot lift her head, slips into a coma and can die within hours.

lookalikes.name: Grass tetany (hypomagnesaemia, low blood magnesium)
lookalikes.howToTell: Grass tetany usually makes cows very excitable and aggressive. They have muscle spasms, stagger, paddle their legs and have fits. It often affects cows at any stage of lactation grazing lush rain-season grass. Milk fever cows are usually quiet, drowsy and floppy, and it happens right around calving. The two can occur together, so the vet may give a treatment that covers both.

lookalikes.name: Calving injury (nerve damage or pelvic/hip injury)
lookalikes.howToTell: After a hard or assisted calving with a big calf, a cow may be bright and alert and still eating, but unable to use her hind legs, or her legs splay out to the sides. Her ears are warm and she does not turn her head to her flank. If a cow does not rise after calcium treatment, the vet will check for these injuries.

lookalikes.name: Toxic (acute) mastitis
lookalikes.howToTell: In toxic mastitis one quarter of the udder is usually hot, hard or swollen, or the milk is watery, clotted or bloody. The cow may have had a high fever before she weakened. Milk fever cows have a normal-looking udder and milk. Toxic mastitis can make a cow go down and feel cold, and it can also follow milk fever, so always check the udder and the milk.

lookalikes.name: Ketosis and acute metritis (womb infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ketosis usually appears one to six weeks after calving. The cow eats less, loses weight and drops in milk, and her breath or milk may smell sweet, like nail polish. Metritis gives a foul-smelling, dark discharge from the vulva a few days after calving, often with fever. Neither usually causes the sudden collapse with cold ears in the first day that is typical of milk fever.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually diagnoses milk fever from the timing, the cow's age and history, and a physical examination. The typical picture is an older, high-yielding cow, within a day or two of calving, that is down with cold ears, a low temperature, a weak heartbeat, no gut sounds and her head turned to her flank. The strongest confirmation is a fast response to calcium given into the vein. The cow often burps, passes dung, trembles and may try to stand within minutes to hours. Where possible, the vet may take a blood sample before treatment to measure calcium, phosphorus and magnesium. This is especially useful if the cow does not respond or if there are several cases in the herd. The vet will also check the udder, the womb, and the legs and hips to rule out mastitis, metritis or injury. If a cow dies, a post-mortem examination plus samples of eye fluid can help confirm low calcium or magnesium. To help your vet, write down the calving date and time, whether the birth was difficult, when you first saw signs, what she ate in the last three weeks before calving (including any lucerne, mineral lick or lime), whether she had milk fever before, and what, if anything, has been given to her.
firstSteps: Call your vet or the nearest animal health assistant at once and say clearly that a freshly calved cow is down. Milk fever is an emergency and a cow can die within a few hours.

If she is down, roll her gently onto her chest with her legs tucked under her, and wedge sacks of feed, hay bales or folded bedding against her side to keep her upright. A cow lying flat on her side can bloat and choke on stomach contents.
Gently turn her head forward so she is not lying on it, and every two to three hours change which side she leans on, so the down leg does not lose its blood supply and get permanently damaged.

Do not pour water, drench or medicine into the mouth of a cow that is down, drowsy or cannot swallow properly, because the liquid can go into her lungs and cause fatal pneumonia. Do not inject calcium yourself, because calcium given wrongly can stop the heart.

Move her, or protect her where she lies, onto soft, dry, non-slippery bedding such as straw, sand or grass. Give her shade from the sun and shelter from rain and cold, and keep other cattle away so they do not trample her.
Keep the calf safe and fed with colostrum from another source or by hand if needed. Until the vet advises otherwise, take only a small amount of milk for the calf rather than fully milking her out.
Do not try to lift her by the tail, beat her or force her up. This can injure her badly. Let the vet decide when and how to help her stand.
Note the time she went down, her signs and anything she has eaten, and keep an eye on any other cows due to calve soon, especially older ones.
detail.vetTreatment: The main treatment is replacing calcium quickly. The vet usually gives a calcium solution, most commonly calcium borogluconate. Sometimes it is a combined solution that also contains magnesium, phosphorus and glucose. It goes slowly into a vein while the vet listens to the heart, because calcium given too fast can cause a dangerous heart rhythm or sudden death. This is why it must be done by a trained person. Part of the dose may also be given under the skin for a slower, longer effect. Once the cow can swallow normally, the vet may give oral calcium in a gel, bolus (large tablet) or drench to keep levels up over the next day. Most cows respond within minutes to a few hours. They burp, pass dung and urine, stop trembling and often get up. About a third of cows or more may relapse within a day or two and need repeat treatment, so keep watching closely. If the cow does not rise, the vet will look for other problems such as low phosphorus or magnesium, muscle or nerve damage from lying too long, mastitis, metritis or a calving injury, and may treat these as well. Antibiotics do not treat milk fever. A vet will only use them if there is a confirmed bacterial problem alongside it, such as mastitis or a womb infection. Using them without need adds to antimicrobial resistance, which is when germs stop responding to medicines. Plain calcium solutions usually have little or no milk withdrawal. However, combination products and any other drugs given, such as anti-inflammatories or antibiotics, can carry milk and meat withdrawal periods. Always ask your vet and follow the label before selling milk or meat. All treatment, products and doses must be prescribed by a vet.
prevention: Feed dry cows separately from milking cows, especially in the last three weeks before calving. Avoid lucerne, desmodium and other legumes in large amounts, high-calcium dairy mineral mixes, lime and chalk at this time, so her body learns to release its own calcium before she calves.

Ask your vet or a dairy nutritionist about a properly balanced 'close-up' dry cow ration. Commercial farms may use anionic salts (special minerals that make the blood slightly acidic and help calcium release). This must be done carefully and measured by a professional, because mistakes can harm the cow.

Make sure the dry cow ration has enough magnesium, for example from a dry cow mineral with magnesium, and avoid too much potassium. Do not give heavy amounts of manure-fertilised young grass, napier or molasses right before calving.

Manage body condition so cows are fit but not fat at drying off and at calving. Dry off at the right time, give dry cows a ration suited to them, not the milking ration, and avoid sudden feed changes around calving.

For high-risk cows, meaning older cows, Jerseys and any cow with a past case, ask your vet about giving oral calcium at calving and again 12 hours later. Some vets may also advise vitamin D3 a few days before the expected date. Vitamin D3 must be timed and dosed by a vet, because too much is toxic.
Keep good breeding and health records so you know which cows are due, which had milk fever before, and can watch them closely from the day before calving until three days after.

Provide a clean, dry, comfortable calving area close to the house with good footing. Reduce stress and long walks at calving, and make sure fresh cows have water and good feed straight away so they keep eating.

Once a cow has calved, she needs good calcium, phosphorus and energy in her milking ration to keep up with milk production. Your vet may advise taking only part of the milk in the first day or two for very high-risk cows.
detail.impact: Milk fever hits the best cows in the herd, the mature high yielders that pay the bills on a Kenyan dairy farm. A cow that dies at calving is a huge loss: the price of a good dairy cow plus a whole lactation of milk, often with a newborn calf that then needs hand-rearing. Even cows that recover often produce less milk in that lactation. They are also more likely to suffer retained afterbirth, womb infections, mastitis, displaced abomasum (twisted stomach), ketosis and delayed return to heat. This means extra vet bills, discarded milk during treatments and longer calving intervals. Cows that stay down for long can develop permanent leg and muscle damage and may have to be culled. Many cows also have 'subclinical' milk fever, low calcium without going down, which quietly lowers appetite and milk and raises the risk of other diseases. On a zero-grazing farm with a few cows, one case can wipe out months of income from milk sold to the cooperative or local buyers.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when treatment starts early. Most cows treated while still standing or lying on their chest get up and recover, often within hours. The longer a cow stays down, the worse the chances. Cows lying flat on their side, bloated, or in a coma have a much poorer outlook. Cows that lie for many hours can suffer crush damage to the muscles and nerves of the legs. They may never rise again even after their calcium is back to normal. Relapses within a day or two are common, so careful watching and repeat vet visits may be needed. Recovery is slower or less likely if there are other problems at the same time, such as low phosphorus or magnesium, a difficult calving, mastitis or metritis. Cows that recover are at higher risk of milk fever at their next calving, so prevention planning with your vet is important.

faqs.q: Can I buy a calcium injection from the agrovet and give it myself?
faqs.a: It is not safe to do this yourself. Calcium given into the vein too fast, or at the wrong dose, can upset the heart rhythm and kill the cow on the spot. A vet listens to the heart while giving it slowly. Injections under the skin and oral calcium also need the right product and dose. Oral calcium should never be given to a cow that cannot swallow well. Call your vet or animal health assistant and let them treat her, then follow their advice for any follow-up.

faqs.q: Why does milk fever affect my best cows and not the heifers?
faqs.a: Older cows produce more colostrum and milk, so they lose more calcium suddenly at calving. Their bones also release calcium more slowly than young animals. First-calf heifers make less milk and are still good at moving calcium around, so they rarely get milk fever. Jerseys are especially at risk because their milk is rich in calcium compared with their body size.

faqs.q: Should I feed extra calcium or lime before calving to prevent milk fever?
faqs.a: No. This is one of the most common mistakes. Feeding a lot of calcium in the last few weeks before calving makes the cow rely on her feed for calcium. When she calves, her body has not yet learned to pull calcium from her bones, so her blood levels crash. Keep calcium moderate in the dry period, avoiding big amounts of lucerne, high-calcium mineral mixes and lime, and ask your vet about a proper dry cow ration. After calving, when she is milking, she needs good calcium and phosphorus in her ration.

faqs.q: My cow had milk fever last year. Will she get it again?
faqs.a: She is at higher risk, but it is not certain. Talk to your vet well before her next calving. Common steps include a correct dry cow ration, keeping her from getting fat, enough magnesium, and having oral calcium ready to give at calving under vet advice. Watch her closely from the day before she is due until three days after calving, and call the vet at the first sign of trembling or wobbling.

faqs.q: Is the milk from a cow treated for milk fever safe to drink or sell?
faqs.a: Milk fever itself does not make milk dangerous to people. Plain calcium treatment usually has little or no withdrawal period. But some combined products and any other medicines, such as antibiotics for mastitis or a womb infection, do have milk and meat withdrawal periods. Ask your vet exactly what was given and how long to wait, and keep that milk out of the cooperative tank until the time is over. The colostrum is still valuable for her calf.

faqs.q: Why are her ears cold if it is called 'fever'?
faqs.a: The name is misleading. Milk fever is not an infection and the cow usually does not have a fever. Low calcium weakens the muscles and heart, so blood flow to the ears and legs drops and the body temperature often goes below normal. Cold ears and a low thermometer reading in a freshly calved cow are actually strong clues that it is milk fever and not an infection.

products.role: After calving only, DCP-18 (dicalcium phosphate) can be part of the milking cow's mineral ration to help replace the calcium and phosphorus she loses in milk, which supports bones and steady recovery. It is a nutritional aid alongside vet treatment and a correct dry cow diet, not a treatment for a cow that is down. Do not feed extra calcium sources like this in the last three weeks before calving, because that can increase the risk of milk fever.

Vitamin D3 helps the cow absorb calcium from her gut and release it from her bones, and vitamins A and E support immunity around calving. Ask your vet whether AD3E fits your herd's dry cow and fresh cow plan, and use it only on their advice for timing and amount, because too much vitamin D is harmful. It supports good management and does not replace calcium treatment or a correct dry cow ration.

milk-fever.imagePrompt: A black-and-white Friesian dairy cow lying on her chest on straw bedding in a simple Kenyan zero-grazing shed, her head and neck turned back and resting against her flank, looking dull and drowsy, with a newborn calf standing nearby in soft daylight.
milk-fever.seoDescription: Milk fever in cattle: spot a down cow with cold ears and head turned to flank after calving, what to do before the vet arrives, and how to prevent it in Kenya.

card.headline: Fresh cow off feed, sweet-smelling breath
card.look: A cow that calved a few weeks ago eats less, especially dairy meal, and her milk drops. She loses weight quickly and her breath or milk may smell sweet, like nail-polish remover or overripe fruit.
card.action: Call your vet early, keep the cow eating and drinking with fresh forage and clean water, and do not give any drugs unless the vet prescribes them.

detail.summary: Ketosis is an energy shortage in high-producing cows, usually in the first weeks after calving. The cow's milk needs more energy than she can eat, so she burns body fat too fast. Her blood then fills with ketones, which are acid by-products of fat breakdown. It cuts milk, weakens fertility and opens the door to other fresh-cow diseases. Many cows also have a hidden, mild form with no obvious signs.
detail.cause: After calving, a dairy cow's milk production rises fast, but her appetite rises more slowly. For several weeks she uses more energy than she eats. This gap is called negative energy balance. To fill it, she breaks down body fat and sends it to the liver. The liver can only process so much fat at once. When it is overloaded, it turns the extra fat into ketone bodies (acetone, acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, often called BHB). In small amounts these are a normal fuel. In large amounts they make the cow feel sick, lower her appetite even more and cause the sweet acetone smell. A vicious circle follows: less eating means more fat breakdown, which means more ketones. Fat can also build up inside the liver (fatty liver), which makes the liver work poorly and slows recovery. Ketosis can be primary, caused mainly by poor energy intake, or secondary, triggered when another illness such as a retained placenta, uterine infection (metritis), mastitis, lameness or a displaced stomach stops the cow eating. In some cows high ketone levels affect the brain, causing nervous ketosis. Silage that has fermented badly (butyric silage, which smells rancid like spoilt butter) contains ketone-like compounds and can add to the problem.
spread: Ketosis is not infectious and does not spread from cow to cow, but several cows in a herd can be affected if they share the same poor feeding or management.
Too little energy in the diet after calving, for example poor-quality napier, dry-season stover or not enough dairy meal for the milk being produced, is the main trigger.
Cows that are too fat at calving eat less after calving and mobilise more fat, so they are much more likely to develop ketosis and fatty liver.
Any disease that reduces appetite around calving, such as milk fever, retained placenta, metritis, mastitis, lameness or a displaced abomasum, can tip a cow into secondary ketosis.
Sudden changes of feed around calving, or putting a fresh cow straight onto a large amount of concentrate the rumen is not used to, upset digestion and reduce intake.
Badly fermented, mouldy or spoilt silage and other feeds can lower appetite and add ketone-like compounds to the diet.
Stress from transport, overcrowding, competition at the feed trough, heat or rough handling around calving cuts feed intake.
Shortage of clean drinking water reduces how much a cow eats, especially in hot, dry weather.
detail.atRisk: High-yielding dairy cows (Friesian, Holstein, Ayrshire, Jersey, Guernsey and their crosses) are most at risk, especially in their second lactation onward. Risk is highest from about the first week to the first two months after calving, with most cases in the first month. Cows that were fat at calving, cows with twins, and cows that had a hard calving, retained placenta, milk fever or uterine infection are at higher risk. In Kenya, zero-grazing and semi-zero-grazing dairy units in places like Kiambu, Nyandarua, Nakuru, Uasin Gishu, Meru and Murang'a see it most. Risk rises in the dry season when forage is poor and in herds that rely on low-quality fodder with uneven concentrate feeding. Local zebu and kienyeji cattle producing little milk rarely get the classic form, but any cow that stops eating late in pregnancy can develop a related condition (pregnancy toxaemia or fatty liver).

early: The cow eats less dairy meal first, often still picking at hay or napier, and may refuse concentrates completely.
Milk yield drops over a few days, sometimes sharply, often during the first month after calving.
Her breath, milk or urine may smell sweet, like nail-polish remover or overripe fruit, though not every farmer can smell it.
Dung becomes firmer, drier and smaller in amount than normal for a fresh cow.
She looks dull, stands apart from the others and is slower to come to the trough.
Rumen movements and cudding are reduced; you see her chewing the cud less than usual.
advanced: Rapid weight loss; her hips, ribs and backbone show clearly within a week or two.
She refuses most feed and may drink less, and milk can fall to very low levels.
Nervous signs in some cows: constant licking of the body, walls or objects, chewing movements with drooling, head pressing, circling, staggering or seeming blind.
Some cows with nervous ketosis become excitable or aggressive and may bellow or charge without warning.
Very weak cows may lie down a lot and struggle to rise if fatty liver develops.
Other fresh-cow problems appear or worsen, such as a displaced abomasum, metritis or mastitis.

lookalikes.name: Milk fever (hypocalcaemia)
lookalikes.howToTell: Milk fever usually strikes within one to three days of calving, with wobbling, cold ears, an S-bend in the neck and the cow going down. Ketosis usually comes later, from the first week to a few weeks after calving, with a gradual drop in appetite and milk and often a sweet smell. A cow can have both, and milk fever raises the risk of ketosis.

lookalikes.name: Displaced abomasum (twisted stomach)
lookalikes.howToTell: This also causes a fresh cow to go off feed and drop milk, and it often causes secondary ketosis. The vet confirms it by tapping the left or right side while listening with a stethoscope for a hollow 'ping' sound. Ketosis that does not improve with treatment should always be checked for this.

lookalikes.name: Rabies
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabies can cause bellowing, drooling, aggression and staggering like nervous ketosis, but it gets steadily worse, often with paralysis, straining and death within days, and the cow may have been bitten by a dog. Nervous ketosis is linked to recent calving and usually improves with energy treatment. If in any doubt, treat it as possible rabies: do not put your hand in the mouth and call the vet at once.

lookalikes.name: Metritis or retained placenta
lookalikes.howToTell: A uterine infection causes a smelly, brown or reddish discharge from the vulva, often with fever and a dull, off-feed cow. It can cause secondary ketosis, so both may be present. Check the back end and the discharge and tell the vet.

detail.diagnosis: The vet will ask when the cow calved, how her appetite and milk changed, what she is being fed and whether she had any calving problems. A full examination checks temperature, rumen movement, heart, lungs, udder, uterus and both sides of the abdomen for a displaced abomasum. Ketosis is confirmed with simple cow-side tests: strips dipped in urine or milk that change colour when ketones are present, or a handheld meter that measures BHB in a drop of blood, which is the most accurate on-farm test. The vet will look for any underlying disease, because secondary ketosis will not clear until the cause is treated. In nervous cases, the vet will rule out rabies, heartwater and poisoning. Blood tests for liver function may be used when fatty liver is suspected. To help, write down the calving date, any calving problems, daily milk records, what she eats and in what amounts, recent feed changes and any other sick cows. Keep the cow confined so the vet can examine her easily.
firstSteps: Call your vet or local animal health service as soon as you notice a fresh cow going off feed and dropping milk, because early treatment works far better than late treatment.
Keep the cow in a clean, dry, shaded pen with soft bedding, away from bullying by other cows, so she can eat and rest in peace.
Offer plenty of fresh, palatable, good-quality forage such as leafy napier, good hay or fresh grass, and remove any mouldy or rancid-smelling feed.
Make sure she has constant access to clean, fresh water, placed where she can reach it easily.
Do not suddenly load her with large amounts of dairy meal, as this can upset her rumen; let the vet advise on a safe feeding plan.
Check her back end for a retained placenta or smelly discharge, check the udder for mastitis and take her temperature if you have a thermometer, then tell the vet what you found.
If she shows nervous signs such as licking, head pressing or aggression, keep people and children away, do not put your hand in her mouth, and handle her calmly from behind a barrier.
Record her calving date, milk yield, feed and signs so the vet can make a quick, accurate decision, and do not give any drugs or home drenches without the vet's advice.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment aims to give the cow energy quickly, stop the fat breakdown and fix any underlying disease. The vet commonly gives glucose (dextrose) solution into the vein for a fast energy boost, which often brings quick improvement but wears off within hours. This is usually followed by oral propylene glycol, a liquid energy source drenched by mouth for several days, because it is converted to glucose in the liver. Some vets add a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone to help raise blood sugar, but this is not suitable for every cow, especially pregnant ones or those with infections. Vitamin B12 and cobalt, or other supporting products, may be used in some cases. If there is a displaced abomasum, metritis, mastitis or lameness, the vet will treat that too, sometimes with antibiotics or surgery. Antibiotics do not treat ketosis itself and should only be used when the vet finds an infection, because misuse drives antimicrobial resistance. All doses and schedules must come from the vet. Some drugs used carry milk and meat withdrawal periods, so ask the vet how long to discard milk and hold back from slaughter, and follow it. Mild cases often improve within a few days; cows with fatty liver or another disease may need longer and repeat treatment.
prevention: Manage body condition: aim for cows to be moderate, not fat or thin, at drying off and calving, roughly 3 to 3.5 on the usual 5-point body condition scale; adjust feeding in late lactation rather than in the dry period.

Feed dry cows well but not excessively, with good forage, and in the last two to three weeks before calving introduce a small amount of the dairy meal she will get after calving so the rumen can adjust.
After calving, increase concentrates gradually over a few weeks while offering plenty of good-quality forage, so energy intake rises without upsetting the rumen.
Plan fodder for the dry season by making hay or silage during the long and short rains, and only feed well-made silage; discard silage that smells rancid, is mouldy or is slimy.
Provide a balanced mineral supplement suitable for dairy cattle, including cobalt and other trace elements, and keep clean water available at all times.
Prevent the diseases that trigger ketosis: good calving hygiene, prompt help with hard calvings, milk fever prevention and early treatment of retained placenta, metritis, mastitis and lameness.
Watch every fresh cow closely for the first six weeks: check appetite, cudding, dung and milk daily, and ask your vet about routine ketone testing of high-risk cows.

Reduce stress around calving with enough trough space, a comfortable, clean calving area and minimal regrouping; for high-risk cows, ask the vet whether preventive propylene glycol drenching after calving is worthwhile.
detail.impact: Ketosis costs Kenyan dairy farmers far more than the vet bill. Milk yield falls during the illness, and many cows never reach their full peak that lactation, which means lost daily income from the cooperative or milk buyer. Affected cows are more likely to get a displaced abomasum, metritis and mastitis, each with its own treatment costs. Fertility often suffers: cows come on heat late, need more inseminations and the calving interval stretches, so fewer calves and less milk over the cow's life. Milk may have to be discarded during drug withdrawal periods. Severe cases with fatty liver can lead to early culling or death of a valuable high-grade cow. The hidden, subclinical form, with no clear signs, quietly reduces milk and fertility across a herd, so herds that see a few clinical cases probably have more mild ones.
detail.humanHealth: Ketosis itself is not infectious and cannot pass to people. The main risks are drug residues: some treatments, such as corticosteroids or antibiotics given for linked infections, carry milk and meat withdrawal periods, so discard milk and delay slaughter for as long as the vet advises. If a cow shows nervous signs and rabies has not been ruled out, do not put your hand in her mouth or touch saliva, keep children away and call the vet immediately.
detail.outlook: Most cows with primary ketosis caught early recover well within a few days of treatment and better feeding, and milk usually returns, though often not quite to the level it would have reached. The outlook is less certain when the cow was very fat at calving, has developed fatty liver, has nervous signs that last, or has another disease such as a displaced abomasum or severe metritis. Secondary ketosis only resolves when the underlying illness is fixed. Cows that have had ketosis are more likely to get it again in later lactations, so careful body condition and transition feeding matter. Delay in calling the vet makes recovery slower and the risk of death or culling higher.

faqs.q: Can I just drench my cow with molasses or sugar water?
faqs.a: Molasses and sugar are mostly fermented by microbes in the rumen, so much less of the energy reaches the blood as glucose than people expect. They can help appetite and are a useful part of the diet, but they are not a reliable treatment for ketosis. The vet usually uses glucose into the vein and propylene glycol by mouth. Drenching a weak or nervous cow can also cause choking or feed going into the lungs, so always ask the vet first.

faqs.q: Is the milk from a cow with ketosis safe to drink or sell?
faqs.a: Ketosis is not infectious, so the disease itself does not make milk dangerous. However, the milk may taste odd, and if the cow has been given drugs with a withdrawal period, that milk must be discarded for the full time the vet tells you. Selling milk with drug residues is illegal and can harm consumers and your reputation with the buyer.

faqs.q: Why does my best cow keep getting ketosis every time she calves?
faqs.a: High-yielding cows have a bigger energy gap after calving, so they are naturally more at risk. Repeat cases are often linked to the cow being too fat at calving, poor dry-cow feeding, sudden diet changes or another disease like milk fever or metritis. Work with your vet or extension officer on her body condition in late lactation and a step-by-step feeding plan around calving.

faqs.q: Can I test for ketosis myself at home?
faqs.a: Yes, cow-side test strips for urine or milk, and handheld blood BHB meters, are available through some agrovets and vets. They are useful for checking fresh cows in the first weeks after calving. A positive test still needs a vet visit, because the vet must find out whether another disease is causing it and decide on treatment.

faqs.q: My cow is licking the walls and acting strange after calving. Is it ketosis or rabies?
faqs.a: Nervous ketosis can cause licking, chewing, head pressing and aggression in a recently calved cow, but rabies can look similar. You cannot safely tell them apart yourself. Keep away from her mouth and saliva, keep children away, confine her safely and call the vet immediately. If rabies is suspected, the vet will advise on reporting and precautions.

faqs.q: Do local zebu or kienyeji cattle get ketosis?
faqs.a: Classic ketosis is rare in cattle that produce little milk, because their energy needs after calving are much lower. However, any cow that stops eating around calving, especially if she is fat or carrying twins, can develop fatty liver or a similar energy problem. Good feeding in late pregnancy and early lactation helps all cattle.

products.role: Can be used, alongside the vet's energy treatment and improved feeding, to support liver function and digestion in fresh cows under the strain of fat breakdown and a reduced appetite. It does not treat ketosis or replace glucose or propylene glycol from the vet.
