Where silage, maize or dairy meal may be mouldy, adding this mycotoxin binder to the feed of transition and fresh cows helps protect them from toxins that can suppress appetite and burden the liver. It supports prevention only and does not replace good-quality feed or vet treatment.

ketosis.imagePrompt: A thin black-and-white Friesian dairy cow standing dull and head-low in a Kenyan zero-grazing stall, ignoring a full trough of chopped napier grass and dairy meal, with her hip bones and ribs clearly visible, in soft natural daylight.
ketosis.seoDescription: Ketosis in dairy cows: spot the sweet acetone breath, falling milk and appetite after calving, what to do before the vet comes, and how to prevent it.

card.headline: Left side of belly swollen high, tight
card.look: The left flank, the hollow just in front of the hip bone, balloons outward and may rise above the line of the backbone. It feels tight like a drum when tapped. The animal stops eating, looks uncomfortable, and breathes fast or through the mouth.
card.action: Remove the animal from the feed at once, keep it standing and walking slowly, and call your vet immediately, because bloat can kill within an hour or two.

detail.summary: Bloat is a build-up of gas in the rumen, the large first stomach of a cow, that the animal cannot belch out. The swollen rumen presses on the lungs and heart, so the animal struggles to breathe and can die quickly, sometimes before the farmer even notices. It often follows a change to lush legumes such as lucerne, clover or desmodium, or heavy grain feeding. It can also follow a blockage in the throat. It is an emergency, but with fast action and good feeding management most cases can be saved and most outbreaks prevented.
detail.cause: A healthy cow produces large amounts of gas every day as rumen microbes ferment feed, and she gets rid of it by belching, called eructation. Bloat happens when this belching fails. There are two main types. In frothy bloat, which is the most common type on pasture and in zero-grazing units feeding legumes, certain feeds release proteins and fine particles that make the rumen contents foamy. The gas is trapped in millions of tiny stable bubbles, like the foam on a shaken soda, and the cow cannot belch it out. Lush young lucerne, clover and desmodium, especially when wet, and finely ground grain rations are common triggers. In free-gas bloat, the gas forms a normal pocket on top of the rumen contents, but something physically stops it escaping. Common causes are choke, which is an object such as a whole potato, avocado, maize cob, mango or piece of sugar cane stuck in the food pipe (oesophagus). Other causes are milk fever (low blood calcium) that stops the rumen muscles working, a cow lying flat on her side for a long time, nerve damage from hardware disease (a swallowed wire or nail), tetanus, and swollen glands or growths in the chest pressing on the food pipe. In both types, the rumen swells, pushes forward against the diaphragm (the muscle sheet that helps breathing), squeezes the lungs and slows blood returning to the heart. Death comes from lack of oxygen and heart failure.
spread: Bloat is not infectious and does not spread from animal to animal, but several animals can bloat at the same time because they share the same feed.
Turning hungry cattle onto lush lucerne, clover or desmodium, or giving them a large load of freshly cut legume, is the classic trigger for frothy bloat.
Grazing or feeding legumes that are wet with morning dew or rain, or very young pre-flowering growth after the long or short rains, raises the risk sharply.

Sudden changes to rations high in finely ground grain, maize meal, wheat bran or other concentrates with too little long roughage can cause feedlot-type frothy bloat and is often linked with acidosis.
Cattle getting into a maize or sorghum store, a heap of brewer's waste, or a field of crop residues they are not used to can bloat.
Whole or large pieces of potatoes, avocados, fruits, root crops, maize cobs or plastic can lodge in the throat and cause free-gas bloat from choke.
Other illnesses, especially milk fever after calving and hardware disease, can cause bloat as a complication rather than feed being the cause.
A cow that falls and is stuck on her side or back, for example in a narrow crush or a ditch, can bloat within a short time because she cannot belch in that position.
detail.atRisk: Any ruminant can bloat, but adult cattle on high-quality feed are most at risk. Dairy cows in zero-grazing units fed cut lucerne or desmodium, grade cows in high-potential areas grazing lush pasture after the rains, and fattening or feedlot cattle on heavy grain rations are the classic risk groups. Some animals and some family lines seem more prone to bloat than others, and an animal that has bloated before is more likely to do it again. Hungry cattle that gorge, for example after a long trek, after being kept off feed for treatment, or after a dry spell, are at higher risk. Calves can suffer bloat too, often linked to milk feeding problems or digestive upsets. Recently calved cows with milk fever, and animals with choke from feeding whole potatoes or avocados, are at risk of free-gas bloat. The long and short rain seasons, when legumes and pastures grow quickly and are full of water and protein, are the most dangerous times.

early: The left flank, the triangular hollow between the last rib and the hip bone, starts to fill out and look rounder than the right side.
The animal stops eating suddenly, even in front of good feed, and stops chewing the cud.
Restlessness and discomfort: getting up and lying down often, shifting weight, kicking at the belly or looking round at the left side.
Frequent passing of small amounts of dung and urine.
Tapping the left flank with your fingers gives a hollow, drum-like sound, and the skin feels tight.
Other animals in the same group may show similar mild swelling, which suggests a feed cause.
advanced: The left flank is hugely swollen and may rise above the line of the backbone; in severe cases the right side swells too.
Fast, laboured breathing with the mouth open, tongue hanging out, neck stretched forward and head held low.
Drooling of saliva, grunting or groaning, and in choke cases, repeated attempts to swallow or drool from the mouth.
Staggering, unwillingness to move, then going down and being unable to get up.
Bluish or very dark gums and tongue from lack of oxygen.
Collapse and death, which can happen within about an hour of signs starting in severe frothy bloat; sometimes the first sign a farmer sees is a dead, bloated animal.

lookalikes.name: Anthrax
lookalikes.howToTell: Anthrax also causes sudden death and a bloated carcass, but there is often dark, tarry blood that does not clot oozing from the nose, mouth, anus or vulva, and the body may not stiffen normally. If an animal is found dead and bloated with no clear feed cause, especially with bleeding from openings, do NOT open the carcass. Anthrax is notifiable, so call the vet and report it. All dead animals swell with gas after death, so a bloated carcass alone does not prove the animal died of bloat.

lookalikes.name: Grain overload (rumen acidosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Acidosis follows eating a large amount of grain or concentrate. The main signs are depression, watery sour-smelling diarrhoea, lameness, weakness and dehydration over several hours, rather than a rapidly swelling drum-tight left flank. Bloat may appear as part of it, so tell the vet exactly what and how much the animal ate.

lookalikes.name: Hardware disease (traumatic reticuloperitonitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: A swallowed wire or nail causes a cow to stand with an arched back, elbows out, grunt when moving or when pressed under the chest, and be reluctant to walk downhill. Any bloat is usually milder and comes back again and again over days, rather than being a sudden severe swelling after feeding.

lookalikes.name: Milk fever (hypocalcaemia)
lookalikes.howToTell: Milk fever affects cows around calving, usually high-producing older cows. The cow becomes wobbly, cold-eared, then lies down with her head turned into her flank and cannot rise. Bloat develops because the rumen stops moving, so a recently calved cow that is down and bloated needs the vet to treat the low calcium as well as release the gas.

detail.diagnosis: Bloat is usually diagnosed on the spot from the history and what the vet sees: a swollen left flank, a drum-like sound when tapped, and signs of distress. The key question for the vet is which type it is, because treatment is different. The vet passes a stomach tube through the mouth down into the rumen. If large amounts of gas rush out and the swelling goes down, it is free-gas bloat, and the vet will then look for the cause, such as an object stuck in the throat, milk fever or hardware disease. If little gas comes out and the tube fills with froth, it is frothy bloat. The vet may feel along the neck for a stuck object and examine the mouth. If an animal has died, a post-mortem can show changes such as a congested upper food pipe with a pale section inside the chest, known as a bloat line, which helps separate death from bloat from normal swelling after death. Post-mortem should only be done by a vet, because anthrax must be ruled out first. To help, tell the vet exactly what the animals ate in the last 24 hours, including any change in feed, fresh lucerne or desmodium, grain or kitchen waste, when the swelling started, how many animals are affected, and whether the animal has calved recently or bloated before.
firstSteps: Remove the animal, and the rest of the herd, from the suspected feed immediately, whether it is a lucerne field, a desmodium plot or a trough of concentrate.
Call your vet or the nearest animal health assistant at once and describe the swelling, breathing and what the animal ate, because severe bloat can kill within an hour or two.
Keep the animal standing and walk it slowly and gently; movement helps the rumen work and belching, while lying flat on its side makes bloat much worse.
If possible, stand the animal with its front feet higher than its back feet, for example facing uphill, to take pressure off the chest and help gas move towards the throat.

Do not force-drench liquids into a distressed, struggling or choking animal, because liquid can go into the lungs and cause fatal pneumonia; give anything by mouth only if your vet tells you to over the phone.

If you suspect choke, look in the mouth carefully from the side of the head without putting your arm deep inside, and do not push objects down the throat with sticks or wires, which can tear the food pipe.
Check the rest of the group closely every 15 to 30 minutes for swelling of the left flank, and move all of them onto dry hay or grass.
Write down what was fed, how much, and when, and the time signs started, so the vet can decide on treatment and prevention quickly.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how severe the bloat is and which type it is, and must be carried out or prescribed by a vet. For free-gas bloat, passing a stomach tube usually releases the gas quickly and the animal improves within minutes. The vet then deals with the cause, for example gently removing or moving an object from the throat in choke, or giving calcium for milk fever. For frothy bloat, a tube alone does not help much because the gas is trapped in foam. The vet gives an anti-foaming agent through the tube or by mouth to break down the bubbles so the gas can be belched or released. Commonly used products include poloxalene, silicone-based agents such as dimethicone, surfactants such as docusate, and vegetable or mineral oils. In life-threatening cases where the animal is about to collapse, the vet may puncture the rumen through the left flank with a trocar and cannula (a sharp hollow tube) to let gas out quickly. In very severe frothy bloat, an emergency surgical opening of the rumen, called rumenotomy, may be the only option. After the crisis, the vet may give supportive treatment, and antibiotics only if there is a clear reason such as infection at a trocar puncture site or aspiration pneumonia; antibiotics do not treat bloat itself and unnecessary use drives antimicrobial resistance. If any drugs are given, follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods your vet tells you and on the label, and do not sell milk or slaughter the animal until the period is over. Expect the animal to be dull and eat less for a day or two; offer good grass hay and clean water, and keep it off legumes and concentrates until the vet advises.
prevention: Introduce lucerne, clover, desmodium and other legumes gradually over one to two weeks, starting with small amounts mixed into grass or hay, so the rumen microbes can adjust.
Never turn hungry cattle onto lush legume pasture; give them a feed of dry hay, maize stover or mature grass first so they are not gorging.
Avoid grazing or feeding legumes when they are wet with dew or rain, or when very young and lush; wait until later in the day, or cut and wilt the fodder for a few hours before feeding.
Keep legumes as a part of the diet rather than the whole meal; mixed grass and legume pastures, or mixing cut legumes with Napier grass, Rhodes grass or hay, greatly reduce the risk.

For grain and concentrate feeding, change rations slowly, avoid very finely ground grain, and always provide enough long roughage such as hay or stover so cattle keep chewing and producing saliva, which protects the rumen.
Chop or slice potatoes, avocados, root crops, mangoes and other bulky foods into small pieces, keep cattle away from fruit trees with fallen fruit, and clear plastic bags and wire from feeding areas.

Ask your vet about anti-bloat products such as poloxalene or ionophore feed additives for herds on high-risk legume or grain diets; these must be used as directed by a vet and need to be fed daily during risky periods to work.

Manage milk fever risk in close-up dry cows with good transition feeding and vet advice, check the herd more often during the rains and after any feed change, and consider culling animals that bloat again and again.
detail.impact: Bloat often kills the best animals on the farm, the high-producing dairy cows and well-fed fattening steers eating the richest feed. A single death of an in-calf grade cow is a heavy loss for a smallholder, as it removes milk income, the future calf and the capital value of the animal at once. Animals that survive usually drop sharply in milk yield for a few days and may lose condition. Repeated mild bloat in a herd reduces feed intake and growth quietly over time. There are also costs for emergency vet visits, and milk that must be discarded during drug withdrawal. Fear of bloat can make farmers avoid legumes like lucerne and desmodium altogether, losing their great value as cheap protein, so learning to feed them safely brings strong economic benefit.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good if bloat is caught early and the animal gets help quickly. Most cases of free-gas bloat respond fast once the gas is released and the cause is dealt with, although choke, hardware disease or chest problems can make it come back. Frothy bloat treated early with anti-foaming agents usually resolves within hours. The outlook is poor when an animal is already down, mouth-breathing heavily or has blue gums, because the heart and lungs may be badly affected; some die even with treatment. Delays are the main reason animals are lost, as severe bloat can kill in under an hour. Complications such as inhaled liquid from forced drenching, infection at a puncture site, or the underlying disease also affect recovery. Animals with recurring bloat may need long-term feeding changes or culling.

faqs.q: Can I give my cow cooking oil for bloat?
faqs.a: Vegetable oil is one of the anti-foaming substances vets use for frothy bloat, and many farmers have used it with success. However, it does not help free-gas bloat from choke, and forcing liquid into a cow that is struggling, choking or breathing with her mouth open can send it into the lungs and kill her from pneumonia. Call your vet first. If the vet advises an oil drench over the phone and the animal can swallow normally, give it slowly, with the head only slightly raised, and stop if she coughs. Never use paraffin, petrol, detergents or other household chemicals.

faqs.q: Should I stab the cow's side with a knife to let the gas out?
faqs.a: Puncturing the rumen is a last-resort life-saving step that vets do with a proper trocar and cannula. A kitchen knife makes a wound that leaks rumen contents into the belly and often causes fatal infection, and it does not release froth well. If you live far from a vet and keep high-risk cattle, ask your vet in advance to show you the correct site and method and to recommend a trocar to keep on the farm. Otherwise, keep the animal walking, keep the front end higher, and get the vet.

faqs.q: Why did only one or two cows bloat when all ate the same lucerne?
faqs.a: Animals differ. Some eat faster or more, some produce less saliva, which naturally helps break down foam, and some individuals and family lines are simply more prone to bloat. A cow that has bloated before is more likely to do so again. When one animal in a group bloats, treat it as a warning that the whole group is at risk and change the feeding for all of them.

faqs.q: Is desmodium from push-pull plots safe for my dairy cows?
faqs.a: Desmodium is a valuable protein fodder and many Kenyan farmers feed it safely. Like other legumes, it can cause bloat if fed in large amounts alone, especially when fresh, young and wet. Wilt it for a few hours after cutting, chop it, mix it with Napier grass or other grasses, and introduce it gradually. Feeding roughage first and avoiding it on an empty stomach lowers the risk further.

faqs.q: I found a cow dead and swollen in the morning. Was it bloat?
faqs.a: Maybe, but you cannot be sure. Every dead animal swells with gas within hours of death, and other sudden killers like anthrax, lightning, poisoning and East Coast fever can look similar. Do not open the carcass or let anyone cut it for meat, especially if there is dark blood from the nose, mouth or anus. Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to examine it safely. Knowing the true cause protects the rest of your herd and your family.

faqs.q: How soon can a cow go back to legumes after bloating?
faqs.a: Follow your vet's advice. Usually the animal is kept on grass hay, stover or mature grass for a few days until she is eating and cudding normally. Legumes are then brought back slowly in small amounts mixed with grass, increasing over one to two weeks. If she bloats again, she may need permanent limits on legumes or a vet-prescribed anti-bloat additive.

products.role: Only after the vet has resolved the bloat and the animal is swallowing normally, K-DIGEST can be used as a digestive stress support aid while the rumen settles and appetite returns. It does not release gas, break down froth or treat bloat, so never use it instead of calling the vet, and do not drench it into a bloated or struggling animal.

bloat.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a Friesian dairy cow standing in a Kenyan zero-grazing shed, viewed from behind and slightly to the left, with the left flank visibly ballooned high and tight above the hip line compared with the right, the cow standing with neck stretched forward, natural daylight, no people.
bloat.seoDescription: Cattle bloat: spot a swollen left flank early, act fast before the vet arrives, and prevent frothy and free-gas bloat from lucerne, desmodium and grain.

card.headline: Swollen foot with stinking crack between claws
card.look: The cow is suddenly lame on one foot, and the skin just above the hoof is hot and swollen so the two claws spread apart. Between the claws there is a split or crack with grey, dead-looking tissue and a strong rotten smell.
card.action: Move the lame animal to a clean, dry, soft-floored pen, gently wash the foot with clean water to look between the claws, and call your vet promptly.

detail.summary: Foot rot is a bacterial infection of the soft skin and tissue between the two claws of a cow's foot. It causes sudden, painful lameness, swelling above the hoof and a foul-smelling crack between the claws. It is one of several common causes of lameness in Kenyan cattle, alongside sole ulcers and laminitis, which are also covered briefly here. Lameness matters because a cow in pain eats less, walks less, gives less milk, loses weight and may fail to get back in calf, and untreated foot rot can spread deep into the joint.
detail.cause: Foot rot is mainly caused by a bacterium called Fusobacterium necrophorum, often working together with other bacteria such as Porphyromonas and Prevotella species. These germs live naturally in the gut and dung of cattle and survive in mud, manure and wet bedding. They cannot easily get through healthy, dry skin. Trouble starts when the skin between the claws is softened by constant wetness or damaged by stones, thorns, sticks, stubble or rough concrete. The bacteria enter through the small wound and release toxins (poisons) that kill the surrounding tissue. This is called necrosis, meaning tissue death, and it is what produces the grey, dead-looking material and the very bad smell. The body reacts with inflammation, so the foot becomes hot, swollen and very painful. If not treated, the infection can travel deeper into the tendons, the coffin joint (the joint inside the hoof) and bone, which is much harder to treat and may end the cow's productive life. Sole ulcers and laminitis are different problems. Laminitis is inflammation of the corium, the sensitive living layer inside the hoof that produces horn. It is most often linked to rumen acidosis, a condition where too much grain or concentrate and too little fibre makes the rumen too acidic, releasing harmful substances into the blood that damage the corium. Weak, poor-quality horn then grows, leading to bruising, sole ulcers (an open sore in the sole, usually near the heel of the outer hind claw) and white line disease (separation where the sole meets the wall).
spread: Wet, muddy conditions during the long and short rains soften the skin between the claws and let bacteria get in, so cases often rise in rainy months.
Dirty, dung-filled walkways, kraals, bomas and zero-grazing units keep feet constantly wet and full of bacteria.
Sharp stones, thorns, maize stubble, broken concrete and rough murram tracks cause small cuts that bacteria can enter.
Infected cows shed large numbers of bacteria from their feet onto the ground, bedding and water points, contaminating the area for other cattle.
Crowding at gates, water troughs, crushes and milking areas increases contact with contaminated mud and dung.
Buying in cattle without checking their feet, or sharing grazing and watering points with other herds, can bring in more bacteria.

For laminitis and sole ulcers, sudden increases in dairy meal or grain, low-fibre diets, long hours standing on hard concrete, poorly trimmed hooves and the stress around calving are the main triggers.
detail.atRisk: Any cattle can get foot rot, from calves to old bulls, but adult dairy cows are most often affected. Zero-grazed cows standing in wet, dung-covered concrete units, cattle walking long distances on stony tracks to water, and herds kept in muddy kraals or bomas overnight are all at high risk. Cases usually increase during and just after the long and short rains, but in very dry, hot conditions cracked, dry skin can also let infection in. High-producing exotic dairy breeds such as Friesian/Holstein and Ayrshire, and their crosses, tend to suffer more from laminitis and sole ulcers because they are fed more concentrate and often housed on concrete. Cows in the weeks around calving are especially vulnerable because their hoof tissue softens and their diet often changes suddenly. Animals with poor nutrition, especially low zinc, vitamin A or overall poor body condition, may have weaker skin and horn. Pastoral herds are generally less affected by laminitis but can still get foot rot around wet watering points.

early: Sudden lameness in one foot, often appearing over a day or two; the cow may hold the foot up or touch it to the ground only lightly.
Swelling of the skin just above the hoof (the coronet) and between the claws, usually even on both sides of the foot.
The two claws start to spread apart because of the swelling between them.
The foot feels warm or hot to the touch and the cow flinches or pulls away when you press it.
The cow is slower to walk to feed and water, lags behind the herd, lies down more and may eat less.
A drop in milk yield, sometimes noticed before the lameness is obvious.
advanced: A split or crack in the skin between the claws with grey, yellowish or cheesy dead tissue.
A strong, rotten, very unpleasant smell from the foot that is typical of foot rot.
Swelling spreading up the leg towards the fetlock, and the cow refusing to put any weight on the foot.
Fever, dullness and marked loss of appetite and body condition.
Pus coming out above the hoof or at the heel, or a hugely swollen, very painful single claw, which can mean the infection has reached the joint or tendon.

For laminitis: cows standing with an arched back, shifting weight, walking stiffly on several feet, with yellow or reddish bruising, ridges or softened horn on the soles and, later, sole ulcers near the heel.

lookalikes.name: Digital dermatitis (hairy heel warts, 'strawberry foot')
lookalikes.howToTell: Digital dermatitis causes a red, raw, strawberry-like or hairy, wart-like sore, usually at the back of the foot just above the heels, not deep in the cleft. There is usually little or no swelling of the whole foot and no cracked, rotting skin between the claws, though the cow is very sensitive to touch. It spreads quickly through a housed herd.

lookalikes.name: Sole ulcer, white line disease or a stone or nail in the sole
lookalikes.howToTell: These problems are in the horny sole or wall, not the skin between the claws. Swelling above the hoof is usually absent or limited to one claw. When the foot is lifted and pared by a trimmer or vet, you find a bruise, hole, black track or foreign object in the sole or along the white line, often on the outer claw of a hind foot.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
lookalikes.howToTell: FMD is a notifiable viral disease. It usually affects many animals at once, with blisters and raw sores in the mouth, on the tongue and teats as well as between the claws, heavy drooling, smacking of the lips, high fever and a sharp milk drop. Foot rot usually affects one foot of one or a few animals with no mouth sores. If you see mouth blisters or many lame animals at once, report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Interdigital fibroma (corn) or injured joint
lookalikes.howToTell: A corn is a firm, fleshy lump of tissue growing between the claws, which may become infected but grows slowly over weeks rather than appearing suddenly. A sprain, fracture or septic joint higher up the leg causes lameness with swelling at the fetlock, knee or hock rather than at the foot itself, and no foul smell from the cleft.

detail.diagnosis: Foot rot is usually diagnosed by the vet on the farm by examining the foot. The vet will restrain the cow safely, often in a crush with the leg lifted, clean the foot and look closely between the claws for the typical cracked, dead tissue and smell, with even swelling of both claws. They will check the sole and white line by paring with a hoof knife to rule out sole ulcers, white line disease, stones or nails, and look at the back of the foot for digital dermatitis. They will also check the mouth and the rest of the herd to rule out foot-and-mouth disease. If the foot is badly swollen, the vet may test whether the infection has reached the joint, and in some cases may suggest an X-ray or sampling, although this is not common in field practice in Kenya. Laboratory tests for the bacteria are rarely needed. For laminitis and sole ulcers the vet will also ask about the diet, how much concentrate is fed and how it was changed, housing and recent calvings. To help, have the cow ready in a crush or safe handling area, note which foot is lame and when it started, how many animals are lame, what you feed (especially dairy meal), any recent rain or change in housing, and any treatments already given.
firstSteps: Move the lame cow to a clean, dry, well-bedded pen or a dry paddock close to feed and water, so she does not have to walk far or stand in mud and dung.
Gently wash the foot with clean water and look between the claws, at the heel and on the sole; note any crack, smell, stone, nail or wound, and remove loose debris if you can do so safely.
Make sure she has easy access to clean drinking water, good fodder and shade, because lame cows often eat and drink less.

Check the mouth, tongue and teats of the lame cow and look over the rest of the herd; if you see blisters, drooling or many lame animals, stop all movement and call the County Veterinary Officer at once.
Call your vet or animal health assistant promptly, because foot rot responds best when treated early, before infection goes deep.
Do not cut deeply into the foot, apply harsh chemicals such as battery acid, used engine oil or undiluted disinfectants, or give leftover antibiotics without a vet's prescription.
Wear gloves when handling the infected foot, wash your hands afterwards, and clean any tools so you do not carry bacteria to other animals.
Record the date, which foot, the signs you see, milk yield and any treatment, so you and the vet can track recovery and spot patterns in your herd.
detail.vetTreatment: Foot rot usually responds well to prompt treatment. The vet will clean the foot thoroughly and gently remove dead tissue from between the claws. A topical antiseptic or antibiotic spray may be applied, and sometimes the foot is bandaged and kept dry for a short time. Because the infection is under the skin, most cases also need a course of antibiotics given by injection. Drugs commonly used include penicillins, oxytetracycline, sulfonamides and, in some situations, cephalosporins such as ceftiofur; the vet chooses the drug, dose and length of course for your animal. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs, such as meloxicam or flunixin) are often given to reduce pain and swelling, which helps the cow get up, eat and keep producing. Most cows begin walking better within a few days, but you should call the vet back if there is no clear improvement, because this may mean deep infection of the joint or tendon, which may need surgery, claw amputation or culling. For sole ulcers and white line disease, the main treatment is corrective hoof trimming to take weight off the sore claw, often by gluing a block onto the healthy claw, together with pain relief. Laminitis is managed by correcting the diet, increasing fibre and reducing concentrates, soft bedding, trimming, and pain relief. All drugs used in cattle have milk and meat withdrawal periods, meaning milk must be thrown away and animals must not be slaughtered for a set time after treatment. Ask your vet for the exact withdrawal period and follow it strictly. Use antibiotics only when prescribed and complete the full course, because misuse speeds up antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines, a serious problem for both animals and people.
prevention: Keep walkways, gates, water points and zero-grazing units as dry and clean as possible: scrape out dung daily, improve drainage, raise or gravel muddy areas and fix leaking troughs, especially during the long and short rains.
Remove sharp stones, thorns, broken concrete, nails, wire and stubble from areas where cattle walk, and repair rough or broken floors in cow units.
Provide clean, dry, comfortable lying areas such as cubicles with mats, sand or dry bedding, so cows spend less time standing in wet dung.

Use a footbath regularly where foot problems are common, with a product such as copper sulphate or zinc sulphate prepared according to the label or your vet's advice; change the solution often, wash feet before the bath if possible, and dispose of used solution safely away from water sources.
Arrange regular hoof trimming by a trained trimmer, often before calving and around mid-lactation in dairy herds, to keep weight evenly spread and catch sole ulcers early.
Feed a balanced diet with enough long fibre such as good hay, napier grass or silage, introduce dairy meal and grain gradually, and avoid sudden diet changes, to reduce rumen acidosis and laminitis.

Make sure the ration supplies enough minerals and vitamins, particularly zinc, vitamin A and biotin, which support healthy skin and horn; ask your vet or nutritionist about a suitable mineral lick or premix.

Check and treat lame animals early, isolate infected cows until healed, and inspect the feet of new animals before mixing them with the herd. Vaccines against foot rot exist in some countries but are not widely available in Kenya, so management remains the main tool.
detail.impact: Lameness is one of the most costly problems on Kenyan dairy farms, even though it rarely kills. A lame cow eats less and walks less to feed and water, so milk yield can drop sharply, and recovery of yield may be slow. Milk must also be discarded during and after antibiotic treatment because of withdrawal periods, adding to the loss. Lame cows lose body condition, show heat less clearly and often take longer to get back in calf, lengthening the calving interval and reducing the number of calves and lactations over a cow's life. Treatment, vet visits, hoof trimming and extra labour add direct costs. Severe or repeated cases, especially sole ulcers and deep joint infections, are a common reason for early culling, often at low prices because of poor condition. In beef and draught animals, lameness slows weight gain and reduces working ability. For smallholders with only a few cows, one chronically lame cow can cut household income noticeably.
detail.humanHealth: Foot rot is not considered a disease that spreads from cattle to people in normal farm work, although the bacteria involved can occasionally cause infections in people with open wounds, so wear gloves, cover cuts and wash hands after handling infected feet. The main human health risk is drug residues: milk and meat from cows treated with antibiotics or painkillers must not be consumed or sold until the full withdrawal period stated by the vet or on the label has passed. Footbath chemicals such as formalin and copper sulphate can harm people and the environment; formalin in particular irritates the eyes, skin and lungs and is a cancer risk, so use protective gloves and eye protection, work in open air, keep chemicals away from children, food and water sources, and follow label instructions.
detail.outlook: Most cases of simple foot rot recover well, often within days to a couple of weeks, when the cow is treated early by a vet and kept in a clean, dry place. Recovery is slower and less certain if treatment is delayed, if the cow keeps standing in mud and dung, or if infection has spread into the joint, tendon or bone; these deep infections may need surgery or lead to culling. Sole ulcers take several weeks to heal and often return in the same cow, especially if diet, flooring and trimming are not improved. Laminitis can leave long-term damage to the hoof, causing repeated problems. The outlook for the herd depends strongly on fixing the cause: drier, cleaner walkways, good bedding, regular trimming and a balanced, fibre-rich diet greatly reduce new cases.

faqs.q: Can I treat foot rot myself with antibiotics from the agrovet?
faqs.a: It is best to have a vet or animal health assistant examine the foot first. Several conditions look similar, including sole ulcers, stones, digital dermatitis and foot-and-mouth disease, and they need different treatment. Antibiotics should only be used when prescribed, with the right drug, dose and length of course, and you must follow the milk and meat withdrawal period. Using leftover or wrong antibiotics can fail to cure the cow and helps create drug-resistant germs.

faqs.q: Why do I get more lame cows during the rains?
faqs.a: Constant mud and wet dung soften the skin between the claws, making it easy for bacteria and small injuries to get in. The rains also make walkways and kraals dirtier and slippery. Improving drainage, scraping dung often, raising feeding and watering areas and providing a dry lying place can greatly reduce cases in the wet season.

faqs.q: Is foot rot the same as foot-and-mouth disease?
faqs.a: No. Foot rot is a bacterial infection of usually one foot, with swelling, a crack between the claws and a rotten smell, and it is not notifiable. Foot-and-mouth disease is a notifiable viral disease that causes blisters in the mouth, drooling, high fever and lameness in many animals at once. If you see mouth sores or several animals suddenly lame, stop animal movement and report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

faqs.q: Can I milk my cow and sell the milk while she has foot rot?
faqs.a: Foot rot itself does not make milk dangerous, but if the cow is treated with antibiotics or other drugs, the milk must be thrown away for the full withdrawal period your vet gives you. Selling milk with drug residues is illegal and can harm consumers and cause milk to be rejected at the cooling centre or processor. Keep a record of the treatment date so you know when the milk is safe again.

faqs.q: Does feeding a lot of dairy meal cause lameness?
faqs.a: It can contribute. Large amounts of dairy meal or grain, especially when increased suddenly and with too little roughage, can make the rumen too acidic. This can lead to laminitis, which weakens the hoof and causes sole ulcers and white line disease weeks later. Increase concentrates gradually, split them into several small feeds a day, and always provide plenty of good fibre such as napier grass, hay or silage.

faqs.q: How often should my cows go through a footbath?
faqs.a: It depends on how many lame cows you have, the season and the product used. Herds with frequent foot problems often use a footbath regularly, sometimes more often in the rainy season. Follow the product label and your vet's advice on strength and frequency, change the solution when it is dirty, and remember that a footbath helps prevent infections but does not replace clean, dry housing or veterinary treatment of lame cows.

products.role: Vitamin A helps keep skin and the tissues of the foot healthy, and vitamins D3 and E support normal bone and immune function. Where a vet or nutritionist judges the diet to be short of these vitamins, for example in dry seasons with poor forage, AD3E can support skin and hoof health and recovery alongside vet treatment of foot rot, clean dry housing and a balanced ration. It does not treat the infection.

foot-rot.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a dairy cow's lifted front foot on a Kenyan farm, showing the two claws spread apart with a swollen, reddened coronet and a visible greyish crack in the skin between the claws, muddy ground in soft focus behind.
foot-rot.seoDescription: Foot rot in cattle: spot sudden lameness, swelling and a foul-smelling crack between claws, plus sole ulcers and laminitis. First steps and prevention in Kenya.

card.headline: Cloudy blue-white patch on the eye
card.look: The eye waters heavily, the animal squints or keeps it shut, and the white of the eye is red. A cloudy blue-white patch, often with a white spot or pit in the centre, appears on the clear front of the eye.
card.action: Move the animal into shade away from flies and dust, check the rest of the herd's eyes, and call your vet early, because prompt treatment saves eyesight.

aka: Ugonjwa wa macho (general Swahili for eye disease)
detail.summary: Pinkeye is a painful, contagious eye infection of cattle caused mainly by the bacterium Moraxella bovis. It inflames the conjunctiva (the pink lining of the eyelids) and the cornea (the clear front window of the eye), and can cause an ulcer that leads to scarring or blindness. It spreads fast through a herd when flies are many, the weather is dry and dusty, or grass is tall and seeding. It is rarely fatal, but it costs farmers through lost weight, lower milk, treatment and blind animals.
detail.cause: The main cause is Moraxella bovis, a bacterium that lives in the eyes and noses of some cattle without causing harm. It becomes a problem when the surface of the eye is damaged first, for example by strong sunlight (ultraviolet light), dust, wind, grass seeds and awns, or the feet and mouths of flies feeding on tears. Once the surface is scratched, the bacteria stick to the cornea and release toxins that kill the cells on its surface. This creates an ulcer, which is a raw hole in the clear layer of the eye. The eye responds with tears, swelling and redness, and the cornea fills with fluid, which gives the blue-white cloudy look. Blood vessels then grow in from the edge to heal it, which is why a pink or red ring sometimes appears around the patch. Other germs can join in or make it worse, including Moraxella bovoculi, Mycoplasma and the IBR virus (infectious bovine rhinotracheitis). Lack of vitamin A, which keeps the eye surface healthy, can also make cattle more likely to be affected. In severe cases the ulcer becomes so deep that the eye bulges forward or bursts, and the animal loses sight in that eye permanently.
spread: Flies are the most important spreaders: they feed on the tears of an infected animal and carry bacteria on their legs and mouths to the eyes of the next animal.
Direct contact between cattle, such as rubbing heads, sharing feed troughs or crowding at water points, passes infected tears from eye to eye.
Dust from dry paddocks, roads and bomas scratches the eye surface and opens the way for infection.
Tall grass with seed heads, thorny bush and stemmy hay scratch eyes while grazing or feeding, especially when cattle push their heads into hay racks.
Strong sunlight during the dry season damages the eye surface, particularly in cattle with white faces and pink, unpigmented eyelids.
Carrier animals that look healthy can keep the bacteria in the herd from one season to the next and start new outbreaks.
People can carry infection on hands, cloths and equipment when they examine or treat one animal's eyes and then touch another's.
detail.atRisk: Young cattle, especially calves and weaners under about two years old, are most often affected because they have not yet built immunity. Breeds with white faces and pink eyelid skin, such as Herefords and some Friesian and Simmental crosses, suffer more because sunlight damages their eyes more easily, while Boran and other zebu cattle with dark pigmented eyelids tend to be less affected, although they can still get it. Outbreaks are most common in the hot, dry months and as the grass dries and seeds after the rains, when flies, dust and sunlight are all high. Animals grazing tall, seeding pasture, feeding from overhead hay racks, or crowded in dusty bomas and feedlots are at higher risk. In pastoral systems, herds that walk long distances on dusty tracks and share water points with many other herds are exposed often. Zero-grazed animals are not immune, especially where manure builds up and attracts flies or where they feed on coarse, dusty hay. Animals that are short of vitamin A, for example on dry, bleached pasture for long periods, or that have IBR, are also more likely to get pinkeye.

early: Heavy watering of one or both eyes, with wet tear stains running down the face that attract flies.
Squinting or keeping the eye partly or fully closed, and blinking often.
Avoiding bright sunlight, seeking shade, or holding the head low and turned away from the sun.
Red, swollen lining of the eyelids and a pink or bloodshot white of the eye.
A small white or grey spot in the centre of the clear part of the eye, which is often the start of the ulcer.
Rubbing the eye on the legs, posts or other animals because of irritation and pain.
advanced: The whole clear front of the eye turns cloudy blue or milky white, so the animal cannot see through it.
A visible pit, crater or raised white area in the centre of the eye where the ulcer has deepened.
A pink or red ring of blood vessels growing in from the edge of the eye towards the cloudy patch.
Thick yellow pus-like discharge instead of clear tears.
Reduced feeding and weight loss because the animal is in pain or cannot see to find feed and water.
The eye bulges forward like a cone, or bursts and then shrinks, leaving the animal permanently blind in that eye.
Blind animals walking into fences, getting separated from the herd, or struggling to find water, sometimes with both eyes affected.

lookalikes.name: Foreign body in the eye (grass seed or thorn)
lookalikes.howToTell: Usually only one animal and one eye is affected, often suddenly. On close look you may see a seed, awn or splinter under the eyelids or stuck to the eye. It does not spread through the herd the way pinkeye does, though a seed can also lead to a pinkeye-like ulcer.

lookalikes.name: IBR (infectious bovine rhinotracheitis) eye form
lookalikes.howToTell: IBR usually affects both eyes, makes the eyelid lining very red, and cloudiness tends to start at the edge of the cornea rather than as a central ulcer. Affected cattle often have fever, nasal discharge, cough or drooling, and milk may drop sharply.

lookalikes.name: Malignant catarrhal fever (MCF)
lookalikes.howToTell: MCF makes both eyes go cloudy from the edges inwards, and the animal is very sick with high fever, thick nasal discharge, crusty nose and mouth sores, and often dies. It is linked to contact with wildebeest, especially around calving season, and needs an urgent vet visit.

lookalikes.name: Eye cancer (squamous cell carcinoma) or eyeworms
lookalikes.howToTell: Eye cancer is mostly seen in older, white-faced cattle as a pink or white growth on the eyelid or third eyelid that slowly gets bigger. Eyeworms (Thelazia) cause watering and redness, and thin white worms may be seen moving on the eye surface or under the lids.

detail.diagnosis: Most vets diagnose pinkeye from the history and a close examination: young animals, several cases in the herd, a dry, dusty or fly-heavy season, and a central ulcer on the cornea. The vet may restrain the animal and drop a harmless orange-green dye called fluorescein into the eye, which glows on damaged areas and shows the size and depth of the ulcer. They will look under the eyelids and third eyelid for grass seeds or thorns, and check for fever, nasal discharge or mouth sores that would point to IBR or MCF instead. If the herd has repeated outbreaks or treatment is not working, the vet can take a swab of the eye for laboratory culture to confirm which bacteria are involved and which antibiotics they respond to. Before the vet arrives, note how many animals are affected, when it started, which eyes, whether any animal has a fever or is off feed, any recent new animals, and what treatments have already been used. Have a crush, cattle race or a strong head rope ready, and a shaded place to examine the animal, because a sore eye is hard to see in bright sun.
firstSteps: Move affected animals into a shaded shed or under trees, out of direct sunlight, wind and dust, which reduces pain and stops further damage to the eye.
Separate affected animals from the healthy herd where possible, and use a separate feed trough and water container to slow the spread.
Put feed and clean water where the animal can easily find them, especially if it cannot see well, and keep it away from ditches, wires and other hazards.
Check the eyes of every animal in the herd, especially calves and young stock, so you can catch early cases with only watering and squinting.
Start reducing flies straight away by removing manure and wet bedding, and cleaning around troughs, feeding areas and the boma.
If you can safely see a grass seed or thorn sitting loosely in the eye, gently flush the eye with clean, cooled boiled water, but do not dig or scrape at it.
Wash your hands well after handling each animal's face, and use a clean cloth per animal so you do not carry infection from eye to eye.
Do not put salt, sugar, ash, chilli, herbal pastes, human eye drops or any powder into the eye, as these damage the cornea further and can cause blindness.
Record each affected animal, which eye, the date and signs, then call your vet or the County Veterinary Office early, because an ulcer can deepen within days.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and given or guided by a vet, as the right choice depends on how deep the ulcer is and how many animals are affected. Because pinkeye is caused by bacteria, antibiotics are the main treatment. Commonly used options include long-acting oxytetracycline injections, penicillin given by the vet as a small injection into the tissue around the eye (subconjunctival injection), and antibiotic eye ointments containing drugs such as cloxacillin. Some vets also give anti-inflammatory painkillers so the animal is more comfortable and keeps eating. To protect the eye from sunlight, flies and dust, the vet may glue a cloth eye patch over the eye, or in severe cases stitch the third eyelid or eyelids closed for a few weeks to let a deep ulcer heal. If the eye has burst or is badly infected and painful, the vet may recommend removing it for the animal's welfare. Most early cases begin to improve within a few days of treatment, but a cloudy patch can take several weeks to clear, and a small white scar may remain. Every drug used has a milk and meat withdrawal period, which is the time you must wait before selling or drinking milk or slaughtering the animal; ask your vet for the exact period and follow the label. Use antibiotics only when prescribed, complete the course, and never share leftover drugs between animals or farms, because careless antibiotic use breeds resistant bacteria that make future infections harder to treat in both animals and people.
prevention: Control flies all year and especially in the dry season: remove manure and wet bedding regularly, keep feeding and water areas clean, and ask your vet or agrovet about approved fly control such as pour-ons, ear tags or sprays, following label withdrawal periods.
Cut or graze down tall, seeding grass and clear thorny bush in paddocks and around troughs so cattle do not scratch their eyes while feeding.
Reduce dust in bomas, sheds and holding pens by avoiding overcrowding and, where practical, wetting dusty walkways and feeding areas.
Feed hay from ground-level troughs or racks at head height rather than high overhead racks, which drop seeds and dust into the eyes.
Provide shade in paddocks and zero-grazing units so cattle can rest out of strong sun, which is especially important for white-faced animals.
Make sure cattle get enough vitamin A, from green forage, good silage or a vitamin supplement, particularly during long dry spells when pasture is bleached and dry.
Quarantine new or returning cattle for a few weeks and check their eyes before mixing them with the herd, since healthy-looking carriers can bring infection in.
Vaccinate against IBR where your vet recommends it; pinkeye vaccines exist in some countries but availability in Kenya is limited and protection varies, so discuss options with your vet.
When choosing breeding stock in high-risk areas, favour animals with dark, pigmented skin around the eyes.
detail.impact: Pinkeye seldom kills cattle, but it quietly drains money from a Kenyan farm. Painful animals eat less, so calves and weaners grow more slowly and dairy cows can drop in milk. Treatment costs include vet visits, antibiotics and labour, and milk must be thrown away during the withdrawal period, which hurts dairy farmers who depend on daily milk sales. Animals with a scarred or blind eye fetch a lower price at livestock markets and are often rejected by buyers, and a blind animal in a pastoral herd can get lost, injured or fail to keep up on long walks to water. In an outbreak, many young animals can be affected at once, multiplying the losses. Prevention through fly, dust and grass control is usually far cheaper than treating a herd outbreak.
detail.humanHealth: Pinkeye bacteria are not considered a significant risk to people, but wash your hands after handling infected eyes to avoid carrying infection to other cattle. The main human risk comes from drug residues: do not drink, sell or give to calves milk from treated cows, or slaughter treated animals, until the withdrawal period given by your vet or on the drug label has passed.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when pinkeye is caught early, before a deep ulcer forms. Most treated animals recover their sight, although the cloudy patch can take several weeks to clear and a small white scar may remain without causing major problems. Recovery is slower or incomplete when treatment is delayed, when flies, dust and sunlight keep irritating the eye, or when other infections such as IBR are present. Deep ulcers that cause the eye to bulge or burst often leave permanent blindness in that eye, though most animals adapt well with one eye if kept in a safe area. Animals that recover may have some immunity, but outbreaks can return in later dry seasons if carriers and fly problems remain.

faqs.q: Is pinkeye contagious to my other cattle?
faqs.a: Yes. It spreads quickly through a herd, mainly by flies carrying infected tears, and by direct contact at troughs and in crowded bomas. Separate affected animals where possible, control flies, and check the whole herd daily so early cases are treated quickly.

faqs.q: My neighbour says to blow salt or sugar into the eye. Is that safe?
faqs.a: No. Salt, sugar, ash, chilli, herbs and battery water are common home remedies, but they scratch and burn the already damaged surface of the eye. This makes the ulcer deeper and raises the chance of blindness. Keep the animal in shade and call your vet instead.

faqs.q: Will my cow go blind?
faqs.a: Most animals treated early recover their sight, though a small white scar may stay. The risk of blindness rises if the ulcer becomes deep before treatment, or if the eye keeps being irritated by sun, dust and flies. That is why calling the vet at the first sign of squinting and a white spot is so important.

faqs.q: Can I still sell milk from a cow with pinkeye?
faqs.a: Pinkeye itself does not make milk unsafe, but most treatments involve antibiotics. Once the cow is treated, milk must be discarded until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed. Selling milk earlier puts residues into the food chain and can get you into trouble with milk buyers and cooperatives.

faqs.q: Why does pinkeye keep coming back every dry season?
faqs.a: Some cattle carry the bacteria without showing signs, and each dry season brings the conditions that trigger outbreaks: lots of flies, dust, strong sun and seeding grass. Year-round fly control, cutting tall grass, providing shade, good vitamin A nutrition and quarantining new animals reduce repeat outbreaks. Talk to your vet about a herd plan, including IBR vaccination where advised.

faqs.q: Is there a pinkeye vaccine in Kenya?
faqs.a: Pinkeye vaccines are made in some countries, but they are not widely available in Kenya and they do not always protect against every strain of the bacteria. Vaccinating against IBR, which can trigger or worsen eye problems, may help where your vet recommends it. Good management of flies, dust, grass and shade remains the most reliable protection.

products.role: Vitamin A helps keep the surface of the eye healthy, so where cattle are on dry, bleached pasture or poor hay, supplementing vitamins A, D3 and E under vet or agrovet guidance can help correct a deficiency that makes eyes more vulnerable. It supports eye health and recovery alongside vet treatment and fly control; it does not treat the infection.

pinkeye.imagePrompt: Close-up photograph of a young Friesian-cross calf in a sunny Kenyan farmyard with one eye squinting and watering, showing a cloudy blue-white patch with a small white central spot on the eye and tear stains down the face, flies near the eye.
pinkeye.seoDescription: Pinkeye in cattle: spot tears, squinting and a cloudy blue-white eye early, act before the vet arrives, and prevent spread with fly and dust control in Kenya.

card.headline: Watery yellow diarrhoea in young calves
card.look: A calf under a month old passes runny yellow, white, grey or green dung that soils its tail and hind legs. Soon it becomes dull, stops sucking well and its eyes start to sink into the head.
card.action: Keep the calf warm and drinking, giving oral fluids between its normal milk feeds, and call your vet the same day, at once if it cannot stand or suck.

detail.summary: Calf scours is diarrhoea in young calves, usually in the first four weeks of life. It is one of the most common reasons calves die on Kenyan dairy and beef farms. The diarrhoea itself is rarely what kills. The calf loses water and salts so fast that it becomes dehydrated, its blood turns acidic and it collapses. With early fluids, good nursing and a vet's help, most calves can be saved, and good colostrum and hygiene prevent many cases.
detail.cause: Scours is usually caused by germs that attack the lining of the calf's gut. The main ones are E. coli bacteria, rotavirus, coronavirus, Cryptosporidium and Salmonella. Often more than one germ is involved at the same time. Certain types of E. coli (called enterotoxigenic E. coli, often K99 strains) mainly hit calves in their first few days. They stick to the gut wall and release a toxin that pulls large amounts of water and salts out of the body into the gut. Rotavirus and coronavirus usually strike from about the first to the third week. They destroy the tiny finger-like structures (villi) that absorb food, so milk passes through undigested and draws even more water with it. Cryptosporidium is a tiny parasite, too small to see, that damages the same villi, usually in calves of one to three weeks. Salmonella can affect calves of any age. It often invades the blood and causes fever and sometimes bloody dung. Whatever the germ, the calf loses water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate. Its blood becomes acidic (a state vets call acidosis), its circulation weakens, and it grows cold, weak and unable to suck. Non-infectious problems make all of this worse or start it off. These include a calf that got too little colostrum, overfeeding milk, sudden changes of milk or milk replacer, cold milk, and dirty feeding buckets.
spread: Infected calves pass huge numbers of germs in their dung. Other calves pick them up by licking contaminated walls, buckets, bedding, teats or the farmer's hands.

Adult cows can carry E. coli, rotavirus, coronavirus, Cryptosporidium and Salmonella without looking sick. They shed these germs around calving, so a dirty calving area infects the newborn within hours.
Dirty feeding buckets, bottles and teats that are not washed between calves pass infection from one calf to the next very efficiently.
Cryptosporidium eggs (oocysts) survive a long time in damp bedding and resist many common disinfectants. One sick calf can contaminate a calf shed for weeks.
People, boots, wheelbarrows and shared equipment carry dung from sick calves to healthy ones, especially when the youngest calves are fed after the sick ones.
Wet, muddy, crowded calf pens during the long and short rains build up germ numbers quickly, and cold, wet calves resist infection poorly.
Failure to give enough good colostrum early is the biggest trigger. Without it the calf has no antibodies and even small numbers of germs can cause severe scours.
detail.atRisk: Calves in their first month are most at risk. E. coli scours peaks in the first week, virus and Cryptosporidium scours in weeks one to three, and Salmonella can appear at any age. Calves that did not suck or receive enough colostrum in the first few hours of life are the most likely to get sick and die. So are calves born after a difficult calving, twins, calves from first-calf heifers (whose colostrum is often lower in antibodies) and calves of thin or poorly fed cows. In Kenya, zero-grazing dairy units with Friesian, Ayrshire and crossbred calves are hit hard. Calves are often separated early, bucket-fed, and kept in shared, damp pens close to adult cows. Problems grow when many cows calve close together, because germ levels build up in the calving and calf areas. Cases often rise in the cold, wet long and short rains. In pastoral and extensive systems, calves born into crowded, dung-soaked night bomas (enclosures) or kraals are also at high risk. Farmers who sell all the first milk, or who believe colostrum is dirty and throw it away, unknowingly put their calves in danger.

early: Dung becomes soft, then watery. It is often yellow, pale white, grey or greenish and may smell sour or unpleasant.
A dirty, wet tail and hindquarters, with dung stuck to the hocks.
The calf is slower to come for its milk, drinks less eagerly or leaves milk in the bucket.
Mild dullness. The calf stands with a slightly hunched back, ears drooping, and lies down more than usual.
Early dehydration. When you pinch a fold of skin on the neck or upper eyelid, it takes more than a second or two to flatten back.
The mouth and nose feel drier and stickier than normal.
advanced: Eyes clearly sunken into the head, with a visible gap between the eyeball and the eyelid.
The calf is very weak and wobbly, cannot stand, or lies flat on its side.
The suck reflex is weak or absent. When you put your fingers in its mouth, the calf does not suck, and the mouth feels cool.
Cold legs, ears and mouth. A very weak calf may be colder than normal, not hotter.
Skin stays tented for many seconds after pinching, and the gums may look pale or bluish.
Blood, mucus or shreds of gut lining in the dung, high fever and a very depressed calf can point to Salmonella or another serious infection.
Swollen, painful joints or a hot, swollen navel appearing with the scours, suggesting infection has spread through the blood.
Coma and death, sometimes within a day in very young calves with E. coli scours.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis is caused by a different parasite and is usually seen in calves older than three to four weeks, often weaned calves in dirty, crowded pens. The dung is often dark, with blood and mucus, and the calf strains hard as if trying to pass dung. Scours in calves under two weeks is much less likely to be coccidiosis. A faecal test separates the two.

lookalikes.name: Nutritional (dietary) scours
lookalikes.howToTell: This follows overfeeding, sudden changes in milk or milk replacer, poorly mixed replacer, or cold milk. The calf usually stays bright and keeps a good appetite. The dung is pasty, often pale, and it clears quickly once feeding is corrected. If the calf becomes dull, stops sucking or gets dehydrated, treat it as infectious scours.

lookalikes.name: Navel ill and septicaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: Navel ill is infection entering through the navel. The navel is swollen, hot, painful or oozing pus, and joints may swell. The calf has a fever and is very dull, sometimes with little or no diarrhoea at first. Navel ill and scours often happen together in calves that missed colostrum, so the vet needs to check both.

lookalikes.name: Worms and older-calf diarrhoea
lookalikes.howToTell: Worm diarrhoea is mostly seen in calves grazing pasture at a few months old, not in newborns. The calves are pot-bellied, have rough coats and grow poorly, with ongoing scour. Faecal egg counts confirm it.

detail.diagnosis: The vet starts by looking at the calf's age, the colour and smell of the dung, and how dehydrated and weak the calf is. They take its temperature and check the navel, joints and suck reflex. They will also ask how many calves are affected and at what ages. The age at which calves start scouring is a strong clue to the cause. To find the exact germ, the vet may collect fresh dung from one or more sick calves, ideally early in the illness and before any treatment. The samples go to a County or regional veterinary laboratory, the Central Veterinary Laboratory at Kabete, or a private lab. Some vets carry quick pen-side test kits that check dung for rotavirus, coronavirus, Cryptosporidium and E. coli K99 within minutes. Blood tests can show how dehydrated and acidic the calf is. In healthy calves aged a few days, a blood test of total protein or antibody level shows whether calves are getting enough colostrum, which is very useful when a whole farm has a problem. If a calf dies, a post-mortem examination by the vet gives the best information for protecting the others. Before the vet arrives, write down each sick calf's age and date of birth, when the scours started, and whether and when it got colostrum. Note how much milk it is drinking, any treatment already given, and how many calves are affected. Keep a fresh dung sample in a clean, sealed container in a cool place.
firstSteps: Separate the scouring calf into a clean, dry, draught-free pen with thick dry bedding, away from other calves, and feed and handle it last.
Keep the calf warm. Put it on deep dry straw or sacks, out of rain and wind, and use a calf jacket or an old blanket in cold weather. A cold calf cannot recover.
Keep offering its normal milk in small, frequent feeds. Do not starve the calf of milk, because it needs the energy to heal its gut and stay alive.

Start oral rehydration solution (electrolytes) as soon as scours begins. Give it as separate feeds between milk feeds, not mixed into the milk, and follow the product label and your vet's advice on amounts.
Check dehydration twice a day using the skin-pinch test, sunken eyes and suck reflex. If the calf cannot stand or will not suck, call the vet urgently, because it needs fluids into the vein.
Do not force fluids down a calf that cannot swallow. Do not use a stomach tube unless you have been trained, as fluid can go into the lungs.
Do not give antibiotics, human medicines or other drugs bought over the counter without a vet's advice. Many scours are viral or parasitic, and the wrong drug wastes money and can harm the calf.
Protect yourself and your family. Wear gloves or wash your hands with soap after handling the calf, its dung and its buckets, and keep children away from sick calves.
Clean and scald or disinfect feeding buckets and teats after every use, and remove soiled bedding often.
Record each case: calf, age, date, colostrum history, signs and treatments. Call your vet the same day, especially if more than one calf is affected.
detail.vetTreatment: Fluid therapy is the most important treatment, whatever germ is involved. Calves that are still standing and sucking are usually treated with oral rehydration solutions. These contain salts such as sodium and potassium, an energy source such as glucose, and an alkalising agent that corrects blood acidity. Milk feeding continues alongside them. Calves that are badly dehydrated, cannot stand or will not suck need intravenous fluids, given by drip into a vein, often over several hours. Only a vet can give these, and they can save calves that look close to death. The vet may give an anti-inflammatory painkiller, such as an NSAID like meloxicam or flunixin. These can help the calf feel better and start eating again. Antibiotics do not cure rotavirus, coronavirus or Cryptosporidium. They are only justified when the vet finds signs of bacterial infection spreading in the body, such as fever, severe depression, blood in dung, a very young calf with E. coli, or suspected Salmonella. If an antibiotic is needed, the vet chooses the drug and the course. Using antibiotics for every scour drives antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines, and this harms animals and people. Where Cryptosporidium is confirmed, some vets use specific anti-parasite products such as halofuginone lactate where they are available. These mainly reduce the severity of the disease and the shedding of eggs. All treatments must be prescribed by a vet. Any drug given has a meat withdrawal period, a time when the calf must not be slaughtered for food, and this applies to calves sold for meat. With good fluids, most calves improve within a few days, but the dung may stay loose for a while as the gut lining regrows. Expect the vet to also review colostrum feeding and hygiene so that more calves do not fall sick.
prevention: Make sure every calf gets good-quality colostrum, the cow's first thick milk, as early as possible, ideally within the first one to two hours of birth. A first feed of around a tenth of the calf's body weight within the first few hours is widely advised. The calf's gut absorbs antibodies well only in the first day.

Do not throw away or sell the first milk. If a cow has little or watery colostrum, use frozen colostrum saved from another healthy cow on the farm, thawed gently in warm water and never boiled or microwaved hot.
Prepare a clean, dry, well-bedded calving area away from the main cow shed and dung channels. Clean it between calvings, and wash dirty udders and teats before the calf sucks.
Dip the navel of every newborn calf in a suitable antiseptic such as iodine solution soon after birth, and keep the calf on clean, dry bedding.
House young calves in individual, dry, draught-free pens for the first weeks, so they cannot lick each other, and keep them away from adult cattle dung.
Wash and scald or disinfect buckets, bottles and teats after every feed. Give each calf its own bucket where possible, and always feed the youngest and healthiest calves first and sick calves last.
Feed milk or milk replacer at the same times, at body temperature, in consistent amounts, and mix replacer exactly as the label says. Avoid sudden changes.

Feed pregnant cows well, especially in the last two to three months of pregnancy, with enough energy, protein, minerals and vitamins (particularly vitamin A and E in the dry season), so they produce good colostrum.

Ask your vet whether vaccines for pregnant cows against E. coli, rotavirus and coronavirus are available and suitable for your farm. They work only if the calf then drinks that cow's colostrum, and availability in Kenya varies.
Clean out and dry calf pens between batches. Leave them empty for a while if possible, and talk to your vet about disinfectants that work against Cryptosporidium if it is a problem on your farm.
detail.impact: Scours is one of the biggest causes of calf deaths in Kenya. Each dead heifer calf is a lost future dairy cow and years of lost milk income. Calves that survive often grow more slowly, take longer to reach breeding weight and calve later. Some remain weak and more prone to pneumonia. Treatment costs include vet visits, intravenous fluids, electrolytes and medicines, and a sick calf needs a lot of extra labour for nursing and cleaning. When many calves on one farm are affected, losses can be heavy and discourage farmers from rearing their own replacements. Antibiotics used without need add cost and fuel drug resistance. For most farms, spending on colostrum management and hygiene is far cheaper than treating outbreaks.
detail.humanHealth: Some causes of calf scours can infect people. Cryptosporidium causes watery diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes fever in humans. It can be serious in young children, elderly people and anyone with a weak immune system, including people living with HIV. Salmonella from calves can cause food poisoning-like illness in people, and some E. coli strains carried by cattle can also make people sick. Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap and clean water after handling sick calves, their dung, bedding or buckets, and always before eating or preparing food. Keep children from playing with scouring calves. Do not use calf buckets for the household. Keep calf dung away from water sources and vegetable gardens. If you or a family member develop diarrhoea after working with sick calves, see a health worker and mention the calves. Any calf treated with drugs must not be slaughtered or eaten until the withdrawal period given by the vet has passed.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for calves that are treated early, while they can still stand and suck. Most recover within several days with fluids, continued milk, warmth and nursing. The outlook becomes guarded to poor once a calf is lying flat, cold, unable to suck or severely sunken-eyed. Many of these calves can still be saved with prompt intravenous fluids from a vet, but delays are often fatal, especially in calves only a few days old. Calves that missed colostrum, have navel or joint infection, or have Salmonella do worse. Recovered calves may scour on and off for a short time and grow slowly for a while. Good feeding helps them catch up. Repeated outbreaks on one farm usually mean colostrum, hygiene or housing need fixing.

faqs.q: Should I stop giving milk to a calf with scours?
faqs.a: No. Older advice was to starve the calf of milk, but this weakens it and slows gut healing. Keep offering its normal milk in smaller, more frequent feeds if it drinks less. Give oral rehydration solution as separate feeds in between, not mixed with the milk. If the calf refuses to suck at all, call the vet.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and inject the calf?
faqs.a: It is not a good idea without a vet's advice. Many scours are caused by viruses or Cryptosporidium, and antibiotics do nothing against these. What saves most calves is fluids and warmth. Unnecessary antibiotics cost money, can upset the calf's gut further, leave residues in meat and help create resistant germs. Your vet will decide whether an antibiotic is truly needed and which one.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my calf is dangerously dehydrated?
faqs.a: Pinch a fold of skin on the neck or upper eyelid and let go. In a healthy calf it flattens almost at once. If it stays up for several seconds, the eyes look sunken, the mouth feels cool or dry, and the calf is weak or will not suck, it is seriously dehydrated. A calf that cannot stand is an emergency and needs a vet to give fluids into the vein.

faqs.q: Is it true that colostrum is dirty and should be thrown away?
faqs.a: No. Colostrum, the thick yellow first milk, is the calf's only source of protective antibodies. It also contains energy and vitamins it badly needs. Calves that miss it are far more likely to get scours and die. Give it to the calf as early as possible after birth. If there is extra, freeze it in clean containers for calves whose mothers have too little.

faqs.q: Can I make my own rehydration fluid at home?
faqs.a: In an emergency, a home mix of clean boiled water, salt and sugar is better than nothing. However, it often lacks the right balance of salts and the alkalising ingredients a scouring calf needs, and mixing it wrong can do harm. A proper calf oral rehydration product, used as the label and your vet advise, is safer. Always keep some in stock before the calving season.

faqs.q: Several of my calves are scouring at the same age. What should I do?
faqs.a: This suggests a farm-level problem, such as a germ building up in the calving area or calf pens, or calves not getting enough colostrum. Call your vet to take dung samples so the cause can be identified, and possibly blood tests from healthy calves to check colostrum intake. Meanwhile, separate sick calves, clean and dry the pens, use separate buckets and feed sick calves last. Also review how quickly and how much colostrum each new calf receives.

products.role: RE-COVER is an oral rehydration solution. It can help replace the water and salts a scouring calf loses, alongside continued milk feeding, warmth and vet care. Ask your vet whether it suits young calves, give it between milk feeds rather than mixed into milk, and follow the label. It does not kill the germs causing scours and cannot replace intravenous fluids for a calf that cannot stand or suck.

AD3E supplies vitamins A, D3 and E. Where pregnant cows are on poor dry-season pasture, it can help prevent vitamin shortages, supporting colostrum quality and newborn calf vigour as part of good late-pregnancy feeding. Use it on your vet's or agrovet's advice and follow the label. It does not treat scours, and it is not a substitute for colostrum and hygiene.

calf-scours.imagePrompt: A young Friesian dairy calf standing in a straw-bedded pen on a Kenyan smallholder farm, with watery yellow diarrhoea staining its tail and hind legs, slightly sunken eyes and a dull, hunched posture, in soft natural daylight.
calf-scours.seoDescription: Calf scours in Kenya: spot watery diarrhoea and dehydration early, keep calves drinking, call the vet, and prevent it with colostrum and clean calf pens.

card.headline: Coughing calf with runny nose, droopy ears
card.look: The calf coughs, breathes fast with its flanks heaving, has a runny or crusty nose and droops its ears and head. It drinks less milk and stands apart from the others.
card.action: Move the sick calf to a dry, draught-free, well-aired pen, take its temperature, and call your vet the same day.

aka: Shipping fever (in transported or newly bought calves)
detail.summary: Calf pneumonia is an infection of the lungs and airways in young calves. Viruses usually start it, and bacteria then move in and cause the serious lung damage. It is one of the most common reasons calves fall sick or die on Kenyan dairy farms, especially in cold, damp, poorly aired calf pens. Calves that survive often grow more slowly and can become weaker, less productive cows later in life.
detail.cause: Calf pneumonia is a 'complex', meaning several germs and stresses work together. It usually begins with a virus such as bovine respiratory syncytial virus (BRSV), parainfluenza-3 (PI3), infectious bovine rhinotracheitis (IBR, a herpes virus) or bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV), which weakens the immune system. These viruses damage the lining of the windpipe and the tiny hair-like cilia that normally sweep dust and germs out of the lungs. Bacteria that already live harmlessly in the calf's nose and throat, such as Mannheimia haemolytica, Pasteurella multocida, Histophilus somni and Mycoplasma bovis, then take the chance to travel down into the lungs and multiply. They cause inflammation, pus and areas of dead, solid lung tissue that can no longer take in oxygen. Stresses such as damp bedding, ammonia from urine, draughts, cold nights, crowding, weaning, transport and poor colostrum make the calf far more likely to get sick. In severe cases the lung damage is permanent, leaving scarred lungs and sometimes abscesses or adhesions (where the lung sticks to the chest wall).
spread: Sick calves cough and sneeze out droplets that healthy calves breathe in, especially in crowded or closed pens.
Direct nose-to-nose contact between calves, and shared buckets, teats and feeders that carry nasal discharge.
Bringing in new calves from markets or other farms, which may carry viruses or bacteria without looking sick.
Poor ventilation lets germs, dust and ammonia build up in the air, so calves breathe in more germs and their airways get irritated.
Damp, wet bedding and cold draughts at calf level chill calves and lower their resistance.
