Big temperature swings between warm days and cold nights, common in the highlands and during the cold June–August season and the rains.
Stress from weaning, dehorning, castration, transport, sudden feed changes or mixing calves of different ages.
Calves that did not get enough good colostrum in the first hours of life have weak protection and fall sick easily.
detail.atRisk: Calves from a few weeks old up to about six months are most at risk, with many cases around weaning and after transport or mixing. Calves that got little or late colostrum, calves recovering from scours (diarrhoea), and underfed or worm-burdened calves are especially vulnerable. Exotic dairy breeds and crosses (Friesian, Ayrshire, Jersey) kept in zero-grazing units are commonly affected, because they are often housed in closed or crowded pens. Risk rises in the cold, wet months of the long and short rains and during cold nights in highland dairy areas such as Nyandarua, Kiambu, Nyeri, Meru, Uasin Gishu and Kericho. Calves kept in dark, damp, low-roofed sheds, iron-sheet structures with no air outlet, or pens shared with older cattle, are at the greatest risk. Bought-in calves from markets are also high risk in their first few weeks on a new farm.

early: Fever: a rectal temperature above about 39.5°C (normal for a calf is roughly 38.5–39.5°C). A cheap digital thermometer catches pneumonia before other signs are obvious.
Dull calf that is slow to come for milk, drinks less, or leaves milk in the bucket.
Clear, watery discharge from the nose, and sometimes watery eyes.
Occasional dry cough, often heard when the calf gets up or is moved.
Slightly faster breathing than the other calves while resting.
One or both ears drooping, or the calf tilting its head to one side.
Standing or lying apart from the group, with less interest in its surroundings.
advanced: Thick, cloudy, yellow or green nasal discharge that may crust around the nostrils.
Frequent, wet or painful-sounding cough.
Fast, laboured breathing with the belly and flanks pumping hard; the calf may breathe with its mouth open, neck stretched out and tongue out.
Grunting or groaning with each breath, a sign of chest pain and severe lung damage.
Complete refusal of milk or feed, sunken eyes and dehydration.
Rapid weight loss, rough dull coat and a hollow-flanked look.
Calf lying down most of the time and reluctant or unable to stand.
Sudden death in some very severe cases, sometimes with few signs seen beforehand.

lookalikes.name: East Coast fever (ECF, ndigana)
lookalikes.howToTell: ECF is spread by the brown ear tick. Look for swollen lymph nodes, especially the gland below the ear and in front of the shoulder, and ticks on the calf. Late ECF causes frothy fluid from the nose and fast breathing because the lungs fill with fluid. Pneumonia does not cause the obvious swollen glands. A vet can confirm ECF with a gland or blood smear. If you see swollen glands, tell the vet urgently because ECF needs different treatment.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm (husk, Dictyocaulus viviparus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Lungworm mainly affects calves that are grazing on wet pastures, not calves kept indoors from birth. It causes a harsh cough, especially after the calf moves, and fast breathing, often with little or no fever at first. Several grazing calves usually start coughing at about the same time. A vet can check dung samples for lungworm larvae.

lookalikes.name: Aspiration pneumonia (from drenching or bottle-feeding)
lookalikes.howToTell: This happens when milk, medicine or liquid goes down the windpipe instead of the gullet, for example when a weak calf is force-fed or drenched with its head held high. Signs often start suddenly within a day or two of the drenching, usually in a single calf, and the breath may smell bad. There is usually no history of spread to other calves.

lookalikes.name: Contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP)
lookalikes.howToTell: CBPP is a notifiable disease that mostly affects older cattle, often in pastoral herds and where animals are moved and mixed across areas. Several adults may have cough, painful breathing, standing with elbows turned out, and deaths spreading through the herd. If adult cattle are also coughing and sick, or there are unexplained deaths, report to the County Veterinary Officer at once.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually diagnoses calf pneumonia from the history and a careful examination. They will take the rectal temperature, count the breathing rate, check the nose, eyes, ears and cough, and listen to the chest with a stethoscope for crackling, wheezing or areas with no breath sounds. Some vets use a scoring system that adds up points for temperature, cough, nose and eye discharge and ear position, to pick out which calves need treatment. Where available, a vet may use ultrasound of the chest to see damaged lung. To find out which germs are involved, the vet can take deep nasal swabs or a wash from the windpipe and send them to a laboratory, such as the County Veterinary Laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, for culture, antibiotic sensitivity testing or PCR tests for viruses. If a calf dies, a post-mortem (opening the carcass to examine the organs) is very useful: the vet looks at the lungs and can send samples to the lab, which helps protect the rest of your calves. Before the vet arrives, write down each sick calf's temperature, age, when signs started, how much milk it is drinking, any recent transport, weaning, dehorning or new arrivals, colostrum feeding at birth, and any drugs already given. Keep a dead calf cool and covered for post-mortem rather than throwing it away.
firstSteps: Separate the sick calf into a clean, dry pen that has fresh air but no draught at calf height, so it can rest and is less likely to infect others.
Give plenty of thick, dry bedding such as dry grass, straw or wood shavings so the calf can nest and keep warm; on cold nights a clean, dry calf jacket or sack cover can help.
Make sure clean, fresh water is always available, and keep offering milk in small, frequent feeds; do not force-feed or drench a calf that is breathing hard, as liquid can go into its lungs.
Take and write down the temperature of the sick calf and of all the calves in the same pen, because others may be in the early stage of disease.
Call your vet or animal health officer the same day; calf pneumonia gets worse quickly and early treatment gives the best chance of full recovery.
Improve air flow in the calf house straight away by opening vents, removing wet bedding, cleaning out dung and urine, and reducing crowding, while avoiding direct draughts on the calves.
Feed and handle the healthy calves first and the sick one last, and wash your hands and buckets after handling the sick calf.
Do not give leftover antibiotics or any drug without the vet's advice, because the wrong drug or an incomplete course can fail and adds to antibiotic resistance.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet. Because bacteria do most of the lung damage, the vet will usually give an antibiotic, chosen according to the likely germs, the farm's history and, where possible, laboratory sensitivity results. Drugs commonly used for calf pneumonia include oxytetracycline, florfenicol, macrolides such as tulathromycin or tilmicosin, and penicillin-based products; some antibiotics, such as fluoroquinolones (for example enrofloxacin), are important for human medicine and should be kept for cases where other drugs have failed or tests show they are needed. Antibiotics do not kill the viruses that often start the disease, but they control the bacteria that cause most of the damage and deaths. The vet will often also give an anti-inflammatory painkiller (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, NSAID, such as meloxicam or flunixin) to bring down fever and lung swelling, which helps the calf breathe and start drinking again. Very weak or dehydrated calves may need fluids by mouth or by drip. A good response usually shows within one to three days as the temperature drops and appetite returns; if not, the vet may change the drug or look for another cause. Always finish the full course exactly as the vet says, even if the calf looks better, and keep records of what was given. Every drug has a meat withdrawal period, which is the time you must wait before the animal can be slaughtered for food, and you must respect it. Using antibiotics only when needed, at the right dose and for the full course, helps prevent antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. Where several calves are sick at once, the vet may advise treating the whole group, but this should be a vet decision, not a routine habit.
prevention: Make sure every newborn calf drinks enough good-quality colostrum (first milk) within the first two to six hours of life, and more within the first day; this is the single most important protection against pneumonia and scours.

Design or modify calf housing so stale air can escape: leave open spaces or vents along the top of the walls or along the roof ridge so warm, moist air rises out, while keeping walls solid at calf height to stop draughts.
Keep bedding deep, clean and dry; if you kneel on it and your knees get wet, it is too wet. Remove dung and urine often to reduce ammonia, which you can smell as a sharp stinging odour.
Avoid crowding and mixing calves of different ages; individual calf pens or small groups of similar age reduce spread, and calves should be housed away from adult cattle.

Reduce stress at weaning: wean gradually, make sure calves are eating enough concentrate and drinking water before milk is stopped, and do not dehorn, castrate, move or vaccinate at the same time as weaning.
Isolate newly bought calves for at least two to three weeks, watch them and take temperatures daily before mixing them with your own calves.

Talk to your vet about vaccination; vaccines against some respiratory viruses (such as IBR, BRSV and PI3) and some bacteria exist, but availability in Kenya varies, and a vaccination plan for cows and calves should be made with your vet.

Feed calves well with enough milk, a good calf starter, clean water and correct minerals and vitamins (including vitamin A, which supports the lining of the airways), and control worms and ticks so their immune systems stay strong.
Clean and disinfect calf pens, buckets and teats between calves, and let pens dry fully before a new calf goes in.
Check calves every day, including temperatures for any calf that seems slightly off, so pneumonia is caught early when treatment works best.
detail.impact: Calf pneumonia is costly for Kenyan farmers in several ways. Some calves die, which means losing the future heifer or bull and all the milk and money already spent raising it. Calves that recover often have scarred lungs, so they grow more slowly, reach breeding weight later, calve for the first time later and may produce less milk in their first lactation. Treatment costs, vet visits and extra labour add up, especially when several calves fall sick together in the rainy or cold season. Repeated outbreaks on one farm also mean more antibiotic use, higher risk of drug resistance and a weaker replacement herd. For a smallholder whose dairy heifer is a major investment, preventing pneumonia through good colostrum and housing is far cheaper than treating it.
detail.humanHealth: Calf pneumonia is not considered a significant risk to people, and the usual germs involved do not commonly infect humans. The main human-health concern is drug residues: if a treated calf is slaughtered or sold for meat before the antibiotic withdrawal period ends, the meat can contain drug residues that are unsafe and contribute to antibiotic resistance. Always follow the vet's withdrawal instructions and keep treatment records. As good practice, wash your hands after handling sick calves. If adult cattle in the herd have a long-lasting cough and are losing weight, ask the vet to check for bovine tuberculosis, which can infect people through raw milk.
detail.outlook: Calves treated early, when they first show fever, dullness and a runny nose, usually recover well, often within a few days. The outlook becomes poorer when treatment starts late, the calf has stopped drinking, breathes with its mouth open or grunts, or has already had several bouts of pneumonia. Some recovered calves are left with permanent lung damage and remain 'poor doers' that grow slowly and may cough for a long time; some of these never become profitable and may be culled. Calves that had good colostrum, are well fed and are housed in clean, dry, airy pens recover faster and are less likely to relapse. Fixing the housing and management problems that caused the outbreak is essential, or new cases will keep appearing.

faqs.q: Should I close the calf house tightly at night to keep the calves warm?
faqs.a: No. Closing the house completely traps damp air, ammonia and germs, which is one of the main causes of pneumonia. Instead, keep the calves warm with deep dry bedding and, if needed, calf jackets, and block draughts at calf level while leaving openings high up so stale air can escape. A good test is the smell: if the air smells stuffy or of ammonia when you enter in the morning, ventilation is not enough.

faqs.q: Can I treat the calf myself with an antibiotic from the agrovet?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Calf pneumonia can look like East Coast fever, lungworm or other problems that need different treatment. The wrong antibiotic or an incomplete course may fail, waste money and help create resistant germs. Call your vet or animal health officer, who can choose the right drug, add an anti-inflammatory if needed, and tell you the withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Why did my calf get pneumonia even though it was well fed?
faqs.a: Good feeding helps, but pneumonia is mostly driven by colostrum, housing and stress. A calf that got little or late colostrum, lives in a damp or poorly aired pen, was recently transported, weaned or mixed with other calves, or faces cold nights can still get sick. Look at all these factors together, not just feeding.

faqs.q: My calf recovered but still coughs sometimes. Is that normal?
faqs.a: A mild cough can last for a while after pneumonia as the airways heal, but a calf that keeps coughing, has a fever again, breathes fast or is losing weight may have a relapse or permanent lung damage. Take its temperature and ask your vet to re-examine it. Some calves with badly scarred lungs never fully recover their growth.

faqs.q: Is calf pneumonia contagious to my other calves?
faqs.a: Yes. The viruses and bacteria spread through coughing, nose contact and shared buckets, especially in crowded pens. When one calf is sick, others in the same air space may already be infected. Isolate the sick calf, check temperatures of the rest daily, and improve ventilation and hygiene straight away.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine against calf pneumonia in Kenya?
faqs.a: Vaccines exist for some of the viruses and bacteria involved, but which ones are available in Kenya changes over time and they do not cover every germ. Vaccination also only works well alongside good colostrum, housing and low stress. Ask your vet whether a vaccine is suitable and available for your farm and how to time it for cows and calves.

products.role: A plant-extract supplement whose label says it relieves respiratory problems; it can be used, with your vet's agreement, as supportive care alongside the vet's prescribed treatment to help calves cope with respiratory stress. It does not cure pneumonia and is not a replacement for antibiotics, good ventilation or veterinary care.

An oral rehydration solution that helps replace fluids and salts in calves that are drinking less or have fever, supporting recovery while the vet's treatment works. Offer it only to calves that can swallow normally, never drench a calf that is breathing hard, and follow your vet's advice on how it fits with milk feeding.

calf-pneumonia.imagePrompt: A young black-and-white Friesian calf standing in a simple wooden calf pen with dry straw bedding, head lowered, ears drooping, with a thick cloudy discharge from its nostrils and visibly heaving flanks, in soft natural daylight.
calf-pneumonia.seoDescription: Calf pneumonia in Kenya: spot cough, nasal discharge, fast breathing and droopy ears early, act fast, and prevent it with colostrum and dry, airy housing.

card.headline: Rough coat and pot belly in calves
card.look: Young cattle look dull and thin, with a rough, staring coat and a swollen, hanging belly. Many have loose, dirty dung on the tail and hind legs and grow more slowly than they should.
card.action: Weigh or weigh-band the affected animals and ask your vet or agrovet for a dung (faecal egg) test before choosing a dewormer, rather than dosing by guesswork.

detail.summary: Internal roundworms are thin, thread-like worms that live in the stomach and intestines of cattle. Almost every grazing animal carries some, but heavy burdens steal nutrients, damage the gut and, with some species, suck blood. Calves and weaners are hit hardest, showing poor growth, diarrhoea, pot bellies and sometimes death. Because the worms are becoming resistant to common dewormers, how you deworm matters as much as whether you deworm.
detail.cause: Several worm species are involved, often together. Haemonchus (barber's pole worm) lives in the abomasum (the true, fourth stomach) and feeds on blood, causing anaemia (thin, pale blood). Ostertagia (brown stomach worm) burrows into the glands of the abomasum, so the stomach cannot digest protein properly and the animal loses weight and scours. Cooperia and Trichostrongylus live in the small intestine and damage its lining, cutting the absorption of food. Oesophagostomum (nodular worm) forms small lumps in the large intestine, and Bunostomum (hookworm) also sucks blood. In very young calves, Toxocara vitulorum, a large white roundworm, passes from the mother to the calf through her milk in the first days of life and can cause severe pot belly, diarrhoea and even blockage of the gut. Overall, worms reduce appetite, leak protein and blood from the gut, and divert the animal's energy into repair, so the animal looks hungry and thin even when feed is available.
spread: Adult worms in the gut lay eggs that pass out in the dung of infected cattle onto pasture, paddocks and around water points.
In warm, moist weather the eggs hatch and develop into infective larvae (the young stage that can infect cattle) within one to two weeks, and these larvae crawl out of the dung onto wet grass.
Cattle swallow the larvae while grazing, especially on short, heavily grazed pasture close to dung pats, and the larvae mature into egg-laying adults in roughly three weeks.
The long and short rains create ideal conditions, so pasture contamination and infections rise sharply during and just after the rains.
Cut-and-carry fodder for zero-grazed animals can carry larvae if it is cut very close to the ground or from wet, low-lying areas where infected cattle have grazed or manure has been spread.
Calves can pick up Toxocara vitulorum from their dam's milk in the first weeks of life, so even calves that have never grazed can be infected.
Some larvae of Ostertagia can lie dormant inside the stomach wall during harsh dry periods and then emerge together later, causing sudden severe disease.
Buying in untreated or poorly treated animals brings new worms, including dewormer-resistant strains, onto your farm.
detail.atRisk: Calves, weaners and young stock in their first year or two on pasture are most at risk, because they have not yet built immunity. Calves under about six months are the main victims of Toxocara. Adult cattle usually develop partial immunity, but cows around calving, heavily milking dairy cows, undernourished animals, and those weakened by other diseases such as East Coast fever or trypanosomiasis can still suffer. Risk is highest during and after the long and short rains, on overstocked communal or free-range grazing, on wet low-lying pasture, and where calves graze the same paddock year after year. Pastoral herds sharing water points and grazing are exposed, and zero-grazed calves are not completely safe if fodder is cut low or calf pens are dirty and damp. Exotic dairy breeds and their crosses often show disease more clearly than hardy local zebu cattle, though all breeds can be affected.

early: Young stock grow more slowly than others of the same age and do not gain weight despite eating.
The coat becomes rough, dull and staring, and calves may keep their long baby coat for longer than normal.
Appetite drops slightly and animals spend less time grazing.
Dung becomes softer than normal, and the tail and hindquarters become soiled.
Milk yield in cows may dip slightly without another obvious cause.
Calves look slightly pot-bellied while the backbone and hips begin to show.
advanced: Persistent watery, dark or greenish diarrhoea with marked weight loss and visible ribs and hip bones.
Pale or white gums and inner eyelids, weakness and tiring quickly, especially with blood-sucking worms like Haemonchus.
Bottle jaw: a soft, cold, fluid swelling under the jaw, caused by loss of protein from the blood.
A very swollen, hanging pot belly in calves, sometimes with a smell of butyric acid (like rancid butter) on the breath or dung in Toxocara infection.
Dehydration, with sunken eyes and skin that stays tented when pinched.
Animals lying down a lot, unable to keep up with the herd, and in severe cases collapse and death, particularly in calves.

lookalikes.name: Liver fluke (fascioliasis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Flukes also cause weight loss, anaemia and bottle jaw, but they are linked to swampy areas with water snails, and adult cattle are often affected as well as young stock. A dung test for fluke eggs (sedimentation) or liver damage at slaughter confirms it. Many common roundworm dewormers do not kill flukes.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: Trypanosomiasis causes anaemia, weight loss and a rough coat, but occurs in tsetse fly areas, often with swollen lymph nodes, fever, tear-streaming eyes and abortion. A blood smear examined by the vet finds the parasites, while worm cases show eggs in the dung.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis mainly affects calves of about three weeks to six months in crowded, dirty pens, and causes diarrhoea that often contains blood and mucus, with straining. A dung test shows coccidia (oocysts) rather than worm eggs, and dewormers do not treat it.

lookalikes.name: Poor nutrition or mineral deficiency
lookalikes.howToTell: Underfed animals are thin with rough coats, but usually without diarrhoea, pale gums or bottle jaw, and the whole herd is affected similarly. They improve once feed improves, and a dung test shows few worm eggs.

detail.diagnosis: A vet confirms worms by examining the animal, checking the colour of the gums and inner eyelids for anaemia, feeling for bottle jaw and assessing body condition, and by testing fresh dung. The faecal egg count (often the McMaster method) counts how many worm eggs are in each gram of dung and gives a guide to the burden, though egg counts in adult cattle can be low even when worms cause harm. A larval culture can show which worm species are present. Blood tests can measure anaemia, and in some labs a test called plasma pepsinogen helps detect stomach damage from Ostertagia. A post-mortem on an animal that has died is very useful: the vet can see and count worms in the stomach and gut. To prepare, collect fresh dung straight from the rectum or immediately after an animal passes it, from several affected animals (around five to ten if possible), place each sample in a clean labelled bag or container with the air squeezed out, keep it cool but not frozen, and get it to the vet or lab within a day or two. Write down ages, weights, grazing history, when and with what product you last dewormed, and any deaths. KALRO, county veterinary laboratories and some private labs and vets can run these tests.
firstSteps: Separate the weakest, scouring or very thin animals into a clean, dry pen so they are not pushed off feed and water by stronger animals.
Provide plenty of clean drinking water at all times, as scouring animals lose a lot of fluid.
Give good quality feed such as fresh fodder, good hay and a suitable concentrate or calf feed to help the animal rebuild, without sudden large diet changes.
Check gums and inner eyelids for paleness and feel under the jaw for swelling, and note which animals are worst so the vet can see them first.
Estimate each animal's weight with a weigh band or scale, because any dewormer the vet recommends must be given for the true weight.
Collect fresh dung samples from several affected animals for a faecal egg count before any treatment is given.
Move young stock off heavily grazed, wet or contaminated paddocks if you have cleaner grazing, and clean calf pens of dung and wet bedding.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer if animals are collapsing, have bottle jaw, very pale gums or severe diarrhoea, and keep a record of dates, signs and any previous deworming.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment uses anthelmintics (dewormers), chosen by the vet according to the worm species, the animal's age and pregnancy status, whether it is producing milk, and the resistance pattern on your farm. The main drug groups are the benzimidazoles (such as albendazole and fenbendazole), levamisole, the macrocyclic lactones (such as ivermectin, doramectin and moxidectin), and closantel, which mainly targets blood-sucking Haemonchus and flukes. Some of these, such as albendazole, should not be used in early pregnancy, and not all are approved for milking cows, so the vet's choice matters. They may be given as drenches (by mouth), injections or pour-ons. Doses must be calculated on accurate body weight and prescribed by a vet; underdosing because weight was guessed is a major cause of resistance. Very sick animals may also need supportive care such as fluids, vitamins, iron or other treatment for anaemia, and good nutrition. Every dewormer has a milk and meat withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment when milk must be discarded and the animal must not be slaughtered; follow the label and your vet's advice strictly. Antibiotics do not kill worms and should only be used if the vet finds a separate bacterial infection. Many vets will suggest a repeat dung test about two weeks after deworming to check the product actually worked; if egg counts do not fall properly, the worms may be resistant and a different drug group will be needed. Most animals start to improve within days to weeks, but weight and condition take longer to recover.
prevention: Deworm strategically rather than routinely: work with your vet to plan treatments around the risk periods, typically at the start and end of the long and short rains and before moving young stock to fresh pasture, instead of dosing every month.
Always weigh or weigh-band animals and dose for the heaviest in a group of similar animals, calibrate drench guns, and never guess weights or dilute products.
Use dung tests (faecal egg counts) to decide which animals and groups really need treatment and to check that your dewormer still works on your farm.

Slow down resistance by leaving some healthy, well-conditioned adult animals untreated when advised by your vet, so that some worms that are not resistant remain on pasture (called refugia), and do not change drug groups every time without reason.

Practise rotational grazing, avoid overstocking, and keep calves off wet, low-lying and heavily contaminated paddocks; where possible graze young stock ahead of adults or alternate with other species or crops.

In zero-grazing units, cut fodder at least a hand's width above the ground, avoid cutting from wet areas where infected animals graze, compost manure well before spreading, and keep calf pens dry and clean.
Feed animals well, with enough protein, energy, minerals and vitamins, because well-nourished cattle resist and tolerate worms much better.

Quarantine and test or treat newly bought animals in a separate pen for some weeks before they join the herd, so you do not bring in resistant worms; ask your vet about treating young calves for Toxocara in their first weeks of life in high-risk herds.
detail.impact: Worms are one of the most common hidden causes of lost production on Kenyan farms. Heavily infected calves and heifers grow slowly, so they reach breeding weight later and first calve later, which delays income from milk. Dairy cows may give less milk and lose condition, and beef and fattening animals take longer to reach market weight and fetch lower prices. Severe cases cause deaths in young stock, and money is lost on repeated, ineffective dewormers when resistance develops or products are underdosed. Weakened animals are also more likely to fall ill with tick-borne diseases and other infections. Because the losses are often gradual rather than dramatic, many farmers underestimate them.
detail.humanHealth: The common cattle roundworms do not pose a significant infection risk to people. The main human health concern is drug residues: milk and meat from treated animals can contain dewormer residues if the withdrawal period is not respected. Always follow the label and vet's withdrawal instructions, discard milk for the full period, and do not sell or slaughter treated animals early. Wash hands after handling dung, sick calves and dewormers, and store products out of reach of children.
detail.outlook: Most animals recover well when worms are diagnosed early, treated with an effective dewormer at the correct dose, and given good feed and clean grazing. Recovery of weight and condition can take several weeks, and young stock that were stunted for a long time may never fully catch up in growth. The outlook is poorer in calves with severe anaemia, bottle jaw or heavy dehydration, in animals also suffering other diseases, and on farms where worms are resistant to the dewormers used. Without changes to grazing and deworming practice, re-infection is likely, especially in the rains.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my cattle?
faqs.a: There is no single schedule for every farm. Deworming every month or two without testing is expensive and speeds up resistance. Most farms do better with a strategic plan made with their vet, focusing on young stock and high-risk seasons such as the long and short rains, and guided by dung tests. Adult cattle in good condition often need less frequent treatment than calves and weaners.

faqs.q: I dewormed my calves but they still look thin and pot-bellied. Why?
faqs.a: Several things can cause this. The dose may have been too low because weight was guessed, the product may not suit the worm species, the worms on your farm may be resistant, the calves may have been put straight back on contaminated pasture, or the problem may be something else such as coccidiosis, liver fluke, trypanosomiasis or poor feeding. Ask your vet to do a dung test before and about two weeks after treatment to check whether the dewormer is working.

faqs.q: Do zero-grazed cattle need deworming?
faqs.a: Zero-grazed cattle usually have fewer worms than free-grazing animals, but they are not completely safe. Fodder cut close to the ground or from wet areas, poorly composted manure and dirty calf pens can all carry larvae, and calves can get Toxocara from their mothers' milk. Use dung tests to decide how often they really need treatment.

faqs.q: Should I keep switching dewormer brands to avoid resistance?
faqs.a: Switching brands does not help if the new brand has the same active ingredient or drug group. What matters is the drug group, for example a benzimidazole versus levamisole versus a macrocyclic lactone. Dose correctly, test whether your current product works, and change groups only when your vet advises, often once a year or when a test shows resistance. Your vet may also suggest combination products.

faqs.q: Can I drink milk from a cow that has just been dewormed?
faqs.a: Only after the withdrawal period on the product label has passed, as confirmed by your vet. Some dewormers are not allowed in milking cows at all. Milk taken during the withdrawal period must be thrown away, not sold or fed to people, because it can contain drug residues.

faqs.q: Is bottle jaw always caused by worms?
faqs.a: No. Bottle jaw is a sign of protein loss from the blood, and in Kenya it is commonly caused by blood-sucking worms like Haemonchus or by liver fluke, but it can also appear with other serious illnesses. It is a sign of advanced disease, so call your vet promptly rather than waiting.

products.role: Oral rehydration support for calves and young stock losing fluid through worm-related diarrhoea, helping replace water and salts while the vet-prescribed dewormer and better grazing deal with the worms; it does not kill worms.

Vitamin A, D3 and E supplementation to support recovery, coat condition and growth in young cattle whose nutrient absorption has been reduced by heavy worm burdens, used alongside vet-directed deworming and good feeding, not as a treatment for worms.

internal-worms.imagePrompt: A thin young East African crossbred dairy calf standing in a dry, sunlit paddock, showing a rough dull staring coat, visible ribs and hip bones, a swollen hanging pot belly and dung-soiled hindquarters.
internal-worms.seoDescription: Internal worms in cattle: spot rough coat, pot belly, scours and weight loss in calves, learn strategic deworming and avoid dewormer resistance in Kenya.

card.headline: Soft swelling under the jaw
card.look: A thin, dull cow with a soft, cool, fluid-filled swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw), pale gums and eyelids, and falling milk, often in herds grazing swamps or along rivers.
card.action: Call your vet or animal health officer to confirm liver fluke with a dung test before buying any dewormer, and move the herd off wet, snail-infested grazing.

detail.summary: Liver fluke disease is caused by a flat, leaf-shaped worm, Fasciola gigantica, that lives in the liver and bile ducts of cattle. Cattle pick it up from grass and water around swamps, dams, rivers and irrigated land where a small water snail lives. It rarely kills adult cattle quickly, but it quietly steals weight, milk, fertility and money, and causes livers to be condemned at slaughter. It is common in Kenya and East Africa wherever cattle graze wet areas, and it can also infect people.
detail.cause: The disease comes from the giant liver fluke, Fasciola gigantica, a flatworm that can grow several centimetres long. Its life cycle needs both cattle and a freshwater snail (mainly Radix, also called Lymnaea, natalensis). Adult flukes in the cow's bile ducts lay eggs that pass out in the dung. If the dung lands in water or wet mud, the eggs hatch into tiny swimming larvae that enter snails. Inside the snail they multiply many times, then leave as another larval stage that sticks to grass and water plants and forms a tough cyst called a metacercaria. When a cow eats this grass or drinks the water, the young flukes hatch in the gut, bore through the gut wall and travel into the liver. For several weeks they tunnel through the liver tissue, causing bleeding, inflammation and scarring. They then settle in the bile ducts (the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the gut), where they feed on blood and damage the duct walls, which become thick and hard, sometimes almost like pipes. The result is blood loss leading to anaemia (thin, watery blood with too few red cells), loss of protein from the blood which causes fluid to collect under the jaw and belly, poor digestion of fat, and a damaged liver that cannot do its normal work. It usually takes around three to four months from swallowing the cysts to eggs appearing in dung, so the farmer often sees the problem long after the infection happened.
spread: Cattle swallow fluke cysts on grass, reeds and water plants growing in or near swamps, dams, slow streams, river banks, irrigation channels and flooded valley bottoms.
Drinking from shallow pools, dams and slow-moving streams where infected snails live can also carry cysts into the animal.
In zero-grazing units, cut-and-carry grass or napier harvested from swampy plots, riverbanks or irrigated land can bring cysts straight into the stall.
Infected cattle, sheep, goats and some wild animals spread eggs in their dung, so the snail habitat keeps getting re-infected; cattle are not infected directly from each other.

Rains and flooding create more snail habitat and help the parasite multiply, and in the dry season cattle concentrate around the few remaining wet areas, so infection risk rises at both times depending on the area.
Buying cattle from fluke areas and bringing them onto your farm can seed new snail habitats with fluke eggs if you have wet ground.
Fresh grass carries the highest risk; hay that has been dried well and stored for several months carries much less risk because the cysts slowly die when dried.
detail.atRisk: Any cattle that graze or drink in wet, snail-friendly places are at risk. This includes herds near Lake Victoria and other lakes, river valleys, swamps and dambos, irrigation schemes such as rice-growing areas, and pastoral herds that gather at watering points in the dry season. Young stock and heifers in their first grazing seasons often show the worst growth losses, but adult cows carry flukes too and lose milk and fertility. Zero-grazed dairy cows are not safe if their fodder is cut from wet ground. Pregnant and high-yielding cows and animals already thin from poor feeding, ticks or other worms suffer more from the same fluke burden. Sheep and goats sharing the same grazing are also infected and keep the cycle going.

early: Slow weight loss or poor growth even though the animal seems to be eating normally.
A gradual drop in milk yield in dairy cows without an obvious reason.
A dull, rough, staring coat and a general lack of shine and energy.
Pale pink or whitish gums, inner eyelids and vulva, a sign of anaemia.
Reduced appetite in some animals and less interest in feed.
Heifers that are slow to come on heat or cows that take longer to get back in calf.
advanced: Bottle jaw: a soft, cool, fluid-filled swelling under the jaw that may be bigger in the morning or after grazing with the head down, and may go down later in the day.
Very pale or almost white gums and eyelids, with weakness and tiring quickly when driven.
Marked loss of body condition, with hip bones and ribs clearly showing.
Fluid swelling along the brisket and belly in some cases, and a pot-bellied look.
Soft dung or diarrhoea in some animals, though many fluke cases have normal dung.
Occasionally yellowish eyes or gums (jaundice) when liver damage is severe.
Rarely, in very heavy sudden infections, young cattle can collapse or die from bleeding in the liver before eggs are even seen in dung.

lookalikes.name: Roundworms in the stomach and gut (especially Haemonchus, the barber's pole worm)
lookalikes.howToTell: These worms also cause anaemia, weight loss and bottle jaw, mainly in calves and young stock. A dung test tells them apart: roundworm eggs float in a salt solution, while heavy fluke eggs need a sedimentation test. Both often occur together, so testing guides which dewormer is needed, because many common roundworm drugs do not kill liver fluke.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: Nagana also causes anaemia and wasting but is spread by tsetse flies, so it is linked to bush and tsetse areas rather than swamps. Animals often have swollen lymph nodes in front of the shoulder, bouts of fever and watery eyes. A blood smear or test by the vet confirms trypanosomes; fluke is confirmed by dung tests or at the liver.

lookalikes.name: Anaplasmosis (gall sickness)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gall sickness is tick-borne and usually comes on faster, with high fever, very pale or yellow gums, constipation with hard dry dung, and sudden weakness, mostly in adult cattle. Fluke is slow and long-term, with no high fever. A vet confirms gall sickness with a blood smear.

lookalikes.name: Poor feeding and protein shortage
lookalikes.howToTell: Underfed cattle in the dry season also get thin and may develop bottle jaw, but the whole herd improves quickly once feed improves. Fluke cases stay thin despite good feed, are usually linked to wet grazing, and show fluke eggs in dung or damaged livers at slaughter.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer will look at the herd's history (grazing near water, cut grass from swamps, timing after rains), check body condition, gums and eyelids, and feel the bottle jaw. The most common confirmation is a dung test using sedimentation, because fluke eggs are heavy and do not show up well in the usual flotation test. Eggs are only passed once flukes are adults, so early infections can give a negative result even when the animal is sick; testing several animals and repeating tests helps. Laboratories may also offer a dung antigen test or blood tests for antibodies, and blood tests showing anaemia, low protein and raised liver enzymes support the diagnosis. At slaughter or post-mortem, a thickened, scarred liver with hard, pipe-like bile ducts containing leaf-shaped flukes is clear proof, so ask your butcher or meat inspector whether livers from your animals were condemned. To prepare, collect fresh dung straight from the rectum or freshly passed from several affected and healthy-looking animals, put each in a clean labelled bag or container, keep it cool and get it to the lab within a day. Write down where the herd grazes and drinks, where fodder is cut, when you last dewormed, which product you used and any slaughter reports.
firstSteps: Call your vet, animal health officer or the County Veterinary Office and ask for a dung test for fluke, rather than guessing and buying a dewormer that may not kill fluke.
Move cattle off swampy, flooded or riverbank grazing if you can, and fence off or avoid snail areas such as reeds, seepage spots and muddy edges of dams.
Give clean drinking water from a trough, tank or piped supply instead of letting animals drink from pools, dams or slow streams.
Stop cutting fodder from wet, swampy or irrigated plots for zero-grazed animals until the problem is confirmed and controlled.
Improve feeding for thin and anaemic animals with good-quality fodder, some protein-rich feed and a mineral lick, and keep weak animals in shade with easy access to feed and water.
Avoid driving weak, anaemic animals long distances or working them hard, because they tire quickly and can collapse.
Record which animals are thin, have bottle jaw or have dropped in milk, along with dates, so the vet can judge how widespread the problem is.
Do not eat raw watercress or other water plants from these swamps and boil drinking water taken from them, as people can catch fluke too.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment uses flukicides, which are medicines that kill liver flukes, and must be prescribed by a vet who knows the local situation. Commonly used active ingredients include triclabendazole, which kills both young migrating flukes and adults; closantel, nitroxynil and oxyclozanide, which act mainly on older and adult flukes; clorsulon; and albendazole, which only kills adult flukes and needs care in early pregnancy. Many ordinary roundworm dewormers such as ivermectin or levamisole on their own do not kill liver fluke, which is a common and costly mistake. The vet chooses the product based on the age of the infection, whether cows are milking or pregnant, and local resistance, since resistance of flukes to triclabendazole has been reported in several countries. The dose depends on correct body weight, so weighing or using a weigh band matters, and under-dosing helps resistance develop. Withdrawal periods (the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be sold or eaten) are important: several flukicides have long meat withdrawal times, and some are not allowed at all in cows producing milk for people, so always follow the label and the vet's advice. The vet may also advise treating roundworms at the same time, supportive care such as better feeding and minerals for anaemic animals, and a follow-up dung test a few weeks later to check the treatment worked. Animals usually start regaining appetite and condition over the following weeks, but damaged livers heal slowly, and cattle returned to infected grazing will pick up new flukes, so treatment must go hand in hand with changes in grazing and water.
prevention: Ask your vet to set up a strategic flukicide programme for your area, with treatments timed to the local pattern of long and short rains and dry-season grazing, so flukes are killed before they cause heavy damage and before they seed the pastures with eggs.
Fence off or avoid swamps, reed beds, springs, seepage areas and muddy dam edges where snails live, especially in the weeks after rains when snail numbers rise.
Provide clean water in troughs or tanks filled from boreholes, roof catchment or piped supply, and keep the ground around troughs well drained so it does not become a snail habitat.

For zero-grazing, cut fodder from well-drained land, avoid cutting close to the ground in wet areas, and where possible wilt or dry grass from risky areas; well-dried hay stored for several months carries far less risk than fresh grass.
Improve drainage of wet patches on your own land, repair leaking pipes and troughs, and clear vegetation from small channels to make them less friendly to snails.
Treat newly bought cattle with a suitable flukicide on your vet's advice and keep them off wet grazing until treated, so they do not bring fluke eggs onto your farm.
Include sheep and goats sharing the same grazing in the fluke control plan, because they also carry flukes and keep the snails infected.

Use slaughter reports: ask your butcher or meat inspector about condemned livers, and do routine dung tests in high-risk seasons to check whether your programme is working and whether drugs are still effective.
detail.impact: Liver fluke is one of the most costly hidden diseases on Kenyan cattle farms. Dairy farmers lose milk every day from infected cows, often without realising why. Growing heifers and bulls take longer to reach breeding or selling weight, and cows may take longer to conceive, which stretches the calving interval and cuts the number of calves and lactations. Thin, anaemic animals fetch lower prices at market. At slaughterhouses, infected livers are condemned and thrown away, a direct loss to traders and butchers that is passed back as lower prices for cattle from fluke areas. Infected animals are also weaker and less able to cope with dry seasons, other worms and diseases. Money spent on the wrong dewormer, which does not kill fluke, adds to the loss. Because the damage is slow and quiet, many farmers only notice it when bottle jaw appears or when the butcher reports bad livers.
detail.humanHealth: Fasciola gigantica can infect people, and human fascioliasis is recognised by the World Health Organization as a neglected tropical disease. People do not catch it from handling cattle or from eating properly cooked meat or liver. They catch it by swallowing the same cysts cattle do: eating raw watercress or other water plants from swamps and streams, or drinking untreated water from these places. In people it can cause belly pain, fever and liver and bile duct problems. To protect your family, do not eat raw water plants from grazing swamps, wash and cook vegetables grown in wet areas, and boil or treat drinking water from dams, pools and streams. Fluke-damaged livers are condemned at meat inspection and should not be eaten. Also respect drug withdrawal periods after flukicide treatment, because selling or drinking milk or eating meat too soon can leave drug residues in food.
detail.outlook: Most cattle with chronic liver fluke recover well if they are correctly diagnosed, treated with a suitable flukicide and given good feed. Appetite and condition usually improve over the following weeks, and bottle jaw slowly goes down as blood protein recovers, but scarred bile ducts and liver damage heal slowly and some animals never return to their full milk or growth potential. Recovery is poorer in very thin, severely anaemic or old animals, in cattle with other diseases or heavy roundworm burdens, and where the drug used does not work on the flukes present. The biggest factor is what happens next: cattle that go back onto the same snail-infested grazing without a control plan will simply be reinfected. Herds that combine strategic treatment, safe water and better grazing management see steady gains in milk, weight and fertility over time.

faqs.q: I dewormed my cows recently, so why do they still have bottle jaw?
faqs.a: Many common dewormers, such as ivermectin or levamisole on their own, kill roundworms but do not kill liver fluke. Others, like albendazole, only kill adult flukes and may miss younger ones. Some drugs may also fail because of under-dosing or resistance. Your vet can do a dung test for fluke eggs, tell you which flukicide suits your animals and check afterwards that it worked. Also remember that cattle returning to wet grazing pick up new flukes soon after treatment.

faqs.q: My cows are zero-grazed and never go to the swamp. Can they still get liver fluke?
faqs.a: Yes. If the grass or napier you cut comes from swampy ground, riverbanks, valley bottoms or irrigated plots, it can carry fluke cysts straight into the stall. Cut fodder from well-drained land where possible, avoid cutting very close to the ground in wet areas, and give clean water rather than water from pools or streams. Ask your vet about testing a few cows if you suspect fluke.

faqs.q: When is the best time to treat my cattle for liver fluke?
faqs.a: It depends on your area's rainfall and grazing pattern. In general, risk rises after the rains as snail numbers grow, and in the dry season when cattle crowd around remaining swamps and watering points. Many programmes treat at strategic points such as after the main rains and during the dry season, but the right timing and drug for your farm should be set with your vet or County Veterinary Office, who know local fluke patterns.

faqs.q: Can I drink the milk or sell the meat after treating for fluke?
faqs.a: Only after the withdrawal period on the product label and as advised by your vet. Some flukicides have long meat withdrawal times, and some are not allowed at all in cows whose milk goes for human use. Selling milk or meat too soon can leave drug residues in food, harm consumers and get your milk rejected. Always tell your vet if a cow is milking or pregnant before treatment.

faqs.q: The butcher said the liver was bad and threw it away. What does that mean for my other animals?
faqs.a: A condemned liver with hard, thickened ducts and flat leaf-like worms is strong evidence that liver fluke is present on your grazing. Other animals that grazed the same places are very likely infected too, even if they look fairly normal. Talk to your vet about testing and treating the herd and about changing grazing and water sources to reduce new infections.

faqs.q: Can I get rid of the snails myself?
faqs.a: You can make your land less friendly to snails by draining wet patches, repairing leaking troughs and pipes, clearing blocked channels, and fencing off swamps and seepage areas. Chemicals that kill snails can harm fish, other water life and the environment and are generally not recommended for farmers to use on their own. Combining good drainage and fencing with strategic treatment of animals is the practical and safer approach.

products.role: Can be used as a supportive aid for liver function and digestion while cattle recover after vet-prescribed flukicide treatment; it does not kill flukes or replace treatment and grazing control.

Can help support vitamin A, D3 and E levels in thin, recovering animals whose damaged livers may store vitamins poorly, alongside good feeding and the vet's treatment plan; it does not treat the fluke itself.

liver-fluke.imagePrompt: A thin East African dairy cow with a dull rough coat standing on green swampy grazing near reeds, clearly showing a soft rounded fluid-filled swelling under its lower jaw, natural daylight, realistic farm photograph.
liver-fluke.seoDescription: Liver fluke in cattle in Kenya: spot bottle jaw, weight loss and anaemia, understand snail-borne spread, vet treatment and prevention on wet grazing.

card.headline: Clusters of ticks on ears, udder, tail
card.look: Grey, brown, blue or colourful ticks cling to the ears, under the tail, around the udder, scrotum and between the hind legs. Heavily infested cattle may look thin and dull, with crusty sores or damaged teats.
card.action: Check the whole herd today and arrange correct acaricide treatment of every animal, with fever, swollen glands or red urine reported to a vet at once.

detail.summary: Tick infestation is when cattle carry large numbers of ticks, small blood-sucking parasites that attach to the skin. Ticks drain blood, damage hides and teats, and cause stress that lowers milk and growth. Most importantly, in Kenya ticks spread deadly diseases such as East Coast fever (ndigana), redwater, gall sickness (anaplasmosis) and heartwater. Good tick control is one of the most valuable things a cattle farmer in East Africa can do.
detail.cause: Ticks are eight-legged relatives of spiders. They climb onto cattle from grass, bushes and the walls and floors of sheds. Then they push their mouthparts into the skin and feed on blood for several days, swelling up as they feed. Each kind prefers a part of the body. The brown ear tick (Rhipicephalus appendiculatus) gathers on the ears and carries East Coast fever. The blue tick (Rhipicephalus decoloratus) spreads over the body and carries redwater (babesiosis) and gall sickness (anaplasmosis). The colourful bont tick (Amblyomma) has long mouthparts and attaches to the udder, teats, scrotum, armpits and between the legs, and carries heartwater. Hyalomma ticks, with striped legs, attach under the tail, around the anus and on the feet. Damage happens in several ways. Many ticks together take a lot of blood, causing anaemia (too few red blood cells), weakness and poor growth. Bites leave wounds that become infected, form abscesses or attract flies that lay eggs, so maggots develop. Bont ticks can destroy teats and quarters of the udder, causing blind quarters and mastitis. Hides become scarred and lose value. Tick saliva can irritate skin and, in a few cases, harm the animal directly. Most serious of all, ticks inject the germs of tick-borne diseases while they feed.
spread: Ticks are picked up from grass and bush where tick eggs have hatched, especially on communal grazing land, roadsides and long grass near sheds.
Newly bought or borrowed cattle, including bulls brought in for breeding, can bring ticks and resistant tick strains onto a farm.
Wildlife, goats, sheep, dogs and stray cattle carry ticks and drop them onto shared pasture and around homesteads.
Cut fodder such as Napier grass and roadside grass carried into zero-grazing units can contain tick larvae.
Cracks in walls, bedding and rough floors in cattle sheds give ticks hiding places to lay eggs and wait for animals.
Warm, wet weather during and after the long and short rains allows ticks to multiply quickly, so numbers rise sharply in these seasons.
Spraying or dipping that is irregular, uses weak or wrongly mixed acaricide (tick-killing chemical) or misses the ears, tail and udder lets ticks survive and breed.
detail.atRisk: All cattle can be infested, but exotic and crossbred dairy breeds such as Friesian, Ayrshire and Jersey suffer most, because they have less natural resistance to ticks and tick-borne diseases than local zebu and Boran cattle. Calves are at high risk of East Coast fever and blood loss, while adult exotic cattle brought from low-tick areas often have no immunity and can die quickly from tick-borne diseases. Risk is highest during and after the long and short rains, and in areas with long grass, bush and wildlife, such as parts of the Rift Valley, Central, Western, Coast and pastoral areas. Free-range and communal-grazing herds pick up ticks daily, but zero-grazing cattle are not safe either, because ticks arrive on fodder and live in sheds. Farms where dipping has broken down, or where one acaricide has been used for years without results, are especially at risk.

early: A few ticks seen on the ears, under the tail, around the udder or between the hind legs when you run your hand over the animal.
Animals rubbing, licking, tail-switching or stamping more than usual because of irritation.
Small raised bumps or scabs on the skin where ticks have fed and dropped off.
Ticks of different sizes, from tiny to swollen grey or blue-grey, showing that ticks are breeding on the farm.
Slight drop in milk or appetite, especially in exotic cows, during the rainy season.
advanced: Dense clusters of ticks packed inside the ears, along the tail fold and over the udder, sometimes hundreds on one animal.
Pale gums, inner eyelids and vulva, weakness and loss of condition from blood loss.
Swollen, hard or damaged teats, blind quarters, abscesses and mastitis on the udder where bont ticks have fed.
Crusty sores, hair loss, deep wounds, pus or maggots under the tail, on the feet or on the scrotum.
Torn or thickened ears from heavy ear tick feeding.

Signs of tick-borne disease, which need a vet urgently: high fever, swollen glands below the ears or in front of the shoulder and breathing trouble (East Coast fever); red or coffee-coloured urine (redwater); yellow eyes and gums with constipation (gall sickness); circling, high stepping, chewing movements or fits (heartwater).

lookalikes.name: Lice
lookalikes.howToTell: Lice are much smaller, flat and move through the hair; you see them and their whitish eggs stuck to hairs on the neck, shoulders and tail head. They are worse in cold, dry months, while ticks are firmly attached, round and swell with blood.

lookalikes.name: Lumpy skin disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Lumpy skin disease causes firm, round lumps in the skin itself across the whole body, with fever and swollen glands. Ticks can be lifted at the edge and have legs; a lump from lumpy skin disease is part of the skin and cannot be pulled away.

lookalikes.name: Mange
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange is caused by tiny mites you cannot see. It gives thickened, wrinkled, hairless and itchy skin, often on the neck and tail head, but you will not find attached ticks unless both problems are present.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial skin infection forms thick crusts that look like paintbrush tufts of matted hair, often on the back after rain. It is often linked with bont ticks, so both may appear together; a vet can confirm it with a skin sample.

detail.diagnosis: Tick infestation itself is easy to see. A vet or animal health assistant will examine the ears, tail, udder, scrotum, armpits, groin and feet, count roughly how many ticks there are and identify the types, because each type points to different disease risks. They check the gums and eyes for paleness or yellowness, take temperature and feel lymph nodes (glands). If tick-borne disease is suspected, they may take a blood smear, a gland smear or blood for laboratory tests such as PCR to find East Coast fever, redwater, gall sickness or heartwater germs. If an animal dies, a post-mortem can confirm the cause. Where ticks survive regular, correct spraying, the vet can collect engorged ticks for an acaricide resistance test at a veterinary or KALRO laboratory. To help, keep records of when you sprayed or dipped, which product and active ingredient you used and how you mixed it, when signs started, which animals are affected, and any recent purchases. Keep some ticks in a closed container if asked.
firstSteps: Inspect every animal carefully, running your hands over the ears, tail fold, udder, between the legs and feet, and note which animals carry the most ticks.
Take the temperature of any dull, weak or off-feed animal if you have a thermometer, and call the vet immediately if you see fever, swollen glands, red urine, yellow gums or nervous signs.
Separate visibly sick animals into a shaded, quiet pen with clean water and good feed, and keep newly bought animals apart until checked and treated.
Do not pull ticks off roughly; the mouthparts stay in the skin and cause sores. If you remove a few, wear gloves and never crush ticks with bare fingers.
Before spraying, read the acaricide label or ask your vet or agrovet; mix exactly as the label says and wet the whole animal, including inside ears, under the tail and between the legs.
Keep wounds clean and protect them from flies; ask your vet what to apply to sores and damaged teats.
Write down dates, products, active ingredients and how the animals responded, so the vet can judge whether resistance is a problem.
Protect yourself when handling acaricides: wear gloves, long sleeves, boots and a mask where advised, do not eat or smoke while spraying, and wash afterwards.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment has two parts: killing the ticks and treating any harm or disease they have caused. For the ticks, the vet will advise on an acaricide and how often to use it. Common classes in Kenya include synthetic pyrethroids (such as cypermethrin, deltamethrin or flumethrin), amidines (amitraz), organophosphates (such as chlorfenvinphos), combination products, and pour-ons or injectable products such as fipronil or macrocyclic lactones like ivermectin for some tick types. These come as dips, sprays, pour-ons or injections. In high-challenge areas, especially for East Coast fever, regular treatment, often weekly in the rainy season, is commonly recommended, but the right interval depends on product, area and season, so follow the label and your vet. Tick grease may be advised for ears and tail. If ticks survive correct use, the vet may suspect resistance and suggest a test and a change to a different chemical class, not just a different brand. For tick-borne diseases, prescription drugs are used, such as buparvaquone for East Coast fever, diminazene or imidocarb for redwater, and oxytetracycline for gall sickness and heartwater. Infected wounds, abscesses or mastitis may need antibiotics; use them only when prescribed and finish the course, because misuse builds antimicrobial resistance. Severely anaemic animals may need supportive care. All treatment must be prescribed by a vet. Many acaricides and medicines have milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before selling or drinking milk or slaughtering; always ask and follow them.
prevention: Set a regular tick-control routine with your vet or extension officer, based on the tick types and diseases in your area, and increase attention during the long and short rains.

Always mix acaricide exactly to the label strength, use clean water, and spray enough to soak the whole animal, paying special attention to ears, tail brush, udder, scrotum, armpits and between the legs.

Prevent resistance: avoid weak mixes, missed animals and too-frequent changes of brand; when a change is needed, rotate to a different chemical class as advised, and ask for a resistance test if control fails.

Vaccinate against East Coast fever where available using the infection-and-treatment method (the Muguga cocktail), given only by trained, licensed vets, especially for valuable exotic and crossbred calves.
Quarantine and treat all newly bought or returning cattle before they join the herd, and check visiting bulls.

Keep grass short around sheds, cut bush, seal cracks in walls, clean bedding regularly, and avoid bringing roadside fodder from tick-heavy areas straight into the zero-grazing unit; wilting cut fodder in the sun can help.
Control ticks on dogs, goats and sheep on the same farm, and avoid letting stray animals and wildlife mix with your herd where possible.
Feed well and give clean water and minerals so cattle stay in good condition and cope better with ticks; consider hardier local or cross breeds in very high-tick areas.
detail.impact: Ticks are one of the most costly livestock problems in Kenya and East Africa. Heavy infestation reduces milk yield and weight gain, and damaged teats and blind quarters can permanently reduce a cow's milk. Scarred hides fetch less. The biggest losses come from tick-borne diseases: East Coast fever alone kills many calves and exotic cattle every year, and redwater, gall sickness and heartwater add to deaths, abortions and long recoveries. Farmers also spend a lot on acaricides, drugs and vet visits, and money is wasted when chemicals are wrongly mixed or ticks have become resistant. For a smallholder with two or three dairy cows, losing one cow or calf can wipe out a large part of the family's income.
detail.humanHealth: Cattle ticks can also bite people. Hyalomma ticks can carry Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a rare but serious viral disease in humans, and Amblyomma ticks can carry African tick bite fever. Never crush ticks with bare hands or teeth, wear gloves when removing them, and check yourself and children for ticks after working with cattle. See a health worker if you get fever, headache, rash or bleeding after a tick bite. Acaricides are poisons: wear protective clothing, avoid breathing spray, store chemicals locked away from children and food, never use drink or food containers for mixing, and dispose of leftover dip safely away from water sources. Respect milk and meat withdrawal periods on acaricide and drug labels so residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: Tick infestation on its own usually responds well when the right acaricide is used correctly and regularly, and skin and ear damage heal over a few weeks. Teat and udder damage from bont ticks may be permanent. The outlook becomes serious when tick-borne disease develops: early vet treatment of East Coast fever, redwater or gall sickness gives a much better chance, while late treatment often fails, especially in exotic cattle and calves. Farms with acaricide resistance struggle until the vet identifies an effective chemical class. Recovery is better in animals that are well fed, in good condition and vaccinated against East Coast fever.

faqs.q: How often should I spray or dip my cattle?
faqs.a: It depends on your area, the tick types, the season, your cattle breed and the product. In East Coast fever areas, especially with exotic cattle, treatment is often done about weekly in the rainy season, and sometimes less often in dry spells. Always follow the product label and ask your vet or extension officer to design a schedule for your farm.

faqs.q: I spray every week but ticks are still there. Why?
faqs.a: Common reasons are weak mixing, using too little spray, missing the ears, tail and udder, spraying in rain so the chemical washes off, or old or poor-quality product. If you are doing everything correctly and ticks survive, they may be resistant. Ask your vet to test ticks and advise a change to a different chemical class, not just a new brand name with the same active ingredient.

faqs.q: Can I sell or drink milk after spraying?
faqs.a: Some acaricides have no milk withdrawal, but many do, and pour-ons and injectables often have longer withdrawal periods. Read the label carefully and ask your agrovet or vet. Never ignore withdrawal periods, because residues in milk and meat harm consumers and can get milk rejected at collection centres.

faqs.q: Is it okay to pull ticks off by hand?
faqs.a: Picking a few ticks is not enough to control them and can leave mouthparts in the skin, causing sores. If you remove ticks, wear gloves, pull slowly and steadily close to the skin, and kill them without crushing them with your fingers. Proper acaricide treatment of the whole herd is the main control method.

faqs.q: Do local zebu cattle need tick control?
faqs.a: Zebu and Boran cattle resist ticks and some tick-borne diseases better than exotic breeds, but they can still carry heavy loads, lose condition and spread ticks to other animals. They need tick control too, though the vet may advise a different strategy than for exotic cows. Never assume local cattle are fully protected.

faqs.q: Is the East Coast fever vaccine worth it?
faqs.a: For many farmers in East Coast fever areas, especially those keeping exotic or crossbred calves, vaccination by the infection-and-treatment method can greatly reduce deaths. It must be given by a trained, licensed vet, and vaccinated animals still need tick control because the vaccine does not protect against redwater, gall sickness or heartwater. Ask your County Veterinary Office whether it is available in your area.

products.role: Can be used as a vitamin A, D3 and E supplement for animals that are run down after heavy tick burdens, to support skin repair and general condition during recovery, alongside correct acaricide use and vet care; it does not kill ticks or treat tick-borne diseases.

tick-infestation.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a Friesian dairy cow's ear and neck in a Kenyan farm setting, with clusters of brown and grey engorged ticks clearly attached inside and along the edge of the ear, natural daylight, no people.
tick-infestation.seoDescription: Tick infestation in cattle: spot ticks on ears, udder and tail, prevent East Coast fever and redwater, and use acaricides correctly to avoid resistance.

card.headline: Round grey crusty hairless patches
card.look: Coin-sized or larger round patches of hair loss with thick, dry, grey-white crusts, often around the eyes, ears, face and neck of calves and young stock. The patches look like ash or asbestos stuck to the skin and usually do not itch much.
card.action: Separate affected animals, wear gloves when handling them, and ask your vet to confirm it is ringworm before you treat.

detail.summary: Ringworm is a skin infection caused by a fungus, not a worm. It causes round, grey, crusty, hairless patches, mostly in calves and young cattle kept close together. It is rarely dangerous and often clears by itself over a few months. It matters because it spreads easily through the herd, damages hides, can slow growth in badly affected calves, and it readily infects people, especially children.
detail.cause: Ringworm in cattle is mostly caused by the fungus Trichophyton verrucosum. Other related fungi sometimes cause it too. These fungi belong to a group called dermatophytes, which means fungi that live on skin and hair. The fungus produces tiny seeds called spores. When a spore lands on skin that is slightly scratched, damp or weak, it grows into the top layer of skin and into the hair roots. It feeds on keratin, the tough protein in hair and the outer skin. The hair breaks off and falls out, and the skin reacts by making thick, dry crusts. This gives the classic round, grey, ash-like patch. The patch grows outwards in a ring as the fungus spreads to new hair. Over time the animal's immune system fights the fungus off, the crust falls away and hair grows back. Spores shed from crusts and broken hair can survive for a very long time in the environment, often months and sometimes years, on wooden posts, walls, feeders and equipment. This is why ringworm keeps coming back on the same farm.
spread: Direct contact between animals, for example calves rubbing heads, licking each other or lying together in a crowded pen.
Indirect contact with spores left on fences, wooden posts, walls, gates, feed troughs, crushes and loading ramps where infected animals have rubbed.
Shared grooming brushes, halters, ropes, blankets and other equipment that are moved from one animal to another without cleaning.
People's hands and clothing, which can carry spores between animals and pens.
Buying in new animals that carry the fungus, sometimes before patches are obvious.
Triggers that make outbreaks worse include overcrowding, damp, dark, poorly ventilated housing, poor nutrition, and stress such as weaning, transport or other illness.
detail.atRisk: Calves and young stock, usually from a few months to about two years old, are most at risk because they have not yet built immunity. Adult cattle usually only get it if they are new to an infected farm, poorly fed or stressed. Any breed can be affected, both exotic dairy breeds and local zebu. Outbreaks are most common in housed calves, so zero-grazing units, calf pens, feedlots and crowded bomas are higher risk than free-grazing herds. Ringworm tends to be worse in cool, damp periods, such as during and after the long and short rains, when animals are kept indoors more and sunlight is less. Animals that are thin, short of vitamins and minerals, or carrying heavy parasite loads may get bigger and longer-lasting patches.

early: Small round areas, about the size of a coin, where the hair looks dull, raised or broken off short.
Patches first appear on the head, especially around the eyes, muzzle and ears, and on the neck.
A light grey or white scaly surface on the patch, like dandruff or ash.
Little or no itching in most animals, although some may rub the patch on posts.
The animal usually stays bright, eats well and has no fever.
advanced: Thick, raised, grey-white crusts that look like dried porridge or asbestos, sometimes 5 cm or more across.
Many patches joining together to cover large areas of the face, neck, shoulders, chest and sometimes the back, legs and tail.
Crusts falling off to leave hairless, slightly pink or moist skin underneath, which slowly regrows hair.
Several calves in the same pen affected at the same time.
In severe, long-standing cases in weak calves, poorer growth and a rough coat, and occasionally secondary bacterial infection with pus or a bad smell if crusts are picked or scratched.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis, rain scald)
lookalikes.howToTell: Dermatophilosis is a bacterial infection that flares in wet weather. It causes tufts of matted hair stuck together like a paintbrush, often along the back and on the legs. When you lift the scab, there is often yellow-green pus or a raw moist area underneath. Ringworm crusts are dry, round and grey, mostly on the head and neck of young stock.

lookalikes.name: Lumpy skin disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Lumpy skin disease is a viral disease that causes firm, raised lumps in the skin all over the body, usually with fever, drop in milk, runny nose and swollen lymph nodes. The animal looks sick. Ringworm patches are flat or crusty rather than deep lumps, and the animal is not ill. If you see lumps with fever, call the vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: Mange (mites) and lice
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange and lice cause intense itching, so animals rub and lick constantly, and hair loss is patchy and irregular, not neat circles. Lice can often be seen on the neck, shoulders and tail head when you part the hair. Ringworm patches are round, crusty and usually not very itchy.

lookalikes.name: Warts (papillomatosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Warts are grey, raised, cauliflower-like growths that stick out from the skin, often on the head, neck and udder of young cattle. Ringworm crusts are flatter, round and scaly, and the hair around them is broken off.

detail.diagnosis: A vet can often recognise ringworm just by looking at the round, grey, crusty patches on young stock. To be sure, especially if it looks unusual or is not getting better, the vet may take hair plucked from the edge of a patch and skin scrapings. These are examined under a microscope to look for fungal spores on the hair, and can be grown in a fungal culture at a laboratory, which can take one to several weeks. The ultraviolet lamp test used for dogs and cats is not reliable for cattle ringworm, because the common cattle fungus usually does not glow. To help the vet, note when the first patches appeared, how many animals are affected and their ages, any new animals brought in, and whether any people in the household have red, itchy rings on their skin. Do not wash or treat patches just before the vet comes, as this can make the samples less useful.
firstSteps: Put on gloves and long sleeves before handling affected animals, and wash your hands and arms with soap and water afterwards.
Separate affected calves from healthy ones where possible, and keep them in a clean, dry, well-ventilated and well-lit pen.
Give affected animals their own brushes, buckets, ropes and halters, and do not use these on healthy stock.
Do not apply used engine oil, diesel, paraffin or other harsh home remedies, as these can burn the skin, poison the animal and contaminate milk and meat.
Avoid picking crusts with bare hands; if they fall off, collect them and burn or bury them, because they are full of spores.
Record which animals are affected, where the patches are and when they started, and take photos so you can track progress.
Call your vet or animal health assistant to confirm it is ringworm and advise on a safe treatment, especially if many animals are affected or the animal seems sick.
Watch children and other family members for itchy red rings on their skin, and keep young children away from affected calves.
detail.vetTreatment: Many cases of cattle ringworm clear on their own within about one to four months, as the animal builds immunity. Treatment aims to shorten the course, reduce spread to other animals and people, and protect hides. A vet usually recommends topical treatment, which means medicine applied to the skin. First, crusts may be gently softened and removed with a stiff brush, and the brush and crusts are then disinfected or burned. Antifungal washes or sprays are then applied to the affected areas, or to the whole animal in bad outbreaks. Products used include enilconazole, natamycin, lime sulphur and some iodine or chlorhexidine preparations, depending on what is registered and available in Kenya. Treatment usually has to be repeated several times, and the vet will tell you the right product, strength and schedule for your animals. Oral antifungal drugs such as griseofulvin are not permitted for food-producing animals in many countries and should not be used in cattle. Antibiotics do not kill the ringworm fungus; they are only useful if the vet finds a secondary bacterial infection, and should be used only on vet prescription to help prevent antimicrobial resistance. Always ask about and follow milk and meat withdrawal periods, which are the times after treatment when milk must be thrown away and animals must not be slaughtered. Where available in some countries, a ringworm vaccine is used for prevention and sometimes in outbreaks, but it is not widely available in Kenya. Expect patches to stop spreading first, then crusts to drop and hair to regrow over several weeks.
prevention: Avoid overcrowding calves and young stock, and give each animal enough space so they are not constantly rubbing against each other.
Keep calf housing dry, well ventilated and as bright as possible, because sunlight and dry air help reduce fungal survival.

After an outbreak, scrape and brush down walls, posts, troughs and crushes, remove crusts and bedding, and then apply a disinfectant your vet or agrovet recommends as effective against fungal spores; repeat cleaning between batches of calves.
Do not share brushes, halters, ropes and blankets between animals without cleaning and disinfecting them.
