Quarantine newly bought animals for at least two to three weeks, check their head and neck closely for patches, and treat any before mixing with your herd.
Feed a balanced diet with enough energy, protein, minerals and vitamins, especially vitamin A, which helps keep skin healthy; good nutrition helps young animals fight off the fungus faster.
Keep internal and external parasites under control, as heavily parasitised animals are weaker and may suffer worse skin infections.
Where a licensed ringworm vaccine becomes available, discuss with your vet whether it makes sense for farms with repeated outbreaks.
detail.impact: Ringworm rarely kills cattle, but it can cost a Kenyan farm money and time. Badly affected calves may grow more slowly, especially if they are also poorly fed or carrying worms. The patches damage the skin and lower the value of hides sold to traders and tanneries. Animals with obvious patches may fetch a lower price at market or be rejected for shows and breeding sales. Outbreaks in zero-grazing units and calf pens can involve many animals, increasing labour and treatment costs, and spores in old wooden housing can cause the problem to keep returning year after year. Infection spreading to family members and farm workers can also mean time lost and medical costs.
detail.humanHealth: Cattle ringworm is a zoonosis, which means it can spread from animals to people. In people it causes red, itchy, scaly rings or patches, often on the hands, arms, neck, face or scalp. It can be quite inflamed, sometimes with pus-filled spots, and children are especially likely to catch it from calves. To protect yourself, wear gloves and long sleeves when handling affected animals, wash hands and arms well with soap and water afterwards, wash work clothes separately, and keep young children away from infected calves. Do not use animal antifungal products on people. If anyone in the household develops itchy red rings on the skin, they should visit a health centre or pharmacist and mention contact with cattle ringworm.
detail.outlook: The outlook is very good for most animals. Healthy, well-fed calves usually recover fully within about one to four months, and hair grows back normally, sometimes slightly lighter in colour at first. Once recovered, most animals have good immunity and rarely get it badly again. Recovery can be slower in animals that are thin, stressed, kept in crowded or damp housing, or have other diseases or heavy parasite loads. Treatment and good hygiene help shorten outbreaks and reduce spread, but because spores survive so long in buildings, new calves can be infected unless housing and equipment are thoroughly cleaned.

faqs.q: Is ringworm caused by worms, and will deworming cure it?
faqs.a: No. Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. It gets its name from the ring-shaped patches. Deworming will not cure ringworm. However, keeping worms and other parasites under control helps calves stay strong, which can help them recover faster.

faqs.q: Will ringworm go away without treatment?
faqs.a: Often, yes. In healthy, well-fed calves the patches usually clear by themselves within about one to four months as the animal's immune system fights the fungus. But during that time the animal keeps shedding spores that infect other animals, people and the buildings. Treatment, isolation and cleaning help shorten the outbreak and protect the rest of the herd and your family.

faqs.q: Can I use used engine oil or diesel on the patches like my neighbours do?
faqs.a: Please do not. Used oil and diesel can burn and irritate the skin, may be licked and swallowed, and contain harmful chemicals that can contaminate milk and meat. They have not been shown to be a safe or reliable treatment. Ask your vet or agrovet for a proper antifungal wash registered for cattle and follow the label and withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Can I still sell milk from a cow with ringworm?
faqs.a: Ringworm itself does not make milk unsafe, as it is a skin infection. However, if you treat the cow with any antifungal or other product, you must follow the milk withdrawal period on the label or as told by your vet. Always milk with clean hands, keep crusts away from the milk, and wash your hands well after handling the cow.

faqs.q: My child has a red itchy ring on the arm. Could it be from our calves?
faqs.a: It could be. Cattle ringworm commonly spreads to children who play with or feed calves. Take the child to a health centre or pharmacist and tell them about the ringworm in your cattle so they can give the right human treatment. Keep children away from affected calves until they have healed, and make sure everyone washes their hands after touching animals.

faqs.q: Why does ringworm keep coming back every year in my calf pen?
faqs.a: The spores from crusts and hair can survive for months or even years in wooden posts, walls, feeders and bedding. Each new group of young calves picks them up. To break the cycle, remove old bedding and crusts, scrub surfaces, apply a disinfectant that works against fungi, let in sunlight and air, avoid overcrowding, and quarantine new animals.

products.role: Vitamin A is important for healthy skin, and vitamins A, D3 and E support normal immunity. Where a vet or nutritionist suspects young stock are short of these vitamins, for example on poor dry-season feed, AD3E can help correct the deficiency and support skin repair and recovery alongside vet-advised antifungal treatment, hygiene and good feeding. It does not kill the ringworm fungus.

ringworm.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a young brown dairy calf's head and neck in a farm pen, showing several round, grey-white, crusty hairless patches around the eye and on the neck, natural daylight.
ringworm.seoDescription: Ringworm in cattle: spot grey crusty hairless rings on calves, stop spread to people, first steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Afterbirth hanging from cow after calving
card.look: Grey-red or brown membranes hang from the cow's vulva 12–24 hours or more after calving. After a few days they often smell rotten and attract flies.
card.action: Do not pull the membranes; keep the cow clean and comfortable, take her temperature, and call your vet, especially if she has a fever or stops eating.

detail.summary: Retained placenta means the cow has not passed her afterbirth within about 12–24 hours of calving. Normally the membranes come out within a few hours. A retained placenta is not a disease on its own, but it rots inside the womb and can cause a serious womb infection called metritis. It cuts milk yield, delays the next pregnancy and can kill a cow if infection spreads, so it needs a vet's attention.
detail.cause: During pregnancy the calf's membranes are attached to the inside of the womb at many button-like points called cotyledons (the calf's side) and caruncles (the cow's side). After a normal calving, these attachments loosen and the womb contracts, pushing the afterbirth out, usually within 3–8 hours. If the attachments do not loosen, or the womb is too weak to contract, the membranes stay stuck. Common reasons include a difficult or assisted calving, twins, abortion or an early calving, a caesarean, and milk fever, which is low blood calcium that weakens the womb muscles. Poor nutrition before calving also plays a big part, especially shortage of selenium, vitamin E and vitamin A, and cows that are too fat or too thin. Infections that cause abortion, such as brucellosis, leptospirosis or neosporosis, often lead to a retained afterbirth. Once stuck, the membranes start to rot within a day or two. Bacteria grow in the warm womb, causing a foul discharge and sometimes toxic metritis, where poisons from the bacteria get into the blood, causing fever, weakness and in bad cases death. Even after recovery, scarring and lingering infection in the womb can make it harder for the cow to conceive again.
spread: Retained placenta is not contagious from cow to cow, but some causes are. Abortion diseases like brucellosis can spread through aborted calves, afterbirth and birth fluids.
Difficult calvings, especially big calves from large bulls or AI sires on small heifers, or calves coming the wrong way, are a common trigger.
Twins, abortions, premature births and stillbirths often leave the membranes stuck.
Milk fever and low calcium around calving weaken the womb muscles so they cannot push the afterbirth out.
A dry-cow diet low in selenium, vitamin E and vitamin A, or poor-quality feed during the last two months of pregnancy, raises the risk.
Cows that are overfat at calving, or very thin, are more likely to retain the placenta.
Dirty calving areas, rough handling and unclean hands or tools during calving assistance bring bacteria into the womb.
Heat stress, overcrowding and other stresses around calving can contribute.
detail.atRisk: High-yielding dairy cows such as Friesians and Ayrshires in zero-grazing units are most often affected, but any cow, including Boran, Zebu and crosses, can retain the placenta. Older cows that have calved many times have weaker womb muscles and a higher risk, as do cows that had a retained placenta before. Heifers having a difficult first calving are also at risk. Cows carrying twins, cows that abort, and cows induced to calve early are at high risk. Herds fed poor dry-cow rations, for example only dry Napier or maize stover in the dry season without minerals, are more affected. Herds with brucellosis or other abortion diseases see more cases. Hot weather, overcrowded or muddy calving areas during the long and short rains, and poor hygiene at calving all increase the chance of infection once the placenta is retained.

early: Membranes hang from the vulva more than 12–24 hours after calving. They may be grey, pink, red or brown and can reach the hocks.
Sometimes nothing is visible from outside because the afterbirth is stuck inside the womb or vagina. Suspect this if you never saw the afterbirth come out.
The cow holds her tail raised or slightly away from her body and may strain now and then.
Milk yield in the first few days may be a little lower than expected.
At this stage many cows still eat and look fairly normal, which can fool farmers into thinking all is well.
advanced: A strong, rotten smell comes from the cow's back end, usually from day 2–4 onwards.
Thick brown, reddish or grey watery discharge with a bad smell runs from the vulva and soils the tail and hind legs.
Flies swarm around the hanging membranes and the tail area.
Fever: rectal temperature above about 39.5°C. In very severe cases the temperature may drop below normal as the cow goes into shock.
The cow goes off feed, stops chewing the cud and milk yield drops sharply.
She looks dull, stands with a hunched back, has sunken eyes from dehydration and may have diarrhoea.
In severe toxic metritis the cow may lie down and fail to rise. This is an emergency.

lookalikes.name: Normal discharge after calving (lochia)
lookalikes.howToTell: After calving it is normal to see some reddish-brown or chocolate-coloured discharge for up to two or three weeks. Normal lochia has little or no bad smell, there are no membranes hanging out, and the cow eats, milks and has a normal temperature.

lookalikes.name: Metritis without retained placenta
lookalikes.howToTell: The cow passed her afterbirth normally, but within the first week or two she develops a foul-smelling, watery brown discharge, fever and goes off feed. It needs the same urgent vet care, but there are no hanging membranes.

lookalikes.name: Prolapsed uterus (womb pushed out)
lookalikes.howToTell: A prolapse is a large, heavy, red, fleshy mass, often as big as a bucket, with button-like lumps on it, hanging from the vulva. Retained membranes are thin and sheet-like. A prolapse is an emergency: keep the womb clean and wet, support it on a clean wet cloth, and call the vet immediately.

lookalikes.name: Abortion due to brucellosis or other infections
lookalikes.howToTell: If the cow calved early, the calf was born dead or weak, or several cows in the herd have aborted, the retained placenta may be a sign of an infectious abortion disease. Handle the membranes and calf only with gloves and ask the vet to take samples for testing.

detail.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually simple: the vet sees membranes hanging from the vulva or feels them with a gloved hand inside the vagina more than 12–24 hours after calving. The vet will take the cow's temperature, check how alert she is, whether she is eating and chewing cud, and how dehydrated she is. A gentle internal examination, and sometimes a rectal examination, helps the vet judge how much membrane is still attached, whether there is a second calf, tears in the birth canal, or signs of serious infection. If the cow aborted or calved early, the vet may take blood samples, or samples of the afterbirth or the dead calf, to test for brucellosis, leptospirosis or other abortion diseases. If several cows are affected, the vet may test blood for calcium, selenium or other minerals and look at the dry-cow diet. To help the vet, write down the date and time of calving, whether you helped pull the calf, whether there were twins or a dead calf, the cow's temperature readings, how much she is eating and milking, and what she was fed in the last two months of pregnancy. Keep any aborted calf or expelled membranes in a closed bag or container in a cool place, handled only with gloves, in case the vet wants samples.
firstSteps: Do not pull, twist or tie a weight such as a stone or bottle to the hanging membranes. Pulling can tear the womb, cause heavy bleeding, leave pieces behind and push infection deeper.
Take the cow's rectal temperature morning and evening with a thermometer and write it down. Call the vet straight away if it is above about 39.5°C, or if she stops eating.
Put the cow in a clean, dry, shaded pen with fresh bedding, away from mud and dung, and keep other animals from stepping on the membranes.
Make sure she has plenty of clean drinking water and good fresh feed in front of her at all times. A cow that keeps eating recovers better.
If membranes hang very low and get dirty, ask your vet whether they can be trimmed with clean scissors at the level of the vulva. Do not cut inside the vulva and never push them back in.
Wear gloves when handling the cow's back end, the afterbirth or any dead calf, and wash your hands with soap afterwards. This protects you from brucellosis and other infections.
Bury deeply or burn any afterbirth that comes out, and do not let dogs eat it, because dogs can spread some abortion diseases.
Keep flies away by keeping the area clean and the tail region washed with clean water, and record everything for the vet.
Do not put herbal mixtures, soil, oils or any objects into the womb or vagina, and do not give antibiotics or other drugs unless your vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how sick the cow is. Many vets now advise against forcefully removing the afterbirth by hand, because it can damage the womb and does not speed up recovery. If gentle traction loosens membranes that are already free, the vet may remove them, and the vet may trim long hanging pieces. If the cow has no fever and is eating well, the vet may simply advise close monitoring of temperature and appetite until the membranes come out on their own, which commonly takes several days to around ten days. Hormones that make the womb contract, such as oxytocin, may help if given soon after calving, but they work less well later. Prostaglandin products are sometimes used, but evidence for them is mixed. If the cow has fever, foul discharge or is off feed, the vet will usually treat for metritis. This often means injectable antibiotics such as penicillin, oxytetracycline or ceftiofur, given as a full course. The vet may also give anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce fever and pain, fluids by mouth or into the vein for dehydration, and calcium if milk fever is suspected. Antibiotic pessaries placed into the womb are still used by some vets, but their value is debated. All of these medicines must be prescribed by a vet, who will choose the drug and dose. Antibiotics should only be used when truly needed and the full course completed, because misuse breeds antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to medicines. Most drugs have a milk and meat withdrawal period, a set number of days when milk must be discarded and the animal must not be slaughtered. Ask your vet for the exact days and follow them strictly. Expect the vet to recheck the cow and to examine her womb again around 3–5 weeks after calving before she is served.
prevention: Feed dry cows well in the last two months of pregnancy with good forage, a balanced ration and a proper dry-cow mineral mix. Avoid both starving them and letting them get too fat.
Make sure the diet supplies enough selenium, vitamin E and vitamin A. In areas or seasons with poor green feed, ask your vet or nutritionist about supplements or injections before calving.
Prevent milk fever by using a dry-cow mineral that is not too high in calcium, avoiding sudden diet changes near calving, and following your vet's advice for high-yielding or older cows.
Choose bulls or AI sires with easy-calving records, especially for heifers, and grow heifers well so they are big enough at first calving.
Provide a clean, dry, well-bedded and quiet calving area, separate from the main zero-grazing unit if possible, and clean it between calvings.
Help with calving only when needed, using clean hands, gloves, soap, lubricant and clean ropes, and call the vet early for difficult calvings.
Test and control abortion diseases such as brucellosis with your County Veterinary Officer. Vaccinate heifers against brucellosis where your vet recommends it.
Keep calving records and watch cows that had a retained placenta before. Check every fresh cow's temperature, appetite and discharge daily for the first 10 days.
detail.impact: A retained placenta costs a Kenyan dairy farmer in several ways. The cow often milks less in the early weeks when she should be reaching her peak, and milk must be thrown away during any antibiotic withdrawal period. Treatment and vet visits add costs. Womb infection often delays the return to heat and lowers conception rates, so the farmer may need extra inseminations and the calving interval gets longer, meaning fewer calves and less milk over the cow's life. Affected cows are also more likely to get other problems after calving, such as ketosis (a metabolic problem from low energy) and displaced stomach. Some cows never get back in calf and must be culled early. Severe toxic metritis can kill a valuable cow. In herds where many cows are affected, the problem usually points to nutrition, hygiene or abortion disease issues that are costing money across the whole farm.
detail.humanHealth: The retained placenta itself is not passed to people, but the membranes, discharge and any aborted calf can carry germs that infect humans, especially if the cow aborted. Brucellosis (which causes undulant fever in people), leptospirosis and Q fever can all spread through birth fluids and afterbirth, and through drinking raw milk. Always wear gloves and, if possible, long sleeves when handling the cow's back end or the afterbirth, cover any cuts, and wash with soap and water afterwards. Pregnant women and children should keep away. Never eat or let dogs eat the afterbirth; bury it deeply or burn it. Boil all milk before drinking. If the cow is treated with antibiotics or other drugs, do not drink or sell her milk, and do not slaughter her, until the full withdrawal period given by your vet has passed, because drug residues can harm people and contribute to antibiotic resistance.
detail.outlook: Most cows with a retained placenta recover, especially if they keep eating and have no fever. In many uncomplicated cases the membranes rot loose and pass on their own within several days to about a week and a half. The outlook is less good when the cow develops fever, stops eating, becomes dehydrated or goes down, which are signs of toxic metritis. These cows need urgent vet care and some may die despite treatment. Cows with milk fever, twins, a difficult calving or underlying abortion disease also tend to recover more slowly. Even after she looks well, the cow may take longer to come back on heat and conceive, so ask your vet to check her womb before breeding. Early detection, good nursing, clean conditions and prompt vet treatment give the best chance of full recovery.

faqs.q: Can I just pull the afterbirth out myself?
faqs.a: No. The membranes are stuck to the womb at many points, and pulling can tear the womb lining, cause bleeding, leave pieces inside and push infection deeper. Many vets themselves no longer remove the afterbirth by force. If it comes away with only a very gentle touch it is already loose, but otherwise leave it, keep the cow clean, watch her temperature and appetite, and call your vet.

faqs.q: My neighbour says to tie a stone or bottle to the hanging afterbirth. Is that good?
faqs.a: No, this common practice is risky. The weight keeps pulling on the womb, which can tear it, cause bleeding or even pull the womb out (prolapse). It also does not make the membranes come out faster. Leave the membranes alone and follow your vet's advice. If they hang very low, your vet may advise trimming them level with the vulva.

faqs.q: How long can I wait before calling the vet?
faqs.a: If the afterbirth is not out by 12–24 hours after calving, tell your vet. Call immediately if the cow has a temperature above about 39.5°C, stops eating, looks dull, has a foul-smelling discharge, is straining hard or goes down. A cow that is eating well with a normal temperature may only need monitoring, but the vet should decide that.

faqs.q: Can I sell or drink the milk from a cow with retained placenta?
faqs.a: If she has not been given any medicines, her milk can be used, but always boil milk before drinking. If the vet treats her with antibiotics or other drugs, you must throw away her milk for the whole withdrawal period the vet gives you. Selling milk with drug residues is harmful to people and illegal, and dairy buyers may test for it.

faqs.q: Will my cow get pregnant again?
faqs.a: Most cows do conceive again, but it may take longer than normal, and some need more than one insemination. Womb infection is the main reason for delay. Ask your vet to examine her about 3–5 weeks after calving and before she is served. If she has a lingering infection, treating it first improves the chance of a successful pregnancy.

faqs.q: Why do several of my cows keep retaining the afterbirth?
faqs.a: When many cows in one herd are affected, there is usually a shared cause. Common ones are a poor dry-cow diet lacking selenium, vitamin E or vitamin A, milk fever problems, cows too fat or thin at calving, difficult calvings from heavy-calf sires, dirty calving areas, or an abortion disease like brucellosis. Ask your vet to review your dry-cow feeding and minerals and to test for abortion diseases. Fixing the herd cause works far better than treating cow after cow.

products.role: Shortage of vitamins A and E before calving is one known risk factor for retained placenta. AD3E can be used as part of a vet-guided dry-cow nutrition plan in the last weeks of pregnancy, especially in the dry season when green feed is scarce. Ask your vet whether your herd also needs selenium, which this product does not provide. It supports prevention alongside a balanced ration and good calving hygiene. It does not treat a retained placenta that has already happened.

An oral rehydration solution can help keep a feverish, dull cow drinking and hydrated while she recovers, alongside the treatment your vet prescribes. Offer it in clean water as well as plain water, never instead of it, and call the vet if she will not drink or is badly dehydrated.

retained-placenta.imagePrompt: A black-and-white Friesian dairy cow standing on clean straw bedding in a Kenyan zero-grazing shed, seen from behind and slightly to the side, with greyish-pink afterbirth membranes hanging from below her raised tail toward her hocks, natural daylight, realistic farm photo.
retained-placenta.seoDescription: Retained afterbirth in cattle: signs, causes, first steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan farmers, and why you should never pull it out.

card.headline: Open-mouth panting and drooling in heat
card.look: Cows stand bunched in shade or by the water trough, breathing fast with mouths open, tongues out and saliva dripping. They eat less and milk drops, especially on hot, humid afternoons.
card.action: Move the cows into shade with plenty of clean, cool water straight away, and wet their bodies with water if they are panting hard.

detail.summary: Heat stress happens when a cow takes in or makes more heat than she can get rid of, so her body temperature rises. Exotic dairy breeds such as Holstein-Friesian and Ayrshire are most affected, especially when heat comes with high humidity. Even mild heat stress cuts feed intake, milk yield and fertility, often before the farmer notices. Severe heat stress, called heat stroke, can make a cow collapse and die.
detail.cause: A cow produces a lot of heat by digesting feed in her rumen (the large first stomach) and by making milk. The more milk she gives, the more heat she makes. She loses this heat mainly by sweating, by panting, and by passing heat to cooler air around her. When the air is hot, the sun is strong and humidity is high, sweat and breath cannot evaporate well, so the heat stays inside her. Her body temperature climbs above the normal of about 38.5°C. To cope, she eats less to make less heat, breathes faster and drools. Heavy panting and drooling lose saliva, which normally contains natural buffers that protect the rumen, so the rumen becomes more acidic. This raises the risk of acidosis (sour rumen) and lameness. Blood flow moves to the skin and away from the gut and reproductive organs, which reduces milk, weakens heat signs and harms early pregnancies. If the body temperature keeps rising, the brain, heart and other organs are damaged, and the cow can collapse.
spread: Heat stress is not infectious and does not spread from cow to cow; it is triggered by the environment and management.
High air temperature combined with high humidity is the main trigger, because humid air stops sweat and breath from cooling the cow.
Direct strong sun with no shade, especially from late morning to late afternoon, adds a large heat load.
Low iron-sheet roofs without insulation, closed walls and poor airflow in zero-grazing units trap heat around the animals.
Shortage of water, or water that is far away, hot from sitting in the sun, dirty or hard to reach, quickly worsens heat stress.
Crowding in small pens or at shade spots raises the heat around each cow and blocks air movement.
Walking or trucking cattle long distances in the heat of the day, or handling them for spraying or treatment at midday, adds heat from muscle work.
Hot nights that do not cool down mean cows cannot shed the heat built up during the day, so stress builds over several days.
detail.atRisk: High-yielding exotic dairy cows, especially Holstein-Friesians, are most at risk because they produce the most metabolic heat; Ayrshires and Guernseys are also affected, while Jerseys tolerate heat somewhat better. Local zebu-type cattle such as Boran, Sahiwal and East African Shorthorn Zebu cope far better, and crosses fall in between. Cows in early lactation, heavily pregnant and dry cows, dark-coated animals, overweight cows and animals that are already sick, lame or recovering from disease suffer more. In Kenya, risk is highest at the coast (Mombasa, Kilifi, Kwale), around Lake Victoria, in lowland and semi-arid areas such as Machakos, Makueni, Kitui and parts of the Rift Valley floor, and during the hot dry months before the long rains and the short rains. Humid spells during and after the rains at the coast and lake region are also dangerous. Zero-grazed cows under low, hot roofs and free-grazing cows on open pasture without trees are both at risk.

early: Cows seek shade, crowd around trees, walls or the water trough and stand together instead of spreading out.
Cows stand more and lie down less, which can also lead to sore feet over time.
Breathing becomes faster and shallower than normal; a resting cow normally breathes roughly 26–50 times a minute, and a clearly faster rate in hot weather is a warning.
Cows drink more often and spend a long time at the water point.
Feed intake drops, especially during the hottest hours, and cows may eat more at night.
Milk yield falls, often by a noticeable amount within a day or two of hot weather.
Less cudding (chewing the cud) than usual.
Cows become restless and kick at flies more, as heat and insects together make them uncomfortable.
advanced: Open-mouth panting with the head stretched forward and the neck extended.
Tongue hanging out and long strings of saliva dripping from the mouth.
Rectal temperature well above normal, often above about 40°C, and in heat stroke 41°C or higher.
Very fast, laboured breathing with the flanks heaving and sometimes grunting.
Dull, weak, wobbly or staggering walk and reluctance to move.
Loose dung and signs of rumen upset or lameness in the days that follow, linked to acidosis.
Weak or missing heat signs, repeat breeding and early abortion over the following weeks.
Collapse, lying flat, trembling or fits in severe heat stroke, which can end in death.

lookalikes.name: East Coast Fever (ECF, ndigana)
lookalikes.howToTell: ECF also causes high fever, fast breathing and drooling, but you will usually find swollen lymph nodes (glands), especially below the ear and in front of the shoulder, plus ticks, watery eyes and frothy nose discharge later. The fever stays high even when the weather is cool or after the cow is shaded and wetted. If cooling does not bring her temperature down, call the vet quickly.

lookalikes.name: Pneumonia (lung infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Pneumonia causes fast or difficult breathing too, but there is usually coughing, nasal discharge, and a fever that continues at night and in cool weather. Often only one or a few animals are affected rather than the whole herd at once on a hot afternoon.

lookalikes.name: Redwater (babesiosis) and gall sickness (anaplasmosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: These tick-borne diseases cause fever, weakness and fast breathing, but look for pale or yellow gums and eyes, red or dark brown urine in redwater, and constipation in gall sickness. Signs do not improve with shade and water, and tick infestation is common.

lookalikes.name: Acute bloat
lookalikes.howToTell: A bloated cow may pant and drool, but the left side of the belly is visibly swollen and tight like a drum, often after grazing lush legumes or eating grain. Heat stress does not cause this swelling.

detail.diagnosis: Heat stress is usually diagnosed from the weather, the setting and the signs: several cows panting, drooling and seeking shade during hot, humid spells, with feed intake and milk falling together. A vet will take the rectal temperature, count breathing and heart rates, check hydration by pinching the skin and looking at the eyes and gums, and listen to the chest and rumen. Because tick-borne diseases and pneumonia can look similar, the vet may check lymph nodes, take blood smears or other samples, especially if only one animal is sick or if the temperature stays high after cooling. Many vets and advisers also use the temperature-humidity index (THI), a single number combining air temperature and humidity, to judge how risky the weather is for dairy cows. To help the vet, record each cow's rectal temperature (a cheap digital thermometer from the agrovet works well), the time and weather, how much water and feed she took, daily milk yields over the past week, any recent tick control, vaccinations and treatments, and whether animals have been moved or handled in the heat.
firstSteps: Move the affected cows into the coolest shade you have, ideally under trees or a high, airy roof, and stop all walking, herding or handling.
Give unlimited clean, cool drinking water in a shaded trough or containers, and make sure timid or low-ranking cows can reach it without being pushed away.

If a cow is panting with her mouth open, wet her down with plenty of water, focusing on the neck, back and legs, then let air move over her; repeat every so often rather than once, and use a fan if you have one.
Open doors, windows and curtains in the cow shed to increase airflow, and reduce crowding by spreading animals out.
Offer feed in the cool early morning, late evening and at night, and keep feed fresh in the trough rather than letting it heat up in the sun.
Take the rectal temperature of the worst-affected animals and write it down with the time, and repeat after cooling to see if it is falling.

Call your vet or animal-health officer urgently if a cow is staggering, collapsing, panting open-mouthed despite cooling, has a temperature of about 41°C or higher, or if her temperature does not fall after an hour of cooling.
Do not give any drugs, including painkillers or antibiotics, unless your vet prescribes them, and avoid forcing liquids into the mouth of a weak cow because she may choke.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no single drug that cures heat stress; the main treatment is cooling the animal and correcting the damage the heat has caused. For severe cases the vet will cool the cow actively with water and air movement while watching her temperature closely. A dehydrated or collapsed cow may receive fluids into the vein or by stomach tube, together with electrolytes (body salts such as sodium and potassium) to replace what was lost in sweat and saliva. The vet may prescribe an anti-inflammatory drug from the NSAID group, such as flunixin or meloxicam, to reduce inflammation and support recovery. Rumen buffers may be used if acidosis is suspected, and calcium may be given if the cow is a fresh calver showing signs of milk fever. Antibiotics do not treat heat stress; they are only used if the vet finds a bacterial infection such as mastitis or pneumonia alongside it, because unnecessary antibiotic use builds antimicrobial resistance, which makes future infections harder to treat in animals and people. All these medicines must be prescribed by a vet, who will advise on the milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before milk or meat from a treated animal can be sold or eaten. Most mildly affected cows improve within hours of shade and water, but milk yield and fertility can take days to weeks to recover.
prevention: Provide good shade for every cow: plant shade trees in paddocks and around sheds, and put up shade nets or roofs where trees are not yet grown, with enough space for all animals to lie down without crowding.

Build or adjust cow sheds with high roofs (higher roofs keep the heat further from the cow), open sides or adjustable curtains, and good airflow; insulate iron-sheet roofs or paint them white or with lime to reflect sunlight.

Make clean, cool water available at all times, in troughs placed in the shade and close to where cows rest and are milked; a milking cow can need well over 50 litres a day and much more in hot weather, so check that supply and flow rate keep up.
Feed at cooler times, giving most of the ration early morning, late afternoon and at night, and feed good-quality, leafy forage, because coarse, stemmy feed produces more heat during digestion.

Work with your vet or nutritionist to balance the ration for hot weather, including correct minerals such as sodium and potassium and appropriate rumen buffers, and avoid sudden heavy grain feeding that can tip a stressed rumen into acidosis.

Cool cows during hot spells by wetting them before or after milking and using fans or sprinklers in the shed or holding area where water and power allow, always followed by good air movement so the water evaporates.
Handle, spray, dip, vaccinate, treat and transport cattle only in the cool early morning or evening, and avoid long walks to water or grazing in the midday sun.

Choose breeds that suit your area: in hot lowland and coastal zones consider Jerseys, crosses with Sahiwal, Boran or other zebu breeds, and seek advice from your County livestock office or AI service provider.
detail.impact: Heat stress is one of the quiet, hidden drains on dairy income in hot parts of Kenya. Milk yield falls during hot spells and may not return fully in the same lactation, so a farmer selling to a cooperative or milk bar loses daily income. Fertility suffers: heat signs become weak and short, conception rates drop and early pregnancies are lost, which lengthens the calving interval and means fewer calves and fewer lactations over a cow's life. Cows that were heat stressed in late pregnancy can give birth to lighter calves and produce less milk afterwards. Linked problems such as acidosis, lameness, mastitis and lowered immunity add treatment costs. In severe cases a valuable exotic cow can die. Because these losses build up gradually, many farmers blame poor feed or bad semen when heat is a major part of the cause.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for mild and moderate heat stress if the cow is cooled quickly and given shade and water; most recover within hours to a day, although milk and fertility can take longer to return. Cows with true heat stroke, meaning very high temperatures, collapse or fits, are at serious risk of dying even with treatment, and survivors may have lasting damage. Recovery is better when the problem is spotted early, when the cow is young and otherwise healthy, and when the farm fixes the underlying shade, water and housing problems so the stress does not keep returning every hot season.

faqs.q: Why does my cow's milk drop so much on hot days even though I give the same feed?
faqs.a: When a cow is hot, she eats less to avoid making extra heat in her rumen, and her body sends blood to the skin to cool down instead of to the udder. Less feed eaten and less energy available means less milk. Panting and drooling also upset the rumen. Feeding at cooler times, keeping feed fresh, providing shade and plenty of water usually helps the milk recover, though it may take some days.

faqs.q: Is it safe to pour water on my cow when she is very hot?
faqs.a: Yes, wetting a hot cow is one of the best ways to cool her, as long as air can move over her afterwards so the water evaporates. Focus on the neck, back and legs and repeat at intervals. Wetting only lightly in a closed, humid shed with no airflow can make things worse by raising the humidity, so open the shed or use a fan. A collapsed or very weak cow still needs a vet.

faqs.q: Does heat stress affect getting my cow in calf?
faqs.a: Yes. Heat stress makes heat signs weaker and shorter, so you may miss them, and it lowers the chance that AI will result in pregnancy. It can also cause early loss of a pregnancy. Many farmers see more repeat breeders after a hot season. Watch for heats in the cool early morning and evening, keep good records, and talk to your AI provider about timing and breed choice.

faqs.q: Should I give antibiotics to a cow that is panting from the heat?
faqs.a: No. Heat stress is not caused by germs, so antibiotics do not help it, and using them without need wastes money, leaves residues in milk and builds antimicrobial resistance. Cool the cow and give water first. If she does not improve, or has other signs such as cough, swollen glands or a high fever at night, call the vet, who will decide whether any medicine is needed and what withdrawal period applies.

faqs.q: Which dairy breed is best for a hot area like the coast?
faqs.a: Pure Holstein-Friesians struggle most in hot, humid areas. Jerseys handle heat better, and crosses with zebu breeds such as Sahiwal or Boran are much more heat tolerant, though they usually give less milk than a pure Friesian in ideal conditions. The best choice balances milk yield against survival, fertility and your ability to provide shade and water. Your County livestock office or AI provider can advise on bulls and breeds suited to your area.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my zero-grazing shed is too hot?
faqs.a: Stand inside the shed in the early afternoon. If it feels much hotter than outside under a tree, if the iron roof is hot to touch from below, or if your cows are standing, panting and crowding near openings, the shed is too hot. Raising the roof, insulating or whitewashing it, opening the sides, planting trees nearby and adding a fan or wetting system can make a big difference.

products.role: An oral rehydration and electrolyte solution that can be added to drinking water during hot spells to help cows replace water and body salts lost through sweating, panting and drooling, supporting thirst, appetite and recovery alongside shade, cooling and vet care. It does not replace cooling or veterinary treatment of a collapsed cow.

A plant-extract supplement labelled for heat-stress relief that may be used during hot seasons to support comfort and recovery, as an aid alongside good shade, ventilation, clean water and correct feeding, not as a substitute for them.

heat-stress.imagePrompt: A black-and-white Holstein-Friesian dairy cow standing in the shade of an acacia tree on a hot sunny Kenyan afternoon, mouth open and panting with tongue slightly out and saliva dripping, other cows bunched nearby around a water trough.
heat-stress.seoDescription: Heat stress in dairy cattle: spot panting, drooling and milk drop early, cool cows fast, and prevent it with shade, water and smart management in Kenya.

card.headline: Cows refuse feed, milk drops suddenly
card.look: Several cows eating the same feed lose appetite, pick at or refuse their dairy meal or silage, and milk falls over a few days. The feed may smell musty, look clumped, dusty, or show green, grey, black or pink mould.
card.action: Stop feeding the suspect feed immediately, keep a sample of it, and call your vet.

detail.summary: Mycotoxin poisoning happens when cattle eat feed contaminated with toxins made by moulds (fungi). The most important in Kenya is aflatoxin, found in mouldy maize, maize germ, dairy meal, cottonseed cake, groundnut cake and badly made silage. It quietly lowers appetite, milk yield, growth, fertility and immunity, and can damage the liver. It also matters for people, because a form of aflatoxin passes into milk that families drink and sell.
detail.cause: Moulds such as Aspergillus (which makes aflatoxin), Fusarium (which makes zearalenone, deoxynivalenol or 'vomitoxin', and fumonisins) and Penicillium (which makes ochratoxin and others) grow on crops in the field or in storage when there is warmth and moisture. They produce chemical poisons called mycotoxins. Cooking, drying or pelleting the feed does not destroy them, and a feed can carry high levels of toxin even when you cannot see mould. The adult cow's rumen (the large first stomach) breaks down some mycotoxins, which is why cattle often tolerate more than pigs or poultry, but aflatoxin is not fully broken down. Aflatoxin is absorbed and processed in the liver, where it damages liver cells. A damaged liver cannot make proteins properly, so the cow loses condition, its blood may not clot well, and its immune system weakens, making it more likely to get mastitis, pneumonia and other infections. Part of the aflatoxin is changed into aflatoxin M1, which comes out in the milk. Zearalenone acts like the female hormone oestrogen and disrupts heat cycles and pregnancy. Vomitoxin mainly makes feed taste bad and upsets the gut, so cows eat less. Often several toxins are present together and their effects add up.
spread: It is not contagious and does not pass from cow to cow; animals are poisoned only by eating contaminated feed.
Maize harvested or stored wet, or left in heaps on the ground after harvest, is a major source, especially after the long and short rains.
Drought and insect damage in the field stress the maize plant and allow Aspergillus to enter the grain, so aflatoxin can be high even in dry years, as seen in parts of Eastern Kenya.
Dairy meal, maize germ, maize bran and oilseed cakes stored too long, kept on damp floors, against walls or under leaking roofs pick up moisture and grow mould.
Poorly compacted or badly sealed silage lets air in, so mould grows on the top, sides and any spoiled pockets; damaged polythene and rats make this worse.
Wet brewers' waste, spent grains and other by-products go mouldy quickly in warm weather if not fed within a short time.
Leftover feed caked in troughs and feeders becomes mouldy and mixes with fresh feed if troughs are not cleaned regularly.
detail.atRisk: Zero-grazing dairy cows on Kenya's smallholder farms are most exposed, because they rely heavily on bought dairy meal, maize germ, silage and stored maize stover. High-yielding cows eat more concentrate, so they take in more toxin and show the milk effects first. Young calves, whose rumens are not yet working fully, are more sensitive than adults, as are pregnant and early-lactation cows whose livers are already working hard. Risk rises in and just after the long rains (March to May) and the short rains (October to December), in humid highland and lakeside areas, and in drought years when field crops are stressed. Farms that buy cheap or unbranded feed, store feed for long periods, or make silage without good compaction are at higher risk. Feedlots and beef animals fed maize-based rations are also affected, mainly through poor growth.

early: Several animals eating the same feed start leaving feed, eating slowly or sorting out the concentrate.
Milk yield drops over a few days to weeks without another clear cause, often across the whole herd rather than one cow.
Cows look dull, with a rough coat and slowly lose body condition even though feed is offered.
Loose or irregular dung, sometimes with mucus, and reduced cudding (chewing the cud).
More cases of mastitis, retained afterbirth, foot problems or infections than usual, because immunity is weakened.
Fertility problems: cows not showing heat, irregular or repeated heats, more repeat breeding, and swollen or reddened vulva in heifers (from zearalenone).
The feed itself smells musty or sour, feels warm or damp, has clumps, webbing or coloured mould patches.
advanced: Marked weight loss, weakness and reluctance to move, with a sharp fall in milk.
Yellow colour (jaundice) of the whites of the eyes, gums or vulva, showing liver damage.
Bleeding problems such as blood in dung, bruising, or bleeding that takes long to stop after injury, because the liver cannot make clotting proteins.
Skin on white or light patches becoming red, swollen or peeling after sun exposure (photosensitisation, sunburn-like reaction due to liver damage).
Abortion, weak calves or calves that fail to thrive.
In calves, severe straining, diarrhoea, and sometimes rectal prolapse (the rectum pushing out).
Nervous signs such as staggering, circling or head pressing in severe cases, and death in very high exposures.

lookalikes.name: Ketosis (acetonaemia)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ketosis usually affects individual cows in the first weeks after calving, and the breath or milk may smell sweet like nail varnish; a cowside ketone test is positive. Mycotoxin problems tend to hit many cows at once, at any stage of lactation, and link to a new batch of feed.

lookalikes.name: Liver fluke (fasciolosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Liver fluke also causes weight loss, poor milk and sometimes jaundice, but it is linked to grazing or cutting fodder near swamps, dams and wet areas, and may cause bottle jaw (swelling under the jaw). A dung test for fluke eggs helps tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Gall sickness (anaplasmosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gall sickness causes jaundice and weakness, but usually with high fever, pale gums, constipation and ticks on the animal, and it often affects one or a few animals. A blood smear by the vet confirms it.

lookalikes.name: Plant poisoning such as Lantana camara
lookalikes.howToTell: Lantana and some other plants cause jaundice and severe photosensitisation, often in animals that have grazed hedges or bush. Check for access to toxic plants, especially in hungry animals, and compare with recent feed changes.

detail.diagnosis: There is no simple cowside test for mycotoxin poisoning, so diagnosis depends on putting the clues together. The vet will examine affected cows, check for jaundice, bleeding, fever and other diseases, and ask about the feed history. The most useful step is testing the feed: samples of dairy meal, maize, maize germ, silage and other suspect feeds can be sent to laboratories such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, KALRO centres, university labs or private feed-testing labs, which measure aflatoxin and other toxins. Milk can also be tested for aflatoxin M1, and some dairy cooperatives and processors test milk routinely. Blood tests for liver enzymes show whether the liver is damaged. If an animal dies, a post-mortem may show a pale, firm or yellow liver, and liver tissue can be examined under a microscope. To help, the farmer should keep at least one kilogram of each suspect feed in a clean, dry, labelled bag (do not throw it all away), keep feed bags with brand, batch number and date, keep receipts, note when the new feed started, and record milk yields and which cows are affected.
firstSteps: Stop feeding the suspect feed straight away, including any mouldy silage face, dairy meal batch or stored maize, and switch to clean, fresh feed from a different source.
Keep a labelled sample of each suspect feed and its bag with batch number, so the vet or laboratory can test it and you can raise it with the supplier.
Clean out all troughs, feeders and storage areas, removing caked and mouldy leftovers, and let them dry in the sun.
Give plenty of clean drinking water and good-quality green fodder or hay to keep the rumen working and help the cows recover appetite.
Keep sick animals in a shaded, comfortable, dry place, and move light-skinned animals with skin reddening out of direct sun.
Do not sell milk from affected cows and do not give it to children until the vet or a milk test says it is safe; ask your vet about testing.
Wear a dust mask and gloves when handling or removing mouldy feed, and do not dump it where other animals, chickens or pigs can eat it.
Record milk yields, feed intake and which animals are affected, then call your vet, and do not give any drugs unless the vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no specific antidote for aflatoxin or most other mycotoxins, so treatment focuses on removing the source and supporting the animal while the liver recovers. The vet will confirm that contaminated feed has been withdrawn and may advise a mycotoxin binder in the ration, which attaches to toxins in the gut so less is absorbed. Supportive care may include vitamins (especially A, D, E and the B group), improved protein and energy in the diet, fluids for weak or dehydrated animals, and vitamin K where there is bleeding. Antibiotics do nothing against the toxin itself; the vet may prescribe them only if there is a secondary bacterial infection such as mastitis or pneumonia, and they should be used exactly as prescribed to avoid antimicrobial resistance. Any drug used has milk and meat withdrawal periods, and milk and meat must not be sold until these have passed. Separately, aflatoxin M1 usually falls in milk within several days of removing contaminated feed, but it is wise to confirm with a milk test before selling. Cows with mild exposure often recover appetite and milk within days to weeks, while cows with serious liver damage recover slowly or may never return to full production, and the vet may advise culling.
prevention: Buy dairy meal and other concentrates from reputable feed millers with the KEBS mark, check the manufacture date, and use bags within a few weeks of purchase.
Inspect every batch before feeding: reject feed that smells musty, feels warm or damp, has clumps, webbing or coloured mould, and return it to the supplier.
Store feed on pallets or raised platforms off the floor and away from walls, in a dry, well-ventilated store with a sound roof, and protect it from rats and insects.

Harvest maize promptly, avoid leaving it in heaps on the ground, dry it well to a safe moisture level (commonly around 13 percent) using tarpaulins or raised racks, and use hermetic bags for storage where possible.
Make silage carefully: chop finely, compact very well, seal tightly with good polythene and weights, keep the feed face clean and move across it quickly, and throw away mouldy top and side layers.
Feed wet by-products such as brewers' waste within a short time, and do not keep them in hot conditions where they spoil.
Clean troughs and feeders daily so old feed does not go mouldy and contaminate fresh feed.

In high-risk seasons or when feed quality is uncertain, ask your vet or nutritionist about including a mycotoxin binder in the ration as an extra layer of protection, alongside, not instead of, good feed quality.
detail.impact: Mycotoxins are often a hidden cost on Kenyan dairy farms. The biggest losses come from lower milk yield, poor feed conversion (cows eat but do not produce), weight loss and slower growth in heifers and calves. Fertility problems such as repeat breeding, missed heats and abortions lengthen calving intervals and cost money in extra inseminations. Weakened immunity brings more mastitis and other illness, adding vet bills and discarded milk. Milk with aflatoxin above legal limits can be rejected by cooperatives and processors, and repeated rejections can damage a farmer's market. Throwing away a bad batch of feed is expensive, but it is almost always cheaper than continuing to feed it.
detail.humanHealth: Aflatoxin is a serious human health concern. Cows that eat aflatoxin pass aflatoxin M1 into their milk, and this toxin is not destroyed by boiling, pasteurising or making mala and yoghurt. Long-term intake of aflatoxin is linked to liver cancer and is associated with poor growth in children, and Kenya has had deadly human aflatoxin poisoning outbreaks from mouldy maize. Children drink the most milk relative to their size, so they are most at risk. Do not sell or drink milk from cows fed suspected mouldy feed until a test or your vet confirms it is safe, and never let the family eat mouldy maize or groundnuts. When handling mouldy feed, wear a dust mask and gloves, because mould dust can cause breathing problems. If drugs are used during treatment, respect milk and meat withdrawal periods to avoid drug residues.
detail.outlook: The outlook is generally good when the contaminated feed is found and removed early, before serious liver damage. Appetite and milk often begin to improve within days to a few weeks. Recovery is slower in cows that ate high levels for a long time, in calves and in pregnant or early-lactation cows. Animals with jaundice, bleeding or photosensitisation have significant liver damage and may not return to full production. Fertility problems may take a few cycles to settle after the toxin is removed. The biggest factor is speed: the sooner the bad feed stops, the better the chances.

faqs.q: Can I just scrape off the mouldy part and feed the rest?
faqs.a: No. Mould roots and toxins spread through feed beyond the visible patch, and feed that looks clean can still carry high aflatoxin levels. Remove and safely dispose of the whole affected batch, or at least a wide margin around spoiled silage, and ask for a feed test if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Does boiling milk remove aflatoxin?
faqs.a: No. Aflatoxin M1 survives boiling, pasteurising and fermenting into mala or yoghurt. The only way to make milk safe is to stop feeding contaminated feed, wait for levels to fall, and ideally confirm with a milk test before drinking or selling.

faqs.q: How long after changing feed is the milk safe again?
faqs.a: Aflatoxin M1 in milk usually drops within several days once contaminated feed is removed, but this varies with how much the cow ate and her condition. Ask your vet or cooperative to test the milk before you return to selling, and remember that any drugs given have their own withdrawal periods.

faqs.q: Can I give the mouldy dairy meal to my chickens or pigs instead?
faqs.a: Please do not. Pigs, poultry, ducks and dogs are more sensitive to aflatoxin than adult cattle and can be poisoned or killed by feed a cow might tolerate. Their eggs and meat may also carry toxins. Dispose of mouldy feed by burning or burying it where no animals can reach it.

faqs.q: If I use a mycotoxin binder, can I keep feeding the mouldy feed?
faqs.a: No. A binder reduces the amount of toxin absorbed from feed with low-level contamination, but it does not make visibly mouldy or heavily contaminated feed safe. Use binders as an extra safeguard with good-quality feed, not as a way to use spoiled feed.

faqs.q: Can I tell if feed has aflatoxin just by looking or smelling?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Mould, clumps and a musty smell are warning signs, but aflatoxin can be present in feed that looks and smells normal. Buying from trusted suppliers, storing feed well and testing batches when problems appear are the best protection.

products.role: A mycotoxin binder that can be added to the ration, as advised by your vet or nutritionist, to help reduce absorption of aflatoxin and ochratoxin from feed with low-level contamination, especially in rainy seasons. It supports prevention alongside clean feed and good storage, and does not make mouldy feed safe to use.
Supports liver function and digestion in cows recovering after contaminated feed has been removed, as an aid alongside the vet's treatment plan and a good diet; it is not a cure for liver damage.

mycotoxin-poisoning.imagePrompt: A dull-looking Friesian dairy cow in a zero-grazing stall standing back from a feed trough that contains clumped dairy meal with visible greenish-grey mould patches, soft natural light, rural Kenyan setting.
mycotoxin-poisoning.seoDescription: Mycotoxin poisoning in cattle from mouldy maize, dairy meal and silage: signs, aflatoxin in milk, first steps, vet care and prevention for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Cattle chewing bones, wood and soil
card.look: Cows lick walls, eat soil, gnaw old bones, wood, plastic or cloth, and often look thin with a dull, rough or faded coat. Growth is slow and cows take a long time to come back on heat.
card.action: Clear old bones, carcasses, plastic and batteries from where the cattle graze, make sure they always have a proper cattle mineral lick and clean water, and ask your vet to check the herd's diet.

aka: Selenium deficiency (white muscle disease in calves)
detail.summary: Mineral deficiency means cattle are not getting enough of one or more minerals their bodies need. The most important ones in East Africa are phosphorus, calcium, copper, cobalt and selenium. A common sign is pica, a strange appetite where cattle chew bones, wood, soil, stones or rubbish. It rarely kills directly, but it quietly steals milk, growth and calves from the herd, and bone chewing can lead to deadly botulism.
detail.cause: Cattle get minerals from grass, fodder, water and supplements. When the soil is poor in a mineral, the grass grown on it is poor too. Many Kenyan soils, especially in rangelands and highly leached areas, are low in phosphorus, and dry season grass is lower still. Phosphorus and calcium build strong bones and teeth. Phosphorus also drives energy use, appetite and fertility. When it runs short, the animal craves it and starts chewing bones, which contain phosphorus. Copper is needed for healthy coat colour, blood, bones, nerves and the immune system. Copper can be short in the soil, or blocked by too much molybdenum, sulphur or iron in grass, water or feed, so animals can be deficient even when the diet seems to contain some copper. Cobalt is used by rumen microbes (the tiny organisms in the first stomach that digest grass) to make vitamin B12. Without it the animal loses appetite and wastes away. Selenium works with vitamin E to protect muscles and cells from damage. Shortage causes weak muscles in calves, retained afterbirth and poor immunity. Over months, these shortages weaken bones, slow growth, lower milk and upset breeding cycles. Several minerals are often short at the same time, so the signs mix together.
spread: Mineral deficiency is not contagious and does not spread from animal to animal, but many animals on the same farm are often affected because they share the same pasture and feed.
Grazing on soils naturally low in phosphorus, copper, cobalt or selenium is the main trigger, and grass from these soils carries the shortage into the animal.
The long dry season makes things worse because dry, mature grass holds much less phosphorus and protein than young green grass after the rains.
Feeding mainly maize stover, Napier grass or crop residues without a balanced mineral supplement leaves zero-grazed cows short, especially high-yielding dairy cows.
Cheap or wrong licks, such as plain table salt, rock salt only, or licks made for other animals, do not supply the needed minerals.
Water or soils high in iron, sulphur or molybdenum can block copper absorption, causing deficiency even when some copper is fed.
High demand times increase need: late pregnancy, early lactation, fast growth in young stock and recovery from illness.
Heavy worm burdens and chronic diseases reduce appetite and absorption, making a borderline deficiency show up clearly.
detail.atRisk: All cattle can be affected, but the highest risk is in high-yielding dairy cows in early lactation, pregnant cows, and fast-growing heifers and calves. Grazing herds in pastoral and semi-arid areas are very prone to phosphorus shortage, especially in the long dry season before the rains. Zero-grazed cows fed mostly Napier, stover or hay without a proper dairy mineral are also at risk. Calves born to selenium- or copper-deficient mothers can be weak from birth. Exotic and crossbred dairy animals have higher needs than local zebu, so they often show signs first. Areas with known low-mineral soils, and farms that do not test soil or forage, should treat this as a standing risk.

early: Chewing or licking unusual things such as bones, wood, walls, soil, stones, cloth, plastic or the hair of other animals.
Slow growth in calves and heifers that look small for their age even when they seem to eat enough grass.
A dull, rough or dry coat, and in black or red animals a faded, rusty or greyish colour, often with pale rings around the eyes ('spectacles') in copper deficiency.
Slightly lower milk yield and lower appetite than expected for the feed available.
Cows taking longer to show heat after calving, silent heats, or repeat breeding even with a good bull or AI.
More cases of retained afterbirth (placenta not dropped within about a day of calving).
Mild diarrhoea in some animals, which can be linked to copper shortage when molybdenum is high.
advanced: Clear weight loss and wasting with loss of appetite, especially in cobalt deficiency, even when grass is available.
Stiff walking, lameness, swollen joints or a hunched back, and bones that break easily in phosphorus or calcium shortage.
Calves with bent legs or enlarged joints (rickets), or weak calves that struggle to stand and suck (white muscle disease from selenium shortage).
Newborn or young calves with a wobbly gait or weak back legs (swayback from copper shortage).
Pale gums and eyelids, a sign of anaemia (shortage of healthy red blood), in long-term copper or cobalt deficiency.
Very poor fertility across the herd, abortions, or weak and stillborn calves.
Sudden weakness, drooling, inability to swallow and floppy paralysis after chewing bones or carcasses, which suggests botulism and needs a vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: Heavy worm burden
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms also cause poor growth, rough coat and weight loss, often with diarrhoea and, for some worms, bottle jaw (soft swelling under the jaw). A dung test by the vet or lab shows worm eggs. Animals improve after correct deworming, while mineral cases keep chewing bones and soil. Both problems often happen together.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana) and other chronic blood diseases
lookalikes.howToTell: Nagana causes wasting, anaemia, swollen lymph nodes and fever, often in tsetse areas, and some animals get sick quickly. A blood smear from the vet confirms the parasite. Pica and bone chewing are not typical of nagana itself.

lookalikes.name: Simple underfeeding (energy and protein shortage)
lookalikes.howToTell: Hungry cattle are thin with low milk, but they mainly eat any grass or hay given and rarely chew bones. When good feed is supplied they recover fast. In mineral deficiency, animals can have enough bulk feed but still lick soil, chew bones and breed poorly.

lookalikes.name: Milk fever (acute low calcium)
lookalikes.howToTell: Milk fever comes suddenly, usually within a few days of calving in a good dairy cow. The cow is weak, cold, trembling, then goes down with her head turned to her side. It is an emergency needing a vet within hours, unlike the slow, months-long signs of chronic mineral shortage.

detail.diagnosis: A vet starts with the history: what the animals eat, which lick or mineral is used, how much, the season, the area, and the breeding and milk records. They examine coat, body condition, teeth, bones, joints and gums, and look for pica. Blood samples can measure phosphorus, calcium, copper, selenium (or a related enzyme) and vitamin B12 status, though some blood results can be misleading and must be read carefully. For copper and cobalt, liver samples are more reliable, and these can come from a liver biopsy or from any animal that dies or is slaughtered. Soil, forage and water testing through KALRO, university or private labs shows what your land is short of or what may be blocking copper. Sometimes the vet suggests a supervised trial of the right supplement and watches the response. To prepare, write down what you feed and in what amounts, keep the bag or label of your current mineral, note which animals are affected and since when, and keep calving, heat and milk records ready.
firstSteps: Walk the grazing area and the shed, and remove old bones, carcasses, skins, plastic bags, wire, batteries, paint tins and rubbish, because pica animals will eat them and can be poisoned or get botulism.
Check that cattle always have a proper cattle mineral lick or mineral powder made for cattle, not just table salt, and that it is kept dry and refilled.
Make sure clean water is available at all times, since animals eat less and use minerals poorly when water is short.
Give the best feed you can, such as good hay, silage or fresh fodder, and avoid relying only on dry stover in the dry season.
Write down which animals are chewing odd things, their body condition, milk yield, coat changes and breeding problems, so the vet sees the pattern.
Do not inject or dose copper, selenium or other minerals on your own, because the gap between a helpful amount and a poisonous amount is small.
If any animal suddenly becomes weak, drools, cannot swallow or goes down after chewing bones, keep it in shade with water and call the vet at once.
Contact your vet or County Veterinary Officer to examine the herd and advise on testing and the right mineral programme for your area.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on which mineral is short, so a vet first works out the likely cause. For phosphorus and calcium shortage, the main fix is a good cattle mineral or dicalcium phosphate in the feed or lick, and in severe cases a vet may give injectable phosphorus or calcium products. For copper deficiency, vets may use copper injections, slow-release copper oxide capsules (boluses) or copper in the mineral, after checking whether molybdenum, sulphur or iron is blocking it. For cobalt deficiency, they may give vitamin B12 injections and cobalt through drenches, slow-release boluses or a cobalt-containing mineral. For selenium shortage, combined selenium and vitamin E injections or selenium in the mineral are used, and selenium is also given to pregnant cows to protect calves. Copper and selenium in particular are poisonous if overdosed, so only a vet should decide the product and dose; never give cattle minerals or injections to sheep, which are very sensitive to copper. Some injectable products carry milk and meat withdrawal periods, so follow the vet's instructions and the label before selling milk or meat. Antibiotics do not treat mineral deficiency; they are only used if a vet finds a separate infection, and should be used responsibly to avoid antimicrobial resistance. Pica usually eases within weeks once the right mineral is supplied, but growth, coat and fertility take months to improve, and bone damage or stunting in young stock may not fully recover.
prevention: Provide a good-quality cattle mineral lick or mineral premix all year round, choosing one made for your type of cattle (dairy or beef) and following the label, and keep it under a roof so rain does not wash it out.
Pay extra attention in the dry season and during late pregnancy and early lactation, when phosphorus and other needs are highest and grass is poorest.
Ask your vet, extension officer or KALRO about known mineral problems in your area, and consider soil and forage testing so you supplement what is actually short.
Feed a balanced ration to dairy cows, including dairy meal or concentrates with added minerals, rather than only Napier, stover or hay.
Keep grazing areas and sheds clean of bones, carcasses and rubbish, and burn or bury carcasses properly, to stop pica turning into botulism or poisoning.
Talk to your vet about botulism vaccination if your cattle graze areas where bone chewing is common, especially in pastoral systems.
Control worms and ticks on a planned programme, because parasites reduce appetite and absorption and make mineral shortage worse.
Improve pasture where possible with fertiliser containing phosphorus, and mix legumes such as desmodium or lucerne into fodder to raise mineral and protein levels.
detail.impact: Mineral deficiency is a hidden thief on Kenyan farms. Milk yield drops slowly, so many farmers do not notice until yields are well below what the cow should give. Heifers grow slowly and reach breeding age late, which delays the first calf and income. Cows come on heat late or repeat breed, so the calving interval stretches and each cow produces fewer calves and fewer lactations in her life. Extra AI services and vet visits cost money. Retained afterbirth and weak calves add losses. In pastoral herds, bone chewing in the dry season can lead to botulism deaths of several animals at once. Weak bones mean more lameness and fractures. Animals with poor immunity also fall sick more often with other diseases. Compared to these losses, a proper mineral programme is usually cheap.
detail.humanHealth: Mineral deficiency itself does not infect people. However, cattle with pica may eat bones, carcasses or soil that carry botulism toxin or anthrax spores, and both can cause disease or death. Never eat meat or drink milk from an animal that died suddenly or became suddenly sick with unknown cause, and do not open the carcass; call the vet, as anthrax is notifiable and must be reported. Wear gloves when handling sick animals and carcasses and wash hands well. If your vet uses injectable minerals or other medicines, respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods on the label to avoid residues reaching your family and customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook is generally good when the deficiency is caught early and the right mineral is supplied. Pica, appetite and coat condition often improve within a few weeks, and fertility and milk yield improve over the following months as body reserves rebuild. Recovery is slower or incomplete in animals with long-standing deficiency, stunted young stock, broken or deformed bones, or severe white muscle disease and swayback in calves. The result also depends on fixing the real cause: if copper is being blocked by molybdenum or iron, or the mineral used is wrong, the problem returns. Herds that keep a year-round, area-appropriate mineral programme rarely see serious cases again.

faqs.q: My cows are chewing bones. Is that just a bad habit?
faqs.a: Usually not. Bone chewing is a strong sign that cattle are short of phosphorus, and sometimes other minerals. It is the body's way of searching for what it lacks. It is also dangerous, because old bones and carcasses can carry botulism toxin, which can kill cattle quickly. Remove bones from the grazing area, give a proper cattle mineral, and ask your vet to review the diet.

faqs.q: Is table salt or rock salt enough as a lick?
faqs.a: No. Salt supplies sodium and chloride, which cattle need, but it does not supply phosphorus, copper, cobalt, selenium, zinc or iodine. Many farmers give only salt and the cattle still show pica, poor fertility and faded coats. Use a complete mineral made for cattle, and keep salt as part of it, not instead of it.

faqs.q: Why is my black cow turning brown or grey?
faqs.a: A faded, rusty or greyish coat, especially with pale rings around the eyes, often points to copper deficiency. It can happen even when the feed contains some copper, if high molybdenum, sulphur or iron in grass or water blocks it. Your vet can test blood or liver and advise on the right product. Do not give copper on your own, because too much copper is poisonous.

faqs.q: Can mineral deficiency stop my cow from getting pregnant?
faqs.a: Yes. Shortage of phosphorus, copper, selenium and other minerals is a common reason for late heats, silent heats, repeat breeding and retained afterbirth. Poor energy and protein feeding also play a big part. Correcting minerals together with good feeding often improves fertility over a few months, but other causes like infections should be checked by your vet too.

faqs.q: Can I give my cattle mineral to my sheep and goats?
faqs.a: Do not give cattle minerals to sheep. Cattle minerals often contain more copper than sheep can tolerate, and sheep can die from copper poisoning. Goats are less sensitive but still have different needs. Buy a mineral made for each species and follow the label.

faqs.q: How quickly will I see improvement after giving the right minerals?
faqs.a: Pica often reduces within a few weeks once the missing mineral is supplied. Appetite and coat usually improve next, and milk and fertility over the following months. Young animals that were badly stunted or have bent bones may never fully catch up, which is why steady year-round supplementation is better than waiting for signs.

products.role: Dicalcium phosphate supplies calcium and phosphorus, the two minerals most linked to bone chewing, weak bones and poor fertility in grazing and zero-grazed cattle. Mixed into the ration or lick as the label and your vet or nutritionist advise, it helps correct and prevent the phosphorus shortage, especially in the dry season and early lactation. It does not supply copper, cobalt or selenium, so it should be used alongside a complete cattle mineral, good feeding and a vet's assessment.

Vitamin D3 helps the body absorb and use calcium and phosphorus for strong bones, vitamin E works together with selenium to protect muscles, and vitamin A is often low when cattle eat dry grass and stover. Used as the label directs and with vet guidance, it can support bone health, fertility and calf vigour in deficient herds. It does not replace selenium or other minerals, so a proper mineral programme is still needed.
